->**Aristotle, Ethics, Book 10.**<-
> <note>original: Εἰ δὴ θεῖον ὁ νοῦς πρὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον, καὶ ὁ κατὰ τοῦτον βίος, θεῖος πρὸς τὸν ἀνθρώπινον βίον· χρὴ δὲ οὐ κατὰ τοὺς παραινοῦντας ἀνθρώπινα φρονεῖν ἀνθρώπους ὄντας, ἀλλ’ ἐφ’ ὅσον ἐνδέχεται, ἀθανατίζειν, καὶ ἅπαντα ποιεῖν πρὸς τὸ ζῆν κατὰ τὸ κράτιστον τῶν ἐν ἡμῖν.</note>
> If the mind is divine in comparison with man, then the life lived according to the mind is divine in comparison with human life. We should not follow those who advise us that, because we are human, we should think only of human things; rather, as far as possible, we should strive to be immortal and do everything to live according to the highest part within us.

# THE GENERAL PREFACE

1. The Author's excuse for such alterations as he has made in this edition of his books. 
2. The general scope of this entire volume. 
3. The excellence and necessity of reason for maintaining the truth of the Christian religion. 
4. His apology for interweaving *Platonism* <note>The philosophy of Plato, often emphasizing the existence of abstract objects and the soul.</note> and *Cartesianism* <note>The philosophy of René Descartes, emphasizing dualism between mind and body and a mechanical view of the physical world.</note> so frequently into his writings. 
5. Certain advertisements <note>original: "Advertisements"; here meaning notices or instructions for the reader.</note> for the more profitable reading of his books. 
6. Divine Intuition <note>original: "Divine Sagacity"; a term More uses for a spiritual or moral sense that precedes logical reasoning.</note>—a principle that comes before successful reason in contemplations of the highest importance. 
7. The aforementioned principle further illustrated and confirmed from the works of *Aristotle*. 
8. The Author’s excuse for omitting, in his *Antidote*, a refutation of the inconclusive <note>original: "unconcluding"</note> reasons some use to prove the existence of God. 
9. His excuse for not adding a treatise on *Superstition* to his work on *Enthusiasm* <note>In the 17th century, "Enthusiasm" referred to the (often criticized) belief that one was receiving direct, private revelations from God.</note>. 
10. That it can be no offense to the knowledgeable and noble-minded <note>original: "ingenuous"</note> that people have a shyness and suspicion <note>original: "jealousy"</note> regarding such truths as they have not been familiar with. 
11. Certain remarkable things concerning *Descartes* and his writings. 
12. Certain considerations brought together which entirely prevent all imaginable objections against the extension of a spirit <note>The idea that a spirit can occupy space, a key point of debate in 17th-century metaphysics.</note>. 
13. The properties and roles <note>original: "Offices"</note> of the Spirit of Nature further cleared and confirmed. A logical deduction <note>original: "Consectary"</note> concerning the guidance <note>original: "Conduct"</note> of souls by the Spirit of Nature. 
14. That the ancient *Jewish Kabbalah* <note>original: "Judaical Cabbala"; a tradition of mystical Jewish interpretation.</note> consisted of what we now call *Platonism* and *Cartesianism*, made further probable by the lineage of the *Pythagorean School*. 
15. Particular considerations from *Pherecydes*, *Parmenides*, and *Aristotle* that might move one to believe that the whole *Pythagorean philosophy*, both *Physical* and *Metaphysical*, was the ancient *wisdom* of the *Jews*. 
16. The unhappy separation of the *physical* part of the *Kabbalah* from the *metaphysical* in the works of *Leucippus*, *Democritus*, and *Epicurus*; with the Author's serious endeavor to reunite them again. 
17. That what he applies to the text of *Moses* in his *Philosophical Kabbalah*, he conceives to be rational and is assured that it fits the text perfectly, though he deliberates further concerning the *truth* of it. 
18. The testimony of several holy persons who either plainly asserted, or at least did not dislike, the doctrine of the soul's preexistence: *Clement of Alexandria*, *Origen Adamantius* (Clement's scholar), *Saint Basil* and *Gregory of Nazianzus*, *Synesius, Bishop of Cyrene*, *Arnobius*, *Prudentius*, *Saint Augustine*, the author of the *Book of Wisdom*, and our blessed Savior. 
19. That there is not the least conflict between the doctrine of preexistence and the derivation of original sin from *Adam*. 
20. That mathematical certainty in purely philosophical speculations need not obligate any man's conscience to make a public profession of them.

### READER,

<margin>The Author's excuse for such alterations as he has made in this edition of his books.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring floral motifs and a central figure, beginning the word "THAT".</image-desc>
1. THAT these writings which you find bound up in one volume may also appear to be held together by some common purpose, I thought it appropriate to say something by way of a general preface to them all. And therefore, if your curiosity leads you to inquire what I have done in these new editions of my books, I am ready to inform you that I have taken the same liberty in this *intellectual* or *theoretical garden* of my own planting that men usually take in their *natural* ones: which is to plant or pluck up, to transplant and graft <note>original: "inoculate"</note>, where and what they please. Therefore, if I have erased some things (which are actually very few), transposed others, and inserted <note>original: "interserted"</note> others, I hope I shall seem harmful to no man by ordering and cultivating this *philosophical plantation* of mine according to my own inclination and preference.

<margin>The general scope of this entire volume.</margin>
2. But these are smaller matters, and hardly any part of what I was about to say. The great bond <note>original: "Cement"</note> that holds these several *discourses* together is one main *design* at which they jointly aim. This design, I think, is admittedly noble and important: namely, the knowledge of God, and within that, of *true happiness*, so far as *Reason* can make its way through those darknesses and difficulties it is burdened with in this life. Although these difficulties are many and great, I would be misrepresenting <note>original: "belie"</note> the sense of my own success if I pronounced them insurmountable. Likewise, if I were deprived of that sense of success, I would lose many pleasures and enjoyments of mind of which I am now aware. Among these, none is so significant as that quiet reflection within myself on what real service may result <note>original: "redound"</note> to *religion* from these labors of mine. For what greater satisfaction can there be to a rational *spirit* than to find himself able to appeal to the strictest *rules* of *reason* and *philosophy* to show that those *doctrines* of the *existence of God* and the *immortality of the soul* are true? And what greater *support* <note>original: "Establishment"</note> for *religion* than to discover these two grand *pillars* so firm and stable, even upon those very grounds that our own faculties naturally agree are true? This cannot help but bring much honor and reverence to the *priesthood* <note>More refers here to the clergy of the Church of England.</note> and silence the mouths of shallow and profane *wits* who are so prone to look upon every *priest* as either a *fool* or an *impostor*.

<margin>The excellence and necessity of reason for maintaining the truth of the Christian religion.</margin>
3. Nor would I want it thought that I limit the *reasonableness* of our *religion* to those two main points only, as if the rest were not reasonable as well. For I conceive *Christian religion* to be rational throughout, and I think I have proved it to be so in my *Mystery of Godliness*. I must confess that this was the main, if not the only, goal of my long and anxious search into *reason* and *philosophy*. Without this goal, I would have proven to be only a lazy and careless inquirer into the nature of things. For to heap up a great deal of *reading*, *notions*, and *experiments* without such a noble and important *design* would have been, as I imagined <note>original: "phansied"</note>, to make my *mind* or *memory* a shop of trinkets <note>original: "small-wares"</note>. But having this eminent goal in my view, and taking up that noble resolution of

# The General Preface.

*Marcus Cicero once said, "I will follow Reason, wherever it leads me" <note>original Latin: "Marcus Cicero, Rationem, quò ea me cunque ducet, fequar"</note>; I consider that I began then to honor my office <note>original: "Function"</note>, and among other priestly garments <note>original: "Habiliments"</note>, in particular to put on the* Logion <note>original Greek: Λόγιον, meaning the "Oracle" or "Word"</note> *or* Rationale <note>The "Rationale" refers to the Breastplate of Judgment worn by the High Priest of Israel, symbolizing wisdom and divine light.</note>, *the priestly breastplate, which most justly claims its place in that region which is the seat of the heart; the simplicity and sincerity of that part being the root or well-spring of the soundest and purest reason. And truly I cannot well imagine what the moral reason might be why* Aaron's *robes should be such an express representation of the universe ("a reflection and a kind of imitation of the universe," <note>original Greek: ἀπηύγασμα καὶ μίμημά τι τοῦ κόσμου</note> as* Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE) was a Jewish philosopher who blended Greek philosophy with biblical tradition.</note>
<margin>* Philo, *On Monarchy*.</margin>
*calls it) unless every priest should endeavor, according to his opportunity and capacity, to be also as much as he can a* rational *man or* philosopher. *(For which reason certainly* universities *were first established, and are still continued to this very day.) <header>The General Preface.</header>

...to be neither under the Gospel, nor yet the people (as far as is possible) whom he presents to God. 

Therefore, to take away reason—under whatever fanatic pretense—is to disrobe the priest and strip him of his breastplate. Worst of all, it robs Christianity of the special privilege <note>original: "Prerogative"</note> it has over all other religions in the world: namely, that it dares to appeal to reason. Those who understand the true interests of our religion will cling closely to this; to do otherwise betrays it to the unjust suspicion of being false and makes it equal to every empty imposture. For if you take away reason, all religions appear equally true, just as when light is removed, all things appear to be the same color. In fact, worst of all, the religion that is most true will seem the most false in this imposed darkness <note>original: "superinduced Darkness"</note>, especially if it strictly and positively declares itself to be the only truth. Such a claim will not be accepted, nor can it be proven in that "region of midnight" where everything looks the same.

<margin>His defense <note>original: "Apologie"</note> for frequently interweaving Platonism and Cartesianism into his writings.</margin>

4. These serious and weighty considerations urged me to search to the very bottom of things with all possible care and vigor, so that my heart might not fail me in the day of trial. Much of the result of that investigation is contained in this present volume. Just as I have gained significant satisfaction from clarifying these major points, I am equally desirous that nothing found here causes the least dissatisfaction to others. And I think it impossible that anything should, if readers will only notice my design: which is not to turn philosophy into theology, but to build an external fence <note>original: "Exoterick Fence"</note> or outer fortification around theology. 

By defending these "outworks" against the assaults of the confident atheist and his massive <note>original: "Gigantick"</note> artillery batteries—raised against the belief in God and a reward in the afterlife—I might show him what a vain and reckless <note>original: "temerity"</note> man he is. He imagines it a simple task to overrun the Holy City and Sanctuary, yet he is easily driven back from its outer walls. This is the true and genuine reason why I so frequently interweave Platonism <note>The philosophy of Plato, which emphasizes the existence of abstract forms and the immortality of the soul.</note> and Cartesianism <note>The philosophy of René Descartes, which emphasizes the use of reason and the distinction between mind and matter.</note> into these writings; I use these hypotheses as invincible bulwarks <note>defensive walls</note> against the most cunning and harmful efforts of atheism. For I am certain that if the suppositions I have selected from those two philosophies are taken as true (and let our adversaries prove them false if they can), there is no objection atheism can make against the doctrines mentioned above that I cannot answer fully and irrefutably.

Thus, it is not hopeless to think that while we put many to flight, others might voluntarily surrender as prisoners, being carried captive by the power of reason into a true belief regarding the most important matters. Having all hope of escaping punishment in the afterlife <note>original: "After-Impunity"</note> cut off by such a clear conviction of the soul’s immortality, they may be persuaded to become real Christians in the basic points of faith. They might be willingly detained in the "Outer Court" <note>In the Temple of Jerusalem, the Outer Court was accessible to those not yet fully admitted to the inner sanctum; here, a metaphor for those who accept the rational basis of faith but not yet its deeper mysteries.</note>, even if, due to their current weak spiritual sight, they are not yet fit to enter the more sacred smoke of the Temple <note>A metaphor for the deeper, more mystical or revelatory aspects of religious life.</note>. Therefore, since I am so faithfully and (I believe) usefully occupied in managing these "outworks," I will not attribute any criticism to over-hasty zeal, but...

<summary>The author argues that reason is the defining feature of Christianity and explains that he uses Platonic and Cartesian philosophy as a rational defense (or "outwork") to protect core religious doctrines from atheist critiques. He hopes this rational approach will lead skeptics toward a basic Christian faith, even if they are not yet ready for deeper spiritual mysteries.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author’s defense of his work, moving from his use of philosophy to specific advice for readers on how to engage with his arguments rationally and spiritually.</meta>

<page-num>vii</page-num>
<header>The GENERAL PREFACE.</header>

...but to mere mishap, if I am pelted behind my back by any volleys of *obloquy* <note>original: "Obloquie"; slander or verbal abuse</note> from any unknown *servant of the sanctuary* <note>A fellow member of the clergy</note>. I presume that if I receive any hurt, the *pain* will be greatest for those who caused it, when they realize they have wounded a true and faithful friend—and even then, at a time when he was so busily and watchfully employed in facing the *common enemy* <note>atheism and irreligion</note>.

<margin>Certain instructions for the more profitable reading of his books.</margin>
5. If any expect or desire any general *instruction* or *preparation* for the *more profitable reading of these my writings*, I must declare that I can give none that is unique to them, but only what would fit all writings written with *freedom* and *reason*. And this one *Royal Rule* I would recommend for all: *Not to judge the truth of any proposition until we have a settled and clear understanding of its terms.* Though this *law* is so necessary and indispensable, there is none so frequently broken. The *effect* of this neglect is the many heaps of voluminous writings and foolish <note>original: "inept"</note> oppositions and *controversies* that fill the *world*. These would be impossible if men had not developed a habit of fluttering *mere words* against one another without taking notice of any fixed *sense*. In this way, they fight as if with *Hercules' clubs* made of *pasteboard*, which make a great sound but do nothing toward ending *disputes*. For just as no man would ever be so eccentric as to affirm that a *triangle* is a *quadrangle*, or a *square* a *circle*, once he has the distinct *ideas* of those *shapes* in his mind, so it would be impossible for him to speak of anything else falsely and absurdly if he had as perfect and settled a *notion* of the things he discusses. But this first and main *principle of wisdom* being neglected, it is no wonder that men clash as ridiculously and needlessly as those two *country clowns* who, in their cups, nearly came to blows because one called himself a *Lutheran* and the other a *Martinist* <note>Martin Luther was the same person as "Martin"; the joke is that the men are fighting over two names for the same thing because they do not understand the words they are using.</note>.

I might also add another *instruction* (which will contribute much toward a greater *conciseness* in *controversies*) which I think I have hinted at on other occasions: namely, that *an argument that could prove anything actually proves nothing*. If this were thoroughly understood, it would not only enable a person to defeat the apparent force of countless irrelevant assaults, but also keep him—if he has any honesty <note>original: "ingenuity"</note> in him—from attacking, or rather disturbing and interrupting, the composure and silence of another man's mind with the empty noise of such weak and groundless *arguments*. I mean those arguments that could support *falsehood* just as well as *truth*. All such *arguments* ought to be rejected <note>original: "exploded"</note>, especially in *philosophy*. I think if this kind of weapon were once out of fashion, conflict would soon end, and such a victory would follow that everyone would benefit from it.

<margin>Divine Sagacity: a principle that comes before successful reason in contemplations of the highest importance.</margin>
6. But in the third and last place—which, though it has considerable influence everywhere, is more particularly required when reading writings on *subjects* such as these I treat—I would recommend to those who wish to philosophize successfully that they believe in and strive after a certain *principle* more noble and inward than *reason* itself. Without this, *reason* will falter, or at least reach only toward mean and frivolous things. I feel a sense of something in me as I speak which I must confess is of so hidden <note>original: "retruse"</note> a nature that I lack a name for it, unless I should venture to term it <term>Divine Sagacity</term> <note>A form of spiritual intuition or intellectual discernment that the author believes is granted by God to help the mind grasp truth.</note>, which is the first *source* of *successful reason*, especi—

...especially in matters of great complexity and importance, without which a man is, as it were, in a thick wood. He may make infinite promising attempts but can find no exit into the open plain <note>original: "Champain"</note>, where one may freely look about in every direction (the plain of truth <note>original: "πεδίον τῆς ἀληθείας"</note>) without the safe guidance of this good genius <note>In this context, "genius" refers to a guiding spirit or an innate intellectual power</note>.

All who claim to be philosophers will indeed be ready to magnify Reason to the skies, to make it the light of Heaven and the very Oracle of God. But they do not consider that the Oracle of God is not to be heard except in his Holy Temple—that is to say, in a good and holy man, thoroughly sanctified in spirit, soul, and body. For there is a sanctity even of the body and temperament <note>original: "Complexion"</note> which the sensually-minded do not even dream of. Did not Aaron's "Rationale"—his Oracle of Reason <note>original: "Λόγιον"; referring to the ceremonial breastplate worn by the High Priest</note>—include the *Urim* and *Thummim*, which signify the purity and integrity of the will and affections, as well as the light of the understanding? Was not that breastplate square, not only in reference to the firmness of reasoning (as Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy</note> suggests), but also to denote the evenness and uprightness of his spirit? One who takes it upon himself to pronounce great truths must be, as Aristotle somewhere says, "a good man, and four-square without blame" <note>original: "ἀνὴρ ἀγαθὸς καὶ τετράγωνος ἄνευ ψόγου"</note>. This is true not only according to the standard of the city, but of the sanctuary; not only to a political degree of virtue, but a purifying <note>original: "Cathartical"</note> virtue, or rather that which <margin>* *Enneads*, book 1, chapter 2.</margin> Plotinus places "in having been purified" <note>original: "ἐν τῷ κεκαθάρθαι"</note>, implying a soul already purged of its lower impulses.

Let a man adorn himself as well as he can with the history of universal nature (represented by the long priestly robe), but if this breastplate with the *Urim* and *Thummim* is lacking to him who would act the part of the priest, he must necessarily fail to prove himself a sound philosopher. He will be unable to utter any oracles himself and will be in a poor position to receive them when they are uttered by another. For if this divine sagacity is missing due to the impurity of a man's spirit, he can neither find the right scent <note>original: "sent"</note> of things himself, nor easily follow it when he is put on the trail by someone else. This odd position of mine may make those people fret and storm who have made the contempt of morality a part of their philosophy; they may think themselves insulted to be pronounced incompetent judges of things they took for granted were within their own reach. Yet I could not conceal such an important truth, especially since it is not at all unphilosophical.

<margin>The above-mentioned principle further illustrated and confirmed from Aristotle. *On Subtlety*, exercise 307, section 25.</margin> 7. For is it not the saying of that so universally-applauded Aristotle: "For the divine within us moves all things in a way; and the beginning of reason is not reason, but something better" <note>original: "Κινεῖ γὰρ πῶς πάντα τὸ ἐν ἡμῖν θεῖον, λόγου δ᾿ ἀρχὴ οὐ λόγος, ἀλλά τι κρεῖττον"</note>? What Plato—nay, what Chrysostom or Augustine—could have spoken more heavenly language? Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger, a leading Renaissance scholar</note>, transported by the sight of this text, breaks out into this admiring question: "What do you say, divine man? Is there something divine in us that is more excellent than reason itself? Were even the rays of the Holy Spirit known to you?" <note>original: "Quid ais, divine vir? For having asked the question, "What is the beginning of motion in the soul?" <note>original: "τίς ἡ τῆς κινήσεως ἀρχὴ ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ;"</note> the full answer follows: <margin>Aristotle, *Eudemian Ethics*, book 7, chapter 14.</margin> "It is clear that as God is in the universe, so everything is in him; for the divine within us moves all things in a way; and the beginning of reason is not reason, but something better. ...except God? <note>original: "πλὴν θεός;"</note> It is evident, *he says*, that it is just as it is in the Universe: God himself, and all things are in him. For it is the same divine power <note>original: "Numen"</note> in us that moves all things in some way or another. And the beginning of reason is not reason, but something which is better; but what can be better than science <note>In this context, "science" refers to systematic knowledge or "episteme," not just the modern natural sciences</note> except God? *The argument of the chapter is a question* concerning good success <note>original: "περὶ εὐτυχίας"</note> *in affairs, whether it happens* by nature, by reason, or by some careful providence <note>original: "φύσει, νόμῳ, ἢ ἐπιμελείᾳ τινί"</note>—*that is to say, whether it be by Nature, Reason, or by the management of some good Genius, of some* good guiding spirit <note>original: "δαίμων ἀγαθὸς κυβερνήτης"</note>; *these are* Aristotle's *own words. I cite them primarily because it is the only place I know where there is such express mention of* Spirits <note>original: "Dæmons"</note>. *Yet he does not even assert their existence here; but on the occasion of this subject, his mind swelling higher, he rose at last to such a pitch as to utter this aphorism so much admired by* Julius Scaliger <note>A renowned 16th-century Italian scholar and physician</note>: *namely, that there is something before and better than reason, from which reason itself has its rise.*

*Though* Aristotle *mainly applies this to external affairs, I must (and may with equal right) transfer it also to the activities of the mind and the success of pure speculation. In this area, "divine success" <note>original: "ἡ θεία εὐτυχία"</note>, as he calls it, is more likely to be continuous and prove constant (because of the natural connection of Truth with an unpolluted soul) than it is in external transactions. This intellectual success, therefore, comes from the presence of God, who* moves all things in some way <note>original: "κινεῖν πῶς πάντα"</note>, *but residing in the undefiled spirit, moves it in the most excellent manner. He endows it with that Divine Sagacity I spoke of, which is a more inward, brief, and comprehensive presentation of Truth. This sagacity always precedes that Reason which, in theories of greatest importance, proves itself afterwards to be most solid and perfect in every way upon the most exact examination. This is truly that wisdom which is uniquely styled the Gift of God, and is hardly attainable by any except those of a pure and unspotted mind. It is of such great importance to sincerely endeavor to be holy and good.*

For I charitably assume that the first inventors of those reasons thought them conclusive, or else they would not have used them. From this it follows that they may still have power with those people who are at the same intellectual level as their first proponents. And he who guesses correctly and continues his journey will as certainly arrive at the place he aims for as he who perfectly knows the way. Besides, it was fitting to show my impartiality, because I have*

<margin>His excuse for not adding a treatise on superstition to the one on enthusiasm.</margin>
9. I cannot easily predict <note>original: "presage"</note> what defect anyone might spot in my *Treatise of Enthusiasm*, nor can I protect myself from appearing deficient to someone who more deeply considers the usefulness of that treatise and wonders why I have not added another on superstition. But I have naturally and inadvertently followed that wise advice of the Poet:

->— And what you despair<-
->can be polished to brilliance, leave behind.<-
<note>original: "Et quæ Desperas tractata nitescere posse relinque," from Horace’s *Ars Poetica*.</note>

For I must confess I do not view that subject as something that can be polished by my hand; it is a topic more suited for rhetoric than philosophy. Besides, I never found my mind low or humble enough to sink into any feeling or concept of that state <note>original: "Dispensation"</note> to experimentally find what lies at the bottom of it. I must honestly confess that I have a natural touch of *enthusiasm* <term>In the 17th century, "enthusiasm" referred to a belief in direct private revelation or religious ecstasy, often attributed to a "complexion" or physical temperament rather than divine grace.</term> in my temperament <note>original: "Complexion"</note>, but one that—I thank God—was always manageable enough and which I have finally found to be perfectly conquerable. By virtue of this victory, I understand what is inside *enthusiasts* better than they do themselves. Therefore, I was able to write what I have written with life and judgment, and I hope I shall contribute significantly to the peace and quiet of this kingdom by doing so.

But having had such a concept of God from my very youth—one that represented Him to me as the most noble and excellent Being possible—it could never enter my mind that He was either easily angered or won over by the omitting or performing of any lowly and insignificant services. Such things neither perfect human nature nor are they the natural result of that perfection. And therefore, I had an early belief that he served God best who was least envious, worldly, or sensual; who delighted most in the common good of the universe; and who had the strongest faith in the bounty and mercy of God. His son, Jesus, is the *most tangible pledge* of this that He could exhibit to the world. This constant state of spirit made me completely incapable of even the slightest trace <note>original: "Tincture"</note> of *superstition*. For it is ignorance of better things that causes those anxieties and terrors of mind concerning matters of less importance.

The *goal of religion* is human happiness and perfection; and he who so serves God as to imagine Him to lack anything of his own, instead of honoring Him, actually insults Him. Therefore, *superstition* is always accompanied by ignorance or hypocrisy. The *first* occurs when, not knowing what that "good and acceptable will of God" is (which is to become like Him—"You will honor God best if you make your mind like God," <note>original: "Τιμήσεις δὲ θεὸν ἄριστα ἐὰν τῷ θεῷ τὴν διάνοιαν ὁμοιώσῃς"</note> as *Pythagoras* taught), they express their zeal and devotion in things that benefit neither themselves nor anyone else. The *second* occurs when those same trifles are offered up to God, not so much out of ignorance of what is better, but out of a kind of silent fraud and cunning deception of God, as it were. They attempt to make such an unequal exchange with Him, whether He wants it or not. Though they may for a while pacify their false hearts and consciences through these delusions, in the meantime, they really only provoke God by these "sacrifices of fools." <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 5:1, implying mindless ritual or superficial worship.</note>

This is the summary of what I am able to conceive regarding this other disease of superstition.

# The General Preface.

...superstition, which I have understood only through reasoning, having had no personal experience of it to sharpen my style or expand my thoughts on the matter. But I believe I may safely affirm, as I have elsewhere, that it is **superstition** (if it is not **vanity**, **self-interest**, or something worse) when men have an excessive zeal for or against religious matters that **God** places little or no value upon, whether they are performed or omitted. If this were seriously and conscientiously considered, it would go a long way toward calming or preventing the usual storms <note>original: "blusters"</note> of **Christendom**. And there could be no better result from writing an entire **volume**. But I must confess that the success and growth of the **Church** is a **secret** <note>original: "Arcanum"</note> that lies deeper in **Divine Providence**. It is a **mystery** of spiritual life rather than of external **reason**. **Paul** may plant and **Apollos** may water, but **God** gives the growth <note>original: "increase"; a reference to 1 Corinthians 3:6</note>.

<margin>
It should not offend knowledgeable and honorable people that men are cautious and suspicious of truths they are not acquainted with.
</margin>

10. As for the letters that follow next, they explain their own purpose. I have added the letter to **V.C.** <note>likely an abbreviation for *Vir Clarissimus*, a Latin honorific meaning "Most Distinguished Man," often used in scholarly correspondence</note> for several reasons, but chiefly to encourage a better opinion of **Descartes** and his writings among those who are not well-acquainted with them. It is inevitable that men of excellent spirit may struggle with prejudice against such a worthy author because of misrepresentations. I must confess that the mere novelty of his work is enough to make even truly honorable men hesitate; that which is strange often seems hostile. This is why the Latin words for **"enemy"** <note>original: "Hostis"</note> and **"foreigner"** <note>original: "Peregrinus"</note> once had the same meaning, as **Cicero** observes. It is a sign of rudeness and lack of skill in understanding the nature of things and the perfection of **Divine Providence** to think that just because a truth is logically self-evident, its opposite will immediately surrender. God has generally implanted in us a stubborn loyalty to what we have customarily received, so that the human mind might be a safer container <note>original: "Receptacle"</note> when it finally encounters what is best. Considering this, honorable people must maintain sincere civility and respect even toward those who suspiciously doubt or oppose new truths. Indeed, it would be a mark of surprising ignorance or inhumanity to feel otherwise toward them.

<margin>
Certain remarkable things concerning Descartes and his writings.

* Letters of Mr. Descartes. Volume 2. Letters 75, 76, 80.
</margin>

11. Nothing specific comes to mind to note regarding that letter, except perhaps to applaud the luckiness of my guess concerning **Descartes's** distortion of the true and natural **idea of motion**. He did this because of **Galileo's** misfortune; Galileo was treated very harshly for his **hypothesis of the motion of the Earth** by a **Council of Cardinals**. It is now very evident from several of his letters to **Mersenne** <note>original: "Marsennus"</note> that Descartes had this event in mind. I did not know about these passages until a few days ago, and my own letter was written before this second volume of **Descartes's** letters was published. In the meantime, I cannot help but notice the harm this external force and fear does to the **community of scholars** <note>original: "Commonwealth of Learning"</note>. Many innocent and deserving young minds have been "put upon the rack," just as **Galileo** was put into prison. For Galileo's imprisonment frightened **Descartes** into such a distorted description of motion that no man's reason could make sense of it, nor could modesty allow anyone to imagine that such an excellent author was simply writing **nonsense**.

My main goal in my letter was to clear **Descartes** <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> from the dizzying and groundless suspicion of **atheism** (which surely could only be believed by those with unrefined and common minds). I believe I have done this fully, and...

<margin>Letter 114.</margin>
...and to effectively stop all such guesses for the future, even in the weakest and most scrupulous people who suspect him. Furthermore, I could have included even more from his first volume of letters: namely, that he not only believed in the existence of God, but also in His specific Providence <note>Providence: the protective care of God or of nature as a spiritual power</note>, which he felt and acknowledged in the special inspiration and success he experienced in his philosophical studies. I am not surprised by this, since he began so piously in his youth, writing his first work on that excellent theme, *The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom* <note>A reference to Psalm 111:10 or Proverbs 9:10</note>. I was informed of this in letters from Mr. Clerselier in Paris when he sent me a list <note>original: "Catalogue"</note> of the writings Descartes <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> had left behind. Learning this pleased me greatly, as it was the very same text upon which I first delivered a sermon <note>original: "common-placed," referring to a scholarly or theological exercise common in universities</note> in our college chapel.

<margin>Letter of Mr. Descartes. Volume 2, Letter 24.</margin>
But what delights me most is that both of us, though setting out from the same starting point <note>original: "Lifts," likely referring to the starting barriers in a race or tournament</note> and taking different paths—the one traveling the lower road of Democritism <note>Democritism: the philosophy of Democritus, focusing on atoms and matter</note> amid the thick dust of atoms and flying particles of matter, the other tracing a path over the high and airy hills of Platonism <note>Platonism: the philosophy of Plato, emphasizing abstract forms and the spiritual</note> in that thinner and more subtle region of immateriality—meet together at last (surely not without divine guidance) at the same goal. Specifically, we meet at the entrance of the Holy Bible, dedicating our joint labors to the use and glory of the Christian Church. We lay at its feet what we believe to be the truest and most acceptable philosophical interpretation of the first three chapters of *Genesis* ever offered to the world since the loss of the ancient Jewish Cabala <note>Cabala/Kabbalah: a traditional system of Jewish mysticism</note>. This is not merely a rhetorical flourish on my part, but a frank admission—or rather, a serious boast—by Descartes himself. In a letter to a friend, he claims that he found his own philosophy to be wonderfully consistent with the text of Moses <note>referring to the Torah, traditionally attributed to Moses</note>, more so than any other interpretation. I have fully demonstrated this in my *Defense of the Philosophic Cabala*, achieving even more than Descartes could have, unless he had discovered the same "key" that I did.

<margin>Several considerations gathered together which completely prevent all imaginable objections against the idea that a spirit has extension.</margin>
12. Regarding my work *The Immortality of the Soul*, I will address only two points of dissatisfaction. Although these seem like major issues to some, they never seemed so to me, but I will now bring them into view. The first is that I have admitted a kind of extension <note>Extension: in philosophy, the property of taking up space or having physical dimensions</note> in the nature of a spirit; the second is that I have not granted perception to the "Spirit of Nature." As for the first point, I can justly defend <note>original: "apologize," in the sense of a formal defense or *apologia*</note> myself by noting that "necessity has no law." If critics consider the provable evidence for these two conclusions: 1. *That there is an immaterial substance that is truly and specifically distinct from the body*, and 2. *That there is no real entity that does not take up space in some sense*, it will be impossible for them not to conclude, as I have, that a spirit must also be "extended" in some way. Therefore, it is a poorly reasoned complaint that nitpicks the conclusion without examining the strength of the premises. I therefore appeal to any impartial reader to judge whether I have not mathematically demonstrated the truth of the first point in both my *Antidote* and my *Treatise on the Immortality of the Soul*.

And for the reader's fuller satisfaction, I shall now demonstrate the second point more precisely: namely, that neither the soul nor anything else can be "the whole" <note>original: *Totum*</note> [in]...

<meta>This page continues the author's philosophical inquiry into the nature of spirits. He moves from defending Descartes to arguing against the traditional Scholastic view that a spirit can be "all in the whole and all in every part" of a space simultaneously without being "extended" (occupying space).</meta>

<header>The Preface general.</header>

...entirely in the whole, and entirely in every part <note>original Latin: "in toto, and totum in qualibet parte"</note>, but that this **Assertion** (as I once had occasion to write to a clever friend of mine) is a mere **sounding contradiction**. I proved it to him this way: namely, that the **Whole** <note>original: "Totum"</note> includes everything that belongs to a thing, both in a **positive sense** and (consequently) in a **negative** one. That is to say, **if all of A is in B, there is nothing left to be in C, which is distant from B**. For it is as if one were to say that there is nothing of A except what is contained within B, and yet at the same moment, not only something of A, but all of A, should also be in C. This is impossible for any singular or individual **Essence** <term>Essence: the fundamental nature or core identity of a thing</term>; and **Universals** <term>Universals: general concepts or categories (like "humanity") rather than specific individuals (like "Socrates")</term> are not **Things**, but **Notions**.

To this we may further add that this supposition makes the thing of which it is affirmed as small as the smallest conceivable thing. For if the Total is in **every** point, it is plain that the size <note>original: "amplitude"</note> of this Total is no larger than the point it occupies. This is intolerable when applied to the Deity, and ridiculous in everything else.

Therefore, since it is so mathematically demonstrable that there is something properly called **Spirit**, and that no Being at all can be totally present in distant points or parts of Matter at once, it unavoidably follows that a **Spirit is in some way extended** <note>The author argues that spirits must occupy space (extension) rather than being points without size or existing in multiple places at once without spanning the distance between them</note>.

But you will further urge: "If Spirit is extended as well as Body, how shall we imagine **Perception** to be more compatible with a Spirit than with a Body?" To this I briefly answer that I have already demonstrated that **Perception** is incompatible with Body, and I challenge anyone to prove the same concerning a **Spirit**. Furthermore, I ask those who imagine a Spirit to be totally present in every part of Matter whether they can any better understand the immediate reason for the power of perception that way. I also ask those who say it is neither like a mathematical point, nor totally present, nor extended, whether they imagine it is any more capable of that **vital Sympathy** and **Coactivity** <term>Coactivity: the ability of different parts of a soul to act together as one</term> that transmits objects in their exact circumstances to the common **Percipient** <note>Percipient: the entity that perceives or senses</note>. I dare say, if they speak honestly about what they find, they will certainly answer that they gain no advantage in understanding the reason for either simple Perception or the aforementioned vital Sympathy through such theories.

And therefore, in the third place, I will be so bold as to inform them that the truth of my 9th Axiom—which declares **that some powers and properties belong immediately to a Subject**—had already fully accomplished my purpose. Since there are other properties in the Body that prevent it from being able to perceive, it was necessarily left to some **Incorporeal** <term>Incorporeal: not composed of matter; having no physical body</term> Substance to be the immediate **Subject** of the power of **Perception**. For it must be the immediate power of some Subject or other, as far as our understanding can reach; nor can we find any other adequate cause besides the Subject itself that explains exactly why anything is able to perceive. It is true that we are conscious within ourselves that any Being that perceives must be very **Unitive** <term>Unitive: having the quality of being a single, indivisible unit</term>. Reason also proves to us that being "One" in a deeper way than Matter is "One" (which is "one" only because its parts are placed next to each other) is a necessary requirement for whatever is capable of the function of **Common-Percipiency**. Therefore, this unity comes first in nature. But that which is as much "One" as anything can be without a contradiction—that is to say, is so much "One" that it immediately possesses, by its own nature, vital Sympathy and the coactivity of parts, so to speak,

### The Preface general.

...speak, and perfect indivisibility <term>indiscerpibility: the quality of being impossible to divide or pull apart into separate pieces</term>, does not for all this immediately imply a power of perception residing within it. For I believe that every Spirit may be unified in this way, but I am not certain that every Spirit possesses perception; on the contrary, I believe some do not. Therefore, although everything that has perception must be a Spirit, not every Spirit needs to be perceptive. Thus, perception must be an inherent power in that class of Spirits that are perceptive. It would be an argument of no small ignorance <note>original Greek: ἀπαιδευσία (apaideusia), meaning a lack of education or unskilfulness</note> to ask or expect a reason why this is so.

Nor can we explain that vital oneness in every Spirit—which consists of the sympathy and shared activity of its parts—unless we claim that it is appropriate, since the nature of a Spirit is opposite to that of Matter, for the first and most immediate consequences of their natures to be opposite as well. Since it is acknowledged here that Matter is "stupid" <note>original: "stupid," meaning dull or lacking sensation</note>—or devoid of vital sympathy and shared activity—it follows that Spirit must be vital and endowed with those very properties. Or, just as Matter lacks the essential unity of indivisibility and is therefore devoid of this vital oneness, so Spirit, which possesses this essential unity, should consequently be endowed with vitality. But this line of reasoning is not as strictly rigorous as I prefer, though the argument is by no means worthless if we consider the direct opposition between the two types of being, and that we are only arguing for the first and most basic level of vitality in this comparison.

However, I did not want to rely on such reasoning <note>original: "ratiocinations"</note>, as I was confident that I had already accomplished my goal. I simply demonstrated that what I claim belongs to the Spirit is incompatible with Matter or Body. Therefore, the Spirit must necessarily be acknowledged both to exist and to be the subject of such powers—namely, vital sympathy, the shared activity of parts, and (the finest of all) the faculty of perception. Who could doubt that these properties are rightly placed there?

For I believe everyone will acknowledge that people generally have either a vague intuition or a more definite notion that whatever possesses this power of sympathy and perception must be the most subtle and unified thing in existence. Now, I challenge anyone to conceive of anything more subtle or more unified than the essential concept of a Spirit, as it is directly contrasted with Matter. For can anything be more "one" than that which is utterly indivisible <note>original: "indiscerpible"</note>? Or more subtle than that which can pass through not only Matter, but also through itself or things of its own kind? For Spirit can penetrate Spirit, though Matter cannot penetrate Matter. Since there is no physical resistance <note>original Greek: ἀντιτυπία (antitypia), meaning "antitypy" or the resistance of matter that prevents two bodies from occupying the same space</note> in a Spirit—neither toward its own kind nor toward anything else—it is evident that it is the most subtle thing that exists. Therefore, the communication of "vital impressions" (and all impressions in this context are vital, though not all are perceptions and none are physical motions) is not caused by parts bumping or crowding into each other. Instead, it happens through spiritual sympathy, which is more fluid and free from the restrictions found in the mechanical laws of matter.

The natural logical result <note>original: "consectary"</note> of this is that explaining a phenomenon through "sympathy" is not always taking refuge in an "asylum of fools" <note>original Latin: "Asylum Fatvorum," a phrase used to mock those who use occult or "magical" explanations for things they don't understand</note>. Nature is such that it is impossible for anyone not to admit that spirits are the proper subjects of sympathy and perception. Therefore, to conclude that something occurs by "sympathy"—when we can demonstrate that it is not caused by mere **mechanical** powers—is not to take shelter in the common refuge of ignorance. Rather, it is to identify the direct and immediate cause of a phenomenon, which is to practice philosophy at its highest level.

Briefly, therefore, to conclude: I have demonstrated with evidence no less than **mathematical** that there are **substances** which are incorporeal (non-physical), and that all **substance** is in some sense "extensional" (occupying space), because there is no **substance** but that which is, or at least may be, essentially present to **matter**. It necessarily follows from this that incorporeal substance is in some way extended. Consequently, a **soul** or **spirit** is capable of no other unity or oneness except that which consists in **indiscerpibility** <term>indiscerpibility: the quality of being impossible to divide or pull apart into separate pieces</term> and in the **vital shared activity** and **sympathy** of its parts. Therefore, finally, resolving the phenomena we experience in ourselves, or observe in other things, which exceed the mere **mechanical** laws of **matter**, into this **vital oneness**—which consists in the shared activity and sympathy of parts—is no empty repetition or merely saying a thing is so because it is so. Rather, it is a distinct **indication** of its proper and immediate cause. All these things, when laid together and seriously considered, will easily prevent whatever objections anyone might otherwise imagine against the **extension** of a **spirit**.

13. The second **dissatisfaction** concerns the **Spirit of Nature**, in that I have not allowed it the **power of perception**. Nor can a man doubt that it is a **universal principle**, if he considers the nature of **God** and the **divine fruitfulness**, and the usefulness of this **spirit** wherever there is **matter** manageable for some helpful end for the good of the whole **creation**. For example: it pulls a stone down toward the **center of the Earth** just as well when the **Earth** is in the constellation **Aries** as when it is in **Libra**; it keeps the **waters** from flying off the **Moon**; it forces the matter of the **Sun** into a round shape (which would otherwise be elongated); it restrains the solid parts of a **star** from flying into pieces into the surrounding **ether**; it carries along those large **regions** of loose **particles** of the "third element" <note>In Cartesian physics, the "third element" refers to the densest particles that form planets and comets</note>, along with the **comets**, in their travels from **vortex** <term>vortex: a "whirlpool" of cosmic matter that carries celestial bodies around a sun or planet</term> to **vortex**; and everywhere it directs magnetic **atoms** on their right **road**; in addition to all the **formative** <note>original: "Plastick," referring to the power of a spirit to give shape and life to matter</note> services it performs in both **plants** and **animals**.

This Spirit, therefore, being a mute copy of the **Eternal Word** (that is, of that **Divine Wisdom** that is entirely everywhere), is in every part naturally appointed to do all the best services that matter is capable of, according to how that matter is modified, and according to that **blueprint** of which it is the **copy**—I mean according to the comprehension and purpose of those **Ideas** of things which are in the eternal **intellect** of **God**. It is unnecessary to repeat what I have already noted regarding the discovery that *Pythagoreanism* was related to the *text* of *Moses*. But besides my observation that *Pherecydes* mentioned *Ophioneus* as the *leader* of the *apostate spirits* <note>referring to the serpent in the Garden of Eden</note>, the beginning of one of his *books* cited by *Laërtius* seems to me like a fragmented reflection of the *beginning* of *Genesis*: *God and Time and the Ground were eternally: But the Ground, when God adorned it, was called Earth.* <note>original Greek: Ζεὺς μὲν καὶ χρόνος εἰς ἀεὶ καὶ χθὼν ἦν· χθονὶ δὲ ὄνομα ἐγένετο γῆ, ἐπειδὴ αὐτῇ Ζεὺς γέρας δίδοι.</note> Of which the plain English is this: *God* and *Time* (by which I suppose he means *Duration*) and the *Ground* existed eternally; *but the Ground, upon God's adorning it, was called Earth.* This latter part was likely a reference to the work of the third day of Creation. But the first part, which claims the *Ground* is eternal, reflects the first day. For this *chthon* <note>original: χθὼν</note>, which I have translated as the *Ground*, is *Hyle* <note>Greek term for "matter" or "substance"</note>, which *Plotinus* calls the *foundation* <note>original: ὑποβάθρα</note> and the *ancient nature* <note>original: ἡ ἀρχαία φύσις</note>. This "Ground" or the *possibility* of the external *creation* is eternal; though it is a kind of *non-entity* <note>nothingness</note>, it is nonetheless the lowest *basis* of *actual being*. *Parmenides* (the fifth in this *Italic succession*) must also be understood in this sense when he makes his two first principles *Fire* and *Earth*, as seen in *Aristotle*: *He posits two principles, the hot and the cold, speaking of them as fire and earth; of these, he ranks the hot as Being, and the other as Non-Being.* <note>original Greek: Δύο τὰς ἀρχὰς τίθησι, θερμὸν καὶ ψυχρὸν, οἷον πῦρ καὶ γῆν λέγων· τούτων δὲ τὸ μὲν κατὰ τὸ ὂν τὸ θερμὸν τάττει, θάτερον δὲ κατὰ τὸ μὴ ὄν.</note> Here, the learned *Stagirite* <note>Aristotle (born in Stagira)</note> is utterly mistaken in his interpretation <note>original: "glosse"</note>, as if *Parmenides* meant nothing more by *Fire* and *Earth* than heat and cold, thereby making two *accidents* <note>properties rather than substances</note> the first principles of all things. The Spirit of Nature is not perceptive itself, being the natural *transcript* <note>original: "Transcript"; a copy or blueprint</note> of that which is knowing or *perceptive*. It is the lowest substantial activity from the all-wise God, containing within it certain general modes and laws of nature for the good of the *universe*. However, the *eye* of particular Providence is not found within it. If it were, why would a roof tile fall upon the head of someone passing by in the street, whether they are going to a play or to a sermon? And how do we explain those mistakes in monstrous births <note>original: "monstrous productions"; referring to birth defects or biological anomalies</note>, or those clumsy and self-defeating attempts of this Spirit in certain experiments regarding the discovery of a *vacuum*? As I have particularly noted in my *Antidote* <note>Henry More's book, *An Antidote against Atheism*</note>. Therefore, neither Omnipotence nor Omniscience acts directly in such cases, but rather this imperceptive Spirit of Nature. Its lack of perception is no more of an obstacle to its natural and plastic <note>term: "plastic"; here meaning "form-giving" or "shaping," as in the biological force that shapes an embryo</note> operations than the soul’s lack of an actual idea of a thing beforehand is a hindrance to her

When these things are well considered and allowed, that *special office of this Spirit of Nature in conducting souls in their "state of silence" <note>the period when the soul is dormant before or after life</note> to animate prepared matter, and so to raise animals into life*, will easily be understood as being as suitable an employment as any of the rest, and not at all more difficult. For *how much harder is it to understand that the Spirit of Nature may direct or carry down a silent soul, rather than a dead stone, to their fit and natural homes?* For the lifeless spirit and the dead stone are equally easy to take hold of, as the Spirit of Nature penetrates them both alike. Body moves up and down so easily within this Spirit of the world that it cannot be imagined that any mechanical power—but only that which is truly called *sympathetic* <note>meaning an attraction or resonance rather than a physical push</note>—must be the bond where any hold is taken. This bond catches and lets go for the direction and transmission of things to their proper places in the various parts of the world for the good of the whole, according to that *essential law* which is the form and *being* of this Spirit of Nature—the final ideal or *omniform efflux* <note>original: "Omniform Efflux"; an outflowing of all possible forms</note> from God. 

Nor is it, as I have already said, any more marvelous that a lifeless soul should be carried away and conducted to duly prepared matter by this imperceptive Spirit of Nature than that a dead stone or the senseless *magnetic* particles should be guided by it. For the thing by which the soul is caught so firmly by its particular body is not its perceptive part, but its plastic or natural part; otherwise, in a fit of pique <note>original: "in a pet"</note>, she might easily leave the body without having to resort to hanging, drowning, or stabbing. Why then may not a Spirit that has more subtle fingers than the finest matter—I mean the Spirit of Nature—lay hold on that imperceptive part of the soul, or on the soul itself in the state of silence or lack of perception, and by the sympathy and shared activity of its own essence carry her away to such services as either she herself had deserved or the *universe* required? Although I will not assert all these things as certain truths, I dare pronounce them to be as intelligible as the union of the soul with the body, which experience makes us understand whether we want to or not.

What we now call *Cartesianism*—because René Descartes <note>original: "Des-Cartes"</note> has so successfully brought it back into view—was actually part of the ancient Jewish *Cabbala* <note>original: "Judaical Cabbala"; a traditional system of Jewish mysticism and philosophy</note>. Clement of Alexandria provides us with very useful insight, in that he testifies of *Parmenides* that he categorized the Earth as one of the "Non-entities." For by this it is clear that he spoke symbolically, and meant the same thing that *Pherecydes* meant by *chthon* <note>original Greek: χθὼν; earth/ground</note>, which is the ancient *Hyle* <term>the fundamental, unformed matter of the universe</term>. For who would say that this physical Earth—which is the most solid and tangible entity in the world—is a "non-entity" any more than fire, air, or the like? 

But *Aristotle* (though he says excellent things at times) very often claims a hollow victory by trampling upon the opinions of the ancient philosophers. This is because he is ignorant of what *Clement of Alexandria* so clearly teaches us: "That their manner of philosophy was Mosaical and symbolical" <note>original Greek: Ὅτι ὁ τρόπος παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς τῆς φιλοσοφίας Ἑβραϊκὸς καὶ αἰνιγματώδης</note>. Since it is so evident that "Earth" is used symbolically by *Parmenides*, there can be no doubt that "Fire" is symbolic as well. It is nothing other than *Or* <note>original Hebrew: אור; light</note> or *Ouranos* <note>original Greek: Οὐρανὸς; heaven/sky</note>, meaning *Ether*. This corresponds in meaning to the "Light" or "Heaven" mentioned in the first day of Creation. This is Parmenides's formative or world-shaping principle <note>original: "Plastical or Demiurgical Principle"</note>—which physical fire cannot be—just as the "Earth" is his material principle. I have produced such evidence as this * to prove that the *Pythagorean philosophy* refers back to the text of *Moses*.

Furthermore, the philosophy which *Pythagoras* received from the *Jews* was not merely *metaphysical* <term>concerned with abstract concepts like being or knowing</term>, but also *physical* or *mechanical*. It was of the same nature as *Cartesianism*. This is proven not only by the "Motion of the Earth"—the famous opinion of *Pythagoras* which implies a *vortex* <term>a whirlpool of cosmic matter</term> around the *Sun*—but also by the acknowledged *Atomic philosophy* of *Leucippus*, *Democritus*, and *Epicurus*, who belong to the *Italic line* of thinkers. It is true that what they say about *vortices* is either a corrupt idea from a decaying school of thought, or was recorded in a broken and confused way by the historian. 

And yet, I have selected something from the life of *Parmenides* that is so perfectly consistent with *Cartesian philosophy* that nothing could be more so; indeed, it is the very heart and marrow of it, and essentially encompasses everything. This is expressed by the translator of *Laërtius* as: "The Sun itself is both cold and hot" <note>original Latin: Solem ipsum frigidum esse & calidum</note>. This is a monstrous statement for *Parmenides* to make, unless the meaning is simply this: "The Sun is either glowing or burnt out" <note>original Latin: Solem esse vel candentem vel extinctum</note>, alluding to the Hebrew terms *Shemesh* <note>original: שמש; the sun</note> and *Kokhav* <note>original: כוכב; a star or planet</note>. Nor can the statement immediately before it be true—that humans were generated from the *Sun*—unless it means the Sun after it has "burnt out" and becomes an *Earth* or a *planet*. *Descartes's* philosophy defines it this way: *That this Earth, out of which man was first made, is of such a nature as if it had once been a Sun*. I dare not define it any further.

The latter is, as it were, the Body, and the former the Soul of that philosophy. The unfortunate separation of these two has been a great evil to both. The metaphysicians have become vain, spinning out needless and useless subtleties and ridiculous falsehoods regarding immaterial beings, because they lacked a simpler object to exercise their reason upon. Meanwhile, the *Atomic philosophers* have become far too ready to believe in the absolute power of matter. I might even say they have been impious and shameless in rejecting the belief in *immaterial beings*, in despising the rules and maxims of *virtue* and *morality*, and in shamelessly forcing their *mechanical guesses* upon the world as if they were necessary demonstrations...

I must admit that although I find myself holding a key whose design fits every ward of the lock in this **Mosaic Treasury** <note>The "Mosaic Treasury" refers to the hidden philosophical and spiritual meanings within the Pentateuch, the first five books of the Bible attributed to Moses.</note>, and which turns easily, locking and unlocking—and within I see, or so I believe, inestimable riches of **knowledge**—I still do not dare to trust my own eyes. I must confess that although I find myself holding a *Key* in my hand whose structure and design is exquisitely fitted to every ward in the lock of this *Mosaic Treasury*, and which turns easily, locking and unlocking, so that I may view—as I imagine—inestimable riches of Knowledge; yet I dare not believe my own eyes. I cannot conclude whether it is a real vision or a dream, for I do not know if this is undoubtedly that ancient golden *Key* of the *Kabbalah* <note>original: *Cabbala*</note> or one made of a cheaper metal. And truly, a man’s suspicion may well be increased because it opens immediately upon those two dazzling paradoxes: the *Motion of the Earth* and the *Preexistence of the Soul*. These are enough to make even the boldest observer step back in sudden amazement—a state in which I confess I remain to this very day. No one can wonder at my hesitation if they consider how cautious the ancient Church Fathers were regarding the *roundness of the Earth* and the existence of the *Antipodes* <term>The "Antipodes" refers to people living on the opposite side of the globe.</term>; this was indeed the opinion of *Pythagoras* in ancient times, but has become certain knowledge in these more recent ages.

C. <note>likely "Vir Clarissimus," a common Latin honorific for a distinguished man.</note>, *nor anything more convincing regarding the preexistence of the soul than what I have presented in my* Treatise on its Immortality. *I brought these into view (along with anything else in my writings that might seem to stray from the common path) to provide more material for precise judgment, which contributes greatly to a correct decision about what is true. Nothing else occurred to me that seemed worth adding regarding the subject of preexistence, except for noting how innocent and harmless that doctrine was in the more pure and uncorrupted ages of the Church. (This is in addition to my showing that it was the opinion of all philosophers who held the soul to be immortal—specifically* Plato, Aristotle, *and* Cicero, *authors assigned to us by the very statutes of our* University; *which is enough to make the opinion respectable.)*

As Clement of Alexandria says, "Just as both non-Greek and Greek philosophy have turned eternal truth into a kind of fragmentation <note>original: 'discerption'</note> of the theology of the *Logos* <note>The Divine Word or Reason</note> that exists forever, breaking it into scattered parts. Ὁ δὲ τὰ διῃρημένα συνθεὶς αὖθις καὶ ἑνοποιήσας τέλεον τὸν λόγον, ἀκινδύνως εὖ ἴσθ' ὅτι κατόψεται τὴν ἀλήθειαν</note>. *I was all the more willing to repeat this because I feel I have attempted a similar task in my own work: fitting together the scattered wisdom of the ancients into one Mosaic Kabbalah <note>original: 'Mosaick Cabbala'</note>.*

Again, in the third book of his *Stromata*, where he argues against the *Marcionites* <note>Followers of Marcion, an early Christian leader who held dualistic views</note>, he cites several sayings from *Plato* that either refer to or directly affirm the *Preexistence of the Soul*. He describes this as a *traditional secret* <note>original: 'Arcanum'</note>: that in this life, we are kept as if in a jail. *He also attributes this wise saying to Heraclitus, Pythagoras, Socrates, and Plato all at once:* "All we see when awake is death, and all we see when asleep is a dream" <note>original: Θάνατός ἐστιν ὁκόσα ἐγερθέντες ὁρέομεν, ὁκόσα δὲ εὕδοντες ὕπνος</note>. 

But the most relevant passage is the one he cites from *Philolaus* the Pythagorean: "The ancient theologians and prophets also bear witness that the soul is yoked to the body as a form of punishment, and is buried in this body as if in a tomb" <note>original: Μαρτυρέονται δὲ καὶ οἱ παλαιοὶ θεολόγοι τε καὶ μάντεις ὡς διά τινας τιμωρίας ἡ ψυχὰ τῷ σώματι συνέζευκται, καὶ καθάπερ ἐν σώματι τούτῳ τέθαπται</note>. *The ancient theologians and prophets (he means, I suppose, especially those of the Jews) testify that the soul is joined to this earthly body as a punishment, and that as long as she is in this body, she is essentially buried.* Clement shows no distaste for these Platonic opinions. Instead, he only blames *Marcion* for abusing them to support his absurd doctrine that marriage is unlawful. He complains that Marcion ungratefully and clumsily used *Plato* as an excuse to hatch his own strange and perverse opinions.

He says he will show that *Cassian* was mistaken once he has completed his *Treatise on the Generation of Man*, but he declines to label it an error for the time being. If he ever wrote such a treatise, it is clear he did not handle these "skins" so roughly that they were not passed down intact to his excellent student, *Origen Adamantius*. <meta>This page continues the defense of the Church Fathers' character, specifically focusing on the life, asceticism, and controversial doctrines of Origen of Alexandria.</meta>

<page-num>xxii</page-num>
<header>The General PREFACE.</header>

*The truth of what we find in* Eusebius <note>original: 'Eusebius' — a 4th-century Greek historian of Christianity</note> *is clear. For certainly (to say nothing of his remarkable talents and abilities, which even his greatest adversaries will not deny), it would be very difficult to find another example of such sincere and zealous devotion to the cause of Christ, even to the point of disregarding death and desiring martyrdom. This was not just a fleeting burst of youthful passion in him, but a permanent faithfulness and fortitude of spirit. It was common for that holy man to assist and encourage all the martyrs—those unknown to him as well as his acquaintances—openly accompanying them to their execution, friendly embracing them, and providing them all the comfort he could, often at the risk of being stoned by the angry crowds.*

*It will seem a smaller matter to notice his tireless reading and meditating on the Holy Scripture day and night, and his total neglect of worldly things for the pleasure of divine contemplation and the service of the Church of Christ; his immense charity to the poor, his frequent fastings and sleeping on the ground, his endurance of cold and lack of clothing, his walking barefoot on the hard stones, his abstinence from wine, and his extraordinary self-control <note>original: 'Temperance'</note> regarding all physical pleasures. His great example of an* **ascetic** <note>original: 'Ascetick' — a lifestyle characterized by abstinence from sensual pleasures, often for spiritual goals</note> *life gained many disciples for the Church and trained many fearless champions of the Christian faith who willingly laid down their lives for the love of the Lord Jesus. Emerging from* Origen's *school were* Plutarchus, *the two* Sereni, Heraclides, Heron, Rhais, *and* Basilides, *who received the crown of martyrdom through the intercession of that illustrious* **virgin-martyr** Potamiæna. *What terrible calamities* Origen *himself also endured in the* **Decian Persecution** <note>A period of intense state-sponsored persecution of Christians by the Roman Emperor Decius, c. 250 AD</note>, *what chains and physical torments, what imprisonments in dungeons, what stretching and racking of limbs, what terrors of fire and burnings—all these are recorded in the annals of Church history.*

<margin>* See Photius, *Library*, Excerpt 234. <note>original: 'Phot. Bibliothec. Excerpt. 234'</note></margin>
<margin>* Photius, *Library*, Excerpt 317.</margin>

*These and similar examples confirm the integrity and holiness of this venerable Father. But I must admit I would be reluctant to be held responsible for the truth of all the opinions attributed to him. For instance, his claim that the* **Sun, Moon,** *and* **Stars** *are living and intelligent creatures shows that he was a better theologian than a scientist <note>original: 'Naturalist'</note>. His claim that the power of God is finite, and that He made only as many things as could be managed by His providence without contradiction—this error (if it truly was* Origen's) *was certainly intended as a defense for God not making the world infinite. It shows that the Reverend Father had a greater concern for the sovereign goodness of God than for His power. Regarding his claim that the punishment of the devils and the damned is not eternal: yet* Jacobus Merlinus <note>A 16th-century French theologian who edited Origen's works</note> *clears him of this by citing at least ten different passages from his writings. Then there is his saying that the bodies of men at the Resurrection will be raised in a* **spherical** <note>original: 'Orbicular'</note> *shape; this is expressly contrary to what* Methodius <note>An early Christian bishop and martyr who opposed some of Origen's teachings</note> *states regarding* Origen: *namely, that his opinion was that everyone at the Resurrection should appear exactly in their own particular form or shape. Finally, there is his assertion that the soul of our Savior was the same soul that was in* Adam; *which is actually impossible for him to have asserted, since he*

*but a mere legend <note>original: 'Romance'</note> built upon the greatness of Origen's name and virtues. For it was to their harm, not their fault, that they were misinformed.*

<margin>Saint Basil and Gregory Nazianzen.</margin>
*Saint <note>original: 'S.'</note> Basil also and Gregory Nazianzen were no enemies to the opinion of the soul's pre-existence, but rather supporters of it. This appears from the great respect they had for Origen, and particularly from the gift that Nazianzen gave to Theodorus Tyaneus: a book of selections from Origen's writings, compiled by himself and Saint Basil, which is titled* Origen's Philokalia <note>original: 'Ωριγένους Φιλοκαλία' — 'Love of the Beautiful or Good'</note>, *wherein there are several passages that plainly imply or directly affirm the pre-existence of the soul.*

<margin>Synesius, Bishop of Cyrene.</margin>
*The next open supporter <note>original: 'Assertour'</note> of the soul's pre-existence is Synesius, Bishop of Cyrene. In a letter to his brother, he seriously declares that he cannot accept that honorable position offered to him without the liberty of enjoying—nay, I may say of professing—certain opinions of his. These had been rooted in him for a long time based on well-considered reasons, the primary one being the pre-existence of the soul. "In good earnest," he says,*
<margin>* Letter 105. <note>original: 'Epist. 105.'</note></margin>
*"I shall never consent to believe that the soul is of later existence than the body or matter" <note>original: 'Αμέλει τὴν ψυχὴν οὐκ ἀξιώσω ποτὲ σώματος ὑστερογενῆ νομίζειν'</note>. He deals so openly that he gives directions to his brother to share the letter with the scholars <note>original: 'Scholasticks'</note>, as he calls them, so that it might be communicated to that reverend Father who offered him the position. This freedom in professing the opinion was nevertheless no obstacle to his promotion <note>original: 'Preferment'</note>.*

...so expressly declaring that the Soul of the *Messiah* <note>original: "Messias"</note> never sinned. And lastly, to omit several others, his supposed teaching of the reincarnation <note>original: "transmitting"</note> of human souls into the bodies of animals. I do not doubt, and could easily prove, that this was falsely attributed <note>original: "falsly fathered"</note> to *Pythagoras* as well as *Origen*. However, some fanciful followers of both did attach these unsightly and ridiculous *additions* <note>original: "Appendages"</note>, thinking every vain addition to be an improvement of those pure doctrines which were anciently delivered to the world. Such was the status of *Preexistence* <note>original: "Præexistence"</note> in the Church of the *Jews*, where no such foolishness was mixed with it. And if it had remained so among the *Origenists* <note>Followers of Origen's teachings.</note>, it certainly would never have fallen under public censure. Yet I dare not lay the blame solely upon them, as their malevolent *adversaries* took enough liberty to charge *Origen* with things that had no basis in fact. 

One such example was that formal story of him casting incense on the altar of an *idol*, supposedly being given the choice between that or the sexual abuse of his body by an *Ethiopian*. This is nothing but a <margin>* See *Epitom. Spondan. Ann.* 253. section 19.</margin> * mere romance built upon the greatness of *Origen*'s name and virtues. Though his reputation may seem much tarnished by that public censure in the fifth *General Council* <note>The Second Council of Constantinople (553 AD), which posthumously condemned Origen.</note>, anyone who considers that the *details* of his condemnation were entirely removed from the *records* of that Council by the same power that first caused his censure, may easily find enough to repair *Origen*'s credit to a great extent. This can be done without damaging the authority of that great *convention*, for it was their *wrong*, not their *fault*, that they were misinformed.

<margin>S. *Basil* and *Gregory Nazianzen*.</margin> Saint *Basil* and *Gregory Nazianzen* were also no enemies to the opinion of the Soul's *Preexistence*; rather, it appears they favored it. This is evident from the great esteem they had for *Origen*, and particularly from the *gift* that *Nazianzen* gave to *Theodorus Tyaneus*: a *book of selections* <note>original: "Book of Exceptions"</note> from *Origen*'s writings, compiled by himself and St. *Basil*. This book is titled *Origen's Philokalia* <note>original: "Ωριγένους Φιλοκαλία"; a collection of Origen's texts compiled by Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus.</note>, and it contains several *passages* that plainly imply or directly affirm the *Preexistence* of the *Soul*.

<margin>*Synesius*, Bishop of *Cyrene*.</margin> The next open *supporter* <note>original: "Assertour"</note> of the Soul's *Preexistence* is *Synesius*, Bishop of *Cyrene*. In a *letter to his brother*, he seriously professes that he cannot accept the honorable church position offered to him without the liberty of enjoying—nay, I may say of professing—certain opinions of his. These had been rooted in him for a long time based on well-considered reasons, the primary one being the *Preexistence of the Soul*. <margin>* *Epist. 105.*</margin> "In good earnest," he says, "I shall never agree that the Soul is younger in existence than the body or matter" <note>original: "Ἀμέλει τὴν ψυχὴν οὐκ ἀξιώσω ποτὲ σώματΘ, ὑστερογενῆ νομίζειν"</note>. He deals so openly that he gives directions to his brother to share the letter with the *scholars* <note>original: "Scholasticks"</note>, as he calls them, so that it might be communicated to that reverend Father who offered him the position. Despite this freedom in professing the *opinion*, it was no barrier to his *promotion* <note>original: "Preferment"</note>.

<margin>*Arnobius*.</margin> To these you may add the authority of two *Latin Fathers*, *Arnobius* and *Prudentius*. The former writes expressly concerning this point: <margin>* *Advers. gent. lib. 1.*</margin> "Do we not all owe to God this very first thing that we are? That we are called humans; and that—whether sent by Him or having fallen through blindness—we are kept within the chains of this body?" <note>original: "Nonne Deo omnes debemus hoc ipsum primum quod sumus, quod esse homines dicimur, quod ab eo vel missi, vel lapsi cæcitate, hujus in corporis vinculis continemur?"</note>. The other writes as follows in his *Hymn for the Burial of the Dead* <note>original: "Hymnus in Exequiis Defunctorum"</note>: <margin>*Prudentius*.</margin>
