*...is true, as we find in the writings of Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the "Father of Church History."</note>. For certainly—to say nothing of his amazing talents and abilities, which even his greatest adversaries will not deny—it would be very difficult to find another example of such sincere and zealous commitment to the cause of Christ, even to the point of defying death and desiring martyrdom. This was no temporary burst of youthful excitement in him, but a permanent faithfulness and fortitude of spirit. It was common for that holy man to assist and encourage all the martyrs, those unknown to him as well as his friends, openly accompanying them to their execution, friendly embracing them, and offering them all the comfort he could, often at the risk of being stoned by the angry crowds.*

*It will seem a smaller matter to notice his diligent reading and meditation on the Holy Scripture day and night, his total neglect of worldly things for the pleasure of divine contemplation and the service of the Church of Christ, his excessive charity to the poor, his frequent fasts and sleeping on the ground, his endurance of cold and nakedness, his walking barefoot on the hard stones, his abstinence from wine, and his remarkable self-control in all the pleasures of nature. His great example of an ascetic <note>original: "Ascetick" — a lifestyle of severe self-discipline and refraining from indulgence for spiritual goals.</note> life drew many disciples to the Church and trained many undaunted champions of the Christian faith, who willingly laid down their lives for the love of the Lord Jesus. Coming out of Origen’s school were Plutarchus, the two Sereni, Heraclides, Heron, Rhais, and Basilides, who received the crown of martyrdom through the intercession of that illustrious virgin-martyr Potamiæna. The terrible calamities Origen himself underwent in the Decian Persecution <note>A period of intense persecution of Christians under the Roman Emperor Decius, c. 250 AD.</note>—the chains and physical torments, being cast into prisons and dungeons, the stretching and racking of his limbs, and the threats of fire and burning—are all recorded in the histories of the Church.*

*These and similar examples confirm the integrity and holiness of this venerable Father. But I must confess I would be reluctant to be held responsible for the truth of all the opinions attributed to him. For instance, his claim that the sun, moon, and stars are living and intelligent creatures; this shows he was a better theologian <note>original: "Divine"</note> than natural scientist <note>original: "Naturalist"</note>. Another is his claim that the power of God is finite, and that He made only as many things as could be managed by His providence without contradiction. This error (if it truly was Origen's) was certainly intended as a defense for God not making the world infinite, and it shows that the Reverend Father had a greater concern for the sovereign goodness of God than for His power. There is also his claim that the punishment of the devils and the damned is not eternal; yet Jacobus Merlinus <note>A 16th-century French theologian and editor of Origen's works.</note> clears him of this by citing at least ten different passages from his writings. Another is his saying that the bodies of men at the Resurrection will be raised in a spherical <note>original: "Orbicular"</note> shape. This is*

*Saint Augustine also speaks very favorably of this opinion in his work "On Free Will" <note>original: "De Libero arbitrio"</note>, where he writes:* "Whether the soul lived in some other life before its union with this body is a great question and a great secret." <note>original Latin: "Utrùm ante consortium hujus corporis aliâ quâdam vitâ vixerit animus, magna quæstio est, magnum secretum."</note> *And then in another place in the same treatise, speaking again of the soul's preexistence, he tells us freely and honestly:* "If we think something about God other than what He is, our intention will drive us not toward blessedness but toward vanity. <note>original Latin: "Si de Deo aliud senserimus quàm est, intentio nostra non in beatitatem sed in vanitatem compellet."</note> Regarding a creature, however, if we think something other than how it actually is—as long as we do not hold it as a known and perceived fact—there is no danger." <note>original Latin: "De creatura verò siquid aliter quàm sese habet senserimus, dummodo non id pro cognito perceptoque teneamus, nullum periculum."</note> *And in a third place, in his discussion of that fourfold question <note>original: "Quære"</note>—namely, whether souls are passed down from parents, created, sent from God out of some hidden storage place where they previously existed, or fell here by their own choice—he says:* "Either this question has not yet been unraveled and clarified by Catholic commentators of the divine books as its obscurity and perplexity deserve, or, if it has already been done, such writings have not yet come into our hands." <note>original Latin: "Aut nondum ista quæstio... à divinorum librorum Catholicis tractatoribus pro merito suæ obscuritatis & perplexitatis evoluta atque illustrata est; ...implied in the question; I say, a person may derive a proof from this: that there is no harm in the opinion, no poison or danger in it. Otherwise, surely our *Savior*, having such a fit opportunity, would not have failed to expose it.

<margin>That there is not the slightest conflict between *Preexistence* and the derivation of *Original sin* from *Adam*.</margin>
19. And that there is not the least evil, or slightest conflict or clashing, in this *Hypothesis* <note>theory or proposition</note> with the ordinary and literal sense of the *Scripture* and the universally acknowledged *Canon of Faith*, I am as certain as that the clear *Air* will not block the light of the *Sun*, but both exist in the same space. What it seems most opposed to is the derivation of *Original sin* from *Adam*. But those who assert the *Preexistence of the Soul* do not understand the mystery correctly if they do not assume that all *Souls* that come by *natural Order* into these *Terrestrial Tenements* <term>earthly bodies</term> are in a state of silence first. This makes it as if they did not exist before, and the whole scene of things clearly begins with *Adam*. God incorporated Adam's *Soul* into such a *Paradisiacal* <note>Eden-like; perfect</note> body that naturally charmed his mind into as full a possibility of not falling as the usual orthodox *Theology* supposes *Adam* to have had. God designed the same advantage—if Adam had remained faithful—to be passed down to his *Posterity*. It is plainly manifest from this that his fall was the cause of what we now call *Original sin*—that is to say, that disproportionate *Proneness* and almost irresistible *Proclivity* <note>tendency or inclination</note> toward evil. This is how far the *Hypothesis* of *Preexistence* is from clashing with the derivation of *Original sin* from *Adam*.

Indeed, I will add further that what is said in *Scripture* about the first and second *Adam* cannot be understood as well as it can through the *Hypothesis* of *Preexistence* and an earlier fall of *Souls* in a previous state. For I ask anyone to consider without prejudice what better meaning there can be for those words <margin>*Rom. 5:14*</margin> of *St. Paul*, where he says that *Adam* was the figure of him who was to come—that is, of *Christ*. He means that the office of *Adam* was a prelude to and *Typical* <note>serving as a "type" or symbolic foreshadowing</note> of the office of *Christ*. This comparison would be very weak if it only meant that he was a public figure as Christ was, but did not have the duty of the *Redemption* of the *sons of men* laid upon him in any sense. Therefore, the office of *Adam* was to pass on that healthy and *Paradisiacal* physical state to his *Seed* (just as our ordinary *Theology* determines) and thereby be, as it were, the *Savior* and *Redeemer* of his descendants from the ill effects of that previous fall they had suffered. Thus, he was perfectly the figure of him who was to come. But this earthly *Adam* failing in his office, the *Heavenly* one was substituted in his place, who *is able to save to the uttermost. <margin>* *Hebrews 7:25*</margin> In my mind, this *Hypothesis* makes *St. Paul* and this part of the *Mystery* of our *Religion* wonderfully easy and intelligible.

These and similar arguments may be made on behalf of that ancient point of *Platonism*: *The Preexistence of the Soul*.

<margin>That mathematical certainty in purely philosophical speculations does not need to force any man’s conscience to profess them against the wishes of his superiors.</margin>
20. <meta>This page continues the author's argument regarding the preexistence of the soul, transitioning into a discussion on the relationship between private philosophical conviction and the authority of the Church.</meta>

*...my superiors. For though those theories were so certain to me, yet I am just as certain that mathematical certainty itself is not absolute, and that God alone is infallible.*

*But so that I do not seem harmful to myself, nor cause a scandal to others by this very free profession, I am required to add this: the conscience of every holy and sincere Christian is as strictly bound in matters of religion—where they are clearly and expressly determined by the infallible oracles of God—as it is free in philosophical speculations. And although, out of a love for his own ease or a reverent regard for the authority of the Church (which undoubtedly every noble spirit is sensitive to), he may have a great desire to say, profess, and do as they would have him; yet in cases of this kind, where anything is expected that is contrary to the plain and express sense of those Divine writings, he cannot help but find himself restricted here. He will certainly be <margin>Herodotus, book 5, number 63.</margin> constrained "to value the things of God more highly than the things of men" <note>original Greek: τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ πρεσβύτερα ποιέεσθαι ἢ τὰ τῶν ἀνδρῶν</note> (as the Lacedæmonians <note>The Spartans</note> are said to have done, though based on a religious mistake). Or <margin>Acts 5:29.</margin> rather, he will use that short but weighty defense of the Apostle: "We must obey God rather than men" <note>original Greek: Πειθαρχεῖν δεῖ Θεῷ μᾶλλον ἢ ἀνθρώποις</note>.*

*These are the unbreakable laws and ties of religion. No man can complain against them without complaining against the very existence of God, or against His essential right to be served first and to bind our consciences to believe—and our tongues to profess—whatever truths He has <margin>Matthew 10:33.</margin> miraculously communicated to the world on those terms: "Whoever denies me before men, him will I also deny before my Father who is in heaven." But in philosophical theories, such as the preexistence of the soul, the motion of the Earth, and the like, where God has not required our profession, nor is our eternal interest at stake, nor is the source of the idea infallible; even if we should imagine ourselves to have a mathematical assurance of our conclusions, I must still declare (as I said before) that I do not see how anyone is bound by conscience to assert them against the authority of the Church under which he lives, if the Church should ever dislike them. Instead, he may with a safe conscience come to an agreement with his superiors and use their language and phrases regarding such things. For if it was a virtue in that holy and venerable lawgiver Moses to condescend with such prudence and fatherly kindness to the capacity of the common people <note>original: "the Vulgar"</note> by describing the creation of the world according to how things appeared to them, then surely it cannot be a vice in us—out of humble submission and reverence to the governors of the Church (whatever our private judgment may be)—to accept their established ways and phrases of speaking in those things where God has not bound us to do otherwise.*

<margin>That if the philosophy which he has applied to the text of Moses is true, it is a real restoration of the Mosaic Cabbala <note>The author suggests his philosophical system (including preexistence) is the original, secret mystical tradition given to Moses.</note>.</margin>
*21. But if Time, which brings all great things along grandly and by degrees, should finally and universally reveal that the philosophy I have dared to apply to the text of Moses is sound, then it will be accepted as commonly and without offense as the doctrine of the Antipodes <note>The concept of people living on the opposite side of a spherical Earth, which was once considered a scientific and theological absurdity.</note> is now, which once seemed so monstrous and crazy to the Christian world. At that point, approval will hardly be able to keep a middle ground; once the theorems are allowed as true, they will also necessarily be acknowledged as most lovely and glorious.*

...my superiors. For though those theories were so certain to me, yet I am as certain that mathematical certainty itself is not absolute, and that God alone is infallible.

But so that I may not seem harmful to myself, nor give scandal to others by this so free profession, I am forced to add: That the conscience of every holy and sincere Christian is as strictly bound in matters of religion plainly and expressly determined by the infallible oracles of God, as it is free in philosophical speculations. # THE PREFACE.

1. *The author's defense <note>original: "Apologie"</note> for writing this treatise, despite there being so many already on the same subject.* 2. *That what he has written are the natural expressions <note>original: "proper Emanations"</note> of his own mind, and may be particularly useful for men of a similar temperament <note>original: "Genius"</note>.* 3. *That he does not strive for rhetoric, nor literary scholarship <note>original: "Philologie"</note>, nor the grand abundance <note>original: "pompous numerosity"</note> of more popular arguments, but for solid and irresistible reason in a clear <note>original: "perspicuous"</note> method.* 4. *That he has undeniably demonstrated the existence of God, provided this one premise <note>original: "Postulate"</note> is admitted:* That our faculties are true. 5. *His unique handling of the first argument of Descartes <note>original: "Des-Cartes"</note>:* 6. *And the reasons for his rejection of the rest.* 7. *His caution and selectivity in managing such arguments as are derived <note>original: "fetch'd"</note> from the more general phenomena <note>original: "Phænomena"</note> of nature:* 8. *As also in those regarding animals.* 9. *His careful choice of such stories <note>original: "Histories"</note> as tend to prove the existence of spirits.* 10. *His confidence in that kind of argument.* 11. *The reason for his refusing to repeat the miraculous stories of Holy Scripture <note>original: "Holy Writ"</note>.* 12. *His intentional humility <note>original: "studied Condescension"</note> and accommodation of the atheist to win him over from his atheism.*

->READER,<-

1. BY what motivations <note>original: "inducements"</note> I was led to publish this present treatise—despite the vast number <note>original: "Numerosity"</note> of writings of this kind—I would rather leave it to your own perceptiveness <note>original: "quick-sightedness"</note> to discover, than be forced into so much immodesty myself as to say anything that might seem to claim any superiority <note>original: "precellency"</note> over what is already available <note>original: "extant"</note> in the world on this same matter. I may only say this: I intentionally avoided reading any treatises on this subject so that I might write the natural expressions <note>original: "easie Emanations"</note> of my own mind without disturbance, and not be distracted from what should naturally flow from myself by biasing <note>original: "prepossessing"</note> my thoughts with the ideas <note>original: "inventions"</note> of others.

2. I have written, therefore, following no model <note>original: "Copy"</note> but the eternal innate traits <note>original: "Characters"</note> of the human mind and the known phenomena <note>original: "Phænomena"</note> of nature.

<summary>Henry More introduces his preface by explaining that his treatise is a product of his own original reasoning rather than a compilation of other authors' works. He outlines twelve key points of his argument, emphasizing a reliance on reason, nature, and the innate ideas of the mind to combat atheism.</summary>

<margin>
By the **objective reality** of an idea, I mean the being of the thing represented by the idea, insofar as that being is present in the idea. For whatever we perceive as being in the objects of our ideas is present in the ideas themselves objectively. <note>original: "Per Realitatem objectivam Idea intelligo entitatẽ rei repræsentatæ per Ideam quatenus est in Idea. Nam quæcunque percipimus tanquam in Idearum objectis, ea sunt in ipsis Ideis objectivè." Descartes, *Replies to the Second Objections*, Metaphysics Definition 3.</note>

6. But as for his following reasons, they assume several things: first, that the <term>objective reality</term> <note>the concept that the "content" of an idea requires a cause as great as the thing the idea represents</note> of the idea of God exceeds the causal power of the human mind. Second, that if the human mind were the cause of its own existence, it would have given itself all the perfections it can imagine. And lastly, they assume that because the mind has no power to preserve its own existence—and because the present moment has no necessary connection to the future—the mind must be continually reproduced (that is, sustained) by some higher cause, which must be God. 

I say that I did not dare to rely on these specific arguments because an atheist can so easily evade them. I would not trust them unless I possessed the original author’s <note>referring to René Descartes</note> brilliant intellect to defend them, for he was skillfully able to justify almost anything. To me, however, these grounds seem vulnerable to certain objections that I cannot find a way to stop.

For an atheist will readily reply that the human mind is capable of creating such an actual **idea** of God on its own. They would argue that this **idea** is merely a current state <note>original: "modification"</note> of the mind, just like any other notion, and is a result of the mind's own essence and power—a power that is a fundamental property of its nature. Therefore, there is no "excess" of an effect over its cause, even if we look no further than the mind itself. In this view, the mind forms this concept of God as naturally and as independently of a higher cause as it does anything else.

And as for the argument that the mind would have given itself the perfections it imagines if it were its own creator: the atheist will say this involves a contradiction. It assumes that a thing could consult about the advantages of its own existence before it even exists. But if the mind exists by its own nature, it simply is what it finds itself to be, and it cannot be any other way.

Therefore, finally, if the mind finds that it exists, it can no more destroy itself than it could produce itself. Nor does it need anything to continue its being, provided there is nothing in nature acting against it to destroy it. For whatever exists continues to exist in that state unless there is some cause to change it.

<meta>This page continues Henry More's preface to "An Antidote Against Atheism." Here, More explains his criteria for selecting arguments for the existence of God. He moves away from abstract Cartesian proofs toward "teleological" arguments—the idea that the specific, complex design of the universe and living creatures proves an intelligent Creator.</meta>

the mind of man, my careful choice made very large reductions <note>original: "defalkations"; meaning subtractions or cuttings-away</note>; focusing instead on things that could have been different, and yet are much better as they are, rather than on things that were necessary and could not have been any other way. For example, when I considered the distance of the sun, I did not think that the fact it is not placed as low as the moon, or as high as the fixed stars, was a very strong argument for Providence <note>Providence: the protective care and wise guardianship of God</note>. This is because someone might reply that it was necessary for the sun to be between those two distances, otherwise the Earth would not have been habitable; thus, mankind might have waited to exist until the movement of matter had worked things into a more tolerable fitness or arrangement for their creation.

Neither is the annual motion of the sun (or rather, of the Earth) by itself any argument for Divine Providence; it is as necessary as a piece of wood being carried downstream or straws caught in a whirlpool. However, the laws of its motion are such that they very clearly convince us of a Providence; therefore, I was compelled to let go of the former argument and focus more extensively on the latter.

I also did not think it appropriate to use flowery rhetoric <note>original: "Rhetoricate"</note> in describing the great variety of things and the excellence of one over another. Instead, I chose to focus closely on the design and the way one thing is organized to serve another. I show that, while the crude motions of matter (by a thousand-to-one chance) might have arranged things differently, the actual production of things is such that our own reason cannot help but approve of them as being for the best—exactly as we ourselves would have designed them.

8. And so, in the consideration of *animals*, I do not base my arguments so much on their diversity or their mere survival (though shaping matter into even the basic survival of an animal is the result of a cause that possesses skill and purpose). Rather, what I am aiming at is the exquisite design of their parts, and the fact that their structure is far more perfect than what would be required merely for their bare existence and continuation in the world. This is an undeniable demonstration that they are the effects of wisdom, not the results of luck or fermented matter <note>fermented matter: a reference to the archaic theory of "spontaneous generation," where life was thought to arise naturally from decaying or "fermenting" substances</note>.

Like the *bat* and the *owl*, such people can see nowhere as well as in the shadowy glimmers of their own twilight.

### CHAPTER 1.

*1. Since this era is prone to freeing itself from the influence of superstition, it is a timely moment to try to steer people away from atheism. 2. Those who follow religion in a purely superstitious and habitual way will easily turn to atheism if that connection fails. 3. The usefulness of this present treatise even to those who are sincerely religious.*

1. <image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring intricate floral and vine patterns within a square border.</image-desc> THE great Truth that we are now engaged in proving is: *That there is a God.* I chose this subject because it is very timely for the times we are in and those that are coming. Divine Providence is now more universally loosening the minds of people from the influence and tyranny of purely habitual superstition, and is permitting a freer examination of religious matters than in former ages. Because of this, the Tempter <note>The Tempter: A traditional name for the Devil or Satan.</note> seeks to take advantage where he can, carrying people captive out of one dark prison into another—out of *superstition* into *atheism* itself.

2. This is easy enough for him to accomplish in people who have followed religion in a purely external way, whether for the sake of fashion or out of blind obedience to the authority of a church. When this external structure of godliness breaks down around them, they are revealed to be at heart devoid of the true fear and love of God. They lack a free and unprejudiced use of their faculties <note>original: "faculties"; meaning the natural powers of the mind, such as reason and judgment.</note> due to the sinfulness and corruption of their natures. Consequently, it is easy to entice them to agree with whatever seems to serve their present interests. Emboldened by the tottering and falling of what they previously considered the main structure of religion, they will gladly, in their own minds, cast down the very Object of that religious worship as well. They will conclude that there is no God just as there is no religion; that is, they wish there to be none, so that they may be free from all

...less necessary; but I know for certain that the reader will be more [convinced]. Whatever is separated from established religion and runs away from it is like a wild colt in a pasture that bolts at the sight of a bridle; its behavior is no better than beating the air and making noise, acting however it pleases.

If it is thought that the lives of the <unclear>Saints</unclear> have influenced many—as we are told men are recognized as knights without sharing in [a specific leader's] folly or wickedness—and have appeared in the simple form of a man, it is so that I might, if possible, win them over from outright atheism. 

For he who wants to lend a hand to help another who has fallen into a ditch must—even if he does not fall himself—stoop and bend his body. And he who speaks with a barbarian <note>original: "Barbarian"; here meaning someone who speaks a different language or is considered uncivilized.</note> must speak to him in his own language. Likewise, anyone who wants to win over the weak and fragile minds of worldly <note>original: "sensual"; referring to people focused only on physical senses and material things rather than spiritual matters.</note> mortals must adapt his efforts to their capacity; such people enjoy nothing and find no enlightenment as easily as the flashy glimmers of their own dim understanding <note>original: "Twilight"; used here as a metaphor for the limited, imperfect light of human reason compared to divine revelation.</note>.

### CHAPTER I.

*1. That the tendency of the world in these times to free themselves from the fear of superstition makes this attempt to steer them away from atheism timely. 2. <image-desc>An ornate square woodcut initial 'T' decorated with scrolling foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc> THE great truth which we are now to be engaged with and to prove is, *That there is a God*. I chose this subject as very timely for the times we are in, and those that are approaching, wherein Divine Providence is more generally freeing the minds of men from the fear and tyranny of purely habitual superstition, and allowing a freer examination of matters of religion than in former ages. The Tempter <note>The "Tempter" refers to the Devil or Satan, traditionally viewed as a deceptive force trying to lead souls astray.</note> seeks to take advantage, where he can, to lead men captive out of one dark prison into another—out of *superstition* into *atheism* itself.

2. For when this external structure of godliness collapses around them, they—being at heart truly devoid of the true fear and love of God, and lacking a more free and unbiased use of their faculties <note>original: "Faculties"; referring to the natural powers of the human mind, such as reason and understanding.</note> due to the sinfulness and corruption of their natures—will find it an easy thing to be enticed to agree with whatever seems to serve their current interests. Emboldened by the crumbling and collapse of what they previously took for the main structure of religion, they will, in their arrogance, gladly throw down the very object of that religious worship as well, and conclude that there is no God just as there is no religion. That is, they have a mind that there should be none, so that they may be free from all

### CHAPTER II.

*1. That there is nothing so demonstrable that the human mind can rationally conclude it is impossible for it to be otherwise. 2. That the soul of man may give full assent to something that might possibly be otherwise, illustrated by several examples. 3. A similar example of dissent. 4. The reasons why he has so carefully established this point. 5. That the atheist gains no advantage from the author's free confession that his arguments are not so compelling <term>convictive</term> as to leave no possibility of the thing being otherwise.*

1. **B**ut when I speak of demonstrating that there is a God, I would not want to be suspected of such vanity and boastfulness as to think I mean to bring only those arguments that are so compelling that a person’s understanding is forced to confess it is impossible to be otherwise than I have concluded. For my own part, I am inclined to believe that nothing at all can be demonstrated in that way. For it is possible that *mathematical evidence* itself might be nothing but a constant, undiscoverable delusion to which our nature is necessarily and perpetually liable <note>original: "obnoxious"; in this context meaning vulnerable or subject to.</note>, and that either by fate or by chance, there has been in the world since time immemorial such a being as we call *Man*, whose essential property is to be most mistaken exactly when he conceives a thing to be most evidently true. And why might this not be as true as anything else, if you insist that all things are fated or accidental without a God? For there can be no check on this wild idea except by supposing that we ourselves exist because of some higher principle that is absolutely *good* and *wise*—which is the same thing as acknowledging *that there is a God.*

2. Therefore, when I say that I will demonstrate *that there is a God*, I do not promise that I will always produce such arguments that the reader will find so strong as to be forced to confess that it is utterly impossible for it to be otherwise. Rather, they shall be such as deserve *full assent*, and will *win full assent* from any unbiased mind.

For I believe that we may give *full assent* to something that might, despite our belief, possibly be otherwise. I shall illustrate this with several examples. Suppose two men reached the top of Mount Athos <note>A mountain and peninsula in northeastern Greece, famous in antiquity and later as a center of Eastern Orthodox monasticism.</note>, and while viewing

...viewing a stone in the form of an **altar** with **ashes** on it, and the footprints of **men** on those ashes, or perhaps some words written or scrawled upon the ashes—such as "To the Best and Greatest" <note>original: *Optimo Maximo*, a Latin title often used for Jupiter or God</note>, or "To the Unknown God" <note>original: *τῷ ἀγνώστῳ Θεῷ*, a reference to the altar found by the Apostle Paul in Athens</note>, or the like. Suppose one person should cry out, "Assuredly, some men have been here and done this!" But the other person, being more fastidious <note>original: "nice"</note> than wise, might reply, "No, it is possible it happened otherwise. For this stone may have naturally grown into this very shape, and the seeming ashes may be no ashes at all—that is, not the remains of any fuel burnt there. Instead, some inexplicable and imperceptible motions of the air, or other particles of that fluid matter which is active everywhere, have worked some parts of the matter into the form and nature of ashes. These particles have moved and played about so much that they have also shaped those intelligible **characters** in the same way." But would anyone not deem it a sign of weakness, or even senility, for the first man to retreat from his original conclusion? Would he not agree as fully as ever with what he first stated, despite this bare possibility of it being otherwise?

The same applies to **anchors** that have been dug up, whether in open fields or mountainous places, or **Roman urns** containing ashes and inscriptions such as *Severianus*, *Julius Linus*, and the like; or **Roman coins** with the **images** and **names** of the **Caesars** on them; or, what is even more common, the skulls of men in every churchyard. These skulls have the correct shape and all the necessary openings for the passage of blood vessels, besides those obvious hollows for the eyes and rows of teeth, the **styloid bone** <note>original: *Os Styloeides*</note>, the **ethmoid bone** <note>original: *Ethoeides*</note>, and so on. If a man were to say of these things that the motion of the particles of matter, or some hidden **formative power** <note>original: "spermatic power," a philosophical concept describing a life-force that organizes matter into specific shapes</note> has generated these **anchors, urns, coins**, and **skulls** in the ground, he is only stating something that human reason must admit is *possible*. No man can ever strictly demonstrate that those coins, anchors, and urns were once the craft of men, or that this or that skull was once part of a living human, in a way that forces someone to admit it is *impossible* for it to be otherwise. Yet, I do not think any man—without doing obvious violence to his own mental faculties—can withhold his agreement. He would freely and fully agree that the skull was once part of a living man, and that these anchors, urns, and coins were certainly once made by human skill, despite the theoretical possibility of it being otherwise.

3. And what I have said regarding **agreement** <note>original: "assent"</note> is also true for **disagreement** <note>original: "dissent"</note>. For the human mind—as long as it is not impaired or prejudiced—will fully and irreconcilably disagree through its own natural wisdom, even when no human wit can prove the rejected thing is impossible. For instance, if we were to invent a **fiction** like this: that **Archimedes**, with the same individual body he had when the soldiers killed him, is now safely focused on his geometrical figures underground at the center of the Earth, far from the noise and din of this world that might disturb his meditations or distract him from the intricate drawings he makes with his rod in the dust. No living person can prove this is impossible. Yet, if anyone does not reject such a fable as irreconcilably as they would any imaginable lie, that person is surely close to madness or senility, or is doing great violence to the free use of his faculties.

<meta>This page concludes the author's introductory argument about the nature of certainty. He argues that we can be rationally certain of something even if it is not "demonstrated" with mathematical necessity, provided that the alternative is absurdly improbable.</meta>

Therefore, it is clear that there can be a very firm and unwavering *agreement* or *disagreement* <note>original: "Assent or Dissent"</note>, even though the thing we agree with might possibly be different, or the thing we disagree with cannot be proven to be an absolute impossibility.

4. I have played around with this point for so long and in so many ways to make a better impression on you, the reader. It is of no small importance, both to inform you that the arguments I will provide—though I do not give them the flashy label of *Demonstration* <note>In this context, a "demonstration" refers to a formal logical proof that is considered indisputable.</note>—can still be just as effective at winning a *firm* and *unshaken agreement* as if they were formal proofs in the strictest sense. I also want to remind you that if these arguments are so strong, so perfectly suited, and so irrefutable to the human mind's abilities <note>original: "Faculties"</note> that you have no reply except to say "for all this, it might possibly be otherwise," you should still give a free and full *Assent* to the conclusion. If you do not, you should suspect your own state of mind, prejudice, or weakness, rather than a lack of strength in the arguments.

5. But if the *Atheist* should instead twist my honesty and fairness and imagine he has gained an advantage because I freely confessed that my arguments are not so convictive that they rule out every tiny possibility of the thing being otherwise, let him calculate his supposed gains. He must consider the limits of this "possibility"—namely, that it is no more possible than the idea that the clearest *mathematical evidence* could be false (which is impossible, if our minds are functioning correctly); or, secondly, that the *Roman urns* and *coins* mentioned earlier might turn out to be the work of *Nature* rather than man-made artifacts. Our minds find this so improbable that it is impossible for us not to fully agree with the opposite. When he has finished his calculations, it will be obvious that only his gross ignorance of this kind of logic <note>original: "Arithmetick"</note> would make him bold enough to think he has won the argument.

### CHAP. III.

> 1. *That we must first have a settled idea of what God is before we try to prove that He exists.* 2. *The definition of God.* 3. *That there is an idea of an absolutely perfect Being in our minds, whether the atheist accepts it as the idea of God or not.* 4. *That the natural origin of this idea is not undermined by the fact that it may be triggered by external events.*

1. Now that I have explained these points, I will move closer to my main goal. To do this, I must first define *what God is* before I proceed to prove *that He exists*. For it is natural for human reason to find arguments for the impossibility, possibility, probability, or necessity of a thing's existence by first explaining what its nature <note>original: "Essence"</note> is.

### CHAPTER III. An Antidote against Atheism.

And now that I have reached this point, I ask any *Atheist* who denies there is a God, or anyone who doubts whether there is one or not, what *Idea* or *Notion* they have of the thing they deny or doubt. If they want to be difficult and hesitant <note>original: "nice and squeamish"</note> and claim they can form no *Notion* of such a thing, I would gladly ask them why they would then deny or doubt something when they do not even know what it is. It is necessary for anyone who wants to rationally doubt or deny a thing to have some settled *Notion* of the thing they are doubting or denying. But if they claim that the very reason they deny or doubt God's existence is because they can form no *Notion* of him, I shall immediately take away that claim <note>original: "Allegation"</note> by offering them a *Notion* that is as appropriate to God as any *Notion* is to anything else in the world.

2. I define God, therefore, as: *An Essence or Being that is fully and absolutely Perfect*. I say *fully and absolutely Perfect* to distinguish Him from the kind of *Perfection* that is not *full and absolute*, but rather the perfection of a specific *Species* or *Kind* of *finite Being*—such as a lion, a horse, or a tree. To be *fully and absolutely Perfect* is to be at least as perfect as the human mind can conceive without a contradiction. For whatever is inconceivable or contradictory is nothing at all to us; we are not meant to move a single atom beyond our own mental powers <note>original: "Faculties"</note>. But what I have proposed is so far from being beyond our powers that I dare appeal to any *Atheist* who still has any sense or reason left in him, to say if it is not very easy and understandable at first sight. If there is a God, he must be thought of by us in the way this *Idea* or *Notion* sets forth.

3. But if he stubbornly denies that this is the proper *Notion* of God, let him indulge his own mood. This much still remains undeniable: that there is in man an *Idea* of a *Being absolutely and fully Perfect*, which we construct by attributing every conceivable *Perfection* to it—whatever does not imply a contradiction. *And this Notion is natural and essential to the soul of man; it cannot be washed out, nor taken away by any force or trick of wit, as long as the mind of man is not broken but has the ordinary use of its own powers.*

4. Nor will it matter if someone claims that *this Notion is not natural or essential to the soul because the soul constructed it based on external experiences.* For all those undeniable conclusions in geometry—which might be helped along or triggered by something external—are nonetheless so natural and essential to the soul that you might as well separate the soul from itself <note>original: "unsoul the Soul"</note> as separate it from its constant agreement with those mathematical truths (assuming the soul's powers are not diseased or forced). As an example: the soul cannot help but acknowledge within itself the several *distinct Ideas of the five regular Bodies*, <note>These are the Platonic solids: the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note> as well as the fact that it is impossible for there to be any more than five. And this *Idea of a Being absolutely Perfect* is as distinct and permanent an Idea in the soul as the *Idea of the five regular Bodies*, or any other Idea whatsoever.

It remains, therefore, undeniable that there is an inseparable *Idea of a Being absolutely Perfect* always residing—though not always active—in the soul of man.

### CHAPTER IV.

*1. Which ideas are specifically included in the concept of a Being who is absolutely perfect. 2. That the difficulty of forming a mental concept of something should not be an argument against its existence; the nature of physical matter is so complex and difficult, yet everyone agrees it exists. 3. That the idea of a spirit is as easy to understand as the idea of any other substance. What powers and properties are included in the concept of a spirit. 4. That if God did not exist, eternity and infinity would have to be attributed to something else; therefore, atheism cannot free the mind from these complexities. 5. Goodness, knowledge, and power are ideas of the highest perfection and are therefore necessarily included in the idea of a Being who is absolutely perfect. 6. Also necessity, as it implies a greater perfection than being dependent or accidental <note>original: "Contingency"</note>.*

1. Now, to lay out more specifically the perfections included in this concept of a *Being who is absolutely and fully perfect*, I believe I can safely name these: *self-subsistence* <note>original: "Self-subsistency"; the state of existing by oneself without needing anything else</note>, *immateriality*, *infinity* of both *duration* and *essence*, *immense goodness*, *omniscience* (all-knowing), *omnipotence* (all-powerful), and *necessity of existence*. Therefore, let this be the description of a *Being who is absolutely perfect*: that it is a spirit, eternal, infinite in essence and goodness, omniscient, omnipotent, and necessarily existent of itself. Since all of these are attributes of the highest *perfection* that the human mind can grasp, and since they have no detectable flaws mixed in with them, they must necessarily be attributed to that which we conceive as *absolutely and fully perfect*. If anyone claims that I am just making up a *concept* from my own imagination, which I then sneakily suggest is the concept of a *God*, I reply that no one can discuss or reason about anything without referring to settled concepts within their own mind. Such an objection leads to the most contradictory absurdities imaginable. It is as if a person should try to reason about something that never entered their mind or is completely beyond the reach of their own mental powers. But such groundless claims only show an unwillingness to admit that they can understand God. They show a heavy tendency to sink into a total forgetfulness of him, becoming as dull and mindless regarding divine things as brute animals.

2. Others, perhaps, will not dismiss this concept because it is easily constructed from familiar ideas our minds naturally form. Instead, they might reject it because of certain difficult or "unintelligible" terms within it, such as *spirit*, *eternal*, and *infinite*. They claim they cannot form any concept of a *spirit*, and they say they do not know how to wrap their minds around the idea of something being *eternal* or *infinite*. Because of this, some would argue that there is no such thing as a *spirit* in the world.

But if the difficulty of forming a mental concept of something were enough to disprove

# CHAPTER IV. An Antidote against Atheism

the existence of the thing itself, there would be no such thing as a *Body* left in the world, and then everything would be either *Spirit* or nothing. For who can form such a certain concept of a *Body* that he can free himself from the complications that its *Extension* <note>original: "Extension"; the property of taking up physical space</note> brings along with it? For this extended *Matter* consists of either indivisible points or of particles that can be divided infinitely <note>original: "in infinitum"</note>. Choose whichever of these two you like (and you can find no third option), and you will be tangled in the most obvious absurdities possible. 

For if you say matter consists of points, I can necessarily demonstrate from that position that every *Spear* or *Church Steeple*, or whatever long body you choose, is as thick as it is long; that the tallest *Cedar* tree is no higher than the shortest *Mushroom*; and that the *Moon* and the *Earth* are so near to one another that the thickness of your hand could not fit between them; that *Circles* and *Squares* are the same shape; that *Even and Odd Numbers* are equal to one another; and that the clearest *Day* is as dark as the blackest *Night*. 

And if you choose the other side of the argument, your imagination will be no better off. For nothing can be divided into parts it does not have; therefore, if a *Body* can be divided into infinite parts, it must have infinite extended parts. If it has an infinite number of extended parts, it is a difficult mystery for the human imagination to understand why those infinite extended parts do not add up to one single, infinite *Extension*. In this view, a *grain of mustard seed* would be as infinitely extended as the entire matter of the *Universe*, and a thousandth part of that grain would be as large as the grain itself. 

Such things are more inconceivable than anything found in the *Concept* of a *Spirit*. Therefore, we should not scornfully and contemptuously reject any *Concept* just because it seems at first to be clouded and obscured by some difficulties in how we imagine it. After all, the very thing we feel most sure of—physical matter—is the most entangled and perplexing thing to understand of anything that can be proposed to the human mind. 

But here you will reply that our *Senses* are struck by such obvious impressions from Matter that, even though its nature is difficult to conceive, its *Existence* is obvious to us because of how it acts upon us. Why then, all I ask is this: when you are reminded of certain *Actions* and *Operations* that come to the notice of your senses or understanding—which, unless we do violence to our mental faculties, we can never attribute to *Matter* or *Body*—that you would not be so picky and reluctant to admit the existence of such a substance as a *Spirit*, even though you find some difficulty in imagining it.

3. For my own part, I think the nature of a *Spirit* is as understandable and easy to define as the nature of anything else. As for the very *Essence* or bare *Substance* of anything at all, any beginner in philosophy acknowledges that it is utterly unknowable. However, the *Essential and Inseparable Properties* are just as intelligible and explainable in a *Spirit* as in any other subject. 

For example, I conceive the entire *Idea* of a *Spirit* in general (or at least of all finite, created, and subordinate *Spirits*) to consist of several powers or properties: namely, *Self-penetration* <note>The ability for two spirits, or a spirit and matter, to occupy the same space simultaneously</note>, *Self-motion*, *Self-contraction* and *Expansion* <note>original: "Dilatation"</note>, and *Indivisibility*. These are the properties I consider most absolute. I will also add one that relates to others, which is the power of penetrating...

He concludes by defining the essential properties of a spirit, such as self-motion and indivisibility.</summary>

# An Antidote against Atheism. BOOK I.

...penetrating, moving, and altering matter. These properties and power, when put together, make up the *concept* and *idea* of a *Spirit*. By this, a spirit is clearly distinguished from a *Body*, whose parts cannot pass through one another, is not *self-movable*, and can neither shrink nor expand. A body is divisible and its parts can be separated from one another; but the parts of a *Spirit* can no more be separated—even if they are expanded—than you could cut the *rays* of the *Sun* with a pair of scissors made of transparent <note>original: "pellucid"</note> crystal. This will suffice for establishing the *concept* of a *Spirit*; the proof of its *existence* does not belong in this section. From this description, it is clear that a *Spirit* is a concept of greater *perfection* than a *Body*, and is therefore more suitable as an *attribute* of something absolutely *perfect* than a physical body is.

4. Now, regarding the other two difficult terms, *eternal* and *infinite*: if anyone seeks to excuse themselves from accepting the *concept* of a *God* because these *attributes* are incomprehensible, let them consider that—whether they want to or not—they will be forced to acknowledge that something is *eternal*, whether it be *God* or the *world*. The complexity is the same in either case. And though one might try to avoid the trouble of understanding an *infinite* *Deity*, they will never escape the complications of *infinite space*; that *concept* will stick as closely to the *soul* as its own power of imagination.

5. If a person consults their own reasoning faculties, they will undoubtedly conclude that *goodness*, *knowledge*, and *power* (the three following *attributes*) are *attributes* of *perfection*; indeed, I know of nothing else one could consult. At least this will be accepted as undeniably true: that an absolutely *perfect* *being* possesses these, or possesses something that contains them in a superior way. It is manifest that *knowledge*, or something like it, exists in *God*, because without *awareness* <note>original: "animadversion"; the act of noticing or perceiving</note> in some sense or other, it is impossible to be *happy*. But it is just as impossible for a *being* to be absolutely *perfect* and yet not *happy*. However, *knowledge* without *goodness* is merely dry cleverness or malicious trickery; and *goodness* with *knowledge* but lacking *power* is simply weak and ineffective. Therefore, whatever is absolutely *perfect* is *infinitely* *good*, *wise*, and *powerful*.

6. Lastly, it is a greater *perfection* for all this to be *stable*, *unchanging*, and *necessary*, rather than *accidental* <note>original: "contingent"</note> or merely *possible*. Therefore, the *idea* of an absolutely *perfect* *being* represents to our minds that the subject of that *idea* must *necessarily* exist; and that which by its own nature exists necessarily must never fail to be. Whether the *atheist* chooses to call this absolutely *perfect being* "*God*" or not does not matter; I have no desire to argue over words. But I believe any other person will see at first glance that we have discovered the true *idea* of *God*.

<header>CHAPTER V. An Antidote against Atheism.</header>

## CHAPTER V.

1. *Why various men have imagined that the Soul is a blank slate <note>original: "Abrasa Tabula"</note>. 2. That the Mind of Man is not a blank slate, but has actual knowledge of its own, and in what sense it does so. 3. A further illustration of this truth.*

1. Now that we have identified this *idea* of a *Being who is absolutely Perfect*, it will be helpful—as further preparation for the arguments we will make later—to briefly touch upon a famous point in philosophy: *Whether the human soul is a blank slate* <note>original: "Abrasa Tabula," literally a "scraped tablet"</note>, *a notebook in which nothing is written; or whether it has some innate notions and ideas within itself.* It has happened that because the soul first begins thinking when prompted by external objects, some people have been misled into judging that the soul has no knowledge or concept except what is impressed or drawn upon it in a *passive* way from the objects of our *senses*. They do not distinguish carefully enough between external occasions and the primary causes of things.

2. But the human mind, being more free and better practiced in closely observing its own operations and nature, cannot help but discover that there is an active and actual *knowledge* in a person, for which these outward objects are reminders rather than the first creators or planters. When I say *actual knowledge*, I do not mean that there are a specific number of *ideas* glowing and shining to the *mind's attention* <note>original: "Animadversive Faculty," the power of the soul to turn its attention toward something</note> like so many *torches* or *stars* in the *sky* <note>original: "Firmament"</note> to our physical sight. Nor do I mean that there are any *figures* written there in distinct places as clearly as the *red letters* or *astronomical symbols* in an *almanac*. Instead, I mean an *active wisdom* <note>original: "sagacity"</note> in the soul, or a quick recollection, so to speak, where a small matter being hinted to it causes it to immediately develop a clearer and larger concept.

3. I cannot better describe its condition than this: Suppose a skilled *musician* falls asleep in a field on the grass. During this time, he does not dream at all about his *musical talent*, so that in one sense there is no *actual skill*, concept, or representation of anything musical in him. But his friend, who is sitting by him and cannot sing at all, nudges and wakes him, asking him to sing one song or another, telling him two or three words from the start of the song. Immediately, the musician takes the lead and sings the whole song based on that slight and slender hint. Similarly, the *mind of man*, being nudged and awakened by the impulses of outward objects, is stirred into a fuller and clearer understanding of what was only imperfectly hinted to it by external events. I venture to call this faculty *actual knowledge*, in the same sense that the sleeping musician's skill might be called *actual skill* even when he was not thinking about it.

<summary>The author argues that the human mind is not a blank slate that only receives information from the senses, but possesses innate "actual knowledge" that is triggered and awakened by external experiences.</summary>

# CHAPTER VI.

1. *Various instances showing actual knowledge in the Soul: such as how she has a more accurate Idea of a Circle and Triangle than Matter can show her. 2. And that from one single consideration, she assures herself of the universal property <note>original: "Affection," here meaning a characteristic or attribute</note> of a Triangle. 3. The same argued from the nature of Mathematical and Logical Notions, which do not enter through the Senses, as they are not physical properties <note>original: "affections"</note> of Matter; 4. Because they are produced without any physical motion upon the Matter; 5. And that opposite types may be entirely in one and the same part of Matter at once. 6. That there are certain sure Complex Notions of the Mind for which she was not indebted <note>original: "beholden"</note> to the Senses.*

1. **A**nd that this is the condition of the Soul can be discovered through various observations. For example, present the figure of a *Circle* to the Soul through the outward Senses; she immediately recognizes this to be one kind of *Figure*, and can immediately add that, if it is perfect, all the lines drawn from one central point to the *perimeter* <note>original: "Perimeter"</note> must be exactly equal. In the same way, show her a *Triangle*; she will immediately declare that if it is to be the true figure she aims for, the *Angles* must be closed in indivisible *points*. But this accuracy, in either the *Circle* or the *Triangle*, cannot be found in any material *Object*; therefore, it remains true that she has a more full and perfect knowledge of things within herself than Matter can lay out before her.

2. Let us add a third example: suppose someone demonstrates that this *Triangle* drawn in *Matter* has its three Angles equal to two right angles. "Yes," says the *Soul*, "this is true—and not only for this specific *Triangle*, but for all flat *Triangles* that could possibly be drawn in *Matter*." And thus, you see, the Soul sings the entire song at the first hint, as though she knew it very well before.

3. Beyond this, there are a multitude of *Relative Notions* or *Ideas* in the Mind of Man—both *Mathematical* and *Logical*—which, if we prove they cannot be the impressions of any material Object from the outside, it will necessarily follow that they come from the Soul herself within, and are the natural equipment of human Understanding. These include concepts such as *Cause, Effect, Whole* and *Part, Like* and *Unlike*, and the rest. So too with *Equality* and *Inequality, ratio* <note>original: "λόγος" (logos)</note> and *analogy* <note>original: "ἀναλογία" (analogia)</note>, *Proportion* and *Analogy, Symmetry* and *Asymmetry*, and similar concepts. I shall easily prove that all these *Relative Ideas* are not material impressions made upon the Soul from the outside, but are her own active conceptions proceeding from herself while she takes notice of external Objects. For it is plain that these *Ideas* can make no impression upon the outward Senses because they are not *sensible* or *physical properties* <note>original: "Physical affections"</note> of Matter. And how can that which is not a *physical property* of Matter affect our physical *Organs of Sense?*

But now, it is clear from these two arguments that these *Relative Ideas*, whether *Logical* or *Mathematical*, are not *physical properties of Matter*:

<header>CHAPTER VI. An Antidote against Atheism.</header>

4. [Arguments continued] First, these concepts may be produced when there has been no *physical motion* nor alteration in the subject to which they belong; indeed, they can occur when nothing at all has been done to the subject to which they accrue. For example, suppose one side of a room is whitened while the other is not touched or meddled with. This second side has thus become "unlike" the first, and now has the notion of *dissimilarity* <note>original: "Dissimile"</note> necessarily belonging to it, although nothing at all has been done to it. 

Likewise, suppose you have two pounds of *lead*, which are therefore two *equal* pieces of that metal. If you cut away half from one of them, the other pound—despite nothing at all being done to it—has lost its notion of being *equal* and has acquired a new notion of being *double* the other. It is useless to answer that although nothing was done to this pound of lead, something was done to the other; for that does not at all weaken the argument. Rather, it shows that the notion of being *half* <note>original: "Sub-double"</note>, which was acquired by the lead that had half cut away, is merely our *mode* <note>original: "Mode," meaning a way or manner of thinking</note> of conceiving, just like the other notion. It is not any *physical property* <note>original: "Physical affection"</note> that strikes the physical organs of the body, as hot and cold, *hard* and *soft*, *white* and *black*, and similar qualities do. Therefore, the ideas of *equal* and *unequal*, *double* and *half*, *like* and *unlike*, and the rest, are not external impressions upon the senses, but the soul's own active manner of conceiving those things which are discovered by the outward senses.

5. The second argument is that one and the same part of *matter* is capable, at one and the same time, of holding two entirely contrary *ideas* of this kind. For example, any piece of matter that is a *middle proportional* <note>The middle value in a geometric progression (e.g., in 2, 4, 8, the number 4 is the middle proportional)</note> between two other pieces is, at once, both *double* (compared to one) and *half* <note>original: "Sub-double"</note> (compared to the other), or *triple* and *one-third* <note>original: "Sub-triple"</note> at once. This is a manifest sign that these *ideas* are not properties of the *matter*, and therefore do not affect our senses. If they did, they would also affect the senses of *animals* <note>original: "Beasts"</note>, and they might also become good geometricians and mathematicians. Since these ideas do not affect our senses, it is plain that we have some *ideas* for which we are not indebted to our senses; rather, they are the mere exertions of the mind, occasionally awakened by the stimuli <note>original: "Appulses"</note> of outward objects. Our outward senses no more teach us these ideas than the person who awakened a *musician* to sing taught him his skill.

6. And now, in the third and last place, it is manifest—besides these single *ideas* I have proved to be in the mind—that there are also several complex notions in the same. These include: *The whole is bigger than the part*; *If you take equals from equals, the remainders are equal*; and *Every number is either even or odd*. These are true to the soul at the very first proposal, as anyone in their right mind <note>original: "in his wits"</note> plainly perceives.

<header>An Antidote against Atheism. BOOK I</header>

## CHAPTER VII.

*1. The mind of man is not lacking in innate truth; therefore, we should confidently listen to her natural and unbiased dictates and suggestions. 2. Some notions and truths are, at the very least, naturally and unavoidably accepted by the soul, whether she possesses actual knowledge within herself or not. 3. The definition of an "absolutely perfect being" is one such truth. 4. This absolutely perfect being is God, the creator and designer of all things. 5. The certainty and stability of this idea.*

1. **A**nd now that we see so clearly that the soul is not unequipped to present truth to us, I ask any man: why—under the pretext that the soul has nothing of her own and can be molded to believe anything, or that she randomly and by chance composes the various impressions she receives from the outside—would he still be so hesitant or fearful as to be afraid to trust his own faculties and receive the natural outputs of his own mind as faithful guides?

2. If my argument seems too complex—though it is not—when I claim that the soul possesses conscious knowledge within herself in the way I have explained, then surely this at least will be admitted as true: the soul’s nature is such that she will certainly and fully agree with some conclusions, regardless of how she first learned them, unless she does obvious violence to her own reasoning abilities. These truths must therefore be concluded to be not accidental or arbitrary, but natural to the soul. I have already named some of these, such as: *every finite number is either even or odd*, and *if you add equal things to equal things, the totals are equal*. Others are not quite as simple as these, but they remain just as firmly in the soul once they are understood, such as: *the three angles in a triangle are equal to two right angles* <note>The sum of a triangle's interior angles is 180 degrees.</note>, and *there are exactly five regular bodies, neither more nor less* <note>original: "five regular Bodies." These are the Platonic solids: tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note>, and the like, which we declare to be necessarily true according to the light of nature <note>The "light of nature" refers to innate human reason or the natural ability to perceive truth without divine revelation.</note>.

3. Therefore, let us now return to what we set aside for a moment: the *idea* of an *absolutely perfect being* proposed earlier. This idea is presented in such a way that a person cannot get rid of it, but must acknowledge it as the true *idea* of such a *being*. It follows that this is not an accidental or random thought, but a necessary one; it is therefore natural to the soul, if it is not always consciously present there.

Consequently, it is obvious that when we consult our own natural reason concerning the notion of an *absolutely perfect being*, this inner voice tells us that it is *a spiritual substance, eternal, infinite in essence and goodness, all-powerful, all-knowing, and necessarily existing of its own accord.*

For this answer is such that, if we understand its meaning, we cannot find a way to deny it; therefore, it is true according to the light of nature.

4. But it is obvious that that which exists of its own accord and is infinitely good,

<header>CHAPTER VIII. An Antidote against Atheism.</header>

...**All-knowing** <note>original: "Omniscient"</note> and **All-powerful** <note>original: "Omnipotent"</note>, is the **Root** and **Origin** of all things. For **omnipotence** signifies a power that can achieve anything that does not involve a logical contradiction; and **Creation** implies no such contradiction. Therefore, this **perfect Being** can create all things. But if it found **Matter** or other **Substances** already existing on their own beforehand, then this **Omnipotence** and power of **Creation** would be useless. The free and unbiased faculties of the human **mind** do not accept this; rather, they view it as a **contradiction**. And according to **Natural Light** <note>A common 17th-century term for human reason or innate intellect</note>, a being who is like this should be adored and worshipped by everyone who knows of it, with all humility and thankfulness. And what is this but to acknowledge him as **God**?

5. Therefore, I believe I have sufficiently demonstrated that the **Notion** or **Idea** of **God** is as **natural**, **necessary**, and **essential** to the **Soul** of **Man** as any other notion or idea whatsoever. It is no more **arbitrary** or **fictitious** than the **notion** of a **Cube** or a **Tetrahedron** <note>original: "Tetraedrum"</note>, or any other of the **regular bodies in Geometry**. These are not invented at our own pleasure (for such **fictions** and **fantasies** <note>original: "Chimæras"</note> are infinite); rather, it can be proven that there can be no more than five of them <note>These are the "Platonic Solids": the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron</note>. This shows that their notion is **necessary**, not an **arbitrary assembly** of whatever we please.

And so, having fully established the notion of God—**what He is**—I proceed now to the next point, which is to prove **that He is**.

## CHAPTER VII.

*1. The Mind of Man is not unequipped with Innate Truth, and we should confidently listen to her natural and unbiased dictates and suggestions. 2. <header>CHAPTER VIII. An Antidote against Atheism.</header>

*All-knowing* and *All-powerful*, is the *Root* and *Origin* of all things. For *Omnipotence* <note>original: "Omnipotency"</note> signifies a power that can accomplish anything that does not involve a contradiction; and *Creation* involves no contradiction. But if it found Matter or other substances existing beforehand on their own, this *Omnipotence* would not belong to this absolutely *All-powerful Being*; a concept which the free and unbiased faculties of the human mind do not accept, but rather look upon as a contradiction. Therefore, the natural concept of a *Being absolutely Perfect* implies that this same *Being* is *Lord* and *Maker* of all things. And according to *Natural Light* <note>The innate spark of human reason.</note>, that which is so must be adored and worshipped by everyone who has knowledge of it, with all humility and thankfulness. And what is this but to be acknowledged as *God*?

5. Therefore, I believe I have sufficiently demonstrated that the Notion or Idea of *God* is as *natural*, *necessary*, and *essential* to the Soul of Man as any other *Notion* or *Idea* whatsoever. It is no more *arbitrary* or *fictitious* than the notion of a *Cube* or *Tetrahedron* <note>original: "Tetraedrum"</note>, or any other of the *Regular Solids* <note>original: "Regular Bodies"; these are the five Platonic solids in geometry.</note> in Geometry. These are not devised at our own pleasure (for such *imaginary creations* and *fantasies* <note>original: "Figments and Chimeras"</note> are infinite), but for these geometric shapes, it can be proven that there can be no more than *five* of them. This shows that their concept is necessary, not an arbitrary assembly of whatever we please.

And thus, having fully established the Concept of *God*—*What he is*—I proceed now to the next point, which is to prove *That he is*.

<header>An Antidote against Atheism. BOOK I.</header>

...thing to reject the *Being of God* because he does not immediately fall under the *Senses* is just as irrational as rejecting the *existence of Matter* because it is so incomprehensible to the *Imagination* <note>original: "Phansy"; in this period, the "fancy" or "phantasy" was the faculty of the mind that handled sensory images.</note>. 14. The biased whimsy <note>original: "factious Humoursomeness"</note> of the *Atheist* who sides with certain *faculties of the soul* while rejecting others, even though they are all equally qualified *judges*.

1. **AND** now, truly, as I look upon the true *Idea* of God which we have discovered, I seem to have ventured further into this matter than I first realized. For if this *Idea* or *Concept* <note>original: "Notion"</note> of God is true—as I have undeniably proved—it is also undeniably true that He exists. This *Idea* of God is no arbitrary invention <note>original: "Figment"</note> created for our own pleasure; rather, it is the necessary and natural outpouring of the human mind. If this idea signals to us that the nature of God implies *necessary existence* (as we have shown it does), then unless we choose to ignore our own natural reason <note>original: "wink against our own natural Light"</note>, we must acknowledge without any further doubt that *God does exist*.

2. Nor is it a sufficient reason to doubt <note>original: "diffide"</note> the strength of this argument simply because our imagination can sneak in this counter-argument <note>original: "Abater"</note>: namely, that while this *Idea of God* shows us that His existence *would be* necessary if He existed, it does not prove that He *actually* exists. Anyone who answers this way fails to see the prejudice that allows them to make such a claim. They are so accustomed to imagining the nature or concept of every other thing without its *existence*—easily separating *Essence* (what a thing is) and *Existence* (that a thing is) in their minds—that they unknowingly take the same liberty here. They attempt to divide *existence* from that very *Essence* to which *existence* itself is essential. This is the clever fallacy in which their own carelessness has entangled them.

3. Furthermore, when we argue that the true *Idea* of God represents Him as a *Being that must necessarily exist*, and therefore that He does exist, you create a manifest contradiction by replying, "If He existed at all." By this answer, you contradict yourself. First, you agree with us that the nature of God is such that His very concept implies *Necessary Existence*; but then you take it back by suggesting that despite this true *Idea* and *Concept*, God might not exist. You are essentially acknowledging that something which is *absolutely necessary* according to the natural expression of our mental faculties might still be otherwise. This is a clear contradiction regarding our own faculties, and we have nothing more internal or immediate than these to guide ourselves by.

4. To make this even clearer, if not stronger: when we say that the *Existence of God* is *Necessary*, we must recognize that *Necessity* is a *Logical Term*. It signifies such a firm connection between the *Subject* and *Predicate* (as logicians call them) that it is impossible for them to be separated or fail to hold together. Therefore, if one is affirmed of the other, they create a *Necessary Axiom* <note>original: "Axioma Necessarium"</note>—an axiom that is necessarily and eternally true. Since there is a *Necessary Connection* between *God* and *Existence*, this statement—*God exists*—is an axiom that is *necessarily* and *eternally true*. We shall make this even clearer...

<header>Chap. VIII. An Antidote against Atheism.</header>

...understand, if we compare *Necessity* and *Contingency* together. For as *Contingency* signifies not only the *manner of existence* in that which is *contingent* according to its *idea*, but also indicates a *possibility of actual existence*; so (to make the analogy true and easy) *Necessity* does not only signify the *manner of existence* in that which is *necessary*, but also that it *actually exists*, and could never possibly do otherwise. For "to be necessary" <note>original: "ἀναγκαῖον εἶναι"</note> and "to be impossible not to be" <note>original: "ἀδύνατον μὴ εἶναι"</note> are one and the same according to *Aristotle* and the rest of the *logicians*. But the *atheist* and the *enthusiast* <note>original: "Enthusiast"; in this period, an "enthusiast" was someone who claimed direct divine inspiration, often viewed as irrational or delusional</note> are usually such declared enemies of *logic*. The one acts merely out of a foolish obsession with outward, physical senses; the other out of a deep devotion to his stubborn and untamed imagination <note>original: "Phansy"</note>—that workshop of mysteries and fine things.

5. Thirdly, we may further add that while we must attribute to the *idea* of God either *contingency*, *impossibility*, or *necessity of actual existence* (since one of these must belong to every *idea* imaginable), we find that *contingency* is incompatible with an *idea* of a *being absolutely perfect*. Much more so is *impossibility* incompatible, as the *idea* of God is composed of no notions except those that are possible according to the *light of nature* to which we now appeal. It remains, therefore, that *necessity of actual existence* is unavoidably assigned to the *idea* of God, and therefore God does actually exist.

6. But fourthly and lastly, if this seems too subtle—though it is no less true for being so—I shall now propose something so obvious that it is impossible for anyone in their right mind to deny it. I say, therefore, that either *God*, or this *physical* and *perceptible world*, must necessarily exist of itself. Or to put it this way: *Either God, or matter, or both*, necessarily exist of themselves. *If both*, we have reached our goal: the *existence of God*.

7. Yet, to acknowledge the necessary *existence* of *matter* by itself is not consistent with or suitable to the *light of nature*. For if anything can exist *independently* of God, then all things can. If that were so, not only might the omnipotence of God be in vain, but moreover, it would allow for all imaginable confusion and disorder. Indeed, it would allow for some great devil of equal power and as large a command as *God* himself—or, if you prefer, six thousand million such monstrous, gigantic spirits, filled with various and mischievous passions as well as armed with immense power. These spirits, appearing in huge shapes out of anger or whim, might grab the planets in their massive clutches and pelt one another with them, just as boys are accustomed to do with snowballs. That this has not yet happened would be due only to the fact that the whim has not yet struck them; yet the frame of nature and the creation of things would still be constantly vulnerable to such ruin and disorder. It is a dangerous thing to ignore the *natural dependencies* and *relationships* of our *innate ideas* and *concepts*.

Therefore, to deny to **God** what is so *necessarily* included in the true *idea* of Him, and to attribute it to something whose *idea* does not contain it at all (for *necessary existence* is not contained in the *idea* of anything except a *Being who is absolutely perfect*), is to speak against our *natural light* and to do clear violence to our own mental faculties.

I have already abundantly proved that there is other knowledge and perception in the soul besides that of the *senses*. Therefore, it is very unreasonable—since we have other faculties of knowledge besides the *senses*—to consult only the *senses* on matters of knowledge and exclude those faculties that penetrate beyond what we can see and touch.
