# CHAPTER VIII. An Antidote against Atheism.

...demonstrated) it is as inconsistent <note>original: "incongruous"</note> to deny there is a ***God*** because ***God*** is not an object perceived by the ***senses***, as it would be to deny there is ***matter*** or a ***body*** because that ***body*** or ***matter***, in our mental concept of it, seems so messy and difficult for our ***imagination*** <note>original: "Phansy"</note> and ***reason***.

In the contemplation of matter, our understanding discovers such contradictory inconsistencies that, were it not for the fact that the ***concept*** is supported by the confident evidence of our ***senses***, ***reason***—appealing to those coarser representations of the ***imagination***—would be able to use clever arguments to prove it does not exist at all. But our ***reason*** is well aware that ***physical matter*** is the proper object of our ***senses***; therefore, she fully believes the information provided by the ***senses*** in their own sphere, ignoring the puzzling objections of a muddled ***imagination***. She freely admits the existence of ***matter***, despite the complications of the ***imagination***, just as she also admits the existence of ***God*** from the contemplation of His ***idea*** in our soul, despite the silence of the ***senses*** regarding Him.

14. Indeed, it would be an inexcusable piece of folly and madness for a man to do otherwise. He has ***cognitive faculties*** <note>original: "Cognoscitive Faculties," the mental powers used for gaining knowledge</note> capable of reaching the knowledge of ***God***, and he has a certain and unchangeable ***idea*** of ***God*** in his soul which he can by no means erase. He also has sensory knowledge that leads to the discovery of ***matter***. It is foolish, therefore, to grant necessary ***self-existence*** to ***matter*** (when no mental faculty tells him it is so) while taking necessary ***existence*** away from ***God*** (even though the natural ***concept*** of ***God*** in the soul informs him to the contrary). To do this simply because ***God*** does not immediately fall under the knowledge of the ***senses*** is to unfairly side with only one faculty of the soul while outlawing <note>original: "proscribing"</note> all the rest.

This is as temperamental <note>original: "humour-somely," meaning acting out of a whim or mood rather than reason</note> and foolish as if a man should create a faction among the ***senses*** themselves and resolve to believe nothing exists except what he could see with his ***eyes***. He might then confidently pronounce that there is no such thing as the element of ***air***, nor ***winds***, nor ***music***, nor ***thunder***. And his reason, forsooth, would be because he can see none of these things with his ***eyes***, and that is the only ***sense*** he intends to believe.

<header>An Antidote against Atheism. Book I.</header>

## CHAPTER IX.

1. *The existence of God argued from the final cause <note>original: "Finall cause," the ultimate purpose or goal for which something exists</note> of the implantation of the Idea of God in the soul. 2. An evasion of the argument, by supposing all things to be such as they are by chance. 3. That the evasion is either impossible, or but barely possible, and therefore of no weight. 4. That we are not to attend to what is simply possible, but to what our natural faculties determine. 5. He urges therefore again the final cause of the indelible <note>original: "indeleble," permanent or impossible to erase</note> idea or image of God in the soul, illustrating its force from an analogy. 6. That supposing God did exist, he would have dealt no otherwise with us for the making himself known unto us than we are in fact <note>original: "de facto"</note> dealt with; which therefore again argues that He does exist.*

1. Up to this point, I have argued from the natural *notion* or *idea* of God as it relates to that which it represents. I shall now try to see what advantage may be gained by looking at how it relates to our *souls*—the *subject* in which this idea resides. I ask, therefore: who put this indelible character of God upon our souls? Why, and for what purpose, is it there?

2. Do not think to brush me off by saying, "We must take things as we find them, and not inquire into the final cause of anything." This argument suggests that things are necessarily as they are of themselves; that their guidance and design comes from no principle of wisdom or counsel, but every substance is now, and ever was, of whatever nature and capacity it is found, having its origin from nothing other than itself. It suggests that all those changes and varieties we see in the world are merely the result of an "eternal scuffle" of equal causes, holding up as well as they can to continue themselves in the state they are in. By acting and being acted upon by others, these varieties of things appear in the world, but every particular substance with its essential properties is self-originated and independent of any other.

3. To this I answer: the very best that can be made of all this is only that it is merely and barely *possible*. In fact, if we consult our own faculties and the *idea of God*, it is utterly impossible. But even if we admit it is possible, this bare *possibility* is so loose, so weak, and so indeterminate a consideration that it ought to have no power to move a mind that has any tolerable use of its own reason. It should have no more power than the faint breath of a light breeze has to shake a mountain of brass. For if bare *possibility* may at all trap our *belief* or *disbelief* in things, we cannot fully disbelieve even the most absurd fables in *Aesop* or *Ovid*, or the most ridiculous fictions that can be imagined. No one can fully disbelieve any of these absurdities if mere *possibility* is allowed the slightest power to tip the scales one way or the other. For none of these scenarios—nor a thousand more like them—imply a perfect and obvious contradiction; therefore, they will all try to claim their right to be considered *possible*.

4. But we are not to focus on what is simply *possible*, but on what our *natural faculties* <note>original: "Natural Faculties," our inherent abilities of reason, perception, and intuition</note> direct and lead us toward. For example, suppose the question were, *whether the stones in the street have senses or not*. We should not leave the point as indifferent—as if it could be argued either way—just because it is *possible* and implies no obvious contradiction that they might have *senses*, even a painful *sense*. Instead, we are to consult our *natural faculties* and see which way they lean. They plainly settle the controversy by telling us that whatever has *senses* and is capable of *pain* ought to also have the power of progressive *motion*, so it can avoid what is harmful and painful. We see this is true in all beings that possess any significant degree of *sense*. And *Aristotle*, who was no great devotee of a *deity*, yet frequently assumes this principle: "Nature does nothing in vain" <note>original Greek: Ἡ φύσις οὐδὲν μάτην ποιεῖ (*Hē physis ouden matēn poiei*)</note>. This is either an acknowledgment of a *God* or an appeal to our own *rational faculties*; I am indifferent as to which, for I gain what I want from either. For if we appeal to the natural suggestions of our own faculties, they will assuredly tell us *there is a God*.

5. I therefore ask again—and I desire to be answered without prejudice or any restraint laid upon our natural faculties—to what purpose is this *indelible image* or *idea* of God in us, if there is no such thing as *God* existing in the world? Or who stamped so deep an impression of that *character* <note>original: "Character," used here in the sense of a distinctive mark, stamp, or written letter</note> upon our minds?

<margin>* See the previous Chapter, Sections 7, 8, 9.</margin>

If we were traveling in a desolate *wilderness* where we could find neither man nor house, and we should come across *herds of cattle* or *flocks of sheep* with certain *marks* or *letters* branded on their bodies, we would conclude without any hesitation that these animals have all been under the hand of some man who has set his name upon them. Truly, when we see written in our souls in such legible characters the *Name*—or rather the *Nature* and *Idea*—of God, why should we be so slow and hesitant to make the same reasonable inference? Assuredly, he whose *mark* is signed upon our souls has been here and has marked us this way so that we and all others may know to whom we belong: *that it is he who has made us, and not we ourselves; that we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture* <note>A reference to Psalm 100:3</note>. And it is evidently plain from the *idea* of God, which includes omnipotence <note>original: "omnipotency," all-powerfulness</note> within it, that we can be made by no one other than him, as I have * demonstrated previously. Therefore, there was no better way to make us acknowledge ourselves as his than by sealing us with this *image*, and to lead us to perform that *worship* and *adoration* to him that is due to our mighty Maker and Creator—that is, to our *God*.

Therefore, since these things align so naturally and easily according to the free suggestions of our *natural faculties*, it is as stubborn and forced an act to withhold our agreement as it would be to doubt whether those *Roman urns* and *coins* I spoke of, dug out of the earth, were the works of nature or the craftsmanship of men.

6. But if we still cannot fully agree with the position *that God exists*, let us at least be patient enough to entertain the idea for a moment. I ask, therefore: assuming God *did* exist, what could the human mind imagine that he would do better or more effectively to make himself known to a creature like man—endowed as we are with specific mental abilities—than what we find has already been done? Since God is an *infinite spirit*, he cannot ever be fully or necessarily made known through appearances to our outward *senses*. For if he were to show himself in any outward figures or shapes—signaling love, wrath, terror, or protection—our faculties could not assure us that this was *God*. It might instead be some specific *spirit* <note>original: "Genius"—referring here to a lesser supernatural entity or guardian spirit</note>, whether good or evil. Furthermore, such dazzling and frightening external displays are neither becoming of the divine nature nor suitable for the condition of the human soul. God interacts with our higher and more free faculties; he does not force or overwhelm us by applying a cruder and more oppressive power upon our weak and animal-like *senses*. What remains, then, but that he should manifest himself to our *inward man*? <note>the soul or internal rational mind, as opposed to the physical body</note> And what way is more fit than the indelible impression of the *idea* of himself? This is not a "divine life and sense" (for that is a higher prize reserved for those who can win it), but a natural representation of the Godhead and a concept of his *essence*. Through this, the human soul could conceive of him in no other way than as an *eternal spirit*, *infinite in goodness*, *omnipotent*, *omniscient*, and *necessarily existing of himself*. As I have fully proved, we find this is done in us *in fact* <note>original: "de facto"</note>. Therefore, since we are treated in every way as if there were an *existing* God, and no *faculty* of ours discovers anything to the contrary, what should hinder us from concluding that he really *does exist*?

### Chapter X. An Antidote against Atheism.

1. We may observe certain traits that cling very closely to human nature, such as a **natural remorse of conscience**, and a fear and disturbance arising from committing acts that are not even punishable by human laws. There is also a **natural hope** of being prosperous and successful when doing things we believe to be good and righteous. Finally, there is **religious veneration**, or **divine worship**. All of these are fruits that grow easily and naturally out of the nature of man; and if we rightly understand their meaning, they all indicate **that there is a God**.

2. First, regarding **natural conscience**: it is clearly a fear and confusion of mind arising from the foreboding of some harm that may befall a person outside the ordinary course of nature or the usual occurrence of affairs, simply because he has done this or that. This does not mean that something supernatural or absolutely extraordinary must necessarily happen to him, but rather that he fears the ordinary calamities and misfortunes of the world will be directed and aimed at him eventually, because he has acted against his **conscience**. In times of heavy **adversity**, a mighty **tempest** at sea, or dreadful **thunder** on land (even though these arise from natural causes), people naturally reflect upon themselves and their actions. They are either overcome with fear or remain unafraid, depending on whether they condemn or acquit themselves in their own **consciences**. From this assumption comes that magnificent expression of the poet concerning the just man:

> *Nor the great hand of thundering Jove,* <note>original: "Nec fulminantis magna Jovis manus"—a reference to Horace’s Odes, describing a man of integrity who does not fear the wrath of the gods or nature.</note>

meaning that he is not afraid of the striking down of thunder and lightning from heaven. This **fear**—that one person should be struck rather than another, or at this specific time rather than another, because of his past actions—is a natural acknowledgment that these events are guided and directed by some discerning Principle. This is the same as confessing **that there is a God**. It does not matter that some argue that sailors curse and swear the loudest when a storm is at its peak; this is because the frequency of such dangers has caused them to lose their sense of the danger, not their sense of a God.

3. It is also very natural for a person who honestly follows the dictates of their own **conscience** to be full of **hope**, ease, and a sense of security that all things at home and abroad will go successfully. This is true even though their actions or sincere thoughts have no physical power to change the course of the world or nature. Therefore, this implies there is a **Superintendent Principle** <note>a higher governing power or intelligence</note> over nature and the material frame of the world. This Principle ensures that nothing happens except what is consistent with the good and welfare of honest and conscientious people. And if things do not happen according to their expectations in this world, this natural hope leads to a belief in a world to come.

4. The strength of this argument is not weakened by the fact that some people have lost the sense of the difference between **good** and **evil** (if indeed anyone is so fully degenerate). If such a person exists, he is a monster, and I suspect he is a monster of his own making. But this does not undermine my goal, which is to argue from the **natural constitution** of man for the **existence**

There is no nation under the canopy <note>original: "cope"</note> of heaven that does not perform divine worship to something or other, and in doing so, to God as they conceive Him. Therefore, according to the ordinary **natural light** <term>Natural light: the innate human capacity for reason and moral understanding, independent of divine revelation.</term> that is in all men, there is a God.

6. Nor can the force of this argument be avoided by saying it is merely a universal **tradition** that has been spread among the nations of the world since time immemorial. For if it were so (which cannot be proved at all), the fact that it is universally received makes it manifest that acknowledging a God is according to the **light of nature**. That which all men admit as true, even when proposed by another, is undoubtedly to be termed true according to the **light of nature**. 

For example, many hundreds of **geometrical demonstrations**, which were first the inventions of a single man, have passed undeniably through all ages and places as true according to the **light of nature** for those who were merely learners, not inventors, of them. It is sufficient to make a thing true according to the **light of nature** if no man, upon perceiving what is proposed and the reasons for it (if it is not clear at first sight and needs reasons to back it), will ever hesitate to acknowledge it as a truth. Therefore, if there were any nations destitute of the knowledge of a **God**—just as they might be, likely, of the rudiments of **geometry**—so long as they will admit the knowledge of the one as well as the other upon proper proposal, the acknowledgment of a **God** is just as much according to the **light of nature** as the knowledge of **geometry** which they receive in this way.

7. But even if it did not stand still, this does not apply to our case. This is merely the victory of **reason** over the general prejudice of the **senses**. Everyone will acknowledge that **reason** may correct...

But there is no faculty that can be claimed to clash with the judgment of **reason** and **natural sagacity** <term>Natural sagacity: innate human wisdom or the ability to perceive truth through reason.</term>, which so easily either concludes or predicts that there is a God. Therefore, that may well pass for a truth according to the **light of nature** that is universally received by men, by whatever faculty they receive it, since no other faculty appears to provide evidence to the contrary. And such is the **universal acknowledgment that there is a God.**

8. Nor is it much more important to reply that, though there is indeed a **religious worship** practiced in all nations upon the face of the Earth, yet many of them worship only **stocks and stones** <note>original: "stocks and stones"—a traditional phrase referring to wooden and stone idols or inanimate objects.</note>, or some particular piece of nature like the **Sun, Moon,** or **Stars**. For I answer that, first, it is very hard to prove that they worship any image or statue without reference to some spirit at least, if not to the Omnipotent God. So we shall at least gain this much: that there are in the universe some more subtle and **immaterial substances** that take notice of the affairs of men. This is as troublesome to a slow-witted atheist as believing that **there is a God.**

And as for the **adoration** some of them give to the **Sun** and **Moon**, I cannot believe they do it to them as mere **inanimate bodies**. Rather, they take them to be the home of some **intellectual beings**, as the verse plainly suggests to us:

-> The Sun, who sees all and hears all: <-
<note>original Greek: Ἠέλιός θ’ ὃς πάντ’ ἐφορᾷ καὶ πάντ’ ἐπακούει</note>

And this is very near the true notion of a **God**.

9. But whatever this **universal religious worship** may be—as absurd as you please to imagine it—it will still go very far in proving the existence of a **Deity**. For there are no **natural faculties** in things that do not have their **object** in the world; just as there is **food** as well as **mouths**, **sounds** as well as **hearing**, **colors** as well as **sight**, **dangers** as well as **fear**, and the like. So, in the same way, there ought to be a **God** as well as a **natural inclination** in men toward **religious worship**, God alone being the proper **object** of it.

The strength of this argument is not weakened by the fact that this deeply-rooted property of **religion** in man (which cannot be lost) displays itself so poorly and ridiculously in mankind.

For just as the moving of a **dog's** feet in his sleep—as if there were some game before him—and the butting of a young **lamb** before he has either horns or enemies to encounter, would not exist in nature if there were not such a thing as a **hare** to be chased or a **horned enemy** to be fought with horns; so there would not be such a **universal** exercise of **religious worship** in the world, even if it is done poorly and foolishly, if there were not really a proper **object** of this **worship**, and a capacity in man for the right performance of it. This could not be unless there were a God.

<summary>The author argues that the universal human instinct for worship, even when misdirected toward idols or nature, proves the existence of a divine object (God), just as physical senses and animal instincts correspond to real-world objects.</summary>

But the truth is, the human soul, in this drunken, drowsy condition she is in, has fallen asleep in the body. Like someone in a dream, she talks to bed-posts and embraces her pillow instead of her friend; she falls down before statues instead of adoring the eternal and invisible God, and prays to wood and stone <note>original: "stocks and stones"</note> instead of speaking to Him who by His Word created all things.

10. But you will reply that a young *lamb* eventually has both his weapon and *enemy* to encounter, and the dreaming *dog* once did and may again pursue real game; and so he that talks in his sleep once conversed with men while awake, and may do so once again. However, entire nations for many successive generations have been very stupid idolaters, and remain so to this day. But I answer that this rather informs us of another great mystery, rather than weakening the present argument at all or obscuring the grand truth for which we strive. For this plainly suggests this much: that mankind is in a lapsed <note>lapsed: fallen or degraded from a superior spiritual state</note> condition, like someone who has fallen down in an *epileptic* fit. By the force of the convulsion, their limbs are moved very clumsily and awkwardly; but we know that the person who currently moves the members of his body so rudely and randomly did previously command the use of his muscles in a graceful exercise of his ability to move, and that when the fit is over, he will do so again.

This therefore implies that these poor, barbarous souls once had the true knowledge of *God* and of His *worship*, and by some hidden Providence <note>Providence: divine guidance or care</note> may be recovered into it again, rather than that this inclination toward *religious worship*, which appears so conspicuously in them, should be utterly in vain—as it would be, both in them and in all other men, if there were no *God*.

### CHAPTER XI. An Antidote against Atheism.

*10. [Ani]mal Spirits and the Body; 11. And therefore is a Substance Incorporeal. 12. The discovery of the Essence of the Soul, of what great usefulness for the easier conceiving the nature of God. 13. And how there may be an Eternal Mind that has both Understanding and power of Moving the Matter of the Universe.*

---

1. We have finished with all those more obvious faculties in the soul of man that naturally tend toward the discovery of the existence of a God. Let us briefly, before we lose ourselves and launch out into the vast ocean of the *external phenomena of nature*, consider the *essence of the soul* herself—what it is, whether it is a mere modification <note>modification: a specific form, state, or property of a physical thing</note> of the body, or a *substance distinct* from it; and then whether it is *corporeal* <note>corporeal: physical or material</note> or *incorporeal* <note>incorporeal: non-physical or spiritual</note>. For by clearing up this point, we may perhaps be convinced that there is a *spiritual substance* really distinct from *matter*; and whoever acknowledges this will be more easily persuaded to believe there is a God.

2. First, therefore, if we say that the *soul* is a mere *modification of the body*, then the *soul* is only one universal faculty of the body, or many faculties put together; and those operations which are usually attributed to the *soul* must, of necessity, be attributed to the *body*. I ask, therefore: to what in the body will you attribute *spontaneous motion* <note>spontaneous motion: voluntary or self-directed movement</note>? By this, I mean a power within ourselves of moving or holding still most of the parts of our body—for example, our hand or little finger. If you say that it is nothing but the release of the *spirits* <note>original: "animal spirits"; in early modern science, these were thought to be extremely fine fluids that moved through the nerves to cause sensation and motion</note> into such and such *muscles*, I would gladly know what *releases* these *spirits* and *directs* them so precisely? Is it *themselves*, or the *brain*, or that particular piece of the brain they call the *conarion* <note>conarion: the pineal gland, which many thinkers of this era believed was the seat of the soul</note> or *pineal gland*? Whatever it is, that which thus *releases* and *directs* them must have *conscious awareness* <note>original: "animadversion"; the act of perceiving or attending to something</note>, and whatever has *conscious awareness* also has *memory* and *reason*. Now, I would like to know whether the *spirits themselves* are capable of *awareness*, *memory*, and *reason*; for indeed, it seems altogether impossible. For these *animal spirits* are nothing else but very thin and liquid matter, whose nature consists in this: that all its particles are in motion and, being loose from one another, shift and play up and down according to the degree and manner of their agitation.

3. I therefore now ask: which of the particles in these many loosely moving parts has *awareness* in it? If you say that they all have it when put together, I appeal to the person who answers this way: how unlikely is it that something so utterly incapable of *memory*, and consequently of *reason*, should have *awareness*? For it is as impossible to imagine *memory* belonging to such a subject as it is to imagine how one might write characters <note>characters: letters or symbols</note> in the water or in the wind.

4. If you say the *brain releases* and *directs* these *spirits*, how can that which has no *muscles* move itself or another thing so freely and spontaneously? Besides, *anatomists* tell us that although the *brain* is the instrument of sense, it has no sensation at all in itself. How then can that which has no sensation spontaneously and arbitrarily direct the *animal spirits* into any part of the body? Such an act plainly requires specific sensation and perception.

# An Antidote against Atheism. BOOK I.

perception. But let the *anatomists* conclude what they will, I think I shall demonstrate almost clearly that the *brain has no sense*. For the same thing in us that has *sense* also has *perception* <note>original: "animadversion"; the act of the mind turning its attention toward something</note>; and that which has *perception* in us also has a faculty of free and arbitrary *imagination* <note>original: "phansy"</note> and *reason*.

5. Let us now consider the nature of the *brain* and see how compatible those operations and powers are to such a subject. Truly, if we take a right view of this loose pith or marrow in a man's head, neither our sense nor understanding can discover anything more in this substance—which might claim such noble operations as *free imagination* and the wise gathering of *reason*—than we can discern in a cake of *suet* <note>original: "sewet"; animal fat used in cooking</note> or a bowl of curds. For this loose pulp that is thus wrapped up within our *skull* <note>original: "cranium"</note> is but a spongy and porous body, permeable not only to the *animal spirits* <note>animal spirits: in 17th-century physiology, these were thought to be very fine, subtle fluids that traveled through nerves to cause movement and sensation</note>, but also to thicker juice and liquid. Otherwise, it could not be well-nourished; at least, it could not be so softened and moistened by drunkenness and excess as to make the understanding unfit and foolish in its operations.

Therefore, I now ask: in this soft substance which we call the *brain*—whose softness implies that it is in some measure *liquid*, and liquidity implies a separate *motion* of loose parts—in what part or portion of it do *imagination*, *reason*, and *perception* lie? In this loose consistency that lies like a net in heaps in the water, I ask: in what knot, loop, or space does this faculty of free *imagination* and active *reason* reside? I believe you would be ashamed to assign me any one part in particular.

And if you say *in all of them together*, you must say that the whole *brain* is shaped into this or that representation, which would erase *memory* and take away all capacity for there being any distinct marks and places for the various *types* <note>original: "species"; here meaning the mental images or forms of things</note> of things represented there.

But if you say there is in *every part* of the brain this power of *perception* and *imagination*, you must remember that the *brain* is, to some extent, *a liquid body*. We must then ask how these loose parts understand each other's various *perceptions* and *notions*. And even if they could (which is still very hard to imagine), and if they could then do anything toward the *sending out* and *directing* of the *animal spirits* into this or that part of the body, we must consider that they would have to do it (after knowing one another's minds) as if by a joint effort of strength. It would be like many men lifting or pulling together at a signal to move a body so massive that the single strength of one person could not handle it. But this is to make the various particles of the *brain* into so many *individual persons*—a better subject for laughter than for even the slightest belief.

6. Besides, how do these many *perceptions* seem like only *one* to us, if our *mind* consists of all of them? Or rather, why, if the shape of *one* part of the *brain* is communicated to all the rest, does not the same *object* seem to be located both behind us and before us, above and beneath, on the right hand and on the left—and in every direction—as the impression of the *object* is reflected against all parts of the *brain*? ->### CHAP. XI. An Antidote against Atheism.<-

...appearing to us as **but one perception** <note>original: "Animadversion"; the act of the mind turning its attention toward something</note>, or as but one view of things, it is a sufficient argument that there is **but one** perceiver. Or, if there are many perceivers, it is clear that they do not communicate with one another across the different parts of the brain, and therefore there can be no such joint effort toward a single design. From this, it is manifest that the brains cannot emit or direct these **animal spirits** into whichever part of the body they please.

7. Moreover, there is a strong argument that the **brain has no sense**, and therefore cannot spontaneously impress any motion on the **animal spirits**. This is shown by the fact that some people, when dissected, have been found **without brains**. **Fontanus** <note>original: "Fontanus"; likely Nicholas Fontanus, a 17th-century Dutch physician</note> tells us of a boy in **Amsterdam** who had nothing but clear water in his head instead of **brains**. Generally, the **brains** are easily dissolved into a watery consistency, which agrees with what I suggested before. Now I appeal to any unbiased judge: how likely is it that these **liquid** particles have the nature and power to organize and join themselves together for a moment of time, acting with a single united strength to cause a voluntary dispatching <note>original: "ablegation"</note> of the **spirits** into this or that specific part of the body? I have already sufficiently hinted at the absurdity of this idea.

Lastly, the **nerves**—meaning the "marrow" or inner core of them, which is made of the very same substance as the **brain**—have **no sense**, as can be proven from cases of **catalepsy** or **catochus** <note>original: "Catalepsis" or "Catochus"; medical conditions characterized by a trance-like state and loss of sensation or voluntary motion</note>. But I will not pile up arguments in a matter that is so obvious.

8. As for that little protruding piece of the **brain** which they call the **pineal gland** <note>original: "Conarion"; the pineal gland, which René Descartes famously proposed as the seat of the soul</note>: the idea that this should be the very substance whose natural faculty is to move itself, and by its motions and nods to determine the course of the **spirits** into this or that part of the body, seems to me no less foolish and fabulous than the story of the man who could change the wind as he pleased by setting his cap on one side of his head or the other.

If you heard only the magnificent stories told about this little, hidden "mushroom"—how it not only hears and sees, but imagines, reasons, and commands the whole structure of the body more skillfully than an **Indian** boy directs an **elephant**; what an acute **logician**, subtle **geometrician**, prudent **statesman**, skillful **physician**, and profound **philosopher** he is—and then afterward, through dissection, you discover this worker of miracles to be nothing but a poor, silly, contemptible knob or protrusion, consisting of a thin membrane containing a little pulpy matter (much the same nature as the rest of the brain):

> **If you were admitted to see such a sight, my friends, could you keep from laughing?** <note>original: "Spectatum admissi risum teneatis amici?"; a quote from Horace's *Ars Poetica*</note>

Would you not sooner laugh at it than go about trying to disprove it? And truly, I may laugh at it more freely now, having already disproven it by the arguments I previously made concerning the rest of the **brain**.

9. I shall therefore take the liberty to conclude that the impulse of **spontaneous motion** comes neither from the **animal spirits** nor from the **brain**. Therefore, those operations that are usually attributed to the **soul** are actually incompatible with any part of the **body**. Consequently, the **soul** is not a mere **modification** of the **body**, but a **distinct substance** from it.

10. Now we are to inquire whether this **substance distinct** from what...

# An Antidote against Atheism. BOOK I.

10. ...whether what we ordinarily call the *Soul* be also itself a **physical body** <note>original: "Corporeal Substance"</note>, or whether it is **non-physical** <note>original: "Incorporeal"</note>. If you say that it is a physical body, you can only mean that it is a type of **matter** more refined and thin than the **animal spirits** <note>original: "Animal Spirits"; in 17th-century physiology, these were thought to be highly refined fluids that traveled through the nerves to facilitate sensation and movement</note> themselves, mixed with them and spread through the vessels and pores of the body. This cannot be true, however, because two physical objects cannot occupy the same space at the same time <note>original: "Penetration of Dimensions"</note>. I do not need new arguments to disprove this foolish notion; for what I said earlier regarding the animal spirits applies just as easily and appropriately to this case. Let it be enough that I remind you of that, so I may be excused from repeating the same points again.

11. It remains, therefore, that we conclude that the thing which triggers **voluntary movement** <note>original: "Spontaneous Motion"</note> in the body (or more directly, in the animal spirits), and which imagines, remembers, and reasons, is an **immaterial substance** distinct from the body. This substance uses the animal spirits and the brain as instruments for its various operations. Thus, we have found a "Spirit" in the proper sense of the word: a being that clearly possesses these faculties—it can both **understand** and **move physical matter**.

12. The prize we have won here will prove to be of great importance for our goal. For it is easy to observe here that the soul of man is, as it were, **an image of God** <note>original: "αγαλμα Θεοῦ" (agalma Theou); a cult image or statue of a deity</note>, a miniature statue of the Divinity; her substance is a **solid likeness of God**. Therefore, just as we can easily study the substance and motion of the vast **heavens** by looking at a small **sphere** or **globe**, we can with similar ease contemplate the nature of the **Almighty** in this small "medal" of God: the human soul. We simply enlarge to infinity those qualities we observe in ourselves when we attribute them to God—just as we imagine the circles we see on a globe to be vastly larger when we picture them drawn across the actual heavens.

13. Therefore, since we are certain that there is a **spiritual substance** within ourselves that possesses both of these properties—namely, **understanding** and **moving physical matter**—let us expand our minds to conceive as best we can of a Spiritual Substance that is able to move and **give life to** <note>original: "actuate"</note> all matter whatsoever, no matter how far it extends, in whatever way it pleases. Let us imagine a Spirit that possesses not just knowledge of this or that particular thing, but a distinct and full **knowledge** <note>original: "Cognoscence"</note> of all things. In doing so, we have a very capable understanding of the nature of the eternal and invisible God. Like the human soul, God cannot be perceived by the **senses**, but He operates everywhere in such a way that His presence is easily inferred from what our outward senses discover.

with me for a while on the wide stage of this **external world**, and diligently attend to those many and most manifest marks and signs that I shall point out to him in this outward frame of things, which naturally indicate to us **that there is a God**.

And now, first, to begin with what is most general, I say that the **phenomena** <note>original: "Phænomena"; observable facts or events</note> of **day and night, winter and summer, springtime and harvest**, and the manner of the **rising and setting** of the **sun, moon, and stars**—all these are signs and tokens to us that there is a **God**. That is, things are so framed that they naturally imply a principle of **wisdom and counsel** in their **Author**. And if there is such an **Author** of external nature, there is a **God**.

2. But here it will be replied that the mere **motion** of the **universal matter** will eventually and necessarily grind itself into those rough and general **outlines** of nature that are observed in the **circuits** of the **sun, moon, and stars**, and their general consequences. But if the **mind** of man grows so bold as to imagine any such thing, let him examine his faculties to see what they naturally conceive regarding the **motion of matter**. Truly, the great master of this **mechanical hypothesis** <note>This likely refers to René Descartes, whose physical theories attempted to explain the universe through the motion of matter alone.</note> does not suppose or admit any **specific difference** in this **universal matter** out of which this outward frame of the world should arise. Nor do I think that any other man will easily imagine anything else but that all the **matter** of the world is of **one** kind in its very **substance** or **essence**.

Now, therefore, I ask regarding this **universal, uniform matter**: does **motion** or **rest** naturally belong to it? If **motion**—it being acknowledged as **uniform**—it must be moved alike in **every part** or imaginable particle of it. For this **motion**, being natural and essential to the **matter**, is the same everywhere within it, and therefore has loosened every **atom** of it to its utmost capacity; so that every particle is alike and moved alike. Therefore, since there is no advantage at all in any one atom over another in size or motion, it is manifest that this **universal matter** (to which **motion** is so essential and intrinsic) will be ineffective for producing any **variety of appearances** in nature. Thus, no **suns**, nor **stars**, nor **earths**, nor **vortices** <note>In Cartesian physics, vortices were giant whirlpools of cosmic matter that carried planets around stars.</note> can ever arise out of this infinitely thin and still **matter**, which must thus eternally remain imperceptible to any of our **senses**, even if our **senses** were ten billion <note>original: "ten thousand millions"</note> times more subtle than they are. Indeed, there could not be any such thing as either **man** or **sensation** in the world. But we see this **matter** shows itself to us in an abundance of varieties of **appearance**; therefore, there must be another principle besides the **matter** to order its **motion** in a way that allows these varieties to appear. And what will that prove to be but a **God?**

3. But if you say that **motion** is **not** part of the **nature** of **matter** (as indeed it is very hard to conceive it as such, given that **matter** is supposed to be uniform), but that it is inert and senseless <note>original: "stupid"; here meaning lacking the power of self-movement or feeling.</note> of itself, then it must be moved by something else. Thus, by necessity, we shall be led to a God, or at least a **spiritual substance** animating the **matter**—which atheists are as much afraid of as children are of **spirits**, or as they themselves are of a **God**.

Therefore, it may be that they will not hesitate to claim that either the parts of matter are **specifically different**, or, though they are not, that some are **movable** of their own accord while others are **inclined toward rest**, and have always been so. They might say it just happened to be that way, even if there is no inherent reason for it in the matter itself. This, however, would wound our mental faculties with such a wide gap that, after accepting this, they would let in any illogical idea and remove any basis for the principles of **knowledge**.

But to fight and struggle with them on their own terms <note>original: "scuffle & combat with them in their own dark Caverns"</note>, let us assume that **universal matter** is a heterogeneous **chaos** of confusion, moved in various ways by chance. I say there is no likelihood that this wild **motion** would ever amount to such a wise design as can be seen even in the general outlines of **nature**. In fact, it would not even result in the natural appearance of what we see and what is thought easiest to produce this way—namely, a round **sun**, **moon**, and **earth**. For it is strongly suspected that if there were no **superintendent** over the motions of those **ethereal whirlpools** <note>original: "Æthereall Whirle-pools"; referring to the Cartesian theory that planets are carried by rotating "vortices" of matter</note> which the **French philosophy** <note>The philosophy of René Descartes, which attempted to explain the universe through mechanical laws and vortices</note> proposes, the form of the **sun** and the rest of the stars would be **oblong**, not round. This is because matter recedes all along the **axis** of a **vortex** as well as from the **center**; therefore, the space left for the finest and most subtle element of all (which the **sun** and **stars** consist of) would naturally be **long**, not round. Therefore, this round shape we see them in must proceed from some higher **principle** than the mere agitation of matter. Whether that principle is simply **generative** <note>original: "Spermatical"; relating to a formative, seed-like power in nature</note>, or also **sensitive** and **intellectual**, I will leave to the investigation of others who have more leisure to deal with such curiosities.

5. The task I have at hand to prove is this: taking for granted what these great **naturalists** <note>Scientists or philosophers who study the physical world</note> would have us allow—namely, **that the Earth moves around the Sun**—I say that the **laws** of its **motion** are such that, if they had been imposed on it by human reason and planning, they would be exactly as they are. So, appealing to our own **faculties**, we must confess that the **motion of the sun and stars**, or of the **earth** (as our **naturalists** would have it), comes from a **knowing principle**, or at least has received the approval and permission of such a principle.

For just as **art** takes what **nature** provides for its purpose and completes the rest itself, so too the **eternal mind**—which set **universal matter** into **motion** (as I believe is most reasonable), or which acts even if **matter** moves itself in confusion (as the **atheist** stubbornly argues)—this **eternal mind**, I say, takes the easy and natural results of this general impulse of **motion** where they serve his purpose; where they do not, he corrects and completes them.

6. In this way, the **intellect** of man, whom **God** created to contemplate the **phenomena of nature** <note>The observable events or appearances in the physical world</note>, may have a more suitable object to study. 1. *The perpetual parallelism of the axis of the Earth is a manifest argument for Divine Providence.* 2. *The great inconveniences if the posture of this parallel axis were perpendicular to the plane of the ecliptic:* 3. *Or coincident with the said plane.* 4. *The excellent advantages of the inclined posture it has, and what a manifest demonstration of Providence it is.* 5. *The same argument made using the Ptolemaic hypothesis <note>original: "Ptolemaical Hypothesis"; the older astronomical model where the Earth is the stationary center of the universe.</note>.* 6. *A further consideration of the axis of the Earth, and of the Moon's crossing the equinoctial line.* 7. *A demonstration from the phenomenon of gravity that there is a principle distinct from matter.* 8. *That neither the air, nor any more subtle matter in the air, has any knowledge or free agency.* 9. *A notable demonstration from the piston <note>original: "Sucker"</note> of the air-pump drawing up so great a weight, showing there is a substance distinct from matter in the world.* 10. *That this phenomenon cannot be explained <note>original: "salv'd"</note> by the elastic power of the air, demonstrated from the phenomenon itself.* 11. *An excuse produced and answered.* 12. *Another excuse anticipated.* 13. *That this stubborn force of nature against the first laws of mechanical motion and against gravity is a clear sign that where things work out perfectly, there is the same immaterial guide, even if the force on matter is not as obvious.* 14. *The ridiculous sophistry of the atheist, arguing from some petty effects of the mere motion of matter that there is no higher principle, plainly discovered and justly mocked.* 15. *Providence concluded from the laws of day and night, winter and summer, etc.*

2. Not a *Perpendicular* posture: for both the pleasant variety and great convenience of *Summer* and *Winter*, *Spring-time* and *Harvest* would be lost. For want of the sun's seasonal approach, those parts of the Earth that currently bring forth fruit and are habitable would be incapable of ever producing any, and consequently could support no inhabitants. And those parts that the full heat of the Sun could reach—with the sun beating down on them always the same way, without any annual retreat or break—would at last grow tired and exhausted. Besides, consulting our own faculties, we observe that an orderly change of things is most pleasant to us and much more gratifies the *Contemplative* nature of Man.

Therefore, I say, we should more naturally conclude that there is some such <term>universal knowing principle</term> that has the power to *move* and *direct* the *matter* of the *universe*, rather than imagining that a confused jostling of its *parts* should arrange themselves into such a condition as if they possessed *reason* and *wisdom* and could *direct* themselves. Instead, they are ordered in a way that our own *reason* must approve as best. It is natural for a man to conceive that they are really ordered by a <term>principle of reason and counsel</term>; that is, that they are made by an <term>all-wise and all-powerful God</term>.

6. I will only add one or two more observations concerning the *axis of the Earth* and the path of the *moon*, and then I will move on to other things.

It must be acknowledged that if the *axis of the Earth* were *perpendicular* to the *plane* of the *sun's ecliptic* <note>The path the sun appears to follow across the sky.</note>, its motion would be more easy and natural; and yet, for the conveniences mentioned before, we see it is made to stand in a *tilted posture*. It is plainly manifest from the second and thirty-second experiments of that learned * gentleman's treatise that neither the **air** itself possesses such **power**, **knowledge**, and **freedom of will**, nor that there are any such **divine particles** scattered within the air that do. In the first of those experiments, the brass stopper <note>original: *stopple*</note> of the cover of the receiver <note>The glass container from which air is pumped.</note> is lifted with great difficulty after the air has been pumped out. In the other experiment, if you apply a tapered brass valve to the lower branch of the stopcock on an emptied receiver and turn the key, the external **air** strikes the valve like a powerful stream to get inside. It suddenly shuts the valve and keeps it closed so tightly that it can support a ten-pound weight. These are evident proofs of an earnest effort in **nature** to refill the receiver with air as it was naturally before, even though this very motion—by which it tries so hard to enter—actually shuts it out more effectively.

It is apparent from this that neither the **air** itself, nor any more **subtle** and divine **matter** (which is more densely packed in the receiver once the air is pumped out), has any **freedom of will**, or any **knowledge** or **perception** to do anything. They are clearly puzzled, acting foolishly <note>original: *fondly*</note> and absurdly <note>original: *preposterously*</note> in their attempts to refill the receiver with air. 

For if the external **air** and that **subtler matter** in the receiver were **knowing** and **free agents**, there would have been coordination <note>original: *correspondence*</note> between them. The exterior **air** would have suspended or withdrawn its pressure from the outside, and the **subtle** and divine **matter** within would have directed its motion against the stopper and valve to let the air in, as nature intended. Or, if only that **subtle body** were **free** and **knowing**, it alone—through mutual coordination (the part in the air outside resisting the pressure of the outward air against the receiver, and the part within pushing against the valve or stopper)—would let in the air, according to the earnest and serious purpose of **nature**. 

But since their acting is so clearly contrary to the intended goal, and their attempts are so clumsy <note>original: *inept*</note>—even though the task would be easy if there were **knowledge** and **free agency** in either the **air** or any other more **subtle matter**—it is a demonstration that the force <note>original: *impetus*</note> of **motion** in all **matter** is blind and necessary. There is no **matter** at all that is **free** and **knowing**; instead, it moves and acts on its own (unless directed by some other **immaterial principle**) according to the mere **mechanical laws of motion**.

The air pump, when the cylinder is well emptied of air, should draw up more than a hundred-pound weight, moving up as if on its own accord. For, as the ingenious experimenter <note>Robert Boyle</note> observed in his third experiment, this forceful attempt of the air to enter <note>original: "subingression"</note> is not caused by the pressure of the surrounding air being strengthened by the addition of the air sucked out. If that were the case, the person operating the pump would find the resistance of the air increasing as the piston <note>original: "sucker"</note> is drawn lower, which is not what happens. We may also reasonably add that since air is nothing but a thin body or collection <note>original: *Congeries*</note> of small particles in perpetual motion, whatever is pumped out will naturally spread into the distances where it can move more freely—that is, into spaces where the air is thinner. Thus, almost instantly, all the air achieves the same consistency. Therefore, any new pressure (based on the idea that the air nearest the pump becomes thicker) cannot be a factor in this case.

10. The most plausible **mechanical** explanation <note>original: *Solution*</note> that can be offered for this phenomenon is the **hypothesis** which the excellent author himself has used, and which would apply to air even in its natural state: namely, that there is an **elastic** power in the air. This can be explained in the **Cartesian** way <note>referring to the philosophy of René Descartes</note>—by the playing and whirling of every particle, through which they attempt to occupy a larger space—or by imagining a compression of particles like the hairs in a lock of wool, which expand when whatever was pressing against them is removed.

But whether this **elastic** power consists of this or something else, although the explanation looks very hopeful and promising at first sight, I must confess (while deferring to better judgments) that the **effect** attributed to the **hypothesis** in this experiment seems to me to be a demonstration against the **hypothesis** itself. For according to the experiment, this **elastic** power has a pressure force of no less than a hundred pounds or more. This pressure—as in all flexible bodies that have a **spring-power** in them—is perpetual and present everywhere in the air, if it exists there at all. Therefore, any cylinder of air at the same height from the ground and with the same diameter as the pump's piston <note>original: "sucker"</note> will press as forcefully as a hundred-pound weight.

Now, suppose a lump of butter is placed in a pair of wooden scales with the same diameter as the **air pump's** piston. It is obvious that this butter would be pressed with the force of two hundred pounds: a cylinder of air from below and another from above each pressing with a force of a hundred pounds. This would necessarily follow if there were this **elastic** power in the air. But the butter is not pressed at all, as is shown by the fact that no watery fluid <note>original: "serose humour"</note> is squeezed out of it, nor is it flattened or spread out by any such compression—even though, according to this **hypothesis** of the **elastic** power of air, it has the force of two hundred pounds pressing on it.

11. Nor can I think up <note>original: "excogitate"</note> any way to avoid <note>original: "Evasion"</note> this demonstration, unless it is argued that the **spring** of the **air** presses against the sides of the butter as well as the top and bottom, keeping it from flattening. But it is

E 2
<meta>easily</meta>

He uses this as evidence that mechanical laws alone cannot explain the behavior of air.</summary>

# BOOK II. An Antidote against Atheism.

11. It is easily answered that this still cannot prevent the butter from being squeezed on all sides and having its milky and watery <note>original: "serose"</note> fluids pressed out, if there were indeed any such pressure as is supposed. To this you may further add that if a lump of butter were reduced to the shape of, for example, a round **plate** <note>original: "Trencher"</note>, whose edge is a hundred or two hundred times smaller than its flat sides, and then placed between two thin, light plates wide enough for the purpose and hung freely in the air with strings—as if in a scale—so that the force of pressure from above and below would exceed the pressure against the round edge of the butter by a hundred or two hundred times; yet, despite all this, the butter will not be pressed any tighter by the **spring of the air**, nor will it have any more effect on it than it had before. This is true even though butter is so soft and yielding that a very small force from our hands will press it between the two plates.

12. Yet this is not because our strength is added to the force of the **spring of the air**. For the excess of the force of the **spring of the air** against the sides of the plates—compared to the force against the round edge of the butter—is far greater than the additional force of our hand pressing against the plates. And yet, there was no new effect from the air.

Moreover, in places where this **spring of the air** does not reach—namely, inside a pail filled with water—you may place a lump of butter, and the butter will yield as easily to the pressure of your hand as it does in the air itself. So, it is indisputably <note>original: "irrefragably"</note> evident that there is no such **spring of the air** as some learned men have supposed; much less is it so strong that it could master a hundred-pound weight, as it is thought to do in this notable experiment of the **air pump**.

13. But just as the **phenomenon of gravity** is entirely contrary to the very first **mechanical laws of motion**—even though it is a **universal law** of **terrestrial** bodies imposed on them by something that is not only not terrestrial, but **immaterial**—so likewise this rising of the **piston** <note>original: "Sucker"</note> of the **air pump** with over a hundred-pound weight attached to it is just as contrary and violent a breach of that **universal law of gravity**. It is so forceful that it is apparent that there is a **principle** transcending the nature and power of **matter** that oversees and rules all. This principle directs the **motion** of every part and parcel of **matter** backwards, forwards, and in contrary ways, in pursuit of such **general** designs as are best for the **whole**. No less a goal than the **living** and **breathing** of animals is intended by this industrious and determined effort to keep the parts of the **air** together, as is well observed by this virtuous and judicious **author** <note>Robert Boyle</note> in his 41st experiment.

Therefore, since it is so manifest that there is a **principle** in the world that struggles so stoutly and resolutely against the **mechanical laws of matter**, and that so forcibly resists or cancels one common **law of nature** for the more timely exercise of another; this, I say, is a very sure pledge to us that when things are done rightly—even if not with this seeming violence and determination—they are still the effects of the same **immaterial principle** (call it the **Spirit of Nature** <note>More’s term for an unconscious but purposeful force through which God acts on the physical world</note> or what you will) which is the **representative power of God** <note>original: "Vicarious Power of God"</note> upon this great **machine** <note>original: "Automaton"</note>, the **world**.

<meta>This page concludes Henry More’s argument against the idea that random mechanical motion can explain the complexity of nature. # CHAP. II. An Antidote against Atheism.

14. But simply because many **bullets** <note>original: "Bullets"; small lead balls</note> shaken together in a man's hat will settle into a specific **shape**, or because the **frost** and the **wind** will draw strange **streaks** like feathers and other trivial patterns upon doors and glass windows—which serve no use or purpose—it is a leap to conclude that all the **contrivances** found in **nature**, even the **frame** of the **bodies** of both **men** and **beasts**, arise from no other **principle** than the random mixing of **matter**. To suggest that because matter **naturally** produces *something*, it is therefore the **cause** of **all things**, seems to me to be reasoning in the same **mood and figure** <note>original: "Mood and Figure"; technical terms for the structure of a logical syllogism</note> as that "wise" tradesman from **Gotham** <note>Gotham: A village in English folklore famous for the "Wise Men of Gotham," who were actually legendary for their foolishness</note>. While walking down a hill carrying his **cheeses** under his arms, one of them fell and rolled down the hill very fast; he then let the others go after it, telling them all to meet him at his house, not doubting that since they began so hopefully, they would be able to complete the whole journey on their own. Or like another man of the same town who, seeing that the **iron trivet** <note>original: "Trevet"; a three-legged metal stand for a pot</note> he had bought had three feet and could stand, expected it to walk as well, saving him the labor of carrying it. So our profound **atheists** and **Epicureans** <note>Epicureans: followers of Epicurus, who believed the world was formed by the random collision of atoms</note>, with the same level of **wisdom**, do not hesitate to conclude that because the confused **motion** of the **parts** of **matter** might result in a rough sketch of hard and **soft**, **rigid** and **fluid**, and the like, it will therefore go further and reach the point of arranging **matter** in such an order that **naturally** implies a **principle** containing exact **wisdom** and **counsel**. Such a position is more suited to the fools mentioned above than to anyone who has the slightest command of their natural wit and faculties.

15. Therefore, having sufficiently exposed the ridiculous folly of this current **sophism** <note>sophism: a clever but false argument</note>, let us attend carefully to the natural **outflowings** of unbiased **reason**. Let us conclude that the **rising** and **setting** of the **stars and planets**, the **cycle** of **day** and **night**, and **winter** and **summer** are so ordered and guided as if they had been established by perfect deliberation and the clearest knowledge. Therefore, the power that ordained them is a **Knowing Principle**, able to move, alter, and guide **matter** according to his own will and pleasure; that is to say, **that there is a God**.

And truly, I do not doubt at all that I shall clearly trace the visible footsteps of this **Divine Counsel** and **Providence** even in all things discoverable in the world. But I will move through them as lightly and briefly as I can.

1. LET us therefore swiftly survey the ***Valleys*** and ***Mountains***, sound the depth of the ***Sea***, range through the ***Woods*** and ***Forests***, dig into the ***Entrails*** of the ***Earth***, and let the ***Atheist*** tell me which of all these places are silent and say nothing of a ***God***. Those that are most dumb will at least agree with the rest: that all things exist by the guidance and determination—let the ***Matter*** move as it will—or at least by the ***permission*** and ***approval*** of a ***Knowing Principle*** <note>A "Knowing Principle" refers to an intelligent, conscious Creator (God) as opposed to blind, unconscious matter.</note>. Just as a mason making a wall sometimes finds a ***stone*** that needs no ***cutting***, and so, merely approving of it, he places it in his work; or as a ***piece*** of ***Timber*** may happen to be cracked in the very place where the carpenter would split it, and he need not close it first just so he can split it apart afterward. Therefore, if the mere ***Motion*** of ***Matter*** can produce any rough, general thing of good consequence, let it stand as acceptable. But we shall also find those things which so manifestly suggest ***Design*** and ***Wisdom*** <note>original: "Counsel"</note> that we cannot naturally withhold our agreement, but must say: There is a ***God***.

2. And now let us set ourselves to the search and see if all things are not exactly as our ***Reason*** would desire them to be. And to begin at the top first, even those roughly scattered ***Mountains***—which seem like so many ***Wens*** <note>original: "Wens"; cysts or unsightly growths on the skin</note> and unnatural ***bulges*** <note>original: "Protuberancies"</note> upon the face of the ***Earth***—if you consider how important they are, once understood <note>original: "reconciled"</note>, you may deem them ornaments as well as useful things.

For these are ***Nature's distillation vessels*** <note>original: "Stillatories"; apparatus used for distilling liquids</note>, in whose hollow caverns the ascending vapors are condensed into that universal ***water of life*** <note>original: "Aqua vitæ"; here used literally to mean fresh water necessary for life, rather than brandy or spirits</note>, that good fresh water, the liquor of life that sustains all the living creatures in the world, being carried through all parts of the Earth in the winding channels of ***Brooks*** and ***Rivers***. Geography would prove this through a large list of examples <note>original: "induction"</note>. I will only mention three or four: the ***Guadiana*** <note>original: "Ana"</note> and ***Tagus*** run from ***Sierra Molina*** in ***Spain***; the ***Rhine*** <note>original: "Rhenus"</note>, ***Po*** <note>original: "Padus"</note>, and ***Rhone*** <note>original: "Rhodanus"</note> from the ***Alps***; the ***Don*** <note>original: "Tanais"</note> from the ***Riphean***, the ***Garonne*** <note>original: "Garumna"</note> from the ***Pyrenean Mountains***; the ***Achelous*** from ***Pindus***; the ***Maritsa*** <note>original: "Hebrus"</note> from ***Rhodope***; the ***Tigris*** from ***Niphates***; the ***Orontes*** from ***Lebanon*** <note>original: "Libanus"</note>; and the ***Euphrates*** from the mountains of ***Armenia***; and so it is with the rest. But I will not dwell on this; I will now turn to what more forcefully declares an ***Eye*** of ***Providence*** directing and determining, as well as approving of, the results of the supposed movement of the parts of ***Matter***.

3. And so that you may better feel the strength of my argument, let us first briefly consider the ***Nature of Man***: what ***Faculties*** he has, and what his rank is in respect to the rest of the ***Creatures***. And indeed, though his body is but weak and unarmed, yet his inward abilities of ***Reason*** and ***technological invention*** <note>original: "Artificial contrivance"</note> are admirable. He is much given to ***Contemplation*** and the viewing of this ***theatre of the world***, to trade and commerce with foreign nations, to the building of ***Houses*** and ***Ships***, to the making of curious instruments of ***Silver***, ***Brass***, or ***Steel***, and the like. In a word, he is the flower and chief of all the products of ***Nature***.

4. I therefore now ask: given that ***Man*** is of this nature, would his noble faculties not be lost and frustrated if there were no materials to exercise them on? And in the second place, I desire to know whether the unrefined, confused ***movement*** of the ***particles*** of ***matter*** would certainly produce such materials fit for ***Man*** to exercise his skill on, or not. That is to say, was there any necessity that could infallibly produce ***stone quarries*** in the Earth, which are the chief materials for all the magnificent buildings in the world? And then, what of ***sea-coal*** <note>original: "Sea-Coal"; an early term for coal, often gathered from the shore or transported by sea, used here as a primary fuel source.</note> and other necessary ***fuel*** fit for the working or melting of these ***metals***? The same may be said of the ***lodestone*** <note>original: "Load-stone"; a naturally magnetized mineral used in early compasses.</note>, that great help to ***navigation***: might it not have lain so deep in the Earth as to never have been reached by ***human*** industry? And the same may also be said of other ***stones*** and ***metals***: that being heaviest, they might have lain lowest. Certainly, moving ***matter***—unless there were some special, overpowering guidance over it—might just as easily have overlooked these necessary, useful things as hit upon them. But if there had not been such a creature as ***Man***, these very things would have been useless, for none of the brute beasts make use of such commodities. Therefore, unless a person will do great violence to his own reason <note>original: "Faculties"</note>, he must conclude that there is a contrivance of ***Providence*** and ***wisdom*** <note>original: "Counsel"</note> in all those things, which reaches from the beginning to the end and arranges all things harmoniously. ***Providence***, foreseeing what kind of creature she would make ***Man***, provided him with materials by which he might be able to adorn his own age and furnish ***history*** with the ***records*** of remarkable <note>original: "egregious"; in the 17th century, this meant "outstanding" or "distinguished," rather than its modern negative meaning.</note> exploits of both ***art*** and ***valor***.

5. But without the provision of these materials, the glory and splendor of both ***war*** and ***peace*** would have been lost. For instead of those magnificent ***buildings*** which are seen in the world, men could have had no better dwellings than a larger sort of beehive or bird's nest, made of contemptible sticks, straws, and dirty mortar. And instead of the usual splendor and bravery of ***war***—where one hears the solemn sound of the hoarse ***trumpet***, the courageous beating of the ***drum***, the neighing and prancing of ***horses***, the clattering of ***armor***, and the terrible thunder of ***cannons*** (to say nothing of the glittering of the ***sword*** and ***spear***, the waving and fluttering of displayed ***banners*** <note>original: "Colours"</note>, and the gallantry of ***cavalry charges*** upon their well-trained steeds, and the like)—I say, had it not been for the provision of ***iron***, ***steel***, ***brass***, and such necessary materials, instead of all this glory and solemnity, there would have been nothing but the howlings and shoutings of poor naked men, striking each other...

6. Besides this, animals are naturally armed, while humans are naturally unarmed with anything except their **Reason**. ## CHAPTER IV.

1. *The distinction between Land and Sea is not without a Providence.* 2. *The consistency of Sea-water is designed so that it can support Ships.* 3. *The great convenience and pleasure of Navigation.* 4. *The admirable series of natural provisions for satisfying human intelligence in such an important curiosity.*

1. Having thus moved past the *hills* and through the *woods* and *hollow depths of the earth*, let us now view the wide *sea* as well. Let us see if it does not also inform us that there is a *God*—that is, whether things there are arranged as a rational Principle would order or approve, even though they could have been otherwise. And now that we have come to view those "floating fields" <note>original: *Campos natantes*</note>, as the Roman poet *Lucretius* calls them—that vast, open plain <note>original: "Champain"</note> of water, the *ocean*—I ask first: Could it not have been *wider* than it is? Could it have been so large as to overspread the entire face of the earth, thereby taking away the home of humans and animals? After all, the wet particles could have easily mixed with the dry ones, so that everything would have been either *sea* or a *quagmire*.

2. And then again, even though this distinction between *land* and *sea* exists, could this watery element not have turned out to be of such a thin consistency that it would not support *shipping*? Such a thing is far from impossible, as there are actually such waters in nature—the River *Silas* <note>A legendary river in India, mentioned by ancient writers like Megasthenes, where it was said nothing could float.</note>, for example. And the waters of the *Borysthenes* <note>The ancient name for the Dnieper River in Eastern Europe.</note> are said to be so *thin* and light that they float on top of the stream of the River *Hypanis* <note>The ancient name for the Southern Bug River in Ukraine.</note>. We also know there are some kinds of wood so heavy that they will sink in any ordinary kind of water.

I appeal, therefore, to any person's reason: Is it not better that there should be a distinction between *land* and *sea* than for everything to be mud or water? And is it not better that *timber trees* provide wood light enough to float on water, or that the water be heavy enough to support the wood, rather than the opposite? Therefore, that which could have been different, and yet is settled according to our own heart's desire, who

Since we are knowing and rational creatures, we ought to believe that these things were established by wisdom and reason.

3. The more closely we examine this matter, the more clearly we shall discern the evident footsteps of **Providence** in it. For the two main properties of humanity being **Contemplation** and **Sociableness** (or a love of **Conversation**), nothing could so highly gratify our nature as the power of **Navigation**. By this, humans ride on the back of the sea's waves and view the wonders of the **Deep**. Because of the fluidity <note>original: "glibness"</note> of that element, a person is able in a reasonable amount of time to prove the truth of those wise suggestions of their own mind. That is, they can discover whether the **Earth** is round in every direction, whether there are any **Antipodes** <note>original: "Antipodes"—people living on the opposite side of the globe</note>, and other such things. By crossing the **Equator** <note>original: "Æquinoctial line"</note>, the traveler decides that controversy regarding the habitability of the **Torrid Zone** <note>The tropics; ancient and medieval geographers often believed the heat there was too intense for human life.</note>—or rather, they wipe away that blot that lay upon **Divine Providence**, as if so great a share of the world had been lost because it was unfit for habitation.

Besides, arriving at **strange coasts** and discovering people with a great diversity of manners different from our own cannot but be a thing of infinite pleasure and advantage. It enlarges our thoughts through what we observe in their **conversation**, **abilities**, and **government** <note>original: "Policy"</note>. Added to this are the various **Rarities of Nature** and **Commodities** specific to several countries, which those who stay at home enjoy through the **travels** of those who go abroad; meanwhile, those who travel grow rich for their adventure.

4. Now, therefore, since **Navigation** is of such great consequence to the **delight** and **convenience** of human life, and since humans possess both the wit and courage to attempt the **seas** if only they were provided with the right **materials** and other necessary advantages: when we see there is so perfect a provision made for this purpose in large **timber** for the building of **ships**; in thick **seawater** sufficient to carry the **ship's** burden; in the **magnet** or **lodestone** for the **compass**; in the steady and parallel direction of the **axis** of the **Earth** for the **North Star** <note>original: "Cynosura"—the constellation Ursa Minor, used for navigation</note>; and then observing our natural **wit** and **courage** to make use of them, and how that innate <note>original: "ingenite"</note> desire for **knowledge** and **socializing**, and for the **improving** of our own abilities and **happiness**, stirs us up to such a notable design—we cannot but conclude from such a train of **causes** so fitly and harmoniously working together, that it was really the counsel of an **Universal** and **Eternal Mind** that laid these **causes** together so carefully and wisely. That is, we cannot but conclude **that there is a God**.

And if we have already gained such a firm foothold in this truth by considering such **phenomena** <note>original: "Phænomena"—natural occurrences or appearances</note> in the world that seem more rugged and general, what will the contemplation of the more **particular** and more **refined** pieces of nature reveal in **plants**, **animals**, and the **human body**?
