### CHAPTER V

1. *That the form and beauty, seed and "signature" of plants are arguments for a Divine Providence.* 2. *That although the mere motion of matter might produce certain "meteors" (weather phenomena) like hail, snow, and ice, it does not follow that this same motion is the sufficient cause for animals and plants.* 3. *That it would not be a major flaw or "gap" in nature if some simpler phenomena were acknowledged as results of the mere mechanical motion of matter.* 4. *That the form and beauty of flowers and plants come from a higher principle.* 5. *That beauty exists and is an object perceived by our intellectual faculties.* 6. *From which it follows that the beautiful forms and shapes of plants and animals arise from an intellectual principle.*

1. So far, we have only considered the more basic and simple outlines of Divine **Providence** in the world, as shown in those broader **phenomena** <note>original: "Phænomena"—observable facts or events.</note> of **day** and **night**, **winter** and **summer**, **land** and **sea**, **rivers**, **mountains**, **metals**, and the like. We now come to a closer view of God and Nature in **plants** <note>original: "Vegetables"—in this period, the term referred to all plant life, not just those we eat.</note>, **animals**, and **humanity**.

And first, regarding **plants**, I shall address only these four topics: their **form** and **beauty**, their **seed**, their **signatures** <note>term: "Signatures"—the historical belief that the physical shape or color of a plant indicated its medicinal purpose (for example, a lung-shaped leaf treating lung disease).</note>, and their great **usefulness** for both **medicine** and **sustenance**. To better understand the advantage of this closer study of nature's works, we must first notice the condition of that substance we call **matter**: how fluid, slippery, and undefined it is by itself; or, if it is hard, how unfit it is to be changed into anything else. Therefore, all things rot into a liquid state before anything can be generated from them—just as we soften wax before pressing a seal into it.

2. Therefore, unless we are so foolish as to conclude that because the uniform motion of the air (or some more subtle physical element) can compress a bit of vaporous moisture into round drops—as some say happens with dew and other experiments—and because this basic and general motion can do *something*, it must therefore do *everything*; we must in all reason confess that there is an **Eternal Mind**, by whose power matter is formed and changed into useful things.

But the idea that mere basic and undirected **motion** will achieve results that clearly imply a wise and deliberate design—just because it naturally produces *some* results—is a ridiculous fallacy <note>original: "Sophism"</note>. As I have already suggested, such an idea is more likely to trick the thoughtless minds of fools and children than men of mature reason who are well-trained in philosophy. Even if we admit that **rain**, **snow**, **wind**, **hail**, **ice**, and similar weather phenomena <note>original: "Meteors"—in the 17th century, this term referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain and wind, not just falling stars.</note> might be the products of **heat** and **cold**, or of the **motion** and **rest** of certain small particles of **matter**, yet that the...

<header>CHAP. V. An Antidote against Atheism.</header>

...the useful and beautiful design of the *branches, flowers,* and *fruits* of *plants* should also be the result of chance (to say nothing yet of the *bodies* of *birds, fish, beasts,* and *humans*) is as ridiculous and lazy a conclusion as to infer that because mere *heat* and *cold* can soften and harden *wax* and put it into some shape or other, that therefore this mere *heat* and *cold*, or *motion* and *rest*, without any art or direction, also made the *silver seal* and engraved upon it so skillfully a *coat of arms* or the shape of some *birds* or *beasts*, such as an *eagle*, a *lion*, and the like. Indeed, this inference would be far more tolerable than the other, as these works of *art* are much easier to produce and less significant than those works of *nature*.

<margin>Regarding these "seminal reasons" <note>original: "Rationes seminales"—the underlying blueprints or vital principles of life.</note>, whether they are distinct or one common Spirit of Nature, see Book 3, chapters 12 and 13, in the *Discourse of the Immortality of the Soul*.</margin>

3. Nor is it a flaw or gap at all in the works of *nature* that some particular **phenomena** <note>original: "Phænomena"—observable events.</note> are simply the easy results of that *general motion* communicated to *matter* by God, while others are the effects of more skillful design, or of *divine art* or *reason*. These are the <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>original: "λόγοι σπερματικοὶ" (logoi spermatikoi)—the "seed-like principles" or divine blueprints that guide the growth of living things.</note> incorporated into matter. This is especially true since matter itself is, in some sense, vital; otherwise, it would not continue the motion it is given when it is moved one way or another. Furthermore, since the *nature* of God is the most perfect fullness of life that can possibly be imagined, it is very fitting that this furthest and most distant shadow of himself (matter) should be in some way vital, however obscurely.

Therefore, as things descend by degrees from the highest perfection, it is a smooth and proportional step to go down from the top of this outward creation—*humanity*, in whom there is a principle of more refined and reflective *reason*. This reason continues on (though not in the same way) in the more perfect kinds of *animals*, just as *sensation* (unwilling to be confined to too narrow a space) also takes hold of some kinds of *plants*, such as various sorts of **zoophytes** <note>term: "Zoophyta"—organisms like sea anemones or corals that appear to be halfway between plants and animals.</note>. In the rest of the plants, no further traces of a **conscious form** <note>original: "Animadvertive form"—a soul or principle capable of perception or attention.</note> are discovered, though they show the effects of an **unconscious form** <note>original: "In-advertent form"—a guiding principle that acts without awareness.</note>, consisting of **embodied art** <note>original: "λόγοι ἔνυλοι" (logoi enyloi)—literally "reasons in matter."</note> or *seminal reason*. I say, then, it is no uneven leap to pass from these faint and obscure examples of *vital life* to the more basic effects of *general motion* seen in *minerals, metals*, and various *weather events* <note>original: "Meteors"—in the 17th century, this referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, snow, or lightning.</note>. The simple and rough shapes of these things may have no need for any principle of life or *seminal form* distinct from the *rest* or *motion* of the particles of *matter*.

4. However, there is such an exquisiteness of *form* and *beauty* in the more noble kinds of *plants*, which carries such a suitability and harmony with the more refined senses and wisdom of the *human soul*, that a person cannot help but acknowledge it. Because the soul's **intellectual touch** <note>This refers to the mind's ability to "feel" or perceive abstract qualities like beauty and order.</note> is so sweetly satisfied by what it finds in such objects, it must admit that some hidden cause, much like its own *intellectual* nature, is the designer and perfecter of these pleasant sights in the world.

5. Nor is it at all useful to object that this matter of *beauty* and *comeliness* of proportion is merely a personal opinion, on the grounds that some people do not acknowledge such things and find all things equally handsome, even though they have the use of their *eyes* as well as anyone else. For I say this actually supports what we are aiming at: that **beauty** <note>original: "Pulchritude"—physical beauty or grace.</note> is indeed conveyed by the outward *senses* to the soul, but a more *intellectual*...

The intellectual faculty is what appreciates beauty; just as a *geometrical diagram* <note>original: "Geometrical Scheme"</note> is perceived by the *eyes*, but the *demonstration* of its truth is discerned by *reason*. Therefore, it is more rational to claim that some *Intellectual Principle* was the author of this *beauty* <note>original: "Pulchritude"</note> in things than to believe they were fashioned this way without the help of such a Principle.

To say that there is no such thing as *beauty* simply because some people's souls are so dull and insensitive that they find all objects equally plain is as absurd and baseless as concluding there is no such thing as *reason* or *logical proof* just because a person born with a mental disability <note>original: "natural Fool"</note> cannot understand it. But the fact that there is such a thing as *beauty*, and that it is recognized by all generations of humanity in *trees, flowers,* and *fruits*, is clearly proven by the way *buildings* have been decorated and beautified in every age. For what is more common than for builders to use flowers and fruit patterns to garnish their work?

Furthermore, I appeal to any person who has not sunk to such a miserable level of degeneracy that they are as insensitive to these things as the lowest of animals: whether, for example, a properly-cut *tetrahedron* <note>original: "Tetraedrum"—a pyramid shape with four triangular faces.</note>, *cube*, or *icosahedron* <note>original: "Icosaedrum"—a solid figure with twenty faces.</note> has no more beauty in it than any rough, broken stone lying in a field or highway. Or, to mention other *solid* shapes—which, though they are not "regular" in the strict mathematical sense, still have a defined *form* and nature, such as a *cone, sphere,* or *cylinder*—do these not please the human mind more and show more elegance of shape than the crude chips of *limestone* <note>original: "free-stone"—a type of fine-grained stone that is easily carved.</note> that fall from a mason’s tools? Such scraps serve for nothing but to fill the inside of a wall, hidden from sight because of their ugliness.

It is worth noting that if nature shapes anything with even a hint of this *geometrical* accuracy, we observe it with great satisfaction and pleasure. This happens if a stone is *exactly round* (like the many such stones found between two hills in *Cuba*, an island of *America*), or *orderly pentagonal* <note>original: "Quinquangular"—five-sided.</note>, or even if its sides are just *parallel* despite having unequal *angles*, as seen in certain small stones and a type of *alabaster* found here in *England*. These stones, I say, please our sight because they share a closer kinship <note>original: "cognation"</note> with the soul of man. The soul is rational and intellectual; therefore, it is well pleased when it encounters any outward object that fits and agrees with the *inborn ideas* <note>original: "congenite Ideas"</note> that its own nature possesses. For *symmetry, equality,* and the *correspondence of parts* are things discerned by *reason*, not merely objects of *physical sense*, as I have proved before.

6. Since it is now evident that there is such a thing as *beauty, symmetry,* and *comely* proportion (to say nothing of the delightful mixture of colors), and that these are the proper focus of *understanding* and *reason* (for animals do not notice these things), I think I may safely infer this: whatever is the first and primary cause of changing fluid and unformed *matter* into shapes as beautiful and symmetrical as those we see in *flowers* and *trees* must be an *intelligent principle*. This principle must know both the nature of man and the nature of those objects it presents to his sight in this outward, visible world. For these things cannot occur by chance or by the random, varied attempts of particles of matter bumping into each other. If that were the case, it is likely that the *species* of things—even if some happened to turn out right—would mostly be deformed and ridiculous;

### CHAPTER VI.

1. *Providence argued from the seeds of plants.* 2. *An answer to an objection concerning stinking weeds and poisonous plants.* 3. *The signature of plants as an argument for Providence.* 4. *Specific examples of signatures.* 5. *An answer to an objection concerning plant signatures that do not relate to medicine.*

1. I say, therefore, that because every *plant* has its *seed*, it is an evident sign of *Divine Providence*. Having seeds is not a necessary result of the *motion of matter* (just as the entire design of the plant is not). Because seeds are of such great importance for the survival and spread of their own *species*, and for the benefit of human *skill*, industry, and needs (for much of *farming* and *gardening* depends on this), it must be an act of deliberate *design* to provide various kinds of *plants* with their *seeds*. This is especially true since the Earth is of such a nature that, although it might have produced all types of *plants* on its own for a while at first (as some claim it also produced all kinds of *animals*), it would eventually become so sluggish that without the advantage of those small, concentrated principles of life—the grains of *seed*—it would produce no such offspring. It is like a pump that has grown dry; it will not yield any water unless you pour a little water into it first, and then for one basin-full of "priming" water, you may draw up many bucket-fulls <note>original: "Soe-fuls"—a 'soe' or 'so' was a large wooden tub or bucket.</note>.

2. Nor is it a significant objection to point out that *stinking weeds* and *poisonous plants* also produce *seeds*, just like the most pleasant and useful plants. Even those *stinking weeds* and *poisonous plants* have their uses. First, human *industry* is put to work by the need to weed them out where they are harmful. If this reason seems trivial, consider that if human *industry* had nothing to conflict and struggle against, the fire of the human *spirit* would be half-extinguished by the laziness of the flesh. When we realize this, we will acknowledge that my argument is neither insignificant nor invalid.

## CHAP. VI.

->1. *Providence argued from the Seeds of Plants.* 2. *An Objection answered concerning stinking Weeds and poisonous Plants.* 3. *The Signature of Plants an argument of Providence.* 4. *Certain Instances of Signatures.* 5. *An Answer to an Objection concerning such Signatures in Plants as cannot refer to Medicine.*<-

1. I say, therefore, that because every **Plant** has its **Seed**, it is an evident sign of **Divine Providence**. For this is no necessary result of the **Motion** of **Matter** (just as the entire design of the **Plant** is not), and it is of such great consequence that they have **Seed** for the continuation and propagation of their own **Species**. This is especially true since the **Earth** is of such a nature that, although at first it might have brought forth all kinds of **Plants** for a while (as some claim it also brought forth all kinds of **Animals**), eventually it would grow so sluggish that without the advantage of those small, compressed **principles** of generation—the grains of **Seed**—it would yield no such births. It would be like a pump grown dry that will yield no water unless you pour a little water into it first; then, for one **basin-full**, you may draw up many **bucket-fulls** <note>original: "Soe-fuls"; a "soe" was a large wooden tub or bucket carried by two men on a stang.</note>.

2. Nor is it important to object that **stinking Weeds** and **poisonous Plants** bear **Seed** as well as the most pleasant and useful ones. For even those **stinking Weeds** and **poisonous Plants** have their use. First, the **Industry** of Man is exercised by weeding them out where they are harmful. If this reason seems slight, let us consider that if human **Industry** had nothing to conflict and struggle with, the fire of man's **Spirit** would be half-extinguished in the flesh. We shall then acknowledge that what I have alleged is neither contemptible nor invalid.

But secondly, who knows but that it is the same with poisonous **plants** as is commonly imagined regarding **toads** and other poisonous **serpents**—that they lick the venom off the **earth**? In this way, poisonous **plants** may well draw all the harmful juice and nourishment to themselves, so that the others may be more pure and refined <note>original: "defæcate"</note>; just as there are receptacles and drainage organs <term>Emunctories: organs or canals in the body that carry off waste or superfluous fluids.</term> in the human body to drain away excess yellow bile <note>original: "Choler"</note>, melancholy, and the like.

But lastly, it is very well known by those who understand anything of nature and **medicine** <note>original: "Phyſick"</note> that the **herbs** which the uneducated and ignorant call **weeds** are actually the ingredients of highly effective **medicines**. It is reported that *Winter Wolfsbane* <note>original: "Aconitum hyemale"</note>, which is otherwise a rank poison, is extremely powerful against the bites of vipers and scorpions—a claim that **Crollius** <note>Oswald Croll (c. 1563–1609) was a German alchemist and physician who promoted the use of chemicals in medicine.</note> agrees with. Nor should we consider those things useless whose purpose we do not yet know; for not everything is to be known at once, so that future generations may always have something left to discover for themselves.

3. We come now to the **Signatures** of plants, which seem to be no less an argument for the fact that the highest origin of nature’s works is some **Understanding Principle** than the careful provision of their seeds. Indeed, this point relates to us more directly and appropriately than the other, serving as a certain **key** to lead mankind into the knowledge and use of nature’s treasures. I ask, therefore, whether it is not a very easy and natural conclusion to make: when we observe that several **herbs** are marked with some **mark** or **sign** that suggests their healing powers <note>original: "virtue"</note> and what they are good for, and since there is a creature like man in the world who can read and understand these **signs** and **characters**, we must conclude that the Author of both man and plants knew the nature of both. It is like the **inscriptions** on **apothecaries'** boxes, which the master of the shop sets there so that the apprentice may read them. In fact, it is even better: for here, the very **nature** and **use** of the **herbs** is inscribed, not just the **name**. 

It is not necessary for all plants to be marked this way, even though some are; the rarity of it provides delight. Otherwise, it would have been dull and tiresome—playing too much on the same string. Besides, Divine Providence intended only to introduce mankind to the useful knowledge of her treasures, leaving the rest to employ our industry so that we might not live like idle loiterers and truants. For the theater of the world is an exercise for man’s wit, not a lazy **encyclopedia** <term>Polyanthea: a large collection of knowledge or commonplaces often used as a reference book.</term> or book of commonplaces. Therefore, all things are to some degree obscure and complex, so that the diligence <note>original: "sedulity"</note> of that divine spark, the soul of man, may have the opportunity for conquest and triumph when he has performed well with the additional help <note>original: "superadvenient assistance"</note> of his God.

4. I shall fully demonstrate that there are some **plants** which bear a very clear **signature** of their **nature** and **use** through the following examples:

The same is true for your several sorts of **Satyrions** <note>A type of orchid named after the lustful satyrs of mythology.</note>, which have the clear resemblance of genital parts upon them—**Aron** <note>Cuckoo-pint or Lords-and-Ladies.</note> especially, and all your **Orchises** that have been named after various beasts, such as *Cynosorchis* <note>Dog Orchid.</note>, *Orchis Myodes* <note>Fly Orchid.</note>, *Tragorchis* <note>Goat Orchid.</note>, and the like. The last of these, notorious also for its goat-like smell and tufts not unlike the beard of that lecherous animal, is of all the rest the most powerful incentive to lust.

The leaves of **Hypericum** <note>St. John's Wort.</note> are very thickly pricked or "pinked" <note>Decorated with a perforated pattern.</note> with little holes, and it is an exceptionally good herb for treating wounds, as it is also useful for clearing obstructions in the pores of the body.

**Scorpioides** (Scorpion-grass), or **Echium**, is shaped like the crooked tail of a scorpion, and **Ophioglossum** (Adder's-tongue) has a very plain and perfect resemblance to the tongue of a serpent, as does **Snake-garlic** <note>original: "ophioscorodon"</note> to the entire head and upper parts of a serpent's body. These are all held to be very good against poison and the biting of serpents. Generally, all such **plants** that are speckled with spots like the skins of **vipers** or other venomous creatures are known to be good against their stings or bites, and are powerful antidotes against poison.

Thus did Divine Providence, through natural **hieroglyphics**, read short **medical** lectures to the unrefined wit of man. This was done so that, having been briefly introduced and engaged by these signs, man might through his own industry and endeavors search out the rest himself. For it is very reasonable that other herbs which did not have such **signatures** might be just as good for medicinal uses as those that did.

5. But if anyone objects here that some herbs resemble things that have no likely connection to **medicine**—such as **Geranium** (Cranesbill), **Crosswort** <note>original: "Cruciata"</note>, **Shepherd's Purse** <note>original: "Bursa Pastoris"</note>, the **Bee-Flower**, **Fly-Orchis**, and the like—I say they answer themselves in the very proposal of their objection. For this is a sign that these were intended only as playful <note>original: "ludicrous"</note> ornaments of Nature, like the decorative flourishes around a large capital letter that signify nothing but are made only to delight the eye. 

Furthermore, it was not an inconvenience to our first ancestors if this hint of **signatures** sometimes failed. On the contrary, it drove them with more courage to test the virtues of those plants that had no such **signatures** at all. It was natural for them to reason this way: "Why might those herbs without signatures not have medicinal virtue in them, just as some that have signatures have no virtue corresponding to the signs they bear?" This was a further confirmation to them of the previous conclusion, and still a greater provocation of their in-

This is manifest in your **Satyrions** <note>A type of orchid whose roots were thought to resemble testicles and thus act as an aphrodisiac.</note>, **Ophioglossum** <note>Adder's-tongue fern; its spike resembles a snake's tongue, suggesting its use against snakebites.</note>, and the like. But I have dwelt too long upon this theory; we will turn our attention to what follows, which is even more undeniably compelling and forceful.

### CHAPTER VII.

1. **The usefulness of plants argues for a Providence, particularly those that provide timber.** 2. **Also, such herbs and plants that serve as medicine for men and beasts.** 3. **Plants fit for food.** 4. **The color of grass and herbs, and the fruits of trees.** 5. **The notable provisions in Nature for husbandry and tillage, with the universal usefulness of hemp and flax.** 6. **The marvelous usefulness of the Indian Nut-Tree.**

1. We have at length come to the fourth and last consideration of **Plants**, namely, their **use** and **profitability**. We shall say nothing now of those larger **trees** that are fit for **timber**, which are the necessary materials for the **building** of ships and magnificent houses, to adorn the Earth and make the life of man more splendid and delightful; as well as for the erecting of those holy **structures** consecrated to Divine Worship. Among these we must not forget that famous edifice, that glorious Temple at **Jerusalem**, consecrated to the great God of Heaven and Earth. Indeed, it was most appropriate that He—whose guidance and providence did not allow the strength of the Earth to waste itself in worthless gravel and pebbles instead of quarries of stone, nor in briars and brushwood instead of pines, cedars, and oaks—should at some time or other have the most stately, magnificent **temples** erected to Him that the wit and industry of man and the best of those materials could provide. It is the most suitable expression of thanks for that act of Providence that can be imagined. It is this very consideration that moved the pious King David to plan the building of a temple to the God of **Israel**: "*See now*," says he, "*I dwell in a house of Cedar, but the Ark of God dwells within curtains.*" <note>2 Samuel 7:2.</note> But, as I said, I will add nothing more concerning these things, being satisfied with what I have touched upon previously.

2. We will now briefly take notice of the **profitability** of plants for **medicine** <note>original: "Physick"</note>.

2. ...**medicine** <note>original: "Physick"</note> and food, and then pass on to the consideration of *animals*. As for their *medicinal uses*, the large herbals that are available everywhere are such ample evidence of this that I have said enough by simply reminding you of them. What is most remarkable here is that brute *beasts* share in these benefits as well as *men*. For the *toad*, when overloaded with the poison of the *spider* (as is commonly believed), turns to the *plantain leaf*. The *weasel*, when she is about to encounter a *serpent*, arms herself by eating *rue*. The *dog*, when he is sick to his stomach, knows his cure: he eats *grass*, vomits, and is well. The *swallows* make use of *celandine* <note>Celandine was traditionally thought to heal the eyes of swallows; its name comes from the Greek word for swallow, 'chelidon'.</note>, and the *linnet* uses *eyebright* <note>original: "Euphragia"</note> to repair their *sight*. And the *donkey*, when he is oppressed with melancholy, eats the herb *asplenium* (also known as *miltwaste*) and thus eases the swelling of his *spleen*. And *Virgil* <note>A famous Roman poet (70–19 BC).</note> reports of *Cretan dittany* <note>original: "Dictamnum Cretense"</note> that *wild goats* eat it when they are shot with darts or arrows; for that herb has the power to work the weapons out of their bodies and heal the wound.

->Those grasses are not unknown to wild goats,<-
->when swift arrows have stuck in their backs.<-
<note>original Latin: "non illa feris incognita Capris / Gramina, cùm tergo volucres hæsere sagittæ."</note>

I believe these things are clear signs <note>original: "indigitation," meaning a pointing out as if with a finger</note> of *Providence*. Since they do by instinct and nature what men (who possess free reason) cannot help but acknowledge is very relevant and appropriate—indeed, something the most skillful physician would approve—and since these creatures have no such reason or skill to become physicians themselves, it must be concluded that they are enabled to do these things by the power of that Principle that designed them and gave them their nature. Therefore, that Principle must possess *skill* and *knowledge*; that is, it must be *God*.

3. We now come to consider plants as they provide *food* for both humans and animals. Here we may observe that just as there was a general provision of *water*—by opening up <note>original: "setting... abroach"</note> the mountains and hills so that spring-heads and continuous streams flow together (eventually creating larger rivers with long, winding branches)—to allow all the earth's creatures to quench their thirst; so *Divine Providence* has spread her *table* everywhere. She has covered it not with a dry green carpet, but with succulent *herbage* and nourishing *grass* upon which most of the beasts of the field feed. Those that do not eat grass feed on the animals that do, and thus all their generations are sustained.

4. But because this seems more a matter of *necessity* than *choice*, I will not dwell on it. For I admit that *counsel* <note>In this context, deliberate planning or wisdom.</note> is most clearly implied where we see variety and the possibility of things being different, yet the *best* option is chosen. Therefore, I will only suggest this: although it was necessary for something like *grass* to exist if such creatures were to live in the world, it was not at all necessary for *grass* and *herbs* to have the *color* they do. They could have been *red* or *white*, or some other color that would have been very offensive and harmful to our sight. But I will not dwell on

these things; let us now consider the *fruits of trees*, where I think it will appear very clearly that there was one and the same Author for both Man and them, and that he certainly knew what he was doing when he made them. For could *apples*, and *oranges*, and *grapes*, and *apricots* <note>original: "Apricocks"</note>, and such similar fruit, be intended for *beasts* that hold their heads downward and can scarcely look up at them, much less know how to reach them? When we feed our dogs, we set the dish or platter <note>original: "trencher"</note> on the ground, not on the table. 

But you will say that eventually these fruits will fall down, and then the animals may reach them. However, for one thing, there are not many animals that desire them, and so they would rot upon the ground before they were consumed; or they would be squandered away in a moment of time, as might easily happen with that most precious of plants, the *vine*. But *Man*, who knows the worth of the *grape*, knows how to preserve it for a long season (for it is both eaten and drunk some years after the vintage), just as he also gathers the rest of the fruits of the earth and lays them up for both himself and his cattle. Therefore, it is plainly discoverable that Man’s arrival into the world is not a matter of *chance* or *necessity*, but a *design*—like the bringing of worthy guests to a well-furnished table.

5. And what I have suggested concerning the *vine* is as remarkably, if not more remarkably, observable in the ordinary kinds of *grain* <note>original: "Bread-corn"</note>, such as *wheat* and *barley* and the like. These also, like the vine, are made either *edible* or *drinkable* by Man’s art and industry. But that is not the point I care most to observe. What I am aiming at now is this: that *grain*, which brings such a considerable increase through *farming* <note>original: "Tillage"</note> and *agriculture* <note>original: "Husbandry"</note>, would scarcely exist at all without it; for that which grows wildly on its own is worth nothing. 

But because it is such a wholesome and strengthening food, the fact that it yields such a plentiful harvest—and that this does not happen without human art and industry—plainly implies that there is a *Divine Providence* that intended to exercise the wit of Man in *agriculture* and *farming*. We may be all the more firmly assured of this if we add to it the careful provision of *tools* so exactly fitted for this employment: namely, the laborious *ox*, and the stout but easily manageable *horse*; *iron* for the plowshare, and *ropes* for the horse harnesses to pull by. 

It is very appropriate to take notice of this last point, as it belongs to this consideration of the *profitability* of *plants*. I appeal to anyone who will take the pains for a moment to consider of what great use and consequence *cordage* (rope-making) is in the affairs of men, whether it was not a palpable *act of Providence* to send such plants out of the earth that would provide it. For we can discover no necessity in Nature that there must be such plants as *hemp* and *flax*. Therefore, if we will only follow the easy suggestions of free reason, we must attribute it to *Providence*. Providence has provided Mankind with such a commodity that no less a matter depends upon it than all the *tackling* of ships, their *sails* and *cable ropes*, and what not? Consequently, this includes all foreign trade, and the transportation of wood and stone and other necessary materials for building, or the carrying of them by land in wagons <note>original: "Wains"</note> and carts, besides the ordinary use of pulleys or other *machines* <note>original: "Engines"</note> for lifting heavy weights, which the strength of Man without these helps would not easily master;

master; besides what I hinted at before concerning the use of *cordage* (ropes) in *farming* <note>original: "husbandry"</note>, for plowing and carrying home the fruits of the Earth. The *uses* indeed of the previously mentioned *plants* are so universal, and play a part in every human affair, that if it were permissible to be a little lighthearted in such a serious matter, one might appropriately apply that verse of the poet to this common commodity:

->*All things for man hang by a slender thread;* <note>original: "Omnia sunt homini tenui pendentia filo"</note><-

that all the business of men depends very much upon these little, long strands <note>original: "sleaks"</note> or threads of *hemp* and *flax*. Or if you say that some clumsy alternative might be made without them, using long iron chains or woolen sails and the like; yet seeing ourselves provided for infinitely better, we should in all reason judge this to proceed from no lesser principle than *Divine Providence*.

6. I might now reach out to *exotic plants*, such as the *cinnamon tree*, the *balsam tree*, the tree that bears the *nutmeg* enveloped in *mace*, as also the famous *Indian nut tree* <note>the coconut tree</note>, which provides almost all the necessities of life at once. For if they only cut the twigs in the evening, a plentiful and pleasant juice comes out, which they collect in bottles and drink instead of *wine*, and from which they extract a *spirit* <note>original: "Aqua vitæ," literally "water of life"</note> that is a very powerful remedy against all kinds of illnesses. They make their *houses* from the branches and boughs; and the trunk <note>original: "body"</note> of the tree, being very spongy inside though hard outside, they easily adapt into the frame and use of their *canoes* or *boats*. The kernel of the nut serves them for *bread* and *meat*, and the shells for *cups* to drink from; and indeed they are not mere empty *cups*, for a delicious, cooling milk is found in them. Besides, there is a kind of *hemp* that encloses the nut, from which they make *ropes* and *cables*, and from the finest part of it, *sails* for their ships. The leaves are so hard and sharp-pointed that they easily make needles or bodkins <note>a thick, blunt needle for piercing cloth or leather</note> from them for stitching their sails and for other necessary purposes. And so that *Providence* may show herself *kind* <note>original: "benign"</note> as well as *wise*, this notable plant is not restricted to one coast of the world—such as the *East Indies*—but is also found in parts of *Africa* and in all the islands of the *West Indies*, like *Hispaniola* and *Cuba*, as well as on the mainland at *Carthagena* in *Panama*, *Norumbega* <note>a name used by early explorers for a region in northeastern North America</note>, and several other parts of the *New World*.

But I thought it best not to dwell on these things, but to limit myself to the scope of such objects as are familiarly and ordinarily before our eyes, so that we may better take the opportunity to return thanks to him who is the bountiful author of all the supports of life.

### CHAPTER 8.

*1. The designed usefulness of animals for man, specifically the dog and the sheep. 2. Also of the ox and other animals. 3. Of man's subduing the creatures to himself. 4. Of those that are as yet untamed. 5. The excellent usefulness of the horse. 6. The usefulness of some animals that are enemies to such animals as are hateful or troublesome to man.*

1. We have now come to take a view of the nature of animals. In contemplating them, we shall use much the same method we did for *plants*, for we shall consider in them also their beauty, their *birth*, their *makeup* and *structure* of body, and their *usefulness* to mankind. To address this last point first: it is wonderfully easy and natural to conceive that, as almost all things are made in some way or other for human use, some are so notoriously and evidently so that we cannot deny it without doing great violence to our reason. To give examples of things that are most obvious and familiar: when we see in the solitary fields a *shepherd*, his *flock*, and his *dog*, how well they are fitted together; when we knock at a farmer's door, and the first to answer is his vigilant *mastiff*, whom from his use and office he ordinarily names *Keeper*. (And I remember *Theophrastus* <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle</note> in his character sketch *On Rusticity* <note>original Greek: "Peri agroikias"</note> tells us that his master, when he has let the stranger in, *taking his dog by the snout* <note>original Greek: "epilabomenos tou rynchous"</note>, will relate long stories of his usefulness and the services he does for the house and those in it: *This is he that keeps the yard, the house, and those within* <note>original Greek: "Houtos phylassei to chorion kai ten oikian kai tous endon"</note>). Finally, when we view in the open countryside <note>original: "Champain"</note> a brace of swift *greyhounds* coursing a good, stout, and well-breathed *hare*, or a pack of harmonious *hounds* and huntsmen on horseback with pleasure and speed pursuing their game, or hear them blowing their horns near a woods-side so that the whole wood rings with the echo of that music and the cheerful yelping of the eager *dogs*—to say nothing of *duck-hunting*, *fox-hunting*, *otter-hunting*, and a hundred more such sports and pastimes that are all performed by this one kind of *animal*—I say, when we consider this diverse harmony and fitness of things in reference to ourselves, how can we withhold from inferring that whatever made *dogs*, *ducks*, *hares*, and *sheep* made them with a reference to us, and knew what it was doing when it made them? And though it is possible to be otherwise, yet it is highly improbable that the flesh of *sheep* should not be designed for food for men, and that *dogs* (which are such a familiar and domestic creature to man) among other clever feats they do for him, should not be intended to supply the place of a *servant* <note>original: "Servitour"</note> as well, and to take away the bones and scraps so that nothing might be lost. And unless we should expect that nature should make jackets <note>original: "Jerkins"</note> and stockings grow out of the ground, what could she do better than afford us such fit materials for clothing as the wool...

<meta>This page continues the argument that animals were designed for human use. It moves from discussing domestic animals like sheep and oxen to the role of wild animals and the specific utility of the horse.</meta>

...the wool of the sheep, since man has the intelligence and skill to make use of it? I will say nothing of the *silkworm*, which seems to come into the world for no other purpose than to furnish man with more costly clothing, spinning away her very entrails to make him elegant on the outside.

2. Again, when we view those large bodies of *oxen*, what can we better imagine them to be than so many living and walking pickling tubs? As *Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher</note> says of fishes, they have "a soul instead of salt" <note>original: "animam pro Sale"</note>; their life serves only as salt to keep them fresh until we have need to eat them. Besides, their *hides* afford us *leather* for *shoes* and *boots*, just as the *skins* of other beasts also serve other uses. Indeed, man seems to be brought into the world on purpose so that the rest of creation might be improved to its utmost usefulness and advantage. For is it not better that the *hides* and *flesh* of beasts should be put to such significant use as to *feed* and *clothe* men, than that they should rot and smell upon the ground? Without man, they would fail to reach such a noble purpose as to be the subject for the exercise of human *intelligence*, and to afford him the necessary conveniences of life. If man did not make use of them, they would either die of old age or be torn to pieces by more cruel masters. Therefore, we plainly see that it is an *act of reason and planning* to have made man, so that he might be a lord over the rest of creation and maintain order among them.

3. Being furnished with fit materials to make himself weapons, as well as with natural intelligence and bravery, man gave battle to the very fiercest of them. He either chased them away into wildernesses and deserts, or else brought them under his control and gave laws to them. Under these laws, they live more peaceably and are better provided for (or at least might be, if men were good) than they could be when they were left to the mercy of the *lion*, *bear*, or *tiger*. And what if he does occasionally and systematically kill some of them for food? Their death is quick, and so less painful than the paw of the bear, the teeth of the lion, or the long-lasting misery and sadness of old age, which would first torture them and then kill them, letting them rot upon the ground, smelly and useless.

Besides, all the intelligence and philosophy in the world can never prove that the killing and slaughtering of a beast is anything more than striking a bush where a bird's nest is located—where you scare away the bird and then seize the empty nest. So, if we could see the final outcome <note>original: "Catastrophe"</note> of things, it might all prove to be nothing but a *tragicomedy*.

4. But as for those *rebels* that have fled into the *mountains* and *deserts*, they provide us with a very pleasant subject for *natural history*. Besides, we make use of them as much as suits our purpose; they are not only ornaments of the universe, but a continual exercise for man’s intelligence and bravery whenever he chooses to encounter them. To expect and wish that there were nothing but such dull, tame things in the world that will neither bite nor scratch is as groundless and childish as wishing there were no *bile* <term>original: "Choler"; one of the four humors in ancient medicine, thought to cause heat and anger</term> in the body, or no *fire* in the universal span of nature.

5. I cannot dwell upon the whole result of this war, nor must I forget how that noble animal the *horse* finally had the sense to submit, to his own great advantage and ours. And truly, he is so fitly made...

# CHAPTER VIII.

1. We have now come to take a view of the nature of *animals*. In contemplating them, we shall use much the same method as we did with *plants*. We will consider their *beauty*, their *birth*, the *structure* <note>original: "Make and Fabrick"</note> of their bodies, and their *usefulness to mankind*. To address this last point first: it is wonderfully easy and natural to conceive that, while almost all things are made in some way or another for human use, some are so obviously and evidently designed for us that we cannot deny it without doing great violence to our reason. To give examples of things that are most common and familiar: when we see in the solitary fields a *shepherd*, his *flock*, and his *dog*, how well they are fitted together; or when we knock at a farmer's door, and the first to answer is his vigilant *mastiff*—whom, because of his job, he usually names "Keeper." (I remember that *Theophrastus* <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle</note>, in his character sketch *On Rusticity* <note>original: Περὶ ἀγροι- κίας (*Peri agroikias*)</note>, tells us that after the master has let a stranger in, he will grab his *dog* by the snout <note>original: ἐπιλαβόμενος τ’ ῥύγχος</note> and tell long stories of the dog's usefulness and the services he performs for the house and the family: *This one guards the farm, the house, and those inside* <note>original: Οὗτος, φυλάσσει τὸ χωρίον κ’ τὴν οἰκίαν κ’ τὸυς ἔνδον</note>.)

Finally, consider when we see in the open *countryside* <note>original: "Champain"</note> a pair of swift *greyhounds* chasing a strong and fast *hare*, or a pack of harmonious *hounds* and *huntsmen* on horseback pursuing their game with pleasure and eagerness; or when we hear them blowing their horns near a forest so that the whole wood rings with the echo of that music and the cheerful yelping of the eager *dogs*. I will say nothing of *duck hunting*, *fox hunting*, *otter hunting*, and a hundred other such sports and pastimes, all performed by this one kind of *animal*. When we consider this diverse fitness of things in relation to ourselves, how can we help but conclude that whatever made *dogs*, *ducks*, *hares*, and *sheep*, made them with us in mind and knew what it was doing? Though it is possible to imagine otherwise, it is highly improbable that the flesh of *sheep* was not designed for human food. It is also unlikely that *dogs*—which are such familiar, domestic creatures to man—were not intended to serve as a servant as well, performing clever feats and cleaning up bones and scraps so that nothing is wasted. Unless we expect Nature to grow jackets <note>original: "Jerkins"</note> and stockings out of the ground, what could she do better than provide us with such excellent materials for clothing as the wool...

# CHAPTER VIII. An Antidote against Atheism.

...the wool of the sheep, given that humans have the wit and skill to make use of it? To say nothing of the *silkworm*, which seems to come into the world for no other purpose than to furnish humans with more costly clothing, spinning away its very entrails to make us elegant.

2. Again, when we view those large bodies of *oxen*, what can we better imagine them to be than so many living and walking powdering tubs <term>original: "Powdring-Tubs"; barrels used for salting and preserving meat</term>? We might say they have *a soul instead of salt* <note>original: "animam pro Sale"</note>, as *Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher</note> says of fish—that their life serves only as salt to keep them fresh until we need to eat them. Besides, their *hides* provide us with *leather* for *shoes* and *boots*, just as the *skins* of other beasts serve other purposes. Indeed, humans seem to have been brought into the world specifically so that the rest of creation might be improved to the greatest usefulness and advantage. For is it not better that the *hides* and *flesh* of beasts should be put to such considerable use as to *feed* and *clothe* mankind, than that they should rot and stink upon the ground? This use allows for a noble improvement, serving as a subject for the exercise of human wit and providing the necessary conveniences of life. If humans did not make use of them, they would either die of old age or be torn to pieces by more cruel masters. Therefore, we plainly see that it is an act of *reason* and *deliberation* <note>original: "Counsel"</note> to have made man, so that he might be a lord over the rest of creation and maintain order <note>original: "keep good quarter"</note> among them.

3. Being furnished with the right materials to make weapons, as well as with natural wit and courage, man waged battle against even the fiercest animals. He either chased them away into solitudes and deserts or else brought them under his subjection and gave laws to them. Under human rule, they live more peacefully and are better provided for (or at least could be, if men were good) than they could be when left to the mercy of the *lion*, *bear*, or *tiger*. And what if he occasionally and orderly kills some of them for food? Their death is quick, and so less painful <note>original: "dolorous"</note> than the paw of the bear, the teeth of the lion, or the tedious misery and sadness of old age, which would first torture them and then kill them, leaving them to rot on the ground, stinking and useless.

Besides, all the wit and philosophy in the world can never prove that the killing and slaughtering of a beast is anything more than striking a bush where a bird's nest is: you scare away the bird and then seize the empty nest. So, if we could see the final outcome <note>original: "Catastrophe"</note> of all things, it might all prove to be nothing but a *tragicomedy*.

4. But as for those *rebels* that have fled into the *mountains* and *deserts*, they provide us with a very pleasant subject for *natural history*. Furthermore, we make use of them as much as suits our purpose; they are not only ornaments of the universe but a continual exercise for human wit and courage whenever we choose to encounter them. But to expect and wish that there were nothing but such dull, *tame* things in the world that will neither bite nor scratch is as groundless and childish as wishing there were no *anger* <note>original: "Choler"; in the medical theory of the time, one of the four "humors" or fluids that governed temperament and health</note> in the body, nor *fire* in the entire scope of nature.

5. I cannot dwell upon the entire result of this war, nor must I forget how that noble animal the *horse* finally had the wit to surrender himself, to his own great advantage and ours. And truly, he is so fitly made

For this purpose, the *cat* is very serviceable. And there is in the *West Indies* a beast in the form of a bear, which *Cardan* <note>Gerolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an influential Italian Renaissance polymath</note> calls the *Ant-bear* <note>original: "Ursus Formicarius"; the Giant Anteater</note>, whose very business it is to eat up all the *ants*, with which some parts of that quarter of the world are sometimes excessively plagued.

We might also add various examples of living creatures that not only have a singular affection for mankind but are also fierce enemies to those things that are very harmful and cruel to man. Such are the *lizard*, an enemy to the *serpent*; the *dolphin*, to the *crocodile*; the *horse*, to the *bear*; the *elephant*, to the *dragon* <note>In historical natural history, "dragon" often referred to large constricting serpents or pythons</note>, and so on. But I do not wish to dwell upon these things.

...fitting parts in all. For not all men and women are exquisitely handsome—indeed, very few are—so that those who are may raise greater admiration in the minds of others, and sharpen their natural abilities for brave adventures in either valor or poetry. But as for the brute creatures, though some of them have a hateful appearance, such as the *toad*, the *swine*, and the *rat*; yet these are like *discords* in music, which make the succeeding chord sound more pleasant. Indeed, most of those momentary inconveniences that human life encounters from time to time only serve to give a greater edge and vigor to our enjoyments.

2. But it is not hard to find many creatures that are either *beautiful things* <note>original: "καλὰ χρήματα" (kala chremata)</note> or *elegant* <note>original: "ἀσεῖα" (asteia)</note>, as the Philosopher distinguishes; they are either very goodly and *beautiful*, or at least *elegant* and *pretty*, as most of your *birds* are. But for *stateliness* and *majesty*, what is comparable to a *horse*? Whether you look upon him alone, with his mane and his tail waving in the wind, and hear him running and neighing in the pastures; or whether you see him with some gallant *hero* on his back, performing gracefully his useful postures and practicing his exploits of *war*; who can withhold from concluding that *Providence* brought these two together? They are fitted so well to each other that they seem like one complete spectacle of nature. This sight even deceived the unrefined people near *Thessaly* <note>A region in Greece famous for its ancient cavalry</note> and gave rise to the fable of the *Centaurs*, as if they had been one living creature made up of *horse* and *man*.

3. *That which I am aiming at is this: there exists a goodliness in the bodies of animals, such as in the ox, greyhound, and stag; or a majesty and stateliness, as in the lion, the horse, the eagle, and the rooster; or a solemn awe-inspiring quality <term>original: "grave Awfulness"</term>, as in your best breed of mastiffs; or elegance and prettiness, as in your smaller dogs and most sorts of birds. All of these are various modes of beauty. Since beauty is an intellectual object—just as symmetry and proportion are (which I proved sufficiently in what I spoke concerning the beauty of plants)—it naturally follows that the Author or Creator of these creatures which are deemed beautiful must himself be Intellectual, as he has designed such pleasing objects for the mind or intellect of man.*

4. After their *beauty*, let us touch upon their *birth* or *manner of reproduction*. And here I appeal to any man: is the design of *male* and *female* in living creatures not a genuine effect of *wisdom* and *purpose* <note>original: "Counsel"</note>? For it is notoriously obvious that these are made for one another, and both for the continuation of the *species*. For even if we should admit, with Cardan <note>Gerolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an influential Italian Renaissance polymath</note> and other naturalists, that the *earth* at first brought forth all kinds of *animals* as well as *plants*, and that they might have been fastened by the navel to their common mother, the earth, just as they are now to the *female* in the womb—yet we see she has grown sterile and barren, and her direct births of *animals* are now very insignificant. Therefore, what can it be but *Providence* that, while the earth was still fertile, she sent out *male* and *female*? This ensured that when her own reproductive power was exhausted, she might still serve as a "dry-nurse" or a helpful grandmother to thousands of generations. And I say it is *Providence*, not *chance* nor *necessity*; for what can be imagined in the parts of *matter* that...

5. For whatever is perpetual does not happen by *chance*. 6. Nor is it useful to reply (if you are willing to take such a large leap as to jump from the land into the water to fish for objections) that the *eel*—which according to *Pliny* and *Aristotle* is an *animal with blood* <note>original: "ζῶον ἔναιμον" (zoon enaimon)</note>—has no distinction of *sex*. If it does not, there is a good reason: that creature arises from the kind of *matter* that will never fail to generate. There will be mud to serve this purpose as long as there are rivers, and rivers will not fail as long as there is a sea. Therefore, this actually points toward a discerning Providence, which knew the nature and course of all things beforehand and made her arrangements accordingly, doing nothing superfluously or in vain.

7. However, in other *generations* that are more risky, even though they sometimes occur through decaying matter, Providence still makes them *male* and *female*, as is evident in *frogs* and *mice*. We should not be shocked that such careful provision is made for such contemptible *vermin* as we imagine them to be. This feeling only comes from *pride* and *ignorance*, or a haughty presumption that because we are encouraged to believe that, in some sense, all things are made for *man*, they are therefore not made for themselves at all. But anyone who speaks this way is ignorant of the nature of *God* and the knowledge of things. For if a good man is merciful to his beast, then surely a good *God* is bountiful and kind, and takes pleasure in the fact that all his creatures—those that have life and sense and are capable of any enjoyment—enjoy themselves. So, regarding the swarms of little *vermin*, *flies*, and innumerable other tiny creatures, we should congratulate their coming into *being* rather than murmuring sullenly and scornfully against their existence. They find nourishment in the world that would be lost if they did not exist, and they are, in turn, useful nourishment for others that prey upon them.

Furthermore, *life* is divided into such infinite numbers of individuals that have their own distinct senses and pleasures, and are sufficiently provided with contentment. These little *souls* are, in a way, just as significant for receiving and experiencing the overflowing goodness of the first Source of all things as the *ox*, the *elephant*, or the *whale*. For it is *sensitivity*, not *size*, that makes things capable of enjoyment.

Therefore, it was fitting that there should be a safe provision made for the propagation and continuation of all *kinds* of living creatures—not only those that are *good*, but also those that we rashly and thoughtlessly call *evil*. For they are at least good enough to enjoy themselves and to partake in the bounty of their Creator. But if they grow annoying and trouble-

8. But to return to the point at hand: there are also other manifest traces of *Providence* <note>Divine care or guidance</note> that the *reproduction* <note>original: "Generation"</note> of living creatures will reveal to us; for example, the manner of the *procreation of fish and birds*. For since there is that notable difference in animals, that some of them are *oviparous* <note>egg-laying</note> and others are *viviparous* <note>bearing live young</note>; the fact that *winged creatures* <note>original: "τὰ πτηνὰ" (ta ptena)</note> (as *Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher</note> categorizes them by that general term), both *fish* and *birds*, should be *oviparous* is a plain sign of purpose and *Providence*. For though it might be granted that their *species* could continue and survive even if they had been *viviparous*, it would have reduced their individual numbers to very few.

For as for *fish*, since *grass* and *herbs* are not the fruit of the sea, it was necessary for them to feed upon one another, and therefore for them to multiply in great abundance. They could not have done this in anything near the numbers they now do if they had been *viviparous*, as four-footed beasts are. But being now *oviparous*, and the smaller kinds being so numerous to begin with and producing such infinite numbers of spawn, their generations are neither extinct nor limited <note>original: "scanted"</note>, but are as plentiful as any creatures on the land.

And the reason why *birds* are *oviparous* and lay *eggs*, but do not bring forth their young alive, is so that there might be a greater abundance of them also, and so that neither birds of prey, the serpent, nor the fowler <note>a hunter of birds</note> should restrict their numbers too much. For if they had been *viviparous*, the burden of their womb—if they had carried any significant number at one time—would have been so big and heavy that their wings would have failed them, and so everyone would *have had the sense to catch the old one* <note>an old proverb meaning the bird would be too slow to escape</note>. Or if they bore only one or two at a time, they would have been troubled all year long with feeding their young or carrying them in their womb; besides, there would have been a necessity for too frequent mating <note>original: "Venery"</note>, which would have been very harmful to their dry bodies <note>original: "carcases"; in the 17th century, this often referred to a living body</note>. It was very reasonable, therefore, that *birds* should propagate by laying *eggs*.

9. But this is not the only advantage we shall gain from this consideration. I ask further: what is it that makes the *bird* prepare her *nest* with such artistry, to sit upon her eggs once she has laid them, and to distinguish between these and her useless waste? Did she learn it from her mother before her? Or rather, does she not do she knows not what, yet does exactly what ought to be done by the appointment of the most exquisite *Knowledge* that exists? Therefore, something else has *knowledge* for her: the Maker and Contriver of all things, the *Omniscient* and *Omnipotent God*.

And though you may reply that the *hatching* of their *eggs* is necessary, otherwise their generations would cease, I answer that all the details and refinements of *brooding* them are not strictly necessary. They might have made do on the ground in the grass, and not made such elaborate and safe *nests* in bushes and trees. Besides, if all

If things were left to *Chance*, it is far easier to conceive that there should have been no such things as Birds at all, than that blind *Matter* should ever have stumbled upon such lucky instincts as those that seem barely necessary for their survival.

10. But you will object that the ostrich lays eggs and does not hatch them herself, so that these things occur by *Chance* rather than *Providence* <note>Divine care or guidance</note>. However, this actually argues for a more exquisitely discerning *Providence* than any argument against it. For the heat of the ground—much like those *ovens* in *Egypt* that *Diodorus* <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE who described Egyptian egg incubators</note> speaks of—where she lays them, proves effective for the production of her young. So *Nature* does not tie the female to this tedious service where it is needless and useless; as is also the case with *Fish*, who, once they have spawned, are discharged of any further trouble. This is a most manifest discovery of a very curious and watchful *Eye of Providence*, which suffers nothing to be done clumsily <note>original: "ineptly"</note> and in vain.

11. I will only make one more use of this observation regarding the *Birth of Animals*, and then pass on to what remains. It is observed by those who are more attentive watchers of the works of *Nature* that the *fetus* is framed out of some *homogeneous* <note>original: "homogeneal"; uniform or of the same kind throughout</note> *liquor* or moisture, in which there is no variety of parts of *Matter* to be shaped into bones and flesh. For example, in an *egg*, around the third day that the *hen* has sat on it, in that part where *Nature* begins her work of formation <note>original: "efformation"</note>, everything is turned into a *crystalline liquid substance* around her. Similarly, several *insects* are bred from little drops of dew. In all other forms of generation, it is supposed by these observers that *Nature* first wipes the writing tablet <note>original: "Table-book"</note> clean, and then portrays upon it whatever she pleases. 

And if this is her course—to break down the subject *Matter* into as perfect an absence <note>original: "Privation"</note> of *Form* as she may, making it as *homogeneous* as possible, yet *liquid* and pliable to her *Art* and *Skill*—it is to me very highly probable, if not necessary, that there should be something besides this *fluid Matter* that must change, alter, and guide it into that wise arrangement of parts that we afterwards find in it. For how should the parts of this *liquid Matter* ever come into this exquisite structure <note>original: "Fabrick"</note> of themselves? This may convince any *Atheist* that there is a *Substance* besides *physical* <note>original: "corporeal"</note> *Matter*; a concept he is as loath to admit as he is to admit that there is a *God*.

For since there is nothing else in *Nature* but *Substance* <note>original: "Substantia"</note> or *Property* <note>original: "Modus"</note>, and since this power of arranging the *liquid Matter* into such order and shape is incompatible with the *liquid Matter* itself, it must be the *Property* <note>original: "Modus"</note> of some other *Substance* hidden within the *fluid Matter* and truly distinguishable from it. This is either the *Soul*, or some seminal Form or *Archeus* <note>original: "Archeus"; a term used by Paracelsian alchemists to describe a hidden "master workman" or vital force that directs life processes</note>, as the *Chemist* calls it. These terms are all equally acceptable to me at this time, as I am aiming here only to prove there is a *Substance* besides *Matter*, so that the *Atheist* may be more easily led to acknowledge the *Existence of a God*.

12. Nor can the force of this argument be escaped by saying the *Matter* is touched and infected by the life of the female while she bore the *egg*, or that her *fancy* <note>imagination or mental influence</note> gets down into her womb.

## CHAPTER X.

1. *That the structure <note>original: "Fabrick"</note> of the bodies of animals argues for a Deity: namely the number and location of their eyes and ears; 2. As also of their legs. 3. The natural defenses <note>original: "Armature"</note> of beasts, and their use of them. 4. Of the general structure of birds and fishes. 5. The admirable structure of the mole. 6. Cardan’s <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath and physician</note> rapture upon the consideration of it. 7. Of the hare and greyhound. 8. Of the structure of the body of the camel.*

1. I come now to the last consideration of *animals*: the outward shape and structure of their bodies. When I have shown you that they could have been designed otherwise, yet are made according to the highest level of *reason* that the wit of man can conceive, it will naturally follow that they were really made by *Wisdom* and *Providence*. Consequently, it follows *that there is a God*. I ask first, in general, concerning all those creatures that have eyes and ears: could they not have had only one eye and one ear each? To make the supposition more tolerable, they might have had the eye on one side of the head and the ear on the other; or the ear on the crown of the head and the eye in the forehead. They might have lived and survived even if they had been no better provided for than this. But it is evident that their having two *eyes* and *two ears*, placed as they are, is safer, more attractive, and more useful. Therefore, since that specific design is constantly chosen—which our own *reason* deems best—we must infer that the choice proceeded from *reason* and *deliberate plan* <note>original: "Counſel"</note>.

2. Again, I desire to know why there are no three-footed beasts (when I speak thus, I do not mean *monsters*, but a constant *species* or kind of *animal*). Such a creature as that would make a limping effort to live just as well as those that have *four* legs. Or why do some beasts not have more than four feet—suppose *six*—with the two middle ones shorter than the rest, hanging like the two legs of a man on horseback by the horse's sides? It is no harder a thing for Nature to make such body frames than others that are more elegant and useful. But since the works of Nature are neither useless nor clumsy <note>original: "inept"</note>, she must either be wise herself, or be guided by some higher...

higher **Principle** of **Knowledge**. Just as a **Man** who does nothing foolishly all the days of his life is either wise himself or consults with those who are.

3. And then again, regarding the **natural defenses** <note>original: "Armature"</note> of **Beasts**, who taught them the use of their **Weapons**? The **Lion** will not kick with his feet, but he will strike such a blow with his **Tail** that he will break the back of his **opponent** <note>original: "Encounterer"</note> with it. The **Horse** will not use his **Tail** except against busy flies, but he kicks with his **Feet** with such force that he lays his **Enemy** on the ground. The **Bull** and **Ram** know the use of their **Horns** as well as the **Horse** knows the use of his **Hoofs**. Likewise, the **Bee** and **Serpent** know their **Stings**, and the **Bear** knows the use of his **Paw**. They know these things merely by **natural instinct**, just as the **Male** knows the use of the **Female**. 

For they do not acquire this skill by observation and experience; rather, the very structure of their nature drives them to it. This is obvious in young **Lambs** that will **butt** their heads before they even have horns. Therefore, it is some higher **Providence** <note>Providence: the protective care and foresight of God</note> that has made them with the nature they possess. This is also evident in **Birds**, which will **flutter** their wings when they have only a little **Down** on them and are still utterly unable to fly.

4. Now that I have mentioned this kind of **Creature**, let me take advantage of the general structure observable in them. The shape of their **Heads** is **narrow** and **sharp** so that they may better cut through the **Air** in their **swift** flight. Also, their **Tails** spread out parallel to the **horizon** <note>horizontal</note> to better support their **Body**; they could have been vertical, like the **Tails** of **Fishes** in the water. It does not matter that the **Owl** has such a broad face, for her flight was intended to be neither as swift nor as frequent.

As for **Fishes**, to say nothing of how elegantly their **Gills** take the place of **Lungs**—being filled with the same abundance of **Veins** and **Arteries** so that their blood may be cooled by the **Water**, just as it is in the **Lungs** of other animals by the **Air**—we will take notice of simpler and more common <note>original: "vulgar"</note> observations. Regarding the **swim bladder** <note>original: "bladder of wind"</note> found in their bodies: who can say it was placed there by **chance**? Is it not clearly designed for their easier swimming? Consider also the form of their **Fins**, which consist of many gristly bones, long and slender like pins and needles, with a kind of skin in between. This design is for greater precision and makes them thin and flat like **Oars**. Such perfect craftsmanship and accuracy could have been omitted, and they still might have managed to move up and down in the water.

But I have touched upon a subject that is infinite and inexhaustible. Therefore, so that I am not too tedious, I will confine myself to a few observations of ordinary **Beasts** and **Birds** (since what is most well-known and obvious serves our purpose best), and then I shall move on to the contemplation of **Man**.

5. Indeed, what is more common and ordinary than a **Mole**? And yet, what is a more obvious argument for **Providence** than her? The parts of her body are so exactly fitted to her nature and way of life. Because her dwelling is underground where nothing can be seen, Nature has provided her with such hidden **Eyes** that **Naturalists** can hardly agree whether she has any **Sight** at all. Providence) I will content myself by only taking notice of the outward frame of a few kinds of this creature that familiarly come into our sight, such as the **cock**, the **duck**, the **swan**, and the like.

4. Now, for **swans**, **ducks**, and similar **waterfowl**, it is obvious to notice how well they are fitted for that manner of life. For those that swim, their **feet** are shaped for it like a pair of **oars**, with their **claws** being connected by a fairly broad **membrane**; and their **necks** are long so that they may dive deep enough into the water. This is also true of the neck of the **heron** and similar **birds** that live on **fish** and are obliged to frequent that element. These birds also walk on long legs like stilts, similar to the people who dwell in the **marshes**; but their **claws** have no such **membranes**, for they would only have been a hindrance to those kinds of birds that only wade in the water and do not swim.

<margin>“And for such as these, the neck becomes like a fisherman's rod, and the beak like a fishing line and a hook.” Aristotle, *On the Parts of Animals*, Book 4, Chapter 12.</margin>
**Aristotle** is clever in comparing the **long necks** of these **waterfowl** to a **fishing rod**, and their **long bills** to the **line** and **hook**. He also adds another observation concerning their **long legs**: that their **tails** are consequently shorter. I do not much admire his reasoning here, as he claims they are short because the "matter" for the tail was used up on the **legs**. Rather, the reason is that they are birds that eat less greedily; and besides, the position of their **long legs**, stretched backward while they fly, performs the function of a larger <term>uropygium</term> <note>original: ὀῤῥοπύγιον (orrhopygion); the fleshy part of a bird's tail from which feathers grow.</note>. Thus, the legs help them fly, whereas a large tail would otherwise be a trouble and a hindrance. Therefore, as I said, their **tails** are short not because the "matter" was spent on their **legs**, but because their **legs** take over the role of the **tail**, according to that excel-
<margin>Chapter 13 of the same book.</margin>
lent aphorism of **Aristotle**: <insert>“Nature does nothing in vain or superfluously.”</insert> <note>original: οὔτε περίεργον οὐδὲν οὔτε μάτην ἡ φύσις ποιεῖ</note>

This is the reason **fish** have no **legs**, though they have **fins**, and that the **torpedo** <note>An electric ray.</note> has no fins at the **sides** of its round body, but only at the sides of its **tail**; the breadth and flatness of its body serves it instead of fore-fins to swim with. Thus, Nature fittingly provides all creatures with features suitable to their temperament, and nothing is created in vain.

3. Nor should we complain about the red, puckered <note>original: "pugger'd"</note> appearance of the *turkey*, and the long *growth* <note>original: "Excrescency," referring to the snood</note> that hangs down over his beak when he swells with pride and anger. It may be a container for his heated blood, which flows so freely to his head; or he may take pleasure in it, just as the *Indians* <note>A historical reference to indigenous peoples of the Americas</note> do, whose jewels hang dangling from their *noses*. If the bird is pleased, we should not be displeased, always remembering that creatures are made to enjoy their own lives as much as to serve us; it is a sign of great ignorance and lack of sophistication <note>original: "Rusticity"</note> to think otherwise.

4. As for *swans* and *ducks*, and other *waterfowl*, it is easy to see how well they are equipped for that way of life. For those that swim, their *feet* are shaped like a pair of oars, their *claws* being connected by a fairly broad membrane <note>webbing</note>; and their *necks* are long so that they may dive deep enough into the water. Similarly, the neck of the *heron* and other such birds that live on *fish* must frequent that element; they also walk on long stilts, like people who live in marshes. But their *claws* have no such membranes, for webbing would only be a hindrance to those kinds of birds that only wade in the water and do not swim.

<margin>“And for such creatures, the neck becomes like a fisherman's rod, and the beak like the line and the hook.” <note>original: Καὶ γίνεται τοῖς τοιούτοις ὁ μὲν αὐχὴν καθάπερ ἁλιευτικὸς κάλαμος, τὸ δὲ ῥύγχος οἷον ὁρμιὰ καὶ τὸ ἄγκιστρον. Aristotle, *On the Parts of Animals*, Book 4, Chapter 12.</note></margin>

*Aristotle* is clever in comparing the long necks of these *waterfowl* to a *fishing rod*, and their long *beaks* to the *line* and *hook*. He also adds another observation concerning their long *legs*: that their *tails* are therefore shorter. I do not particularly admire his reasoning here, as he claims they are short because the "matter" <note>the biological building blocks</note> was used up on the *legs*. Instead, the reason is that they are less greedy <note>original: "voracious"</note> birds; furthermore, the position of their long *legs* stretched backward while they fly performs the function of a larger *uropygium* <note>original: ὀρροπύγιον, the fleshy part of a bird's tail from which feathers grow</note>. Thus, the legs help them fly, whereas a large tail would be a trouble and a hindrance. Therefore, as I said, their *tails* are short not because the material was spent on their *legs*, but because their *legs* serve the purpose of the *tail*, according to that excellent maxim of *Aristotle*: <margin>“Nature does nothing superfluously or in vain.” <note>original: ἔτε περίεργον ὀδὲν ἔτε μάτην ἡ φύσις ποιεῖ. Chapter 13 of the same book.</note></margin> *Nature does nothing in vain or excessively.*

This is the reason *fish* have no *legs*, though they have *fins*; and why the *torpedo* <note>a type of electric ray</note> has no *fins* at the sides of its round body, but only at the sides of its *tail*. The breadth and flatness of its body serve in place of front fins for swimming. But this study of *waterfowl* has drawn me into the subject of *fish* further than I intended.
