5. I shall return and make a short stay with the *birds*—specifically those *martial* ones, by which I mean *birds of prey*. Regarding these, the Philosopher <note>Referring to Aristotle</note> has observed that a short neck is best suited for strength. He noted that none of the *hook-taloned birds* <note>original: "γαμψώνυχα" (gampsonycha)</note> have long necks or straight beaks, but rather crooked ones; and that all carnivorous birds forced to hunt for <margin>On the Parts of Animals, book 4, chapter 12.</margin> their prey are built this way. "A creature that eats raw flesh has a crooked beak; for such a shape is useful for seizing its prey, which it must necessarily obtain from other animals" <note>original: "Γαμψὸν δ' τὸ ὠμοφάγον· χρήσιμον γὰρ πρὸς τὸ κρατεῖν τὸ τοιοῦτον· τὴν δὲ τροφὴν ἀναγκαῖον ἀπὸ ζώων πορίζεσθαι."</note>. Therefore, their crooked talons are fit to hold fast the live prey that would otherwise wriggle away from them, and their crooked beaks are designed to tear tough flesh (acting like a sharp hook) which would not be easily ripped apart by a straight beak. In contrast, the bills of *geese* and *ducks* are of an entirely different form, suited for rooting in the ground or mud, or for shearing herbs and grass—much easier ways of feeding.

Aristotle also ingeniously observed concerning *hook-taloned birds* that their bodies are quite small in comparison to their *wings*, as their greatest safety lies in flight if they are attacked. However, heavier birds are provided with other means of defense, namely either by *spurs* that grow on their legs, or by the strength and sharpness of a single claw <note>original: "cley"</note> on their foot, as I have observed in the *cassowary* <note>original: "Cassoware"</note> or *emu*. But he gives it as a maxim: *That the same birds are never hook-taloned and spur-bearing* <note>original: "γαμψώνυχα and πληκτροφόρα" (gampsonycha and plēktrophora)</note>; they never have crooked claws and spurs together. This is because the weaponry of *spurs* is only suitable for birds that fight on the ground, while hook-taloned birds are hardly equipped to even walk upon it. Therefore, none of the heavy-bodied fowl have crooked talons.

But the most remarkable thing in nature regarding these *birds of prey* is the extraordinary quality of their *sight*. Through a specialized structure of the *eye*, they are enabled to spy their prey from high up in the air; they see best at a great distance and can hardly see at all close at hand. Thus, they act as both the *archer* and the *arrow* <note>original: "Shaft"</note>: taking aim from far off, and then shooting themselves directly at the desired mark, they seize the prey the moment they strike it. The works of *Providence* are infinite. I will conclude this section with a description of that strange *Bird of Paradise*, which has become famous for its unusual nature.

6. There is a *bird* that falls dead out of the air and is sometimes found in the *Molucca* Islands which has no feet at all. The size and shape of its body and bill are much like a swallow's, but the span of its wings and tail is no less than that of an eagle. It lives and breeds in the air and never comes near the earth except for its burial; for the great size and lightness of its wings and tail support it without exhaustion <note>original: "lassitude"</note>. It is said that the laying of its eggs and the brooding of its young take place on the back of the male, which is hollowed out for this purpose, as is the breast of the female, to make incubation easier. Also, two strings—resembling two *waxed threads* <note>original: "Shoe-makers ends," referring to the heavy, waxed thread used by cobblers</note>—extend from the hind parts of the male. It is believed that he uses these to fasten himself more closely to the female while she hatches the eggs in the hollow of his back. The dew of heaven is appointed as her food, as her habitat is too far removed from the reach of flies and similar insects <note>original: "Infects"</note>.

This is the entire story and philosophy of this miraculous bird according to *Cardan* <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian polymath</note>, who claims to have seen it no fewer than three times, and to have...

7. However, so that the reproach of being too gullible does not fall on Cardan <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an influential Italian polymath</note> alone, Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a scholar who often criticized Cardan</note>—who was always looking for a chance to catch him making a mistake—does not argue with anything in the whole story except for the large size of the wings and the smallness of the body. Scaliger attempts to correct this based on a specimen sent to him from Java by Orvefanus. In fact, he confirms what his rival wrote, partly through history and partly through logic. He claims that he himself found two little birds in his own garden with membrane-like <note>original: "membranaceous"</note> wings and no legs at all; their shape was similar to a bat's. Nor is he discouraged from believing that the *Manucodiata* <term>Bird of Paradise</term> flies perpetually by the gaps in its wing feathers (which might seem to make them less able to support its body). Instead, he makes the story more plausible by what he has observed in kites hovering in the air for a whole hour, as he says, without any flapping of their wings or moving from their spot. He also found an explanation for how the bird might sleep in the air by looking at the example of fish, which he has seen sleeping in the water without sinking to the bottom or moving, but lying perfectly still, "only moving their fins with some sort of slight motion" <note>original Latin: "pinnulis tantùm nescio quid motiuncula meditantes"</note>—just as heedlessly and unconcernedly as horses flick their ears while asleep to shoo away the flies landing on them. Therefore, since Scaliger admits that the *Manucodiata* is perpetually flying in the air, he must also necessarily admit the manner of incubation Cardan describes <note>The myth that the female laid eggs on the male's back while in flight</note>; otherwise, how could their species continue?

<margin>
* Nieremberg, *Natural History*, book 10, chapter 13.
</margin>
*Francisco Hernandez* <note>A physician and naturalist who studied the flora and fauna of Mexico</note> confirms exactly what Cardan said in every detail. So does *Eusebius Nierembergius* <note>Juan Eusebio Nieremberg, a Spanish Jesuit and naturalist</note>, who is so enchanted by the story of this bird that he could not resist celebrating its miraculous properties in a short but elegant set of verses; later, though it was confidently opposed by others, he asserted the main facts again in prose.

8. Such are the supporting opinions of Cardan, Scaliger, Hernandez, and Nierembergius. However, *Aldrovandus* <note>Ulisse Aldrovandi (1522–1605), a renowned Italian naturalist</note> rejects the fable of the bird feeding on the dew of heaven and its incubation on the male's back with much scorn and indignation. Regarding the first point, his reasons are not at all trivial. He argues that dew is found near the earth and not at all times of the year, nor except on clear days and only in the morning. He also argues that the bird's constant flight would surely exhaust its energy. Lastly, he claims that dew is not a substance that is complex or varied enough to serve as food, nor is the bird's hard beak designed for such easy tasks as sipping soft moisture.

I do not know how Cardan and the others would answer this, unless they meant by "dew" the more oily moisture of the air. This moisture might not be the same everywhere, so these birds might be equipped with a natural instinct to find it where it exists. There is "dew" in this sense day and night (as well as in the morning) and in all seasons of the year; therefore, there would be a constant supply of moisture and energy to

9. In response to his great impatience regarding their method of *Incubation* <note>The process of sitting on eggs to hatch them</note>, they might conveniently offer this answer: that the method is not ridiculous, but perhaps even necessary, based on what *Aldrovandus* <note>Ulisse Aldrovandi (1522–1605), a celebrated Italian naturalist</note> himself not only acknowledges but insists upon—namely, that they have *no feet at all*. For from this it is clear that they cannot land on the ground, nor rest anywhere on their bellies and be able to take flight again. They cannot crawl out of holes in rocks as *Swifts* and other such short-footed birds can, because they have no feet at all to crawl with. Besides, as *Aristotle* rightly argues concerning the long legs of certain *waterfowl*, they were made so long because they had to wade in the water and catch fish. He adds that excellent aphorism: "For nature makes the organs for the task, not the task for the organs" <note>original Greek: Τὰ γὰρ ὄργανα πρὸς τὸ ἔργον ἡ φύσις ποιεῖ, ἀλλ' οὐ τὸ ἔργον πρὸς τὰ ὄργανα</note>. So, they will say, we may rationally conclude that just as the long legs of these waterfowl imply they are meant to frequent the water, the lack of legs in these *Manucodiatas* <term>Birds of Paradise</term> proves they are never meant to come down to the Earth, because they can neither stand there, nor walk, nor take flight again. And if they never come to the Earth or any other resting place, where can their eggs be laid or hatched but on the back of the male?

Additionally, *Cardan* <note>Girolamo Cardano, the polymath mentioned on the previous page</note> is pleased with that *Antiphony* <term>A system of natural opposites or balances</term> in nature: that just as the *Ostrich* is a bird that never flies in the air, this *Bird of Paradise* should always be in the air and never rest upon the earth. As for *Aldrovandus*’s assumption—based on the five different *Manucodiatas* he had seen—that he could observe no physical structure implying they were fit for such a method of *Incubation*, *Cardan* would answer: "I myself have seen three, and *Scaliger* has seen one, and we both agree against you."

10. However, you see that *Cardan*, *Aldrovandus*, and the rest all agree in stating that the *Manucodiata* has no feet, and in describing two strings <note>Likely referring to the long, wire-like tail feathers of certain species</note> hanging from the rear parts of its body. *Aldrovandus* claims these are found in the female as well as the male, though *Cardan's* experience did not go that far.

11. But *Pigafetta* <note>Antonio Pigafetta (c. 1491–c. 1531), an explorer who chronicled Magellan's voyage</note> and *Clusius* <note>Carolus Clusius (1526–1609), an influential botanist and naturalist</note> will easily end this great controversy between *Cardan* and *Aldrovandus*, if what they report is true, and if they are speaking of the same kind of Birds of Paradise. For they both affirm, with all imaginable confidence, that these birds have feet a palm <note>A unit of measurement based on the width of a hand</note> long.

On the contrary, *Nierembergius* <note>Juan Eusebio Nieremberg (1595–1658), a Spanish Jesuit and natural historian</note> affirms that an eyewitness—one who had handled one of these birds shortly after it died—told him that it had no feet at all. *Johnston* <note>Jan Jonston (1603–1675), a Polish scholar and physician who wrote extensively on natural history</note> also agrees with *Nierembergius* on this point, although he joins *Aldrovandus* <note>Ulisse Aldrovandi (1522–1605), a celebrated Italian naturalist</note> in rejecting their supposed method of *incubation* <note>The process of sitting on eggs to hatch them</note>.

However, unless they can lift themselves from the ground using the stiffness of their wing feathers, or perhaps by means of nervous strings they may be able to stiffen while alive by sending "spirits" into them—making them serve as well as legs to push off the ground, or to hang from tree branches (since very little is needed to lift or hold up their light, feathery bodies in the air, just as a small twig can support us in water)—I am more inclined to believe the testimony of *Pigafetta* <note>Antonio Pigafetta (c. 1491–c. 1531), an Italian explorer who accompanied Magellan</note> and *Clusius* <note>Carolus Clusius (1526–1609), an influential Flemish botanist and naturalist</note> than the judgment of the others. I believe the sailors who told Pigafetta that the legs are pulled off by those who catch the birds, who then disembowel <note>original: "exenterate"</note> and dry them in the sun for personal use or for sale.

<margin>History of Animals, book 1, chapter 1.</margin>
This conclusion would best protect the reputation of *Aristotle*, who long ago so decisively pronounced: "There is no creature that only flies, just as the fish is the only creature that only swims." <note>original: Ὅτι πτηνὸν μόνον οὐδέν ἐστιν, ὥσπερ νηκτικὸν μόνον ἐστὶν ἰχθὺς</note>

12. Thus, our Bird of Paradise has completely flown away and vanished into a myth or fable. But if anyone mourns the loss of such a convincing argument for a *Providence* <note>The concept of God's intervention and design in the universe</note> that fits one thing to another, I must take the liberty to tell him that, unless he values novelty more than the logical consequences of things, I shall provide his meditations with something just as conclusive. I remind him that it will be his own fault if he cannot find as clear a conclusion from an ordinary *Truth* as from either an *Uncertainty* or a *Fiction*. In this regard, bringing this doubtful story into the discussion was not useless, as it carries with it a serious and corrective kind of irony.

The idea that the *Manucodiata* <note>An archaic name for the Bird of Paradise, from the Malay "manuk dewata" meaning "bird of the gods"</note> lives on *dew* is not what makes this story a convincing proof of *Providence*. Rather, it is the fact that it is so excellently provided with wings and feathers—*adorned with such a light apparatus* <note>original: tantâ levitatis supellectile exornata</note> (as *Nierembergius* puts it)—being so well-furnished with every advantage for lightness that it seems harder for the bird to sink down (as he imagines) than to stay afloat in the air. If a bird thus fitted for that region had no legs to stand on the earth, this would be a significant sign of a discerning *Providence* that intentionally avoids all uselessness and redundancy.

The other remarkable feature—and it is a notorious one—is the cavity on the back of the male and in the breast of the female for incubation. And the third and last is the use of those strings (as *Cardan* <note>Gerolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian polymath</note> suggests) to better keep them together during this hatching process.

If these details of this strange story affect you so strongly as to convince you of a *Providence*, consider it a matter of whim rather than judgment if the ordinary truths I offer in their place do not have the same force with you.

13. For is not the fish's lack of feet (as we observed before)—since she is sufficiently supplied with **fins** in so **thick** an element as the **water**—as great an argument for **Providence** as the fact that so light a bird lacks feet in that **thinner** element of the **air**, the extreme lightness of her physical features <note>original: "furniture"</note> being proportioned to the **thinness** of that **element**? And is not the same Providence seen, and just as clearly, in granting only very short legs to those birds called **Apodes** <note>original: *Apodes*; Greek for "footless ones"</note> (mentioned by both **Pliny** and **Aristotle**), upon whom she has bestowed such large and strong wings and a power of flying so long and swift? This is just as evident as it is in giving no legs at all to the **Bird of Paradise** <note>original: *Manucodiata*</note>, who has an even greater power of wing and lightness of body.

And as for the cavities on the back of the male and in the breast of the female <note>referring to the myth that these birds hatch eggs in a hollow on each other's bodies while flying</note>, is that design of Nature any more certain and plain than in the genital parts of the male and female in every kind of animal? What greater argument of **design** <note>original: "Counsel"</note> and purpose—of fitting one thing for another—can there be than that? And if we should make a more inward search into the construction of these parts in an ordinary **hen**, and consider how or by what force an **egg** of such great growth and size is moved from the **ovary** <note>original: *Ovarium*</note> through the **infundibulum** <note>the funnel-like opening of the oviduct</note> into the **uterine passage** <note>original: *processus of the uterus*</note> (the membranes being so thin and the passage appearing so very small), the principle of that motion cannot be thought of as anything less than **Divine**. And if you would compare the **protruding teats** <note>original: "protuberant Paps"</note> in the females of beasts with that **cavity** in the breast of the female Bird of Paradise, which of them do you think is the clearer pledge of a knowing and designing Providence?

And lastly, regarding the strings that are imagined to hold together the male and female during their **incubation** <note>original: "Incubiture"</note>, what a trivial thing <note>original: "toy"</note> it is when compared with those invisible links and ties that compel ordinary birds to sit upon their eggs, though they have no visible enticement for such a tedious service?

### CHAP. XII.

# CHAP. XII. An Antidote against Atheism.

---

1. But we did not need to wander so far into the works of Nature to seek arguments to prove a **God**, since we are so plentifully provided with proof at home that we took the trouble to search for abroad. For there can be no more ample testimony of a **God** and **Providence** than the **frame and structure of our own bodies**. The admirable **craftsmanship** <note>original: "Artifice"</note> of which **Galen**, though he was only a **naturalist** <note>original: "mere Naturalist"; someone who studies the physical world without necessarily invoking the supernatural</note>, was so captivated by it that he could not help but award the honor of a **hymn** to its wise Creator. The design of the **whole** and **every specific part** is so evident an argument of exquisite skill in the Maker that, if I were to pursue everything that suits my purpose, it would fill an entire volume. I shall therefore only hint at a few things, leaving the rest to be explained by **anatomists**. And I think there is no man who has any skill in that art but will confess that the more diligently and accurately the **frame of our body** is examined, the more it is found to be exquisitely conformable to our **reason**, **judgment**, and **desire**. Thus, assuming the same matter that our bodies are made of, if it had been in our own power to create ourselves, we would have formed ourselves no differently than we are.

2. To provide a specific example: in our **eyes**, their **number**, **location**, and **structure** <note>original: "fabrick"</note> are such that we can think of nothing to be added or altered, whether for their **beauty**, **safety**, or **usefulness**. As for their **beauty**, I will leave it to the delicate wit and pens of poets and lovers, rather than venture upon such a sensitive and subtle subject with my more serious style. I will only note how **safely** they are **guarded** and **fittingly designed** for the **use** for which they are intended. **The brow and the nose** save them from harder blows. But because a part as delicate as the **eye** is inevitably vulnerable to harm from smaller things, the **sweat of the forehead** is kept away by those two wreaths of hair which we call the **eyebrows**, and the **eyelids** are fortified with little stiff bristles—like **palisades** <note>original: "Palisadoes"; a fence of wooden stakes used for defense</note>—against the assault of flies, gnats, and similar bold **tiny creatures** <note>original: "Animalcula"</note>. Besides, the **upper lid** quickly snaps down and is as good a defense as a **portcullis** <note>a heavy, vertically-closing gate used in medieval fortifications</note> against the persistence of the enemy. This is also done every night, whether there is any immediate assault or not, as if Nature kept a garrison in this **Acropolis** <note>Greek for "high city"; a fortified citadel. Here it refers to the head</note> of man’s body and ensured that such laws were duly observed as were most necessary for his safety.

3. And now for the **use of the eye**, which is **sight**: it is evident that this organ is so exquisitely framed for that purpose that not the smallest refinement could be added. For, first, the **humors** <note>the fluids within the eye</note> and **membranes** <note>original: "Tunicles"</note> are purely **transparent**, to let in **light** and **colors** pure and uncorrupted <note>original: "unsophisticated"</note> by any internal staining. And then again, the parts of the eye are made **convex**, so that there might be a direction of many rays coming from one

the point of the object onto a corresponding point at the bottom of the *eye*; for this purpose the *crystalline lens* <note>original: "Crystalline Humour"</note> is of great importance, and without it, sight would be very obscure and weak. Thirdly, the *uvea* <note>original: "Tunica Uvea"</note> has a *muscular power* and can expand or contract that round hole within it called the *pupil* of the *eye*, to better regulate the transmission of light. Fourthly, the inside of the *uvea* is blackened like the walls of a tennis court, so that the rays falling upon the *retina* may not be reflected back onto the *uvea* and then returned from the *uvea* to the *retina* again; for such a reflection <note>original: "repercussion"</note> would make the sight more confused. Fifthly, the *arachnoid membrane* <note>original: "Tunica Arachnoides"</note>, which surrounds the *crystalline lens*, uses its *ciliary processes* <note>original: "Processus Ciliares"</note> to push forward or draw back that precious and useful part of the *eye* as the nearness or distance of the object requires. Sixthly and lastly, the *retina* <note>original: "Tunica Retina"</note> is *white*, for the better and more accurate reception of the *images* <note>original: "species"</note> of things (as they are usually called), just as white paper is best suited to receive images in a dark room. If the wit of man had been tasked to invent this *organ* for himself, what could he have possibly conceived <note>original: "excogitated"</note> that was more accurate? Therefore, to think that the *mere motion of matter*, or any other blind cause, could have hit upon such a precise design (for creatures might have survived without such exact provision) is to be either mad or foolish <note>original: "sottish"</note>.

4. And the *eye* is already so *perfect* that I believe human reason would have easily been satisfied with this and admired its own design; for since a person is able to *move* his whole *head* upward, downward, and to every side, he might have unconsciously thought himself sufficiently well-provided for. But Nature has added *muscles* to the *eyes* as well, so that no perfection might be lacking. For we often have occasion to *move our eyes* while our *head* remains *still*, as when reading or looking more closely at an object set before us; and so that this may be done with more ease and accuracy, she has furnished that organ with no less than six different *muscles*.

5. And indeed, this framing of *muscles* not only in the *eye* but in the whole *body* is remarkable. For is it not a wonder that all our flesh should be so handsomely organized into distinct pieces, whose origins and attachments <note>original: "Rise and Insertions"</note> are placed with such advantage that they serve to move some part of the body or another with such ease? And the parts of our body are moved not only as conveniently as needed for us to walk and survive, but they are able to move in every way imaginable that will benefit us. For we can swing our *legs* and *arms* upward and downward, backward, forward, and around, like those who spin wool or those who would flatten a molehill with their feet. I will say nothing of *breathing* <note>original: "Respiration"</note>, the tightening of the *diaphragm* to keep down the *intestines* <note>original: "Guts"</note> and enlarge the *chest* <note>original: "Thorax"</note> so that the *lungs* may have room to work, and the assistance of the inward *intercostal muscles* during deep sighs <note>original: "Suspirations"</note>, when we take larger gulps of air to cool a heart overcharged with love or sorrow. Nor will I speak of the curious structure of the *larynx*, so well-fitted with muscles for the control <note>original: "modulation"</note> of the *voice*, musical *speech*, and delightful *singing*. Nor, lastly, of Nature’s industriousness in making holes in the *tendons* of the second joints of both fingers and toes, and her careful threading of the tendons of the third joints through them.

6. You may add to these the remarkable design <note>original: "contrivance"</note> of the *Heart*, its two *Ventricles* and its many *valves* <note>original: "Valvulæ"</note>, so framed and situated as is most fit for the reception and transmission of the *Blood*, which comes through the *Heart* and is sent away from there warm to comfort and cherish the rest of the Body. For this purpose also the *valves* in the *Veins* are made, so that the *Blood* may more easily ascend upwards.

7. But I will rather insist upon such things as are easy and intelligible even to the unlearned <note>original: "Idiots," referring to those without specialized education</note>, who, if they can but count the *Joints* of their *Hands* or know the use of their *Teeth*, may easily discover it was *deliberate design* <note>original: "Counsel"</note>, not *Chance*, that created them. For why do we have three *Joints* in our *Legs* and *Arms*, as also in our *Fingers*, except that it was much better than having only *two* or *four*? And why are our *front teeth sharp* like chisels to cut, while our *back teeth* <note>original: "inward-teeth"</note> are *broad* to grind, except that this is more precise than having them all sharp or all broad, or the *front teeth broad* and the *others sharp*? We might have made a difficult shift to live even in that worse condition. Again, why are the *Teeth* so luckily *placed*, or rather, why are there not *Teeth* in other bones as well as in the *jawbones*? For they might have been as capable as these. But the reason is, nothing is done foolishly or in vain; that is, there is a *Divine Providence* that orders all things. Again, to say nothing of the internal complexity <note>original: "curiosity"</note> of the *Ear*, why is there that outward frame of it, except that it is certainly known to be for the improvement of our *Hearing*?

8. I might add to these that *Nature* has made the *hindmost* parts of our body which we sit upon most *fleshy*, providing for our *Ease* and making us a natural *Cushion*, as well as providing instruments of motion for our *Thighs* and *Legs*. She has made the back *part* of the *Head* stronger, as it is otherwise unprotected <note>original: "unfenced"</note> against falls and other accidents. She has made the *Backbone* of several *vertebrae* <note>original: "Vertebræ"</note>, as it is more fit to bend, more tough, and less in danger of breaking than if it were all one entire bone without those cartilaginous *joints* <note>original: "gristly Junctures"</note>. She has strengthened our *Fingers* and *Toes* with *Nails*, whereas she might have ended that substance at the first or second joint; which would not have been so handsome or useful, but rather somewhat troublesome and hurtful. And lastly, she has made all the *Bones* devoid of *sensation* <note>original: "sense"</note>, because they were to bear the weight of themselves and of the whole Body. Therefore, if they had possessed *sensation*, our life would have been continually painful and full of sorrow <note>original: "dolorous"</note>.

9. And what she has done for *us*, she has done proportionately in the design of all other *Creatures*; so that it is manifest that a *Divine Providence* runs through all things.

10. And therefore, since things are designed with such exquisite *detail* <note>original: "Curiosity"</note> as if the most watchful *Wisdom* imaginable attended to them, to say they are thus framed without the assistance of some *Principle* that possesses *Wisdom*, and that they come to pass from *Chance* or some other blind, unknowing *Origin*, is to stubbornly and whimsically <note>original: "humorously"</note> assert a thing just because we wish to assert it. Under the pretense of avoiding *Superstition*, this falls into the very thing that makes *Superstition* itself hateful or ridiculous: that is, a willful and groundless adhering to fancies without any support of *Reason*.

11. Now that I have considered how well the parts of the human body are suited for the good of the whole person, let me briefly consider the fitness of the *emotions* <note>original: "Passions"</note> of his *mind*. I will look at those that are *unique* to man, as well as those he *shares* with the rest of the animals, and also the fitness of man as a *part of the universe*. Then I shall conclude.

It is clear that *Anger* so stimulates the spirits and heightens the courage of both men and animals <note>original: "Brutes"</note> that it allows them to break through the difficulties they encounter with greater ease. *Fear* is likewise for avoiding danger, and *Hope* is a pleasant anticipation of enjoyment—much like a dog waiting while his master finishes picking a bone. There is no *Hope*, *Fear*, *Hate*, nor any specific emotion or instinct in *animals* that is in vain. Why then should we think that Nature would fail more in *us* than in any other creature? Why would she be so careful in the construction <note>original: "Fabrick"</note> of our bodies, yet so forgetful or unlucky in framing the faculties of our *souls*? If the *Fear* so naturally unique to us—namely, the *fear of a God* <note>original: "Deity"</note>—were in vain, it would be a strange oversight. The same is true of the pleasant hope and heavenly joys of the mind which humans are naturally capable of, along with the earnest direction of the spirit toward God. If these had no real object in the world, then the *religious affection* which Nature has so clearly implanted in the human soul would serve no use, except to make man either ridiculous or miserable. In contrast, we find no *emotion* or *affection* in *animals*, whether common or unique, that is not for their own good and welfare.

12. It is not for nothing that the *hare* is so afraid of the *dog*, and the *sheep* so afraid of the *wolf*. Even if there is a *fear* or *hostility* <note>original: "Enmity"</note> in some creatures for which we cannot easily see a reason regarding their own survival, we may still consider it reasonable in regards to us and serving a good purpose. But I think it is obvious that *attraction and repulsion* <note>original: "Sympathy and Antipathy"</note>, *love and hostility*, *aversion*, *fear*, and the like, are notable tools that sharpen and quicken the spirit of life in all animals. Being vulnerable <note>original: "obnoxious"</note> to dangers and encounters binds their vital powers more closely together and makes them more consciously relish their present safety. They are more pleased with an escape than if they had never met with any danger at all. Their greedy assaults upon one another, while there is *hope* of victory, also highly gratify them both. If one is conquered and killed, the conqueror enjoys a fresh increase in the pleasure of life—the triumph over his enemy. These things seem to me to be designed even for the sake of the creatures themselves, so that their vital heat and fluids <note>original: "moisture"</note> may not always merely simmer in one sluggish routine, but sometimes boil up higher and overflow when the fire of life is kindled more than usual by some sudden occasion.

13. It is beyond dispute that many of these unique *emotions* of animals are *useful* to men (such as the *lizard’s* hostility toward the *snake* <note>A reference to the historical belief that lizards would warn humans of snakes or attack them</note>). All of them highly gratify man's capacity for contemplation, and some even seem designed on purpose to make him <note>original: "his Worship," referring to Man</note> laugh. For what else could Nature intend by the *dislike* <note>original: "Antipathy"</note> between the *ape* and the *snail*? It is a funny sight that a beast which seems to so boldly claim a relation to man because of his outward shape should have so little wit or courage...

14. But if *Nature* were to implant such a strong inclination <note>original: "propension"</note> toward *Religion* in *Man*—which is the reverence of a *God* <note>original: "Deity"</note>—when there is actually no *God*, *Angel*, or *Spirit* in the world, it would be such a grave error <note>original: "Slur"</note> on her part that no excuse could be devised. If there were a higher *species* of beings to laugh at us as we laugh at the *Ape*, it might seem more tolerable. This happened in *America*, where the remorseless *Spaniards*, under the pretense of being raised in a better *religion* than the *Americans*, dehumanized the poor *natives* so much that they thought nothing of killing them <note>original: "knocking them on the head"</note> merely to feed their dogs with their bodies. There were many such unheard-of *cruelties*. 

Or consider the great affliction that this severe *governess* of human life brings upon the *souls* she seizes: terrifying horrors of *conscience*, confusing and making fools of them in the free use of their *reason*, and blocking deeper searches into the pleasing knowledge of *nature*. It brings anxious cares and disturbing fears concerning their state in the *life to come*, while restraining them from the natural and healthy enjoyments of their *present life*, making bitter all its pleasures and comforts with pangs of *conscience* and suspicions that they are doing something now for which they may suffer eternally hereafter. 

Beyond these are the unspeakable *agonies of mind* endured by those who are more profoundly <note>original: "generously"</note> *religious*. They strive to share in the *Divine Nature* and are willing—though with incredible pain—to be torn from their own desires to become one with that *Universal Spirit* which ought to guide all things. Through an insatiable desire for a just and proper state of mind (where all *arrogance* <note>original: "Arrogancy"</note> should completely vanish, and all that we have or can do is vividly and sensibly attributed to *God*), they heartily acknowledge themselves to be nothing. That is, they seek to be so little conceited, or to relish the glory and praise of *men* no more than if they had done nothing or did not exist at all. In doing so, they plunge themselves into such dampness and deadness of *spirit* that being buried alive <note>original: "buried quick"</note> would be far less torture than such dark deprivations of all the joys of life, and such sad, heart-sinking *mortifications* <note>spiritual disciplines intended to subdue the ego or physical desires</note>.

...himself to be safe and comfortable, he will dismiss all these things by asking a question similar to the one asked by the man to whom the priest of *Neptune* showed the many *offerings* <note>original: "Donaria"</note> hung up in his temple by his *followers* <note>original: "Votaries"</note> who were saved from shipwreck, and therefore boasted much of the power of that God of the Sea. *But what has become of all those,* he asked, *who despite their vows have been lost?* So, I say, the *atheist*, to evade the force of this argument, will whisper to himself, *But how many proud, blasphemous, atheistical men like myself have escaped, while those who have been considered good have died untimely deaths?*

Such were *Aesop* and *Socrates*, the *Prophets*, *Apostles*, and *Martyrs*, along with various other wise and good men in all ages and places. These men, not being fully aware of the ill condition and stubbornness of this wicked world—of which they have truly declared themselves not to be citizens, but strangers—have suffered the greatest mischiefs that can happen to human nature because of their innocent intentions and their intervening in the <term>affairs of another state</term> <note>original Latin: "aliena Republica"</note>. It has usually been safer to craftily and cautiously undermine the honor of God than to plainly and honestly seek the good and welfare of men.

2. Furthermore, the *atheist* will reply that outrageous insults committed on purpose against *Religion* have not only been applauded by the world, but left unpunished by Divine Justice. This is notorious in the case of that sacrilegious wit, *Dionysius* of *Syracuse*. When he stripped *Jupiter Olympius* of his costly robe, which was very stiff and heavy with gold, he added this mocking excuse to his sacrilege: *That this golden garment was too heavy for the summer and too cold for the winter, but one made of wool would fit both seasons.*

Similarly, at *Epidaurus*, he commanded the golden beard of *Aesculapius* to be cut off and carried away, alleging that it was very unfit for the son to wear a beard when his father *Apollo* wore none.

Another incident was not inferior to any of his sacrilegious jokes: when taking away the golden cups and crowns held out by the hands of the statues of the gods, he excused himself by saying that he received only what they gave him of their own accord. He added that it would be a very gross piece of foolishness, when we pray to the gods for all good things, not to take them when they offer them so freely with their own hands.

These and other such irreligious pranks did this *Dionysius* play, yet he fared no worse than the most serious and innocent people, dying no other death than that which other mortals usually do. It is as if in those ages there was as great a lack of *wit* as there once was a lack of *Latin* here in *England*, and that he escaped a more severe sentence by the <term>benefit of his clergy</term> <note>In historical English law, "benefit of clergy" allowed literate defendants to escape the death penalty for certain crimes by proving they could read. Here, the author uses it metaphorically to suggest Dionysius's cleverness saved him.</note>. Others think that he was paid back and punished in the person of his son who succeeded him. But the *atheist* will reply that this is merely "whipping the absent," as *Aristotle* wittily said to the person who told him that someone was unmercifully slandering him behind his back.

Therefore, I hold it more convenient to omit such arguments that may entangle us in such endless disputes, and to bring forward only those that cannot be explained by any *natural causes*, or imagined to happen by *chance*. These events are so *miraculous* that they imply the presence of some free, subtle, understanding Essence distinct from brute *matter* and the ordinary power of nature.

## BOOK III.

### CHAP. I.

*1. That good men do not always fare best in this world, so the great examples of Divine Vengeance upon wicked and blasphemous persons are not so convincing to the stubborn atheist. 2. The irreligious jeers <note>original: "Feers"—likely a typo for "Jeers," referring to Dionysius's mockery</note> and sacrileges of Dionysius of Syracuse. 3. The reason for the atheist's disbelief in things supernatural or miraculous. 4. That there have been true miracles in the world as well as false ones. 5. And what are the best and safest ways to distinguish them, so that we may not be deceived by history.*

<margin>1.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial letter H within a square frame featuring floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>
Up to this point, I have insisted upon such arguments for proving the existence of God as were taken from the ordinary and known phenomena of nature; for such is the history of plants, animals, and man. I shall come now to such effects discovered in the world as are not deemed natural, but extraordinary and miraculous. I do not mean unexpected discoveries of murders, or a conspicuous vengeance upon proud and blasphemous persons, such as Nicanor, Antiochus, Herod, and the like, of which all histories, both sacred and secular <note>original: "Profane"</note>, are very full. All these tend to impress this divine precept from the poet upon the minds of men:

> Learn justice, being warned, and do not despise the gods. <note>original Latin: "Discite Justitiam moniti & non temnere Divos." From Virgil's *Aeneid*.</note>

For though these examples cannot but move impartial <note>original: "indifferent"</note> men to an acknowledgment of Divine Providence and a superior power above and different from matter, I am now dealing with the stubborn and resistant atheist. Though he is a hardened despiser of the Deity, finding...

3. While nothing would be more compelling than these *miraculous effects* if they could be believed, there is also nothing harder for an *atheist* to believe than they are. Because <term>religious partisans</term> <note>original: "Religionists," referring here to those who zealously promote a faith</note> have—for "pious purposes," as they claim—forged so many false *miracles* to deceive and exploit a credulous public, they have thereby, along with their *atheism*, destroyed all belief in those miracles that are actually true. Furthermore, the childish and superstitious fear of *spirits* in <term>melancholic persons</term> <note>In the 17th century, "melancholy" was seen as a physical imbalance that could cause hallucinations or irrational fears</note>, who create strange *monsters* for themselves and see terrible *apparitions* in the dark, has also provided atheists with a further excuse to attribute all <term>specters</term> and strange *apparitions* to mere <term>melancholy and a disturbed imagination</term> <note>original: "Phansie"</note>.

4. But the fact that there should be such a *universal* reputation and fear of something that never was, nor is, nor ever can be in the world, is to me the greatest *miracle* of all.

For if there had not been *true miracles* at some time or another (as indeed there must be, unless the human faculties, which so easily listen to and accept such things, were created in vain), it is very improbable that priests and cunning deceivers of the people would have ever been able to impose upon them so easily with *false* ones. Just as an <term>alchemist</term> would never go about <term>counterfeiting metals</term> <note>original: "sophisticate Metalls"</note> and then passing them off as *true gold* and *silver* if it were not already acknowledged that *true gold* and *silver* exist in the world. In the same way, the very attempt to delude people with *false miracles* is a sign that there have been, and may be, those that are true.

5. But you will say there is a <term>touchstone</term> <note>a stone used to test the purity of gold; here meaning a standard of truth</note> by which we may discern the truth of <term>metals</term>, but that there is nothing by which we may discover the truth of *miracles* recorded everywhere in history. To this I answer: there is, and it is this:

First, if what is recorded was sworn to by people who had no personal goal or *interest* in swearing to such things.
Secondly, if there were many <term>eyewitnesses</term> to the same matter.
Thirdly and lastly, if these things which are so strange and miraculous leave any <term>perceptible effect</term> <note>original: "sensible effect," meaning an effect that can be perceived by the senses</note> behind them.

Though I will not claim that all those <term>stories</term> are *false* that lack these conditions, I still dare affirm that it is mere whim and stubbornness for a man to reject the *truth* of those that do have them. To do so is to believe nothing except what he sees for himself, from which it would follow that he should read nothing of history at all—for history offers neither pleasure nor usefulness if it deserves no belief.

## CHAPTER II.

*1. The moving of a sieve by a charm: Coskinomancy. 2. A magical cure of a horse. 3. The charming of serpents. 4. A strange example of one struck dead as he walked the streets. 5. A story of a sudden wind that nearly threw down the gallows at the hanging of two witches.*

1. **A**nd now that I have set out these preliminaries, I will briefly recite a few of those many *miraculous events* we meet with in writers. I will begin first with the mere and *simple actions of spirits*—as I will venture to declare them beforehand—and then afterwards we shall come to the *apparitions of spirits themselves.*

<margin>
* *On the Demon-mania of Sorcerers*, Book 2, Chapter 1. <note>original: "Mag. Dæmono-man. lib. 2. c. 1." by Jean Bodin</note>
</margin>
Of those *mere effects*, we will start with what might seem the slightest. *Bodin* relates how he himself and several others in *Paris* saw a young man move a *sieve* up and down using a *charm* spoken in *French*. And 
<margin>
* *On the Types of Ceremonial Magic*, Chapter 21. <note>original: "De speciebus Magiæ Ceremonialis, c. 21."</note>

that ordinary way of divination which they call <term>Coskinomancy</term> <note>divination using a sieve and shears to identify a thief or wrongdoer</note>—finding who stole or spoiled this or that thing by the *sieve* and *shears*—*Pictorius Vigillanus* <note>Georg Pictorius, a 16th-century physician and writer on magic</note> confesses he made use of three times, and it was successful.

2. A friend of mine told me this story concerning *charms*: He himself had a *horse* which, if he had remained healthy, would have been of great value. His servants took the horse to several <term>farriers</term> <note>blacksmiths who specialized in horse medicine</note>, but none of them had the skill to cure him. At last, without their master's knowledge, they led him to a farrier who apparently possessed some tricks beyond the ordinary, and who dealt in *charms* or *spells* and similar ceremonies. By virtue of these, he made the horse healthy again. After the owner observed how well his horse was, he asked his servants how they got him cured. When he understood the whole matter and also noticed that there was an *S.* branded on the horse's buttock—which he imagined stood for *Satan*—he scolded his servants very roughly for doing something that was unjustifiable and impious. Upon this profession of his dislike for the deed, the horse immediately fell as ill as he had ever been; he became so useless that he was forced to be turned loose in the pasture. But a kinsman of the owner, coming to his house and later chancing to see the horse in the fields, took advantage of a low price for such a handsome gelding and bought him. The horse had no sooner changed his master than he immediately changed his physical condition also, becoming as healthy as ever.

At last, one huge serpent arrived, far bigger than the rest. It leaped upon him, wound itself around his waist like a belt, and pulled him into the ditch, killing the *charmer* himself in the end.

3. And these *miraculous effects*—though nothing is more convincing if they could be believed—are the hardest things for an *atheist* to believe. Because religious figures <note>original: "Religionists"</note> have, as they claim, for "pious purposes" forged so many false *miracles* to trick and exploit gullible people, they have, in the eyes of the *atheist*, ruined the credibility of those that are actually true. 4. But that there should be such a *universal report* <note>original: "fame"</note> and fear of something that never was, nor is, nor ever can be in the world, seems to me the greatest *miracle* of all. For if there had not been *true miracles* at some point in time (as indeed there must be, if the human mind—which so easily listens to and accepts such things—was not created in vain), it is very unlikely that priests and clever deceivers of the people would have ever been able to trick them so easily with *false* ones. Just as an *alchemist* would never try to adulterate <note>original: "ſophiſticate"</note> *metals* and pass them off as *true gold* and *silver* unless it was already established that *true gold* and *silver* actually exist in the world. In the same way, the very attempt to deceive people with *false miracles* is a sign that there have been, and can be, those that are *true*.

5. But you will say that there is a *touchstone* <note>a stone used to test the purity of gold and silver; metaphorically, a standard for testing truth</note> by which we may judge the quality of *metals*, but there is no such thing for discovering the truth of *miracles* recorded throughout *history*. But I answer: There is, and it is this.
First, if what was recorded was vouched for by people who had *no personal gain or interest* in claiming such things.
Second, if there were many *eye-witnesses* to the same event.
Third and finally, if these strange and miraculous events leave any *tangible effect* <note>original: "ſenſible effect," meaning an effect that can be perceived by the senses</note> behind them.
While I will not admit that all stories lacking these conditions are *false*, I dare say it is pure stubbornness and cynicism for a person to reject the *truth* of those that do meet them. To do so is to believe nothing except what he sees for himself; from this it would follow that he should read no history at all, for history has neither pleasure nor usefulness if it deserves no belief.

...*husband*, who, being in the flower of his youth, in good health, and very cheerful, went out of his house in the morning intending to return for dinner. At *Cambridge*, during the reign of *Queen Elizabeth*, there were two *witches* to be executed: a *mother* and her *daughter*. When the *mother* was called upon to repent and forsake the *Devil*, she said there was no reason to do so, for he had been faithful to her for these sixty years, and she would be faithful to him as long as she lived; and thus she died in this stubbornness. But as she was hanging there upon the *gallows*, her *daughter*—being of a contrary mind—renounced the *Devil* and was very earnest in prayer and repentance. Because of what happened next, the people believed the *Devil* took this very offensively. For there came such a sudden blast of wind (even though it had been completely calm before) that it drove the *mother's* body against the *ladder* so violently that it nearly overturned it. It shook the *gallows* with such force that the officials were forced to hold the posts for fear of everything being flung down to the ground.

<header>CHAPTER III. An Antidote against Atheism.</header>

## CHAPTER III.

1. *That winds and storms are raised based on mere ceremonies or forms of words.* 2. *The unreasonableness of Weyer’s doubting the Devil's power over the atmospheric phenomena <note>original: "Meteors of the Aire"; in the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any weather event, including rain, wind, and lightning.</note>.* 3. *Examples of that power in rain and thunder.* 4. *Margaret Warine thrown onto an oak tree during a thunderclap.* 5. *Amantius and Rotarius cast headlong out of a cloud onto a house roof.* 6. *The Witch of Constance seen by shepherds riding through the air.* 7. *That he might add several other instances from eyewitnesses regarding the strange effects of invisible demons.* 8. *His concise retelling of the most remarkable exploits of the Demon of Mâcon <note>A famous case of a poltergeist or "demon" reported in Mâcon, France, in 1612.</note> instead.* 9. *The reasons for giving himself the trouble of this retelling.*

1. **Weyer** <note>original: "Wierus"; referring to Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a physician who argued that many accused witches were actually suffering from mental illness, though he still believed in demons.</note>, that industrious *defender of those accused of witchcraft*, recites several *ceremonies* that they use for the raising of *storms*, and he acknowledges that *storms* do follow the performance of those *ceremonies*. However, he claims that they would have happened anyway without them; the *Devil*, foreseeing the weather, excites the deluded women to use those *magical rites* so that they may be better persuaded of his power. But whether there is any causal connection between those *ceremonies* and the following *storms*, I will not precisely decide. <margin>* *Weyer, On the Illusions of Demons, Book 3, Chapter 16.* <note>original: "Wierus de Præstig. Dæmon. l. 3. c. 16."</note></margin> But that the connection between them is *supernatural* is plain at first sight. For what is the casting of *flint stones* behind their backs toward the west, or flinging a little *sand* into the *air*, or striking a *river* with a *broom* and sprinkling the *water* toward *heaven*, or the stirring of *urine* or *water* with their finger in a hole in the ground, or the boiling of *hog bristles* in a *pot*? How are these follies capable, by themselves, of gathering *clouds* and covering the *sky* with *darkness*, and then making the ground smoke with peals of *hail* and *rain*, and making the *air* terrible with frequent *lightning* and *thunder*? Certainly, they have no such power at all. Therefore, the arrival of these *storms* after such *ceremonies* must come either from the foreknowledge of the *Devil* (as *Weyer* would have it), who set the *witches* to work, or else from the power that the *Devil* has in his kingdom of the *air*.

<margin>*On the Illusions of Demons, Book 3, Chapter 12; Book 4, Chapter 19. See Bodin, On the Demon-Mania of Witches, Book 2, Chapter 4.* <note>original: "De Præstig. Dæmon. l. 3. c. 12. l. 4. c. 19. See Bodin. Mag. Dæmon. l. 2. c. 4."</note></margin>
2. And it seems strange to me that *Weyer* should doubt this power when he attributes an even greater power to him; for what is the transporting of vapors or driving them together compared to the carrying of men and cattle through the *air* (of which he is a confident supporter), unless it requires larger *demons* or greater numbers? And that there are sufficient numbers of such spirits will seem as credible to anyone as the idea that there are any at all. But now, regarding the truth of this—that certain words or ceremonies do seem, at least, to cause an alteration in the *air* and to raise *storms*—*Remigius* <note>Nicolaus Remigius (c. 1554–1612), a notorious witch-hunter and judge in Lorraine.</note> writes that he had this witnessed to him by the voluntary confessions of nearly two hundred men whom he examined. To this, he adds a story or two in which, there being neither *fraud* nor *melancholy* <note>Mental illness or delusion.</note> to be suspected, I think them worth mentioning.

3. The first story is of a **witch** who, to satisfy the curiosity of those who had the power to punish her, was set free so she could demonstrate the power she claimed she had to raise **tempests**. Once released, she immediately went to a place thick with trees, scraped a hole with her hands, filled it with **urine**, and stirred it for so long that she eventually caused a thick, dark **cloud** filled with **thunder** and **lightning**, to the terror and fright of the beholders. But she told them to take courage, for she would command the cloud to strike whatever place they chose; she proved this in the sight of the **spectators**.

The other story is of a **young girl** who, to please her father who was complaining of a drought, raised a **cloud** with the guidance and help of the evil **Master** to whom her mother had dedicated and consecrated her. She watered only her father's ground, while all the rest remained dry as before.

4. Let us add to these the account of **Cuinus** and **Margaret Warine**. While **Cuinus** was busy making hay, there suddenly arose great **thunder** and **lightning**, which made him run home and abandon his work; he saw six **oaks** near him overturned from their very **roots**, and a seventh shattered and torn to pieces. In his haste, he lost his hat and had to leave his fork or rake behind. Even so, he was not fast enough, for another crack of thunder overtook him and rattled around his ears. Upon that **thunderclap**, he suddenly spotted **Margaret Warine**, a reputed witch, at the top of an **oak tree**, and he began to scold her. She begged him for secrecy and promised that she would never cause him any injury or harm at any time.

<margin>See Remigius’s *Demonolatry*, Book 1, Chapter 29. <note>original: "Remigius his Dæmonolatr."; Nicholas Rémy (c. 1554–1612) was a French judge who claimed to have overseen the execution of hundreds of people for witchcraft.</note></margin>
This **Cuinus** testified under oath before the magistrate, and **Margaret Warine** acknowledged the truth of it several times before her death and at the time of her death, without any force being used against her. **Remigius** believes she was dropped onto the top of the **oak** during that last **thunderclap** and hung there among the branches; he is led to believe this because of two stories he tells later.

5. The first is about a **storm** of **thunder** and **lightning** that frightened herdsmen tending their cattle on the ridge of **Alman Hill** in the field of **Guicuria**. Running into the **woods** for shelter, they suddenly saw two countrymen on the tops of the **trees** next to them. The men were so dirty, in such a mess, and so out of breath that it seemed as if they had been dragged through thorns and muddy places. But when the herdsmen had looked at them closely, they vanished in a moment, and they did not know how or where they went. These herdsmen spoke of the incident, but the truth of it came out not long after. The free confessions of the two men they had seen exactly matched what the herdsmen had reported, making the whole matter clear and certain.

The other story involves the same individuals, later identified by name as **Amantius** and his partner **Rotarius**. Having flown high in the **air** again and being thrown headlong out of a **cloud** onto a house, the latter man—being only a novice and inexperienced in those supernatural exploits—was greatly astonished and afraid at the strangeness of the matter. But **Amantius**, being used to such feats from his youth,

His parents, having dedicated him to the **Devil** from his childhood, treated the matter as a joke. Laughing at his friend, he called him a fool for his fear and told him to be brave; for their Master, in whose power they remained, would safely carry them through even greater dangers than those. No sooner had he said these words than a whirlwind snatched them up and set them both down safely on the ground. However, the house from which they were carried shook so violently that it seemed as if it would be overturned from its very foundations. Both men, when examined separately, confessed to this using the exact same words, without changing their story at all. Their confessions matched every detail observed by the local people regarding the time and the nature of the **storm** <note>original: "Tempest"</note> and the shaking of the house.

6. I will add only one more account of this nature, and that is of a **witch of Constance**. She was annoyed that all her neighbors in the village where she lived had been invited to a wedding—where they were drinking, dancing, and celebrating—while she was left solitary and neglected. She got the **Devil** to transport her through the air in the middle of the day to a hill near the village. There, she dug a hole and poured urine into it, raising a great **hailstorm** <note>original: "Tempest of Hail"</note>. She directed the storm so that it fell only upon the village, pelting the dancers with such violence that they were forced to stop their sport. When she had finished her exploit, she returned to the village. Upon being seen, she was suspected of having raised the storm; the shepherds in the field who saw her riding through the air already knew the truth. When they brought their witness against her, she confessed to the deed.

The evidence so thoroughly convinced him of the reality of witches and spirits that he could not help but admit it in a letter to a friend in his own handwriting.

7. We could provide many more examples of this kind (I mean supernatural effects that occur without miraculous appearances) if I were to include everything I have been told myself, either by eyewitnesses or by those who received the accounts directly from them. 

For example: bricks being carried around a room without any visible hand; many stones being thrown down from the roof of a house at a certain time of day for many months together, to the amazement of the whole country; pots being moved off a fire and set back on again without anyone touching them; the violent flapping of a chest lid when no hand was near it; the carrying of linens that were out bleaching so high into the air that tablecloths and sheets looked no larger than napkins—and this when there was no wind, but the air was calm and clear; glass windows being struck with such violence that it sounded as if they were being shattered into pieces, the glass jingling all over the floor for fifteen minutes, yet everything was found intact the next morning; \* boxes that were carefully locked unlocking themselves and throwing out the flax inside; bread tumbling off a **bench** <term>fourm: a long wooden bench</term> on its own; women's **pattens** <term>pattens: wooden overshoes with elevated soles to keep the wearer's feet out of mud</term> rising up from the floor and whirling at people; a comb breaking into two pieces by itself in a window, with the pieces then flying into men's faces; a knife also rising from the same place and flying handle-first; and stones being thrown about the house without hurting anyone. There are several other such incidents, which would be too long to repeat with all their details, and they are less necessary to include,

...since there are already accounts published and available to us that will provide us with enough examples of this kind.

8. Among these, the account by *Mr. Francis Perreand* <note>Francis Perreaud (1572–1657) was a Huguenot minister whose account of the "Devil of Mascon" became a famous 17th-century case of poltergeist activity.</note> concerning an unclean spirit that haunted his house at *Mascon* in *Burgundy* is of primary importance, both for the variety of its details and the authenticity of the story. For though this *Demon* <note>original: "Dæmon"</note> never appeared visible to the eye, its presence was clearly detectable by many tricks and pranks that it played. These included drawing the curtains at midnight and pulling off the blankets; holding doors shut and rolling logs <note>original: "billets"</note>; knocking and throwing things against the wood paneling; whistling tunes such as those taught to birds, and singing vulgar and indecent songs; repeating the Lord's Prayer and the Creed aloud; imitating the voices and accents of various people, as well as the cries of hunters, the croaking of frogs, and the speeches of street performers and charlatans; mocking and jeering and uttering witty remarks—such as the one about *Pays de Vaud* <note>original: "Pays de Vaux"</note>, where he said they made fine grilled meats <note>original: "Carbonado’s" — meat scored and grilled over coals; here used as a dark joke about burning witches</note> out of witches, and laughed very loudly at the thought; bringing greetings from distant friends and telling stories of fights and murders; revealing things done in private to those who had done them; and shaming a serious clergyman for singing a vulgar song in a tavern.

The spirit also tossed a roll of cloth fifty yards long <note>original: "fifty ells" — an ell was a unit of measurement, usually about 45 inches</note>; it tangled skeins of yarn and pulled men's coats backward while they worked; it threw one man’s hat at his face while he was asleep in his house and snatched a candlestick out of a servant girl’s hand. It tangled and tied things into such knots that it was impossible for anyone to untie them, yet the spirit itself untied them in an instant. It would toss a bed into the middle of the floor as soon as it had been made and take books down from their shelves in the study. It made a noise like a volley of gunfire and imitated the sound of four hemp-dressers beating together. It made music with two small bells it found among some rusty iron in the house; it used these not only there but in several other places, where the sound could be heard passing by them through the air, though they could see nothing. It hid a goldsmith’s jewels and tools for a while and then dropped them out of the air onto a table. It threw stones around the house, but without causing harm, as in the previous account. It frequently beat a new servant girl in her bed and poured water on her head until it forced her to leave. And lastly, it pulled a certain lawyer by the arm into the middle of the room, whirled him around on his tiptoes, and then threw him to the ground.

This is a short summary <note>original: "Epitome"</note> of the most remarkable exploits of that invisible devil of *Mascon*. For, as I recall, he was not even seen once in any form during all this time, unless it was he whom *Lullier* and *Repay* met at a corner of the street in the clothes of a countrywoman spinning by moonlight, who vanished from their sight as they approached.

9. <margin>* This account was not written by just one person. For *Marcelin*, a preacher then at *Mascon*, wrote the same story; and *Ternus*, a frequent eyewitness of the pranks of this *Demon* <note>original: "Dæmon"</note>, left an account written and signed with his own hand, which *Perreand* kept with him.</margin>

This story is included partly for both the richness <note>original: "copiousness"</note> and the suitability of the story to the current theme; but lastly and chiefly, for the undeniable truth and authenticity of the account. These strange events were observed not by *one solitary person, but by many together*. Furthermore, they were not observed by someone of suspect integrity, but by a person of exceptional seriousness and exemplary life. Nor was it done carelessly or out of credulity, but cautiously and diligently, by searching every corner of the house and setting bolts and barricades to all its doors and windows—even stopping up the cat-holes in the doors—leaving nothing that might allow for a suspicion of fraud <note>original: "Imposture"</note>. A candle also burned every night, all night long. The places where the voice came from during the day were searched, along with the *objects* inside, by several people. When one *Simeon Meissonier* brought away a bottle from one of those places, the Devil burst out laughing that anyone would think him such a fool as to enter it, since he would then be liable to be trapped inside by a person’s finger. Finally, the experience happened not just once or twice, but almost every day for three months <note>original: "a quarter of a year"</note>.

To further prove the miraculous nature of the account, the silence of the dog also provides evidence <note>original: "suffrage"</note>. The dog was otherwise very watchful and ready to bark at the slightest noise, yet it never barked at the loud speaking and hideous noises made by the *Demon*. The profane Goblin itself took notice of this, mischievously claiming that it was because he had made the sign of the cross on the dog's head; for the spirit was then in a merry mood <note>original: "on a merry pin"</note> and full of jeering.

To all of this, you may also add the authority of the Reverend and learned Mr. *P. Du Moulin* <note>Pierre Du Moulin (1568–1658), a prominent Huguenot minister and author.</note>, father to the current Dr. *Du Moulin*, and the sharp, judicious reasoning of his accomplished son in his preface to Mr. *Perreand's* account: 

> *That this familiar interaction with the Devil did not take place in some corner or desert (where the melancholy of witches is often supposed to make them imagine they talk with him), but in the middle of a great city, in a house where there was a great daily gathering of people to hear him speak. Men of opposing religions met there, whose readiness to bring disgrace upon the dissenting parties led them to examine the matter closely and fully confirm its truth, both by the magistrate and by the local bishop <note>original: "Dioceasan"</note>.*

And lastly, so that nothing may be missing to convince those who are hard to believe, we add the testimony of that excellently learned and noble gentleman, Mr. *R. Boyle* <note>Robert Boyle (1627–1691), the famous Irish natural philosopher and chemist, known for his skepticism and scientific rigor.</note>. He spoke with Mr. *Perreand* himself in *Geneva*, where he received a copy of his book as a gift before it was printed. There, he had the opportunity to inquire about both the writer and several passages in the book. He was so well satisfied that he confesses his usual reluctance <note>original: "indisposedness"</note> to believe strange things was overcome by this special conviction.

### CHAPTER IV.

1. *The supernatural effects observed in the bewitched children of Mr. Throckmorton and Mrs. Muschamp.* 2. *The general remarkable features in them both.* 3. *The possession of the religious virgins of Weert, Hessimont, etc.* 4. *The story of that famous Abbess Magdalena de la Cruz <note>original: "Magdalena Crucia"</note>, her useless and ridiculous miracles.* 5. *That she was a sorceress and was married to the Devil for thirty years.* 6. *That her story is neither a priestly invention nor a delusion caused by melancholy.*

1. We will now pass to those *supernatural effects* which are observed in *persons who are bewitched or possessed*. These include *predicting things to come*; telling exactly what certain people are saying or doing as if they were standing right next to them, even when the *possessed* person is at one end of the town inside a house, and the parties acting and talking together are outdoors at the other end of the town; being able to *see some people and not others*; playing at cards with one specific person and not being able to perceive anyone else at the table besides him; acting, talking, and moving about, and predicting how things will turn out and what is happening during those *fits of possession*; and then, as soon as the possessed or bewitched person comes out of the fit, *remembering nothing at all*, but instead asking about the well-being of the very people they seemed to be looking at just moments before while in their *fits*. All of these can be symptoms or signs of nothing else but the *Devil* having entered a person's body and taking over all the functions of their soul—acting, speaking, and playing as he pleases in the miserable tenement <note>original: "Tenement"; here meaning the human body as a temporary dwelling for the soul</note> he has crowded himself into, using the organs of the body at his own pleasure to perform pranks and feats that are far beyond the capacity, strength, or agility of the person who is *bewitched* or *possessed*.

All these things are fully confirmed by long and detailed observations recorded in *The Discovery of the Witches of Warboys in Huntingdonshire, in the year 1593* <note>original: "1594"</note>. The memory of this event is still kept fresh by an annual sermon preached at *Huntingdon* by some of the Fellows of *Queen's College in Cambridge*.

There has also lately been published a narrative about how *Mrs. Muschamp's* children were treated in *Cumberland*, which is very similar to the case of *Mr. Throckmorton's children of Warboys*.

2. What is generally observed in both cases is this: that during their *fits*, they are as if they had no soul at all in their bodies; and whatever operations of sense, reason, or motion appear to be in them, it has nothing to do with them, but belongs entirely to that stranger <note>the possessing spirit</note> who has entered them. For as soon as their *fits* are over, they are as if they had been in such a deep sleep that they did not even dream, and so they remember nothing at all of what they either said or did, or where they had been. This is clear from an infinite number of examples in the aforementioned accounts.

3. Since we are very well-assured of the truth of these occurrences here at home, we may with more confidence venture to consider what is recorded concerning others abroad. For example, the possession of the *Religious Virgins* <note>Nuns</note> in the Monastery of *Weert* <note>original: "Werts"</note>, others in *Hessimont*, others also not far from *Xantes*, and in other places. In those locations, there were enough eyewitnesses to notice how strangely they were handled: they were thrown up from the ground higher than a man's head and fell back down without harm; they climbed up trees as nimbly as cats and hung from the branches; and their flesh was torn from their bodies without any visible hand or instrument. There were many other wild antics which are not appropriate to name, but those who are interested may read about them at length in the works of Weyer.

<margin>*On the Deceptions of Demons* <note>original: "De Præstigiis Dæmon."</note>, Book 6, Chapter 6.</margin>
4. I would move on now to other *effects of witchcraft*, such as the transferring of *knives, balls of hair*, and *nails* into the bodies of those who are *bewitched*. However, the mention of these *nuns* reminds me of that famous story in Weyer regarding *Magdalena de la Cruz* <note>original: "Magdalena Crucia"</note>, who was first a *nun* and then an *abbess* of a nunnery in *Cordoba* <note>original: "Corduba"</note> in *Spain*. The things about her that were considered miraculous were these: she could tell from almost any distance how the affairs of the world were going, such as the consultations or transactions occurring in all the nations of Christendom. Because of this, she gained the reputation of being a very *holy woman* and a *great prophetess*. 

But other things happened through her, or for her sake, that were no less strange and miraculous. For instance, during the celebration of the holy *Eucharist*, the priest would always find himself missing one of his round *wafers*; it was supposedly secretly conveyed to *Magdalena* by the assistance of angels. She would receive it into her mouth and eat it in full view of the people, to their great astonishment and high reverence for the *Saint*. At the "elevation of the Host" <note>The moment in the Catholic Mass when the bread is held up for worship</note>, while Magdalena was nearby but separated by a wall, it was believed that the wall would open up to reveal Magdalena to those in the chapel, allowing her to partake of the consecrated bread. When this *abbess* entered the chapel herself on a special holy day, she would enhance the solemnity of the occasion with some notable and conspicuous miracle. Sometimes she would be lifted up above the ground three or four cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches</note> high. At other times, while holding an image of Christ in her arms and weeping fervently, she would cause her hair to increase to such a length and thickness that it would reach her heels and cover her entirely, along with the image of Christ in her arms; yet shortly afterward, it would shrink back to its usual size. These were many such impressive, though ultimately useless, miracles.

5. But you will say that the narration of these things is not *true*, but that they are faked for the advantage of the *Roman Catholic religion*, and that it was profitable for the Church to forge them and record them for posterity. A person who is unwilling to admit to anything *supernatural* would satisfy himself with this general dismissal and excuse. But when we come to the *conclusion* of the story, he will find it quite otherwise. For this *Saint* at last began to be suspected of being a *sorceress*, as it is thought. Being conscious of her guilt, she did of her own accord—in order to save herself—make a confession of her wickedness to the Visitors of the Order (as they are called); namely, that for thirty...

# CHAPTER IV.

*1. The supernatural effects observed in the bewitched children of Mr. Throckmorton and Mrs. Muschamp. 2. The general remarkable features in both cases. 3. When this Abbess entered the chapel herself on special holy days, she would enhance the solemnity of the occasion with some notable and conspicuous miracle. For example, she would sometimes be lifted up above the ground three or four cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note> high. At other times, while holding the image of Christ in her arms and weeping fervently <note>original: "favourly"</note>, she would cause her hair to grow to such length and thickness that it would reach her heels and cover her entirely, as well as the image of Christ in her arms; yet soon after, it would shrink back to its usual size. These were many such impressive, though useless, miracles.

But when we come to the *conclusion* <note>original: "Catastrophe"</note> of the story, he will find it to be quite different. This *Saint* at last began to be suspected of being a *sorceress*, as it is thought; and she, being aware of this, voluntarily confessed her wickedness to the Visitors of the Order <note>Official inspectors of the religious community</note> to save herself. ### CHAPTER V.

### CHAPTER VI.

->1. *The apparition Eckerken*. 2. *The story of the Pied Piper*. 3. *A Triton or Sea-God seen on the banks of the Rubicon*. 4. *On the imps of witches, and whether those old women are as senile as the atheist imagines them to be*. 5. *That the interactions between them and their imps are impossible to attribute to melancholy*. 6. *The examination of John Winnick of Molesworth*. 7. *The reason for sealing covenants with the Devil*.<—

There is such clear proof of this in the town of **Hamelin** <note>original: "Hammel"</note> where it occurred that it should not be discredited at all.
