3. There is also an account that seems to me beyond any objection or excuse, which **Suetonius** relates regarding a **spirit** <note>original: "Spectrum"</note> appearing on the banks of the River **Rubicon**. The story is as follows: **Julius Caesar** had marched with his army to this river, which divides **Cisalpine Gaul** <note>original: "Gallia citerior"</note> from **Italy**. While he was feeling very doubtful whether he should cross into **Italy** or not, a man of enormous size and form was seen on the riverbank, playing on a reed flute. The strangeness of his appearance as well as the beauty of his music drew several shepherds toward him, as well as many soldiers, including some trumpeters. This **Triton** (as **Melanchthon** <note>Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560), a German Protestant reformer</note> ventures to call him) or **sea-god**, seeing them, nimbly snatched a trumpet out of one of their hands, leaped immediately into the river, and sounded a "March" with such strength and violence that he seemed to tear the heavens. He made the air ring with the mighty force of the blast as he crossed to the other side of the river. Thereupon **Caesar**, taking this as an **omen**, stopped arguing with himself and led his army across into **Italy**, certain of success because of such obvious signs of favor from the gods.

4. To confirm the truth of these **apparitions**, if we would only accept the voluntary confessions of **witches** regarding their **imps**—whom they see and talk with frequently, know by name, and bow down to—the point would be settled beyond all doubt. The proofs would be so numerous that no book would be large enough to hold them. But of course, some claim these must all be **mentally ill old women** <note>original: "Melancholy old women"</note> who are senile and bring themselves into danger through their own **fancies** and **delusions** <note>original: "Conceits"</note>. However, I am more certain that they are not senile than I am of the sanity of those who claim they are. To satisfy my own curiosity, I have examined several of them, and they have spoken as cleverly as anyone of their social status and education. From what I have read and observed, I can see they serve a very treacherous master, who often plays **tricks** <note>original: "wreaks"</note> on them specifically to betray them. But that is only a side note.

5. I ask regarding these **witches** who confess to their contract and frequent conversation with the **Devil**—some seeing him in one shape, others in another—whether mere **mental illness** <note>original: "Melancholy"</note> and **imagination** can put **powders**, **rods**, **ointments**, and similar things into their hands and tell them how to use them? Can it brand **marks** upon their bodies so deep that they lose all feeling in that spot? Can it put **silver** and **gold** into their hands, which later usually turns out to be nothing but **tokens** <note>original: "Counters"</note>, **leaves**, **shells**, or some other useless material? These **real effects** cannot be caused by mere mental illness. If a man receives anything into his hand, no matter what it is, there must have been someone there to give it to him. Therefore, when a witch receives a physical object from a figure that appears to her, it is clear evidence that what she saw was an external object, not just a product of her **depressed imagination**. There are countless examples of this kind, but the phenomenon is so common and ordinary that it needs no specific proof. I will only record one instance, which involves the appearance of three spirits.

3. It may perhaps be objected that these were merely some poor ragged boys who plotted with Anne Bodenham to get money by pretending to conjure and foretell future events, when it was actually nothing more than a cheat within the power of an ordinary, mischievous wit. The transformation of a boy into a snake, and of that snake into a shaggy dog with staring eyes, is a feat far above any human art or wit whatsoever.

7. All these things the maid testified under oath. I believe it is now evident beyond all controversy that, unless she knowingly committed perjury, these events are certainly true; for they cannot be attributed to dreams, imagination, or melancholy <note>In the 17th century, "melancholy" was often used as a medical explanation for hallucinations or perceived supernatural experiences</note>. Several arguments prove that the maid did not commit perjury or invent these stories she swore to.

First, it is entirely unlikely that a simple girl <note>original: "sorry Wench"</note> who could neither read nor write would be able to devise <note>original: "excogitate"</note> such magical forms and ceremonies, with all the specific details of their effects, and describe them so precisely, unless she had actually seen them done before her eyes.

Secondly, if she had been so clever at inventing lies, she would have had enough wit to frame them better for her own advantage and for the benefit of those who employed her. Or, she would have told only as much of the truth as would not have harmed herself or anyone else by being revealed.

Because of this, the maid *Anne Styles* was sent to the witch under the pretense of finding out when this poisoning would happen and how to prevent it. When the two sisters learned they were suspected of trying to poison their mother, and that they had recently bought an ounce and a half of arsenic at the apothecary's <note>An apothecary was a medical professional who prepared and sold drugs and medicines; a precursor to the modern pharmacist.</note>, they made a diligent search of all the apothecary shops throughout Salisbury <note>original: Sarum</note> to clear their names of this suspicion. If she had only confessed to buying the arsenic with the purpose of preventing her mistress from being poisoned through the help and skill of the witch or "wise woman" <note>original: Wife-woman; likely a typo for "Wise-woman," a term for a folk healer or practitioner of magic.</note>, it might have been seen as a tolerable piece of folly. It will appear from several circumstances that the grievous troubles and agonies she later experienced were not merely whims of her own disturbed imagination <note>original: Phansy</note>, but the tyranny of Satan.

*...was thrown down and extinguished. At that time, there was a little boy who was almost asleep, but he was so frightened by this noise that he did not have the power to leave the room with the others. He stayed there and saw a spirit in the form of a large black man without a head in the room, struggling with the maid. The spirit took her and set her in a chair, telling her that she must go with him because he had come for her soul, which she had given to him. But the maid answered that her soul was not hers to give; he had already taken her blood, but as for her soul, he should never have it. After tossing and throwing the maid about for a while, he vanished.*

*The witch's condition in another room at that same time clearly suggests that what the boy heard and saw was not a figment of his imagination, but a real experience of his senses. She was seen then with her clothes off, in her shackles <note>original: fetters</note>, running around like a madwoman. When asked why she ran about the room, she replied that she could not stay in her bed but was pulled out by force. When asked for the reason, she replied, "I pray you, what is the matter in your room?" "Nothing," they said, "only a child is unwell." To which she answered, "Do not lie to me, for I know what is happening as well as you do."*

10. But to return to the maid, from whom we may draw further arguments relating also to the witch. For instance, when the maid had not rested for many days and nights together and was suffering through the most grievous agitations <note>original: hurryings; referring to the violent physical movements or convulsions of possession</note> and tortures of the body, the witch was brought into the room where she lay. The plan was unknown to the maid, as was the time of the witch's entry; yet as soon as the witch set one foot into the room, the maid gave a most hideous look with her eyes and shut them immediately after, falling asleep in an instant. She slept for about three hours so deeply that when they tried to waken her, they could not by any method or force whatever, such as by stopping her breath, putting things up her nostrils, holding her upright, striking her, and the like. The witch also declared her refusal to let the maid be wakened, crying out, *"Oh, I pray you, by no means wake the maid, for if she should wake, I would be torn to pieces, and the Devil would carry me away bodily."* A further piece of evidence that this sleep of the maid depended in some way upon the witch is that as soon as the witch had left the house where she was, the maid woke up on her own. As soon as the maid awakened and was at ease (the Devil, as she said, having gone out of her stomach but doing her no violence, only making her body tremble a little), the witch began to roar and cry out, *"The Devil will tear me in pieces."* You may read these things more fully and in greater detail in the account by Edmond Bower, who was an eyewitness to them. I believe what I have transcribed from there is sufficient to convince any impartial <note>original: indifferent; in the 17th century, this meant unbiased or objective</note> man that what happened to the maid after she revealed the secrets she was entrusted with was not faked but real—indeed, I may safely say, supernatural.

<header>CHAPTER VII. An Antidote against Atheism.</header>

...it would have been argument enough for any unprejudiced person that she swore to nothing but what she was certain was true. Furthermore, those floods of tears and her bitter weeping after the sentence was passed on the witch—along with her grieving over her own wickedness and madness, and her stated willingness (if it could be done without sin) for the witch to be reprieved—should further wash away all suspicion of either fraud or malice.

12. Nor can the witch's denial (even until her dying day) of what the maid swore to weaken <note>original: "enervate"</note> her testimony. For the maid tells the whole truth as it happened, even at the risk of her own life; the witch indeed denies it, but only to save her own. It is no wonder that someone who would curse the executioner <note>original: "bid a pox on the Hangman"</note> when he asked for her forgiveness at her death would lie and impudently deny anything to save her life.

But you will object that this reputed witch may indeed be wicked enough, and willing enough to do anything; but because the power of her wickedness could not reach such feats as the maid witnessed against her, we should believe the witch rather than the maid. The meaning of this objection, if I understand it, can be nothing but this: that either this *Anne Bodenham* was no witch, or else the things charged against her were absolutely impossible. The meaning of the latter is surely that it is impossible for anyone to be a *witch*, because there are no such things as *spirits* to be conjured up by them. This is an unskillful argument that ignores the evidence <note>original: "let goe the Premisses"</note> because it is too strong, and instead quarrels with the conclusion.

13. But if the meaning is (admitting that witches exist) that she was not one, I think it may be clearly proven that she was, based on what she undoubtedly both did and said. For example, she showed the maid the shapes of various people in a glass <note>A scrying glass or mirror used for divination.</note>, including their actions and postures in several rooms of her master's house. When the maid returned from the witch, she told the family exactly what they had been doing in her absence; this made *Elizabeth Rosewell*, a member of the household, declare that she thought *Mrs. Bodenham* was either a witch or a woman of God. 

Besides what happened regarding the maid’s fits, which has already been discussed, there are strong <note>original: "shrewd"</note> suspicions of her being a witch. These include what she boasted of to *Mr. Tucker's clerk* regarding *a purse that hung about her neck on a green string, claiming she could perform many feats with it; and that if he would give her half a dozen portions of ale, she would make a toad spring out of it.* 

There was also her confession to *Mr. Langley of Salisbury* <note>original: "Sarum," the Latin name for Salisbury.</note> that she lived with *Dr. Lamb* <note>Dr. John Lambe (c. 1545–1628) was a notorious astrologer and magician who was eventually murdered by a mob.</note> and learned the art of raising spirits from him. She also confessed this to *Edmund Bower*, to whom she also acknowledged her skill in curing diseases by *charms* and *spells*, her ability to discover stolen goods, and her power to show anyone a thief in a glass. When asked by him for the *Red Book* (which was half written in blood and served as a catalogue of those who had made a pact with the Devil), she did not deny knowing about the book, but said it was with someone in *Hampshire*. She also claimed that she used many "good prayers," said the Creed both backwards and forwards, and that she prayed to the planet *Jupiter* for the curing of diseases.

She also acknowledged she had a book with which she raised *spirits*, calling it a *Book of Charms*, and said it was worth thousands of other books. She claimed there was a particular *charm* in it for finding a *treasure* hidden by the old *Earl of Pembroke* in the northern part of *Wilton Garden*.

To another person, who asked her whether there were any *spirits*, she replied that she was sure there were. She confirmed this to him by mentioning several recent incidents <note>original: "passages of late"</note>, particularly that of a man forced to *walk about all night with a bundle of fencing stakes <note>original: "Pales"</note> on his back in a pond of water*, which is mentioned at the end of the fourth conjuration recited above. She also boasted greatly about <note>original: "magnifie"</note> her own art to him, using *astrological* terms and phrases. She expressed much scorn and blame for the ignorance of the people, asserting to him with all earnestness and confidence that there was no harm in these *spirits*. Instead, she claimed they would do a person all kinds of good favors, attending to him and guarding him from evil all his life.

But certainly her *ragged boys* <note>A term for familiar spirits or demons who appeared in the form of children.</note> were no such thing; they released the maid from keeping the Commandments of God and told her they would teach her a better way, as she also confessed to the same person.

Add to all this that this *Anne Bodenham* was searched both at the jail <note>original: "Gaol"</note> and before the judges at the <term>Assizes</term> <note>Periodic courts held in England and Wales for civil and criminal cases.</note>. There was found on her shoulder a certain mark or teat about the length and size of the nipple of a woman's breast, and it was hollow and soft like a nipple, with a hole on the top of it.

14. Therefore, to conclude: there were things found upon her, and things done and spoken by her, which clearly indicate <note>original: "indigitate"</note> that she is a witch and has the power of raising spirits. Furthermore, she was accused of raising them by a witness who, in all likelihood, could not have invented <note>original: "excogitate"</note> any such magical formulas, effects, or circumstances as are recited above. This witness tells her story so impartially that it implicates <note>original: "touches"</note> herself nearly as much as the witch. Moreover, upon her revealing this villainy, the witness was affected in a way that was plainly beyond any imaginable natural illness <note>original: "distemper"</note>. I say, therefore, that any man who is not utterly blinded by prejudice and stubbornness must fully agree that what the maid confessed concerning herself and the witch is most certainly true.

## CHAPTER VIII.

*1. Two memorable stories, and why they are believable. 2. The first concerns a shoemaker from Breslau <note>Modern-day Wrocław, Poland.</note> who cut his own throat. 3. His appearance after death in his usual clothes, and how he troubled the whole town. 4. That when he was dug up eight months after being buried, his body was found intact and fresh, with his joints supple and flexible. 5. That the ghost stopped appearing once the body was burned. 6. A similar event happened with one of his maids after she had disturbed people for an entire month. 7. The person who told the story lived in the town when these events occurred.*

1. **I** have focused for so long on the previous account partly because it is very recent, so that anyone who doubts such things can verify the truth for themselves. It is also so notorious that it is almost unmatched by anything we find in other writers, considering all the circumstances. Yet, if they were as recent, I think the accounts by Martinus Weinrichius—a Silesian physician and philosopher—might be just as convincing. These stories are found in the preface to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's <note>original: "Picus Mirandula"</note> book *The Witch* <note>original: "Strix"</note> or *On the Deception of Demons* <note>original: "De ludificatione Demonum"</note>.

The stories are two and very memorable. They are all the more believable because the events happened during the lifetime of the narrator, only a few years before he wrote them down, and in his own country. He declares with all imaginable confidence that they are certainly true. The first of them is this:

2. A certain shoemaker in one of the chief towns of Silesia, on Friday, September 20, 1591, early in the morning, cut his own throat with a shoemaker’s knife in the back part of his house near a small garden. To hide the shame of the act and protect his widow from disgrace, the family claimed he died of a stroke <note>original: "Apoplexie"</note>. They turned away all visits from friends and neighbors. In the meantime, they washed him and laid him in linens so neatly that even those who saw him later—such as the parson and others—had not the slightest suspicion that he had committed suicide. Thus, he received a proper burial, with a funeral sermon and other ceremonies fitting for a man of his rank and reputation. 

Six weeks had not passed before a strong rumor broke out that he had not died of any disease, but had laid violent hands upon himself. This rumor became so strong that the local authorities <term>magistracy</term> <note>The group of officials or town leaders responsible for upholding the law.</note> were forced to bring everyone who had seen the corpse to a strict examination. At first, the family dodged the matter as well as they could with many fair excuses on behalf of the deceased to remove any suspicion of such a heinous act. But when the matter was pressed more urgently to their consciences, they finally confessed he died a violent death. However, they begged for mercy and leniency for his widow and children, who were not at fault, adding also that it was uncertain whether he might have been killed by some external accident,

# CHAPTER VIII.

1. *Two memorable stories and the evidence for their credibility.* 2. *The first story: a shoemaker from Breslau who cut his own throat.* 3. *His appearance after death in his usual clothing, and his troublesome haunting of the entire town.* 4. *His body was dug up after being buried for eight months and found to be intact and fresh, with joints that were still supple and flexible.* 5. *The haunting ceased once the body was burned.* 6. *A similar event happened with his servant girl after she had disturbed the town for an entire month.* 7. *The man who related the story lived in the town when these events occurred.*

1. **I** have dwelt so long on the previous account partly because it is very recent, so that any man who doubts such things can satisfy himself regarding its truth. It is also so notorious that it is hard to find a parallel in other writings, considering all the circumstances. Yet, if they were as recent, I believe the accounts by Martin Weinrich <note>original: *Martinus Weinrichius*</note>, a Silesian physician and philosopher, might seem just as convincing. These stories are included in his preface to Pico della Mirandola’s <note>original: *Picus Mirandula*</note> book, *The Witch, or On the Deceptions of Demons* <note>original: *Strix* or *De ludificatione Dæmonum*</note>.

The stories are two and very memorable. They are all the more credible because the events happened during the narrator's lifetime, only a few years before he wrote them down, and occurred in his own country. He vouches for them with every possible confidence as being absolutely true. The first of them is as follows:

2. A certain shoemaker in one of the primary towns of Silesia <note>Specifically, Breslau, modern-day Wrocław, Poland.</note>, on Friday morning, September 20, 1591, went into the back parts of his house near a small garden and cut his own throat with a shoemaker’s knife. They turned away all visits from friends and neighbors. In the meantime, they washed him and laid linens so neatly around him that even those who saw him later—such as the parson and others—had not the slightest suspicion that he had died of anything but that disease. Thus, he received a proper burial with a funeral sermon and other honors fitting a man of his rank and reputation. 

Within six weeks, however, such a strong rumor broke out that he had not died of a disease, but had committed suicide <note>original: "laid violent hands upon himself"</note>, that the local authorities were forced to call everyone who had seen the body for a strict examination. At first, they dodged the questions with many excuses on behalf of the deceased to remove any suspicion of such a heinous act. But when the matter was pressed more urgently upon their consciences, they finally confessed he died a violent death. However, they pleaded for mercy and clemency for his widow and children, who were not at fault. ...or if he did it to himself in some irresistible fit of frenzy <note>original: "phrensie"</note> or madness.

Because of this, the Town Council <note>original: "Councel"</note> deliberated on what should be done. When the widow heard this, she feared they might decide on something harsh that would discredit both her husband and herself. Encouraged by some local busybodies, she made a major complaint against those who had spread these reports about her husband. She resolved to take legal action against them, earnestly arguing that there was no reason—based on mere rumors and the idle slanders of malicious people—that her husband’s body should be dug up or treated as if he had been either a magician or a suicide <note>original: "Self-murtherer"</note>. This bold persistence <note>original: "pertinacity"</note> from the woman—even after the facts had been confessed—influenced the Council to some extent and brought their proceedings to a halt.

3. But while these matters were being debated, to the astonishment of the local inhabitants, a ghost <note>original: "Spectrum"</note> appeared in the exact shape and clothing <note>original: "habit"</note> of the deceased man. It appeared not only at night but even at midday. It terrified those who were asleep with horrible visions; those who were awake it would strike, pull, or press, lying heavy upon them like a nightmare <note>original: "Ephialtes"; a term for a spirit or medical condition where one feels a heavy weight pressing on the chest during sleep</note>. Consequently, there were constant complaints every morning throughout the whole town about the previous night’s lack of rest. 

But the more strange tricks this ghost played, the more diligent the friends of the deceased became in suppressing rumors about them—or at least in trying to prevent those rumors from having any effect. Therefore, they made their appeals to the President, complaining about how unjust it was that so much weight was given to idle reports and blind suspicions. They begged him to stop the Council from digging up the corpse and from treating it with any shame. They added that they intended to appeal to the Emperor’s Court, so that his high officials might decide the controversy rather than let the case be determined here based on the light conjectures of malicious men.

But while the business was being delayed in this way, such disturbances and riots broke out all over the town that they are hard to describe. For as soon as the sun set, this ghost <note>original: "spectrum"</note> was sure to appear, so that everyone was forced to look around and stay on guard. This was a great distress to those who, exhausted by the day's labor, felt the lack of sleep even more acutely at night. This terrible apparition would sometimes stand by their bedsides or throw itself onto the middle of their beds. It would lie close to them and miserably suffocate them. It would strike and pinch them so hard that not only blue bruises <note>original: "blew marks"</note>, but plain impressions of its fingers, would be found on various parts of their bodies in the morning. 

Indeed, the ghost was so violent and relentless that even when men left their beds and stayed in their dining rooms with candles lit—many of them gathering together to better protect themselves from fear and disturbance—it would still appear and attack <note>original: "have a bout with"</note> some of them despite all these precautions. In short, it was so troublesome that the people were ready to abandon their houses and seek other homes. The magistrates were so stirred up by the perpetual complaints that they finally resolved, with the President's agreement, to dig up the body.

### CHAP. VIII. An Antidote against Atheism.

4. He had been buried for nearly eight months, from September 22, 1591, to April 18, 1592. When he was exhumed <note>original: "digged up"</note>, which was done in the presence of the town's magistrates, his body was found whole and undecayed <note>original: "not at all putrid"</note>. There was no foul smell about him, except for the mustiness of the grave-clothes. His joints were supple and flexible, like those of a living person. His skin was only loose <note>original: "flaccid"</note>, but a fresher layer had grown in its place. The wound on his throat was wide open, but there was no discharge <note>original: "gear"</note> or decay in it. A magical mark was also noticed on the big toe of his right foot: a growth <note>original: "Excrescency"</note> in the shape of a rose. His body remained unburied from April 18 to April 24, during which time many people from the town and elsewhere came daily to see him. These restless disturbances did not stop despite all this; the authorities later attempted to calm the situation by burying the corpse under the gallows, but it was in vain. The hauntings continued as much as ever, if not more; the ghost did not even spare his own family. Consequently, his widow finally went to the magistrates herself and told them she would no longer object if they decided to take more drastic measures regarding her husband.

5. Therefore, on the seventh of May, he was exhumed again. It was noticeable that he had become significantly more fleshy since his last burial. To be brief, they cut off the head, arms, and legs of the corpse. Opening his back, they removed his heart, which was as fresh and intact as that of a newly slaughtered calf. They placed these parts, along with his body, on a funeral pyre and burned them to ashes. They carefully swept the ashes together and put them into a sack (so that no one could use them for evil purposes) and then poured them into the river. After this, the ghost <note>original: "Spectrum"</note> was never seen again.

6. A similar thing happened with his maidservant who died after him. Within eight days of her death, she appeared to her fellow servant and lay so heavily upon her that she caused her eyes to swell greatly. She treated a child in a cradle so roughly that if the nurse had not come to his aid, he would have been severely harmed <note>original: "quite spoiled"</note>. However, when the nurse crossed herself and called upon the name of **Jesus**, the ghost <note>original: "Spectre"</note> vanished. The next night, she appeared in the form of a **hen**. When one of the housemaids followed it, thinking it was a real bird, the hen grew to an enormous size and suddenly grabbed the maid by the throat. This caused her throat to swell so much that she could not eat or drink properly for a long time afterward.

She continued these disturbances for a whole month, slapping <note>original: "flapping"</note> some people so sharply that the sound of the blows was heard by those standing nearby. She also pulled beds out from under people and appeared in various forms: as a woman, a dog, a cat, and a goat. Finally, after her body was exhumed and burned, the apparition was never seen again.

7. These events took place in Wrocław <note>original: "Breslaw"</note> in Silesia <note>a historical region now mostly in Poland</note> where this Weinrichius <note>Martin Weinrich, a contemporary physician and author who recorded these events</note> lived at the time, which makes the account more credible. I believe he concealed the names of the people involved as a gesture of respect toward his deceased fellow citizen, the widow, and their family.

# CHAP. IX.

1. **The second story of one Cuntius, whose first biographer not only lived in the town but was a personal sufferer in the tragedy.** 2. **The social standing of Cuntius, the fatal blow he received from his horse, and his desperate mental affliction.** 3. **Prodigies attending his death.** 4. **A crushing spirit** <note>original: "Spiritus Incubus"</note> **appearing in his shape, along with other disturbances.** 5. **More hideous disorders, as well as his appearing to a close friend** <note>original: "Gossip"</note> **of his on behalf of his child.** 6. **Several tragic effects of his appearances on various people.** 7. **His miserable treatment of the parish priest and his family, who is the original writer of the story.** 8. **A brief rehearsal of many other wild pranks played by this specter.** 9. **A remarkable event regarding his gravestone.** 10. **The healthy, ruddy condition** <note>original: "florid plight"</note> **of Cuntius after he had been buried for nearly half a year; his grasping of a staff, and the movement of his eyes and blood.** 11. **The extraordinary weight of his body.** 12. **Also the fact that his body could not be burned.** 13. **How difficult it will be for the atheist to find a way to explain away this story.**

1. Instead, he transcribed it from someone who not only lived in the location but was frequently harassed by the foul intrusions of that troublesome ghost, which caused so much harm to the town where he lived. The account is quite long, so I shall condense it as much as I can.

2. Johannes Cuntius was a citizen of Pentsch in Silesia <note>a historical region in Central Europe, mostly in modern-day Poland</note> and was nearly sixty years old. He was an Alderman of the town, known for being very fair in his behavior and, to all appearances, blameless in his conduct throughout his life. Having been sent for to the Mayor's house—as he was considered a very knowledgeable man and skilled at handling business—to settle some disputes concerning certain wagon drivers and a merchant from Hungary <note>original: "Pannonia"</note>, he finished those affairs and was invited by the Mayor to supper. He asked permission to go home first to organize some business, leaving behind this remark: "It is good to be merry while we may, for mischief grows up fast enough daily."

This Cuntius kept five strong horses <note>original: "lusty Geldings"</note> in his stable. He ordered one of them to be brought out, and because its shoe was loose, he had it tied to a post. The master and a servant busied themselves with lifting the horse's leg to look at its hoof, but the horse, being wild and high-spirited, struck them both down. Cuntius received the worst of the blow. Someone standing nearby helped them both up again. As soon as Cuntius was on his feet and regained his senses, he cried out, "Woe is me, how I burn! I am all on fire!" He repeated this often. His nose was whole and full, not sharp as it is in those who are ghastly sick or quite dead. And yet Cuntius’s body had lain in the grave from February 8th to July 20th, which is almost half a year.

## CHAPTER X.

1. *The nightly secret meetings of witches; two examples from Paulus Grillandus. 2. The Witch of Lochiæ, with a reflection on how these instances are beyond doubt as proof of spirits. 3. The piping of John of Hembach to a secret meeting of witches. 4. The dancing of men, women, and cloven-footed satyrs at midday. 5. 1. Paulus Grillandus reports of a man not far from Rome who, at the persuasion of his wife, anointed himself as she had done. He was carried away through the air to a great assembly of sorcerers <note>original: "Wizards"</note> and *witches*, where they were feasting under a nut tree. But this stranger, not enjoying the food without salt, finally saw the salt arrive. When he thanked God for it, at the mention of that *Name*, the whole assembly disappeared. The poor man was left alone and naked a hundred miles from home. When he finally returned, he accused his wife; she confessed to the deed, identifying her companions, who were burned along with her.

2. So the husband of the witch of Loches <note>original: "Lochiæ"; a town in France</note>, whom she brought into a similar assembly, made everyone vanish by saying, *"O my God, where are we?"* He found himself alone and naked in a field, fifteen days' journey from home.

Jean Bodin <note>original: "Bodinus"</note> records several other accounts for this purpose. These tangible results—being found so far from home and being discovered naked in the fields—show that these events are not just delusions caused by depression <note>original: "freaks of Melancholy"; skeptics often argued that "melancholy" caused hallucinations</note>, but **certain truth**. The fact that the Devil appears to the guests at these feasts <note>original: "junquetings"</note> in the form of a **satyr**, a **black goat**, or sometimes in the shape of an ugly **black man**, is the common confession of witches who are discovered and convicted in this way.

3. I will only add a story or two from Nicolas Rémy <note>original: "Remigius"</note> concerning these types of secret meetings <note>original: "Conventicles"</note>, and then I will proceed to other proofs.

<margin>See Nicolas Rémy, *Demonolatry*, Book 1, chapter 14.</margin>

*John of Hembach* was taken by his mother, who was a witch, to one of these meetings. Because he had learned to play the **pipe**, she commanded him to use his skill and climb into a tree so they could hear his music better. While doing this, he looked down at the dancers and saw how strange and ridiculous their movements and gestures were. Struck with wonder at such a strange sight, he suddenly blurted out, *"Good God, what a mad company we have here!"* No sooner were these words spoken than *John* fell down, pipe and all, and hurt his shoulder in the tumble. When he called to the group to help him, he found himself alone, for they had all vanished. *John of Hembach* told others what had happened, but people did not know what to make of it until some of that mad crew who had danced to his pipe were arrested on other suspicions—such as *Catherine Prevost* <note>original: "Catharina Prævotia"</note>, *Kelver’s Orilla*, and others. They confirmed every bit of what *John* had previously said (though they knew nothing of his testimony), adding specifically that the place where he played for them was *Maybuch*.

<margin>*Demonolatry*, Book 1, chapter 14.</margin>

4. The other memorable story I shall relate from *Rémy* is this: One *Nicolea Langbernhard*, while walking along a hedge toward Assenoncourt <note>original: "Assenunturia"</note>, spotted a group of men and women dancing in a ring in the next field (it was about noon). Their body postures were so strange and unusual that she watched them more closely, and she noticed that some of them had cloven feet like oxen or goats (it seems they were **spirits** in the shape of vigorous **satyrs**). He dropped his oven-cleaning stick <note>original: "Maulkin"; a bundle of rags on a pole used to clean out bread ovens</note>, and she herself was pushed so hard by a gust of wind that it almost knocked the breath out of her. She was forced to stay in bed for three days afterward.

2. 3. But for my own part, though I will not undertake to decide the controversy, I think it is not wrong to declare that Bodin may very well defend his own position, despite anything those others allege to the contrary. For that which Weyer and Rémy seem to insist upon so much—that it is too great a power to grant the Devil, and too great an indignity to man, that he should be able to transform him—are, in my mind, but slight rhetorical flourishes, not sound arguments.

For what is that outward mishapenness of the body compared to the inward deformity of their souls, which the Devil helps along so notoriously? And since they have given themselves over to him so completely, why may he not use them this way *here*, when they shall be treated worse by him *hereafter*? And as for the changing of the species of things: if that were a power too great to be granted to the Devil, yet no more is done here, when he transforms a man into a wolf, than when he transforms himself into the shape of a man. For this wolf is still a man, and that man is still a Devil. For it is just as the poet says it was with Ulysses' companions, whom Circe turned into hogs: they had the head, the voice, the body, and the bristles of hogs;

->— But their mind remained firm as it was before <note>original: Αὐτὰρ ὁ νοῦς ἦν ἔμπεδος ὡς τὸ πάροςπερ</note>,<-

but their understanding was unchanged; they had the mind and memory of a man as before. As Pierre Burgot <note>original: *Petrus Bourgotus*</note> professed: when his companion Michel Verdun <note>original: *Michael Verdung*</note> had anointed his body and transformed him into a wolf, and he looked upon his hairy feet, he was at first afraid of himself.

4. Now, therefore, it being plain that nothing material is alleged to the contrary, and that men confess they are turned into wolves and acknowledge the savage cruelties they then committed upon children, women, and sheep—and that they find themselves exceeding weary, and sometimes wounded—it is more natural to conclude they were really thus transformed, than that it was a mere delusion of the imagination <note>original: "phansy"</note>.

...melts the yielding structure <note>original Latin: *Compages*</note> of the body to such a consistency—and as much of it as serves his purpose—and makes it pliable to his imagination. 5. And he who has this power, we can never hesitate to grant him that which is lesser: namely, to instruct people how they shall for a time *leave their bodies* and return again. For can it be a hard thing for him, who can thus melt and take apart the particles of the body, to have the skill and power to loosen the soul? The soul is a substance really distinct from the body and separable from it, which at last is done by the easy course of nature at that final dissolution of soul and body which we call *death*. But no course of nature ever transforms the body of a man into the shape of a wolf; so this transformation is more difficult and further removed <note>original: "exorbitant"</note> from the order of nature than the other.

6. But, you will say, the greatness and incredibility of the miracle is this: that there should be an actual *separation of soul and body*, and yet no *death*. However, this is not at all strange if we consider that *death* is properly a disconnection of the soul from the body because the *body is no longer fit* to host <note>original: "entertain"</note> the soul. This unfitness may be caused by extreme *disease*, outward *violence*, or *age*. If the Devil could restore such bodies as these to life, it would be a *miracle* indeed. But this is not such a *miracle*, nor is the body properly dead, even though the soul is out of it. For the *life of the body* is nothing else but that *fitness* to be animated <note>original: "actuated"</note> by the soul. The preservation of this fitness is helped, as I understand it, by the *anointing* of the body before the *trance* <note>original: *Ecstasie*</note>. This ointment, filling the pores, keeps out the cold and keeps in the heat and spirits so that the frame and condition of the body may continue in a fit state to receive the soul again at her return. Thus, with the vital vapors <note>original: "steams"</note> of the body not yet spent, the original operations of life are quickly rekindled. It is like a candle newly blown out and still smoking <note>original: "reeking" - meaning emitting vapor</note>, which suddenly catches fire from the flame of another, even at some distance, as the light glides down along the smoke.

7. Therefore, since there is nothing in the nature of the thing that should make us skeptical <note>original: "incredulous"</note>, and since these *witches* <note>original: "Sorceresses"</note> so confidently declare that they are *out of their bodies* at such times—seeing and doing various things, meeting one another, bringing messages, discovering secrets, and the like—it is more natural and easy to conclude they are really *out of their bodies* than in them. We would be even more easily persuaded to believe this if we could give credit to that story Johann Weyer <note>original: "Wierus"</note> tells of a soldier. While he was asleep, a creature in the shape of a weasel came out of his mouth. It scurried <note>original: "nudling"</note> along in the grass and finally came to a brook-side, where it busily attempted to get over. Not being able to do so, one of the bystanders who saw it made a bridge for it with his sword. The creature passed over it and, coming back, used the same bridge, then entered the soldier's mouth again while many people watched. When he awoke, he told how he dreamed he had gone over an iron bridge and...

* Wierus <note>Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a physician who argued that many accused witches were actually suffering from mental illness.</note> acknowledges the truth of the report, but insists that it was the **Devil**, not the **Soul** of the man. He does this out of a protective regard for the witches; he fears that if such stories were proven true, they would be under even greater suspicion. He wants to maintain that their **trances** <note>original: "Ecstasies"</note> are nothing but **dreams** and **delusions** caused by the **Devil**, rather than events accompanied by real, physical effects.

8. I will not take it upon myself to decide such a subtle <note>original: "nice"</note> **controversy**. However, I will venture to intervene this far: to declare that the opinion of **Bodinus** <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and political philosopher.</note> is not at all unworthy of a rational and perceptive man. It is true that Bodin was very fond of such speculations and might attribute some natural effects to the work of **spirits** when there was no need to do so. Yet, his judgment in other matters of this kind should not be dismissed for that reason—any more than **Cartesius** <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), the famous French philosopher and mathematician.</note>, that extraordinary mechanical mind, should be rejected. Descartes' excellent discoveries regarding the general **phenomena** of nature are still valid, even though his success emboldened him to stretch his principles too far by claiming that **animals** themselves were merely **machines**. He is like **Aristoxenus** the Musician, who claimed the **soul** was nothing but a **harmony**; of whom **Tully** <note>The Roman orator Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> pleasantly observes, **"that he did not depart from his own art"** <note>original Latin: Quòd non recessit ab arte sua</note>.

Every **character** and **temperament**, like the various sorts of beasts and living creatures, has its own particular byproduct <note>original: "excrement"</note>. It is the part of a wise man to notice this and choose what is profitable, while abandoning what is useless and waste.

2. And indeed, there is very good reason that the *Bodies of Devils*, being nothing but *condensed air* <note>original: "coagulated Aire"</note>, should be *cold*, just like *condensed water*, which is *snow* or *ice*. It should even have a more keen and piercing cold, as it consists of more subtle particles than those of *water*, and is therefore better able to penetrate <note>original: "insinuate"</note> and more sharply and stingingly touch and affect the nerves.

3. Therefore, since *witches* so frequently confess that the *Devil* lies with *them*, and they also complain of his tedious and offensive *coldness*, it is a strong indication <note>original: "shrewd presumption"</note> that he actually does lie with them, and that it is not a mere *dream*, as their friend *Weyer* <note>original: "Wierus"</note> would have it.

4. From this, we may also discover the folly of the opinion that makes the very *essence of spirits* to be *fire*. It is plain at first sight how unfit fire would be to condense the air. It would *melt* and dissolve these forms rather than bind them together <note>original: "constringe"</note> and, in a sense, freeze them. Instead, it is manifest that the essence of *spirits* is a substance categorically distinct from all physical matter whatsoever. But my intent is not to *philosophize* concerning the nature of *spirits*, but only to prove their *existence*.

5. The *ghost* <note>original: "Spectre"</note> at *Ephesus* may serve as further evidence of this. That old man, whom *Apollonius* told the *Ephesians* was the walking plague of the city, appeared in the shape of a huge *black dog* as big as the largest lion when they stoned him and uncovered the heap. This could not have been a delusion caused by mental illness <note>original: "imposture of Melancholy"</note>, nor a *fraud* perpetrated by any priest. And the learned *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a major Dutch jurist and philosopher.</note>—a man far removed from all lightheartedness and foolish gullibility—is so certain of the truth of the *miracles* of *Apollonius of Tyana* <note>original: "Tyaneus"</note> that he does not hesitate to call anyone "impudent" who has the gall to deny them.

Our *English chronicles* also tell us of *apparitions*—*armed men*, *infantry* and *cavalry*—*fighting* on the ground in northern *England* and in *Ireland* for many evenings together. These were seen by many hundreds of men at once, and the grass was found trodden down in the places where they were seen to fight their *battles*. This agrees with the account of *Nicole Langbernard* <note>A woman accused of witchcraft in the late 16th century.</note> regarding the cloven-footed *dancers* who left the prints of their hooves in the *ring* they trod down for a long time afterward.

7. But this *skirmishing* upon the *earth* reminds me of the final part of this argument and bids me look up into the *air*. There, omitting all other omens <note>original: "Prodigies"</note>, I shall only take notice of what is most notorious, and of which no other account can possibly be given except that it is the effect of *spirits*. This is the appearance of *armed men fighting* and encountering one another in the *sky*. There are so many examples of these wonders in the works of *historians* that it would be superfluous to provide examples for all of them. The account from before the great slaughter of no fewer than eighty thousand people made by *Antiochus* in *Jerusalem*, recorded in the second book of *Maccabees*, chapter 5, is famous. The historian there writes, "That throughout all the city, for the space of almost forty days, there were seen horsemen running in the *air* in cloth of gold, and armed with lances, like a band of

8. Similar *apparitions* were seen before the Civil Wars of *Marius* and *Sylla*. *Melanchthon* <note>Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560), a German reformer and colleague of Martin Luther</note> affirms that a vast number of such *prodigies* were seen all over *Germany* from 1524 to 1548. *Snellius*, among other places, specifically mentions *Amersfoort*, where these *battles* were seen not much higher than the rooftops. However, a *lion* appearing alone at the end of that *apparition*—though it may be true for all I know—makes the story susceptible <note>original: "obnoxious"</note> to suspicion and skepticism, rendering it useless for my purpose. But *phenomena* of this kind, whose reports cannot be suspected of serving any *political agenda* <note>original: "politick design"</note>, ought in reason to be held as true when there have been many professed eye-witnesses. Since these cannot be explained by any natural causes, it is evident that we must acknowledge *supernatural* ones, such as *spirits, intelligences*, or *angels*—call them what you please.

### CHAPTER XIII. An Antidote against Atheism.

2. This person, who seemed to be a holy and pious man and was an acquaintance of *Bodin*’s <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French philosopher and jurist known for his writings on law and demonology</note>, freely told him that he had a certain *Spirit* that accompanied him at all times. He first became aware of this Spirit when he was about thirty-seven years old, but he believed the Spirit had been present with him his entire life. He gathered this from certain *warning dreams* and *visions* <note>original: "Monitory Dreams"</note> that had forewarned him of various dangers and vices. This *Spirit* revealed itself to him after he had spent an entire year earnestly praying to God to send a *good angel* to be the guide and governor of his life and actions. He added that, before and after prayer, he used to spend two or three hours in meditation and reading the Scriptures, diligently asking himself which *religion*, among the many disputed in the world, might be the best, and beseeching God to direct him toward it. He noted that he did not approve of the methods of those who recklessly <note>original: "at all adventures"</note> pray for God to confirm them in the opinions they already hold, whether they are right or wrong. While he was occupied with these religious matters, he came across a passage in *Philo Judaeus* <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher</note> in his book *On Sacrifices* <note>original: "De Sacrificiis"</note>, where Philo writes that *a good and holy man can offer no greater nor more acceptable sacrifice to God than the offering of himself*. Therefore, following *Philo*’s counsel, he offered his soul to God. After that, among many other divine *dreams* and *visions*, he once seemed to hear the voice of God in his sleep saying to him, "*I will save your soul; I am the one who appeared to you before.*" Afterward, the *Spirit* would knock at the door every day around three or four o'clock in the morning. Although the man would rise and open the door, he could see no one; yet the *Spirit* persisted in this practice and would rouse him up if he did not get out of bed.

3. This disturbance and roughness <note>original: "boisterousness"</note> made him begin to imagine that it was some *evil spirit* haunting him. Therefore, he daily prayed earnestly to God that He would be pleased to send a *good angel* to him; he also often sang Psalms, having most of them memorized.

Consequently, the *Spirit* afterward knocked more gently at the door. One day it revealed itself to him while he was awake, which was the first time he was certain by his own senses that it was the spirit; for it often touched and moved a drinking glass that stood in his chamber, which amazed him quite a bit.

Two days later, while he was hosting a certain friend for supper—a *Secretary to the King*—this friend was greatly startled when he heard the *Spirit* thumping on the bench right next to him and was struck with fear. But the man told his friend to be of good courage, as no harm was intended; and to better reassure him, he told him the truth of the whole matter.

From that time on, says *Bodin*, he affirmed that this *Spirit* was always with him and always notified him of things by some physical sign. For example, the spirit would touch his *right ear* if he did anything wrong, and otherwise, his *left*. If anyone came to deceive <note>original: "circumvent"</note> him, his right

## CHAP. XIV.

1.  Certain *inquiries* into the preceding *narrative*; such as, what these *guardian spirits* may be. 
2.  Whether one or more of them is assigned to every man, or to some, none at all. 
3.  What might be the reason spirits so seldom appear? 
4.  And whether they have any settled shape or not. 
5.  How they assist men in either *devotion* or *prophecy*. 
6.  Whether every man's temperament <note>original: "complexion"; referring to the balance of humors in a person's physical and mental makeup</note> is capable of the society of a good *spirit*. 
7.  And lastly, whether it is lawful to pray to God to send such a *spirit* or *angel* to someone, or not. 
8.  What is the most effective and divine *magic*.

It is beyond my present scope, as I have already stated, to enter into any more specific and more inquisitive investigations concerning the nature of *spirits*; my aim now is only to demonstrate their *existence* by those strange *effects* recorded everywhere in history. But this last *narrative* is so extraordinarily remarkable that it would be a sign of disrespect to dismiss it without at least some *inquiries* into the *problems* it naturally offers for our consideration; though it may well seem clearly beyond the power of human *intelligence* <note>original: "Wit"</note> or the laws of *modesty* to determine anything for certain in this matter.

In the first place, therefore, it cannot but amaze a man's mind to think what these helpful <note>original: "officious"; in the 17th century this meant performing a duty or service, rather than being meddlesome</note> *spirits* might be that so willingly sometimes offer themselves to associate with a man: whether they may be *angels* incapable of taking on human bodies (as is commonly conceived); or whether they are the *souls* of the deceased, who have more affinity with mortality and human frailty than the others, and so are more sensitive to our necessities and infirmities—having once felt them themselves. This is a reason cited for the *incarnation* of *Christ* by the author of the Epistle to the *Hebrews*.

Hebrews; this opinion has no less-regarded supporters than *Plutarch*, *Maximus Tyrius*, and other *Platonists*. Or lastly, whether there may not be *both sorts*. For separate souls being *equal to the angels* <note>original: <term>ισάγγελοι</term>; a Greek term meaning "angel-like" or "equal to the angels," often used in a theological context</note>, in a condition not unlike *the angels themselves*, it is easy to conceive that they may very well undergo similar duties.

2. Secondly, we are invited to inquire whether every person has his own *Guardian Genius* or not. That *witches* have many—of their own kind—their own confessions testify. The *Pythagoreans* <note>Followers of the ancient Greek philosopher Pythagoras</note> were of the opinion that every man has *two Genii*, a *good one* and a *bad one*. *Muhammad* <note>original: "Mahomet"</note> has taken this into his religion, adding also that they sit on men's shoulders with notebooks <note>original: "table-books"; portable writing tablets used for quick notes</note> in their hands, and that one writes down all the *good* and the other all the *evil* a man does. But I look upon such expressions as symbolic rather than literal. I think it is more reasonable that a man, by changing the state of his mind, changes his *Genius* as well. Or rather, unless a man is very sincere and single-hearted, he is left to common *Providence*. Similarly, unless a man is desperately wicked or deplorably miserable, hardly any particular *evil spirit* intervenes or offers itself as a perpetual *assistant* in his affairs and fortunes. 

But extreme poverty, tiresome old age, a lack of friends, and the contempt, injury, and hard-heartedness of evil neighbors—working upon a soul sunk low into the body and wholly devoid of a divine life—sometimes kindle such a sharp, eager, and piercing desire for *satisfaction* and *revenge* that it acts as a magnet. The shrieks of men while they are being murdered, the howling of a wolf in the fields at night, or the squeaking and roaring of tortured beasts do not call those of their own kind to them as certainly as this powerful *magic* of a grieving and complaining soul, in the bitterness of its affliction, attracts the aid of these over-helpful *spirits*. Therefore, it is most probable that those who are the most eager to *hang witches* are the very ones *who first made them*. They have no more goodness nor true piety than those they so willingly prosecute; they are just as wicked, though they have better luck or more discretion, offending no further than the law will permit them. Therefore, they securely starve the poor, helpless *person*, even while they seek revenge for the death of their *hog* or *cow* with a great deal of loud talk about "justice."

3. Thirdly, it would be worth our investigation why *spirits* so seldom *appear* nowadays, especially those that are *good*. Is it because of the *wickedness* of the present *age*, as I have already suggested? Or is it because of the general *prejudice* men have against all *spirits* that appear—that they must immediately be *devils*? Or is it the frailty of human nature, which is usually unable to bear the appearance of a *spirit*? Other animals cannot bear it either; the agonies into which horses and dogs are cast upon a spirit's approach is a common report, and it is a good piece of evidence to distinguish a *real apparition* from our own imaginations. Or lastly, is it the *condition* of the *spirits* themselves, who perhaps cannot become *visible* without doing some violence to their own nature? It may be as troublesome a thing for them to keep themselves in one steady, visible consistency in the air as it is for men who dive to hold their breath in the water.

# CHAPTER XIV. An Antidote against Atheism.

Fourthly, it may be worth our investigation to ask whether spirits have any settled form or shape. Angels are commonly depicted like plump, cherry-cheeked boys. This is no surprise, as the boldness of these same **Artists** did not hesitate to depict God Almighty in the shape of an old man. In both cases, the appearance is whatever pleases the **Painter**. But this story seems rather to favor the opinion of those who say that **Angels** and separated **Souls** <note>original: "separate Souls"; souls that have departed from the body</note> have no fixed **form** except what they choose to give themselves when the occasion arises, through the power of their own imagination. **Ficinus** <note>original: "Ficinus"; Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), an influential Italian Renaissance philosopher who revived Neoplatonism</note>, as I remember, somewhere calls them "Aerial Stars." And the good **Genii** <note>Guardian spirits or protective deities</note> seem to me to be like the benevolent eyes of God running to and fro in the world, beholding with love and pity the innocent efforts of harmless and sincere people, always ready to do them good and to help them.

What I conceive regarding separated souls and spirits, I cannot express better than I have already in my **Poem** on the ***Preexistence of the Soul***; which, therefore, will not be entirely irrelevant to repeat in this place.

> *Like to a light fast locked in lantern dark,*
> *Whereby by night our wary steps we guide*
> *In muddy streets, and dirty channels mark;*
> *Some weaker rays from the black top do glide,*
> *And fuller streams perhaps through the translucent side:* <note>original: "th' horny side"; lanterns in this period were often made with thin, translucent sheets of animal horn instead of glass</note>
> *But when we’ve passed the peril of the way,*
> *Arrived at home, and laid that case aside,*
> *The bare light, how clearly it does shine,*
> *And spread its joyful beams as bright as summer's day!*
>
> *Even so the soul in this contracted state,*
> *Confined to these narrow instruments of sense,*
> *More dull and narrowly does operate;*
> *At this hole hears; the sight must shine from thence;*
> *Here tastes, there smells: But when she’s gone from hence,*
> *Like a bare lamp she is one shining sphere,*
> *And round about has perfect cognizance* <note>original: "cognoscence"; full knowledge or awareness</note>
> *Of whatever in her horizon does appear;*
> *She is one orb of sense, all eye, all airy ear.*

And what I say there regarding the condition of the soul outside of the body, I think is easily applicable to other **Genii** or spirits.

5. The fifth inquiry may be: how do these good **Genii** become serviceable to men, either for heightening their **Devotions** or enabling them to **Prophesy**? Can it be by any other way than by descending into their bodies and possessing the heart and brain? For the **Euchites** <note>A 4th-century Christian sect (also called Messalians) who believed in continuous prayer and claimed to see demons and the Trinity with their eyes</note>, who sought the gift of **Prophecy** through familiarity with evil spirits, utterly wiped out in their souls the paternal symbols <note>original: <term>πατρικὰ σύμβολα</term>; the innate divine principles or "sparks" of goodness and honesty implanted in the soul by God</note> (as you may see in **Psellus’s** *On the Operation of Daemons* <note>original: <term>περὶ ἐνεργείας δαιμόνων</term>; a famous 11th-century treatise by Michael Psellus on demonology</note>), so that the evil spirits might enter their bodies. They claimed that those sparks of virtue would drive the spirits away, but those be—

being extinguished, they could come in and possess them, enabling them to *prophesy*. And that the imps of witches do sometimes enter their own bodies as well as those of the people to whom they send them, is plain in the story of the Witches of *Warboys* <note>original: "Warbois"; a famous 1593 trial of the Samuel family for witchcraft in Huntingdonshire</note>. It is also the opinion of *Trismegistus* <note>original: "Trismegist"; Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with mystical and alchemical writings</note>, that these spirits get into the veins and arteries of both men and beasts.

Wherefore, concerning the *dreams* and *visions* of this holy man who so freely shared his experiences with *Bodin* <note>original: "Bodin"; Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and writer on demonology</note>, it may be considered reasonable that the *good Genius* <note>original: "good Genius"; a benevolent guardian spirit</note> insinuated himself into his very body, just as the *bad* spirits enter the bodies of the wicked. By residing in his *brain* and shaping it—by thinking of this or that object, just as we ourselves *shape* images when we think—the external *senses* being asleep, those shapes would easily be represented to his *common sense* <note>original: "Common sense"; the internal faculty that integrates sensory data into a single perception</note>. When his *memory* recovered them upon waking, they could not but seem to him as other *dreams* did, except that they were better, as they always signified something of importance to him.

But those raptures of *devotion* during the day might be caused by the spirit kindling a purer kind of *love-flame* in his *heart*, as well as by strengthening and elevating his *imagination*. How far a man may be carried beyond himself by this "redoubled soul" within him, no one, I think, can well conceive, unless they have experienced it themselves.

6. And if this is their manner of communion, it may well be asked, in the sixth place, whether *all men* are capable of association with these *good Genii*. *Cardan* <note>original: "Cardan"; Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian polymath</note> somewhere suggests that their approaches are detectable <note>original: "deprehensible"</note> by certain *sweet smells* they emit. From this, it seems not improbable that those bodies that naturally smell *sweet* themselves—provided the mind does not "stink" with *pride* and *hypocrisy*—have some natural advantage for gaining their company. But if a specific *complexion* <note>original: "complexion"; a person's physical and psychological constitution or "humors"</note> or *natural condition* is required, it will be less hopeful for everyone to obtain their acquaintance. Yet *regeneration* <note>The process of spiritual rebirth or moral improvement</note>, when it reaches its full development—though this cannot happen without much pain and anguish—may well rectify all uncleanness of nature. Thus, no singularly good and sincere man can reasonably despair of their familiarity. For when someone is so highly in favor with the *Prince* <note>Referring to God</note>, it is no wonder he is noticed by the Prince's *courtiers* <note>Referring to angels or spirits</note>.

7. But the last and most significant question is whether it is lawful to *pray* to God for such a *good Genius* or *Angel*. The example in the preceding story seems to be a sufficient warrant. However, I believe *faith* and *desire* ought to be "at full sail" to make such *voyages* successful, and our end and purpose must be pure and sincere. But if *pride*, *conceitedness*, or a *craving* <note>original: "Affectation"</note> for some special privilege above other mortals drives a man to such a bold enterprise, his devotions will no more move either *God* or the *good Genii* than the whining voice of a fraud <note>original: "Counterfeit"</note> will stir the affection of a truly charitable person. Indeed, this high presumption may invite some real *fiends* to play a worse trick on him than was played on that tattered rogue *Guzman* <note>original: "Guzman"; the protagonist of the picaresque novel *Guzmán de Alfarache*</note> by those *mocking spirits*, for his impudent pretending to be related to, and his bold intrusion into the company of, the gentry and nobility of *Genoa*.

Those who keep their eyes solely on these virtues will find everything their heart can desire coming to them. But those who reach out their hands to grab at "high things," as they imagine them, while neglecting these virtues, prove in the end to be only a plague to themselves and a laughingstock to the world.

These are the various speculations that the previous narration would naturally produce in the minds of the curious. But I imagine I hear the *Atheist* replying to all of this, saying that I have developed a long argument based on uncertain foundations, and asking me—not without some scorn and anger—whether I really believe that diverse fable I have repeated from *Bodin* <note>original: "Bodinus"; Jean Bodin, the French jurist previously mentioned</note> and commented upon so much. To this I answer: I will not swear an oath that even the most likely passage in all of *Plutarch's Lives* or *Livy's History* <note>two famous works of ancient Greek and Roman history</note> is absolutely true. However, I am not ashamed to profess that I am as well-assured in my own judgment of the *Existence of Spirits* as I am that I have met men in *Westminster Hall* <note>the center of the English legal system in London</note> or seen livestock in *Smithfield* <note>London's famous livestock market</note>.

## CHAPTER XV.

1. *The structure of the human body and apparitions are the most convincing arguments against the atheist. 2. His first evasion of the former argument, pretending that there were always men, women, and other species in the world. 3. The author's answer to this claim: first, that every man was mortal, and therefore was either created or rose out of the earth. 4. The further usefulness of this answer for completely dismantling the atheist's first evasion.*

1. Thus we have gone through the many and varied effects represented to our senses on this wide theater of the world. The faintest and most obscure of these are arguments enough to prove the *existence*

existence of a *deity*. But since some proofs are more obvious <note>original: "palpable"</note> than others, and better suited <note>original: "accommodate"</note> to awaken the dull and slow belief of the *atheist* into the acknowledgment of a *God*, it will not be out of place to take notice of what *evasions* he attempts to make to untangle himself from those proofs that he imagines most sensibly entangle him and most strongly hinder his escape.

And such are especially these last two I insisted upon: *the curious frame of man's body* and *apparitions*.

2. And some endeavor to evade the force of the former like this: "That there has ever been man and woman and other *species* in the world, and so it is no wonder that like should propagate its like, and therefore that there is no need for any other invisible or material cause but the *species* of things themselves; and so these admirable contrivances in nature must imply no divine *wisdom* nor *counsel*, nor any such thing."

3. But here I ask: whether there was *ever* any *man* who was not *mortal*, and whether there is any mortal who did not have *a beginning*? And if he had, it must be either by *generation* <note>meaning natural reproduction</note> or *creation*. If by *creation*, there is a *God*. If by spontaneous *generation* <note>original: "equivocal Generation"; the archaic belief that living organisms could be produced from non-living matter like earth</note>, as rising out of the *earth*, our argument will still hold good notwithstanding this evasion. But if you say there was never any man in the world who was not born of a *woman*, this must amount to nothing more than this: that there has been an infinite number of *successive* births. If anything more than this is meant by it, it will not make sense.

4. For though our *imagination* <note>original: "Phanſie"</note> cannot run through an *infinite series* of *effects*, yet our *reason* is assured there is no *effect* without a *cause*. And let the progress of *causes* and *effects* be as *infinite* as it will, at last we naturally resolve it into some *First*. And he who denies this seems to me to willfully shut his eyes <note>original: "wink"</note> against the light of nature and do violence to the faculties of his mind. And therefore, of necessity, there must be at least one *first man* and *woman* who are first *in the order of nature* <note>original: "ordine Naturae"</note>, even though the infinity of time (counting back from the present) causes a confusion and obscurity in our understanding. And these which are thus *first* in *order of nature* or *causality* must also exist first before there can be any other men or women in the world. And therefore concerning these *first* ones, it being manifest that they were born of no *parents*, it follows they were *created* or rose out of the *earth*, and so the *evasion* will be frustrated.

5. Besides, if you affirm that there was *never* any *man* in the world but who was born of a *woman*, and so grew to man's estate by degrees, it will fall to some man's share to be a *babe* and a *man* at once, or to be both *father* and *child*. For as soon as mankind existed (let it be from eternity, and beyond eternity is nothing), those who then existed were begotten by *somebody*; and since there was *nothing* before them to beget them, therefore they begot *themselves*.

6. But to claim that they should at once then have been *perfect men*—their substances being made of alterable and passive matter that is worked diversely and by degrees into the frame it has, according to the perpetual testimony of nature—is as rash as if they should say that *boots* and *shoes*

and stockings, and pies and peels <note>original: "Peels"; a long-handled shovel used by bakers to slide bread into an oven</note> and ovens, have existed together throughout all *eternity*. For it is obvious that there must be an orderly interval of time before these things can exist. The killing and skinning of oxen and sheep must happen first, as must tanning, spinning, cutting, and many other such circumstances. 

So it is enormously ridiculous to say that mankind might have existed all at once from all *eternity*—unless the omnipotence of a God (who can do whatever we can imagine and more) should, by his irresistible command <note>original: "Fiat"</note>, cause such a thing in a moment as soon as he himself existed. And he has existed forever, and was never lacking in either power or skill.

But the idea that fluid and blind *matter* could, by itself, have been raised up from all *eternity* into such complete *species* of things is entirely groundless and irrational. I say, that there should ever be such a thing in the world as *a man existing by himself in this physical body* that we see—who nevertheless afterwards died like other mortals—is a fable beyond all poetic fictions. It is more incredible than the most foolish legend that any religion ever offered for an *atheist* to believe.

7. Others, therefore, deserting this way of *evasion*, betake themselves to another, which, though it seems more plausible at first glance, is just as frivolous. They say:

> "That all the *species* of things—*man* himself
> not excepted—first came out of the earth by the 
> manifold <note>original: "omnifarious"</note> attempts of the *particles* 
> of *matter* upon one another. These at last 
> happened upon such a lucky construction and 
> structure of the bodies of creatures as we see. 
> Since they had an infinite *series* of time to try all 
> possible combinations <note>original: "tricks"</note>, they would by 
> necessity eventually arrive at the state they are in now."

But I answer: these *particles* might commit infinite repetitions <note>original: "Tautologies"</note> in their collisions and motions. Therefore, there was no such necessity at all of falling into those forms and shapes that appear in the world.

Again, there is such excellent design in the *body*—for example, that of a man, as I have previously demonstrated—that it can be nothing other than the effect of very accurate *knowledge* and *deliberation*.

And lastly, if this collision of *atoms* were left without a guide, it is a miracle beyond all understanding that they should produce no unfit species <note>original: "inept species"</note> of things. For example, creatures that by their own nature have only three legs, one eye, or one ear, or rows of teeth along the vertebrae of their backs, and the like, as I have suggested above. These clumsy designs <note>original: "Ineptitudes"</note> would be much easier to hit upon by chance than such accurate and faultless frameworks of creatures.

8. But to escape the force of this argument against the accidental collision of *atoms*, they will devise <note>original: "excogitate"</note> this mad *evasion*:

> "That nature did indeed at first bring forth 
> such malformed <note>original: "ill-favoured"</note> and poorly equipped 
> *monsters* as well as those of a more exquisite 
> frame. But those that were more perfect fell 
> upon the others and killed and devoured them. 
> The monsters, not being as well provided with 
> either limbs or senses as the others, were never 
> able to hop fast enough away from them, or to 
> discover the approaching dangers that were 
> constantly coming upon them." 

But this unjust and audacious slander...
