...accusations cast upon God and Nature will be easily revealed and proven false, if we only consider:

First, that **Trees**, **Herbs**, and **Flowers**, which do not move from their places or practice such violent cruelty upon one another, are all in their various kinds **attractive** and **elegant**, and have no **clumsiness** <note>original: "ineptitude"</note> or **defect** in them.

Secondly, that all creatures born of **decaying matter** <note>original: "putrefaction"</note>—such as mice, frogs, and the like—as well as those many hundreds of **insects**, such as **grasshoppers, flies, spiders**, and others, also have a most precise arrangement of **body parts**. There is nothing made carelessly or poorly in any of them.

Lastly, we see this in more complex creatures, such as the **Scotch Barnacles** <note>The "Barnacle Goose" was a legendary bird once believed to grow on trees or from driftwood rather than hatching from eggs.</note> that **historians** write about. Even if there is any doubt about those, **Gerard** <note>John Gerard (c. 1545–1612), a famous English herbalist and author of "The Herball or Generall Historie of Plantes."</note> reports from his own knowledge (which is just as wonderful and relevant to our purpose) that there is a kind of **bird** in **Lancashire** called **Tree-Geese**. They are bred out of rotten pieces of broken ships and tree trunks cast upon a little island in **Lancashire** called the **Pile of Foulders** <note>Now known as Piel Island or the Piel of Fouldrey.</note>. The same author says he has also found the same thing in other parts of this kingdom. 

Those **birds**, in all respects—though born this way from **decaying matter** (and the fact that they are born this way is undeniably true, as anyone may satisfy themselves by consulting the very last page of **Gerard’s** *History of Plants*)—have as perfect a body and are as well-designed for the life of such a creature as any of those produced by **breeding** <note>original: "propagation"</note>. Indeed, these kinds of birds also breed themselves, which has so deceived some foolish people that they have denied the other way they are born. In reality, being born one way does not exclude the other, as is seen in **frogs** and **mice** <note>At the time, it was commonly believed that some animals could be produced both by parents and by "spontaneous generation" from mud or rot.</note>.

Therefore, since these things produced from the earth and from **decaying matter** are as perfect and precise in every way as any others, it is a clear discovery that Nature never created any **species** of things poorly or foolishly. Therefore, she was always guided by **wisdom** and **divine foresight** <note>original: "Counsell and Providence"</note>—that is, Nature itself is the creation of an all-knowing God.

9. This consideration does not only remove this current **excuse** <note>original: "Evasion"</note>, but it more clearly and understandably weakens the previous one. For what good does it do for them to flee to the idea of an infinite breeding of **individuals** within the same eternal **species** (as they imagine), so that they might always be able to point to a cause equal to the effect? Even in these products of decay, **wisdom** and **design** are just as clearly visible as in others. Thus, they are nevertheless necessarily **trapped** <note>original: "illaqueated"</note> in the same difficulty they thought they had escaped through such a clever trick.

### CHAPTER XVI.

*1. The atheists' **excuses** <note>original: "evasions"</note> against **apparitions**: first, that they are mere products of the imagination. 2. Second, that although they are external realities, they are caused by the force of imagination; with a refutation of these ideas. 3. Their foolish idea that the battles seen in the **air** are caused by shedding particles <note>original: "exuvious effluxes"</note> of things; with a refutation of this. 4. A detailed refutation of their last excuse (namely, that those battles are reflections of battles on the Earth) based on the distance and weakness of reflection. 5. Based on the rough surface <note>original: "rude politure"</note> of the clouds. 6. Based on the clouds' inability to reflect even the image of the stars, which would be much easier; first, because the stars do not appear to shrink in size. 7. Second, because of the purity of the stars' light. 8. Third, because of the position of our eyes within the Earth’s shadow. 9. Finally, because stars are scattered everywhere and would be reflected from every part of the sky if the clouds actually had any such reflective quality. 10. That if clouds did have enough reflectivity to represent battles from such a great distance, it would have to be through some supernatural mechanism. 11. That this mechanism is governed by limited laws. 12. Therefore, at least some of these aerial battles cannot be reflections from the Earth. 13. **Machiavelli’s** <note>Niccolò Machiavelli (1469–1527), the Italian political philosopher.</note> opinion regarding these battles in the sky. 14. Nothing in philosophy is as provable as the existence of a God. 15. Where the arrogant display <note>original: "pedantick affectation"</note> of atheism likely originated. 16. The true reasons why someone might be genuinely prone to atheism. 17. That men should not set their personal temperaments <note>original: "complexional humours"</note> against the principles of reason and the evidence of nature and history. The author’s apology for including so many stories of spirits.*

1. **N**ow, as for the **excuses** whereby they would try to escape the force of the argument for **spirits** drawn from **apparitions**, these excuses are so weak and foolish that one can be almost certain the atheists were actually convinced in their judgment of the truth of such stories. Otherwise, it would have been better to flatly deny them rather than invent such useless and empty reasons for them.

For first, they say these sightings are nothing but **imaginations**, and that there is nothing real outside of ourselves in such **apparitions**.

2. However, when they are forced away from this superficial account—because many people often see the same thing at once—they then retreat to a claim of such miraculous power in the **imagination** <note>original: "phansy"</note> that it could supposedly change the air into a real shape and form. This would mean others could behold it just as clearly as the person who created it through the power of their own imagination.

Now I ask anyone: is this not a more difficult **mystery** and more unbelievable than all the **magical transformations** attributed to **demons** <note>original: "devils"</note> or **witches**? For it is much easier to imagine that some **intelligent entity** in the **air** could transform the air into this or that shape while being present in that part of the air it transforms, than to believe that the **imagination**...

But suppose it could; can it *animate the air* that it thus changes <note>original: "metamorphize"</note>, and make it speak, and answer questions, and put things into people’s hands, and the like? Oh, the gullibility of drunken <note>original: "besotted"</note> *atheism*! How intoxicated and foolish they are in their ideas, being surrendered to their senses and having lost the free use of the natural faculties of their minds!

But should this force of *imagination* reach as high as the *clouds* as well, and make men fight full-scale battles in the *air*, running and charging at one another?

<margin>In his 51st Dialogue on Apparitions <note>original: "Dial. de Apparitionibus"</note>.</margin>
3. Here the same bold pretender to wit and philosophy, * *Julius Caesar Vanini* <note>original: "Caesar Vaninus"; an Italian philosopher (1585–1619) executed for atheism and remains a frequent target for More's criticism.</note> (who cunningly and deceitfully tries to inject the poison of *atheism* into the mind of his reader at every opportunity) resorts to those old, discarded ideas <note>original: "cast rags"</note> of *Epicurus's* school, the *shedding of particles* <note>original: "Exuvious Effluxes"; the Epicurean theory that objects constantly shed thin layers of atoms that fly through the air and strike our eyes.</note> from things. He attempts to explain these *phenomena* this way: that the vapors of *men’s bodies*—and apparently of *horses* too—are carried up into the *air* and fall into a certain organized arrangement, and so they imitate those shapes high among the clouds.

But I ask: how do the *vapors* of the *horses* find the *vapors* of their *riders*? And when and how long does it take for them to come together? And don’t they appear before there are even any armies in the field to send up such *vapors*? And do *armor* <note>original: "harness"</note> and *weapons* send up vapors too, such as *swords, pikes*, and *shields*? And how do they happen to land so perfectly in the hands of those aerial soldiers—especially the vapors of *metals* (if they have any), which are likely heavier than the breath <note>original: "reek"</note> of *animals* and *men*? Finally, how do they manage to *fire* at one another and to *fight*, since there is neither life nor soul in them? And do *sounds* also have *shed particles* <note>original: "Exuviae"</note> that are saved until these events? For at *Aldeburgh* <note>original: "Alborough"</note> in *Suffolk* in 1642, very loud beatings of *drums*, shooting of *muskets*, and *cannons* <note>original: "Ordnance"</note> were heard in the *air*. Other similar omens <note>original: "Prodigies"</note> have included the sounding of *trumpets*, as *Snellius* <note>Willebrord Snellius (1580–1626), a Dutch astronomer and mathematician.</note> writes.

<margin>* Natural History, book 2, chapter 57 <note>original: "Hist. Natural. lib. 2. cap. 57."</note>.</margin>
And * *Pliny* <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman author who compiled ancient scientific knowledge.</note> also mentions the sounding of *trumpets* and clashing of *armor* heard from the heavens around the time of the *Cimbrian Wars*, and often before. But here at *Aldeburgh*, everything ended with a melodious noise of *musical instruments*.

The *shed particles* of fiddles apparently fly up into the *air* too? Or were those *musical notes* frozen there for a time, and then, at the heat and firing of the cannons, the *air* softened and thawed, becoming harmoniously vocal? Men who willfully close their eyes against the light of nature and are distanced from the true knowledge and acknowledgment of a God are intoxicated with such vain ideas!

But in nature, this is clearly impossible. For by necessity, if these armies were fighting at such a *distance* from the spectators that the news of the battle never reaches their ears, then their eyes could never see—

# CHAP. XVI. An Antidote against Atheism.

...it by any *reflection* from the clouds. For besides the fact that *reflection* makes images dimmer than direct *sight*, such a great distance from the army to the clouds, and then from the clouds to our eye, will diminish the *visual images* <note>original: "species"; in 17th-century optics, these were the visual likenesses or "forms" of objects that were thought to travel through the air to the eye</note> so exceedingly that they will not be *visible* at all.

5. Or if we could imagine that there might sometimes be such an advantage in the shape of these clouds that it might in some way remedy this lessening of the *visual images*, yet their surfaces are so extremely roughly polished—and *reflection* (*which, as I said, is always dim enough by itself*) is here so extraordinarily imperfect—that they can never be able, according to the laws of nature, to return the *visual images* of *terrestrial objects* back again to our *sight*. It is evident that they are unfit for this because they cannot even perform a far less difficult task: for we never find them able to reflect the image of a *star*, whereas not only glass, but every troubled pool or dirty puddle of water in the highway usually does so.

6. Several reasons will sufficiently inform us that it is far easier for a *star* than for any of these *objects* here upon Earth to be *reflected* to our eyes by those crude natural looking-glasses placed among the clouds.

First, the stars do not decrease at all from their usual magnitude in which they ordinarily appear to us by this reflection; a difference of many hundreds of leagues makes no difference in their size. Indeed, the distance of the diameter of the *Earth's orbit* makes no difference, as must be acknowledged by all those who admit the *annual motion* <note>The Earth’s yearly orbit around the sun in the Copernican system.</note> of the Earth. But a very few miles exceedingly diminish the usual size of the *visual image* of a *horse* or *man*, even to the point that they become invisible. What then will become of his *sword, shield,* or *spear*? And in these cases we are now speaking of, I have already mentioned how long a journey the *visual images* must take from the Earth to the cloud that reflects them.

7. Secondly, it is manifest that a star has preeminence over these *terrestrial objects* in that it is as pure a light as the *sun*, though not so *large*, while they are merely opaque, colored bodies; therefore, there is no comparison between the vigor and strength of the *visual image* of a *star* and of them.

8. Thirdly, in the *night-time*, because the eye is positioned in the shadow of the Earth, those *reflections* of a star will be even more easily visible; whereas the great light of the sun by day must certainly weaken these reflected images of objects upon the Earth, as his beams strike our eyes with such strong vibrations.

9. Fourthly and lastly, since there are stars all over the firmament, it should seem a hundred times easier for natural causes to produce a *Paraster* or *Parastron* <note>More coins these terms from Greek roots: "paraster" for a "mock star" and "parastron" for a "mock constellation."</note> (let *analogy* embolden me to call these seldom or never seen *phenomena* <note>original: "Phænomena"</note>—the image of a single star or whole constellation reflected from the clouds—by these names) than a *Parhelion* <note>original: "Parelios"; a mock sun or "sun dog."</note> or *Paraselene* <note>A mock moon or "moon dog."</note>. But the history of these latter two is more than a hundred times more frequent than that of the *Paraster*. For it is so seldom discovered that it is doubted whether it exists or not, or rather acknowledged not to exist; for which there can be no reason, except that the clouds are so poorly polished that they...

10. Therefore, it is plain that these *apparitions* high in the air are no reflections of any objects on Earth. Or, if it were imaginable that they were, some *supernatural cause* must assist to solidify <note>original: "conglaciate"; to freeze or thicken into a smooth surface</note> and polish the surfaces of the clouds to such an extraordinary accuracy of shape and smoothness as would be required for such amazing reflections. 

And I know no reason at all in nature or philosophy for any man to deny that those *spirits* who rule in the air may act upon the materials there, just as *men* here upon the Earth work upon the land and the neighboring elements as far as they can reach—shaping, perfecting, and directing things according to their own purpose and pleasure. The timing of these appearances seems like a strong argument that the help of some active *spirits* <note>original: "officious Genii"; "officious" here means "dutiful" or "active" rather than "annoying"</note> is employed in such omens as these. According to the observations of historians, they are the **forerunners of civil unrest and troubles in all kingdoms and commonwealths.**

11. Yet, even though they are as skilled as the craftsmen I imagine, since they are working upon nature, they must be bounded by the laws of nature. *Reflection* has its limits just as *refraction* does, whether for carrying *visual images* or for focusing heat. The discerning intellectual René Descartes <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> was well aware of these laws and limits, and he generously and wisely declared: *That a magnifying glass <note>original: "burning-Glass"</note>—if the distance from the glass to its focal point is not smaller in proportion to its diameter than the distance from the Earth to the Sun is to the Sun's diameter—will burn no more intensely than the direct rays of the sun would without it. This is true even if the glass were as perfectly shaped and carefully polished as if it were made by the hand of an angel.*

<margin>
* See chapter 12, section 6.
</margin>
12. Therefore, even if the surface of the clouds were polished perfectly and fitted for reflection, it is still evident that some of these *apparitions* cannot be mere reflections of armies skirmishing on the ground. For those that are observed to fight specifically over a particular city, if they were merely reflections of real fights, they would necessarily have to be from some armies not far off; and if so, they could not help but be discovered, or at least quickly reported. 

From this, it is manifest that such skirmishings in the clouds are real encounters taking place there, not the images or reflections of battles on the ground. And considering that there have been such real omens of fighting on the ground itself by these supernatural horsemen <note>original: "Aereal Coursers"</note>, as I have mentioned above, it is only reasonable to believe that most of the rest of these miraculous skirmishings—even those not tied to a specific city—are really in the clouds or sky, and are not a shadow or reflection of battles upon the Earth. 

It would be easy to prove from history that these fights have been seen over specific cities. I shall only mention the report by Willebrord Snell <note>original: "Snellius"</note> regarding Amersfoort <note>original: "Amortsfort"</note>, stating that such skirmishes were seen there, and that near...

Machiavelli <note>original: "Machiavell"</note> reports similar things concerning Arezzo <note>original: "Aretium"</note>, and acknowledges that these kinds of prodigies are very frequent in history. He also notes they are certain forerunners of the troubles and disturbances of the state and country in which they appear.

13. His own words are so candid and sincere, and his judgment is so significant (though he does not pretend to be a philosopher) regarding the reason for these strange sights, that I think it is worth the time to transcribe them. <margin>\*Discourses on the Republic, Book 1, Chapter 56. <note>original: "Disput. de Republica lib. 1. cap. 56."</note></margin> \* "I believe that the causes of such things can be explained by those who are distinguished in the knowledge of natural and supernatural things—of which I confess I am ignorant—unless perhaps we should conclude, along with certain philosophers, that the air is full of spirits and Intelligences. These spirits, foreseeing future events and pitying human misfortunes, announce them to men through signs of this kind so that they may prepare and fortify themselves against them more opportunely. However the matter stands, we certainly know from experience that such signs are usually followed by great political upheavals." <note>original: "Hujusmodi rerum causas ab iis explicari posse credo... talia signa sequi solere magnos aliquos motus."</note>

14. I have now completed this current treatise against *Atheism* in all three of its parts. As I look back and see that clear and irrefutable evidence for the cause I have undertaken—the external *appearances* of things in the world so faithfully supporting the undeniable dictates of the innate *principles* of our own minds—I cannot help but confidently declare that there is no single concept in all of philosophy more certain and demonstrable than *that there is a God*.

And truly, I think I have searched through every corner of every kind of philosophy that could claim to have any influence in this controversy with such diligence that I may safely pronounce this: it is mere brutish *ignorance* or *shamelessness*—not any *skill* in *nature* or the *knowledge* of things—that can encourage any person to profess *Atheism*, or to embrace it when it is proposed by those who claim it.

15. But I suspect the reality is this: at first, some famously learned men, because they were not as foolishly zealous or superstitious as others, were misunderstood by the *unlearned* <note>original: "Ideots"; in this period, the term often referred to those lacking formal education rather than those with a mental disability</note> and slandered as *Atheists*. Ever since then, one vainglorious fool or another has pretended to be *atheistical*—whenever he thought it was safe—so that he might, forsooth, be thought of as more *learned* or a more profound *scientist* <note>original: "Naturalist"</note>.

16. But I dare assure anyone that if they only look into the bottom of this enormous *disease of the soul*, as Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Trismegist"</note> truly calls it, they will find the cause is nothing but either *vanity* of mind or *brutish sensuality*. It stems from an untamed desire to satisfy one’s own *will* in *every thing*, a guilty *conscience*, and a base *fear* of divine *vengeance*. It comes from *ignorance* of the limitations and insufficiency of physical causes <note>original: "second causes"</note>, or a jumbled foulness and *disorder* of the spirits caused by constant intemperance and luxury. Or else, it is a dark, deadening *Melancholy* that so starves and kills the soul’s ability to perceive divine matters that it makes a person as unfit for such contemplation as if their head were filled with cold earth or dry grave-mold.

17. And to such dull temperaments <note>original: "slow Constitutions"</note> as these, I shall not wonder if, just as the *first part* of my discourse must seem marvelously subtle, so the *last* appears ridiculously incredible. But they are to remember that I do not...

...I do not here appeal to the *humors of the temperament* <note>original: "Complexional humors"; the Early Modern belief that a person's physical health and personality were determined by the balance of four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> or the peculiar *tastes* <note>original: "Relishes"</note> of men that arise out of the condition of the *Body*. If I have insisted somewhat more fully upon the last of these, it should not be attributed to any vain gullibility on my part, or because I take pleasure in telling strange stories. Rather, I thought it appropriate to fortify and strengthen the faith of others as much as I could. I am well assured that a scornful disbelief in such narrations concerning *Spirits*—and any attempt to make them all seem ridiculous and incredible—is a dangerous prelude to *Atheism* itself; or else, it is a more secretive and crafty way of professing and implying it. For certainly, that saying is no more true in politics—*No Bishop, no King* <note>A famous maxim used by King James I, suggesting that the hierarchy of the Church supported the authority of the Monarchy</note>—than this one is in *metaphysics* <term>the branch of philosophy that deals with the first principles of things, including abstract concepts such as being, knowing, substance, and cause</term>: *No Spirit, no God*.

### CHAPTER I.

*1. The Author's reason for adding this Appendix to his Antidote. 2. A list of the chief objections made against the First Book of the work.*

<margin>1.</margin>
Suspected *innocence* and doubted *truth* can win no greater credit than by the strictest examination. For the world is thereby *more fully* assured of the *blamelessness* of the one and of the *solidity* of the other, more than is possible without such a public trial. Therefore, so that such a great advantage may not be missing from the important cause we have in hand, I was not content only to set down those *reasons* for the *existence of God* which in my own judgment I believed to be irrefutably firm. Instead, so that their strength may appear more obvious to all men, I have brought into view the primary and most significant *objections* I could find—whether raised by those who have themselves questioned any argument I used, or by those who were invited to more carefully search for and discover, where they could, any weakness or inconsistency in any reasoning throughout the entire treatise. And the primary exceptions and objections against the First Book are these:

2. First, that the basis of our *demonstration* of the *existence of God* from his *ideas*—namely, that there are *innate ideas* <note>Innate ideas are concepts thought to be present in the mind from birth rather than learned through experience.</note> in the mind of man—is false, as they say.

Secondly, that there is no such *idea* of God at all like the one we have described.

<summary>In this opening to the Appendix, Henry More explains that he is addressing criticisms of his work to further prove the solidity of his arguments. He identifies two major objections to his first book: the denial of innate ideas and the rejection of his specific definition of God's idea.</summary>
<keywords>innate ideas, existence of God, objections, philosophical method, Henry More, epistemology, theology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Henry More’s "Appendix to the Antidote Against Atheism," specifically concluding a list of eight objections to his original arguments and beginning his detailed rebuttal in Chapter II. It follows the start of a list of objections from page 145.</meta>

<page-num>146</page-num>
<header>*An Appendix to the foregoing Antidote.* CHAP. II.</header>

neither **innate** nor **acquired** <note>original: "acquisititious"</note> or **transcribed** <note>original: "transcriptitious," meaning copied from something else</note>; because it involves the concept of a **spirit**, which again consists of such particular concepts as are utterly inconceivable.

Thirdly, that **existence** is not a **term of perfection**, and therefore it is not so inseparably involved in the concept of a **being absolutely perfect**, or of **God**.

Fourthly, that although **necessary existence** is included in the **idea** of God, our inferring from that fact that he **does exist** is nothing but a sophism <note>A sophism is a clever but false argument intended to deceive.</note>; because a being **absolutely evil**, as well as one **absolutely perfect**, would include **necessary existence** in its **idea**.

Fifthly, that if there is any **necessarily existing** thing, it is plainly **matter**, which we ill-advisedly call **space**, which we cannot imagine except as having always and forever **necessarily existed**.

Sixthly, that God did not put this **idea** of himself into the mind of man; rather, it was the more subtle sort of **politicians**, who have always used religion as a mere **engine of state** <note>An "engine of state" refers to a tool or mechanism used by a government to maintain control over its citizens.</note>.

Seventhly, that the **fear** and **hopes** of a **natural conscience** are really nothing but **passions** raised by a belief in a God which men have acquired through **tradition** or **education**.

Lastly, that these **arguments** by which we prove the **incorporeity** <note>Incorporeity means the state of having no physical body or being immaterial.</note> of the soul of man will also prove the **incorporeity** of the soul of a beast, and therefore they are false arguments.

To these, I shall answer in order with as little pomp and wordiness, and as much clarity and plainness, as I can in such a subtle and difficult matter.

---

...what we have written, he must plainly see that the weight <note>original: "stress"</note> of our argument does not rely on this notion of **innate ideas**, but upon the accepted truth that there are some things so plain that, however the soul came to know them, she cannot help but agree with them and acknowledge them to be undeniably true.

2. Now, the **idea** of an **absolutely perfect Being** is such that it must be acknowledged, according to the light of nature, to be the true idea of such a Being. Whether you call it **innate** or not, it makes no difference; the proof will follow as inevitably as if it were admitted to be an innate idea. We can see this more clearly if we look at other ideas—for example, the idea of a **triangle**, of a **regular geometric body**, and of a **round solid**. The nature of these ideas is such that the human mind cannot possibly deny that they are distinct ideas, or that certain characteristics belong to them.

For example: every **triangle** is either **equilateral** <note>original: "Isopleuron," Greek for "equal-sided"</note>, **isosceles**, or **scalene** <note>original: "Scalenum"</note>. Thus, there are exactly **three** kinds of triangles in relation to their sides, and no more. There are **five regular bodies** in geometry, no more and no less: the **cube**, the **tetrahedron** <note>original: "Tetraedrum"</note>, the **octahedron** <note>original: "Octaedrum"</note>, the **dodecahedron** <note>original: "Dodecaedrum"</note>, and the **icosahedron** <note>original: "Eicosaedrum"</note>. There is only one kind of round **solid**: the **sphere** or **globe**. So, when contemplating the **idea** of an **absolutely perfect Being** (whether the idea is innate or not), we must conclude that there can be only **one such being** in existence, and that this one being cannot fail to exist, as we have demonstrated at length.

3. However, although we do not strictly need the principle of **innate ideas** to carry out our demonstration, I still believe it is true. It is important to encourage the reader to pay attention to the concepts of his own mind and to appreciate the excellence of the "Judge" (reason) we must appeal to. Therefore, I thought it appropriate to emphasize it. I am now ready to prove that this principle is true, despite anything alleged against it.

4. In the sixth chapter of the first book, I argued that the exact **idea** of a **circle** or a **triangle** is suggested <note>original: "hinted"</note> to us by shapes found in **matter**, rather than being taught to us by them. This remains true despite the objection that these shapes seem exact to our **outward senses** when we look at them carelessly. We eventually correct ourselves, not only because we can see that physical figures are always **imperfect**, but because of our **innate knowledge**. This knowledge tells us that the physical senses cannot see an exact triangle, because an **indivisible point** (where the angles must meet) is completely invisible to the outward sense.

Furthermore, we should consider that even if a triangle could be drawn so perfectly that it appeared exact to our eyes—even looking through **microscopes**—people who have never seen such a precise drawing still form an exact **idea** of a triangle in their minds based on rougher sketches. Since they did not learn this from any external object, it must be an internal representation from their own minds.

...as we have written, he must plainly see that the weight of our argument does not depend upon this concept of **Innate Ideas**, but upon that admitted truth: that there are some things so plain that, however the soul came to the knowledge of them, she cannot help but agree with them and acknowledge them to be undeniably true.

2. Now the idea of a **Being who is absolutely perfect** is such that it must be acknowledged—according to the light of nature—to be indeed the true **idea** of such a being. Whether we call it **innate** or not, it makes no difference; the demonstration will follow as inevitably as if it were admitted to be an innate idea. We shall see this more clearly if we look at examples of other **ideas**: for example, the **idea** of a **triangle**, of a **regular geometric body**, and of a **round solid**. For the nature of these **ideas** is such that the human mind cannot possibly deny that they are distinct ideas, and that certain properties <note>original: "affections"</note> belong to them. 

For example: every **triangle** is either **equilateral** <note>original: "Isopleuron"</note>, **isosceles**, or **scalene**. Thus, there are exactly **three** kinds of them based on their sides, and no more. There are **five regular bodies** in geometry, neither more nor less: the **cube**, the **tetrahedron**, the **octahedron**, the **dodecahedron**, and the **icosahedron**. There is only one kind of **round solid**, namely the **sphere** or **globe**. And so, when contemplating the **idea** of a **Being who is absolutely perfect** (whether the idea is innate or not, it makes no difference), we cannot help but conclude that there can be only **one such being** in number, and that **that one** also cannot fail to exist, as we have demonstrated in detail.

3. However, even though we do not need such a principle as **Innate Ideas** to carry out our demonstration, I still believe it is true. Because it is important to encourage the reader to pay attention to the **notions** of his own mind and to appreciate the excellence of that "judge" <note>the mind or reason</note> we are to appeal to, I thought it appropriate to insist upon it. I am ready now to prove that this principle is true, despite anything I find claimed against it.

4. In the sixth chapter of this first book, I argue that the exact **idea** of a **circle** or a **triangle** is hinted to us by those shapes found in **matter** rather than being taught to us by them. This remains true despite the objection that these shapes seem exact to our **outward senses** when we look at them casually, even if they are not actually perfect. We clearly correct ourselves afterward, not only because of the **figure** (which we may always perceive as imperfect), but by our **innate knowledge**. This knowledge tells us that the **outward senses** cannot see an exact **triangle** because an **indivisible point**, where the angles are supposed to end, is utterly invisible to the **outward sense**.

Besides, one should consider that even if we admitted that a **triangle** could be drawn so perfectly that it appeared exact to our **outward sense**—even looking at it as closely as possible through **microscopes**—those who have never seen or noticed such an accurate drawing still form the exact **idea** of a **triangle** in their minds based on the hint of rougher sketches. Since they did not learn this from any outward object, it must necessarily be the inward representation of their own minds.

### An Appendix to the foregoing Antidote. CHAP. II.

5. But now for other objections: that a **blind man** would be able to talk about **colors** if there were any **innate ideas** in his soul. I say that this does not follow at all, because these **ideas** that I argue are in the soul are not **sensory** <note>original: "Sensible"</note> but **intellectual**. These include many **logical**, **metaphysical**, **mathematical**, and some **moral notions**. We employ all of these as our own ways <note>original: "Modes"</note> of considering sensory objects, but they are not the sensory objects themselves. We have no **idea** of sensory objects in ourselves, but only a capacity—due to the organs of our body—to be affected by them. Therefore, the reason for a blind man's inability to speak of **colors** is simply that he has no foundation <note>original: "Substratum"</note> or mental image <note>original: "Phantasm"; here referring to a sensory perception stored in the mind</note> of the subject of the conversation. Without that, he cannot apply these innate patterns or frameworks of notions that are naturally in his mind, and which he can use when contemplating various other sensory objects.

<margin>See Book 1, chapter 6, section 3.</margin>
6. It is further objected that these **logical** and **mathematical notions** also come through the **senses** because **animals** <note>original: "Brutes"</note> have knowledge of them—and we certainly would not grant animals such a rich internal store as these **innate ideas**. I answer that **animals** do not have the knowledge of any such **notion**. Rather, what they do results from a mere chaining together <note>original: "Concatenation"</note> of sensory **mental images** representing things as **pleasant** <note>original: "grateful"</note> or **unpleasant** to the **senses**. To use the examples provided: a **dog** will bark at one noise, such as a knock at the door, but not at another, like a stool or a dish falling from a shelf. He will follow one scent, like that of a **hare**, and ignore another, and so on. These things are done not because he has any **notion** of **cause and effect**, but by a mere chaining of **mental images** representing things as pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral to his **senses**; in the neutral case, he is not moved at all. If a **dog** snaps at the larger morsel, it is not because he considers the **notion** of **inequality**, but because the sensory object more powerfully moves his appetite. Similarly, if he takes one single side of a **triangle** to get to the corner where a piece of bread is placed, it is not because he considers that a **straight line** is the shortest distance between two points <note>original: "terms"</note>. Instead, he simply feels that by going directly to it, he will arrive sooner than if he went around. Zeno <note>Zeno of Elea, a Greek philosopher known for his paradoxes</note> gave a good example of this with an **ass** at one corner of a pasture and fodder in the other; the ass would go directly to the corner where the fodder lay. Zeno thought this was a very clever joke at the expense of **Euclid's** **demonstration** that **any two sides of a triangle are larger than the third**, implying it was such an obvious truth that no **ass** could miss it.

7. But with the indulgence of such a **critical** philosopher, we may very well suspect that neither **dog** nor **ass**, in moving toward an object, goes in a straight line because he considers that a curved one is further. Rather, he does so because his line of sight guides him straight to the object he sees. He follows this path as naturally—without any reflection on mathematical notions—as a stone thrown from a sling tries to steer its course with a **straight-line motion** <note>original: "Motion rectilinear"</note>. Since a stone does not even possess **senses**, we cannot possibly suspect it of being capable of even the simplest notion in geometry.

8. Therefore, it is a total fallacy to argue that animals, because they do things that appear reasonable or mathematical, therefore do them...

1. # An Appendix to the Foregoing Antidote. CHAP. III.

2. Therefore, since we have defined a *Spirit* (meaning specifically a created one) by its absolute powers of *self-contraction* and *expansion* <note>original: "dilatation"</note>, as well as its relative abilities to *penetrate, move, and alter matter*, we will now address the objections made against both.

Against the first point, it is objected that it is impossible for the human mind to imagine any substance having a power of *self-expansion* and *contraction* to be *unextended* <note>occupying no space</note>. It is argued that *extension* cannot be imagined without a *diversity of parts*, and *diversity of parts* cannot be imagined without the *possibility of dividing or separating them*. This is because a "diversity of parts" in any substance implies a "diversity of substances," and "diversity of substances" implies they are independent of one another. From this, it would follow that *indivisibility* is incompatible with a *Spirit*—even though we included indivisibility in our definition.

I confess this objection is very clever and hits the mark. However, I also believe the difficulty is easily resolved if we acknowledge that something exists in the nature of a *Spirit* similar to what thousands of scholars have acknowledged in the nature of *intentional species* <note>original: "Intentional Species"; in Scholastic philosophy, these are the forms or "images" of objects that travel through the air to the senses and the mind</note>. We will, therefore, represent the property of a Spirit using this *symbolic image* <note>original: "Symbole or Hieroglyphick"</note>.

Suppose a *point of light* which radiates a *luminous sphere* according to the known principles of *optics*. This *sphere of light* closely resembles the nature of a *Spirit*, which is spread out <note>original: "diffus'd"</note> and extended, yet *indivisible*. For we will suppose that in this *Spirit*, the center of life is indivisible, yet it spreads itself out by a kind of *limited omnipresence* <note>original: "circumscrib’d Omnipresency"</note>, just as the *point of light* is visible in every part of the luminous sphere. Even if we assume that the central shining point is *indivisible*, there is nothing divisible in that entire sphere of light. It would be ridiculous to think that any machine or art could separate the rays of light from the shining center and keep them apart by themselves; any person who carefully considers the nature of light will acknowledge this.

Now, there is no difficulty in imagining such a *sphere* as a *substance* rather than just a *quality*. Indeed, this *sphere of light* itself—since it does not exist as a part of any other object in the space it occupies—looks much more like a substance than an *accidental property* <note>original: "Accident"; a philosophical term for a quality that cannot exist on its own, like "redness"</note>. We often mistakenly think that *light* and *colors* radiate in spheres from every point, but it is more rational to apply this concept to *spiritual substances*. Their central essence spreads out into a *secondary substance*, just as rays of light are conceived to shoot out from a glowing point. From this, we can answer the greatest difficulty in the previous objection: namely <note>original: "viz."</note>, that the imagined parts of a *Spirit* have an inseparable dependence upon its central essence. They flow from it and are fundamentally contained within it. Therefore, although there is an *extension* of this entire substantial power, one part cannot be separated or distinguished from another. The entire substance, both *secondary* and *primary* (or *central*), is *indivisible*.

3. But let us look again at this glowing point and the radiant sphere we have used as an example. It is clear that those rays which are hindered from

Thus, there is no generation of a new ray, but an emission of what already existed. By this, we are well-equipped with an answer to a further objection, which would suggest that this *emanation* or *outflow* <note>original: "Efflux"</note> of the *Secondary Substance* from the *Central* is *Creation* properly so called—an act which is considered impossible for any created being to perform.

But we answer that both the *Central* and *Secondary Substance* of a *Spirit* were created at once by God. We might also further wonder whether any *emanation* may be properly called *Creation*, but enough has already been said to satisfy this objection.

4. But we are pushed even further regarding this *self-contraction* and *expansion* <note>original: "dilatation"</note>. It is asked why the *Soul* of Man, which we acknowledge to be a *Spirit*, does not contract itself or withdraw itself from parts that are in pain, or why she does not expand herself beyond the boundaries of the *Body*. To which it is answered: the <term>plantal faculty</term> <note>The "vegetative" or biological part of the soul responsible for the unconscious maintenance of the body.</note> of the *Soul*, by which she is joined to this terrestrial *Body*, is not subject to the will <note>original: "arbitrarious"</note>, but is fated or natural. This union cannot be dissolved unless the bond of life is loosened, and that <term>vital congruity</term> <note>The specific physical state of the body that makes it compatible with the soul.</note> (which exists in the *Body* and necessarily holds the *Soul* there) is either temporarily hindered or utterly destroyed.

<margin>See my *Immortality of the Soul*, Book 2, chapter 11, section 10; also Book 3, chapter 2, sections 3–4.</margin>
5. The last objection against the *self-extension* of a Spirit is that there would be as many *Wills* and *Understandings* as there are *Parts*. But in the *symbolic representation* I have used, I have described the *extension* of a *Spirit* in such a way that it is also acknowledged to be *indivisible*. Therefore, the objection is answered as soon as it is proposed; that logical defense stands ready to receive all such assaults.

<margin>See also this *Appendix*, chapter 10, sections 9–10.</margin>
6. Now, as for the objections made against the *relational powers* <note>original: "Relative faculties"</note> of a *Spirit*—namely, *the power of penetrating, moving, and altering Matter*—there is mainly this one: that *Matter* cannot be altered except by *Motion*, nor can *Motion* be communicated except by *Impulse* <note>physical impact</note>, nor can there be *Impulse* without *Impenetrability* in the thing striking it. Therefore, it is argued that one cannot imagine how a *Spirit* could move *Matter* which it simply passes through <note>penetrates</note>.

But I answer, first, that our *Reason* often proves things to be true that our *Imagination* is baffled by. For example, our *Reason*, considering the nature of an exact *Globe* and a *Plane* <note>a flat surface</note>, will undoubtedly declare that they will touch at a single *point*, and that they may be moved against one another. But our *Imagination* cannot help but make this exception: that the *Globe* thus drawn upon the *Plane* describes a *line*...

...which must necessarily consist of *points*, one point perpetually following another in the entire description. The thought of how monstrous it would be to admit such a thing is something I have already suggested in the preceding Discourse.

Similarly, geometricians demonstrate through *Reason* that the *Angle of Contact* <note>The infinitesimal angle between the circumference of a circle and a tangent line touching it.</note> contained between the *Periphery* <note>original: "Periphery"; the outer boundary or circumference of a circle.</note> and a *Perpendicular* line falling on the end of a circle's *Diameter* is smaller than any acute *Angle* whatsoever. It is so small, in fact, that another *line* cannot fall between the *Periphery* and the *Perpendicular*. Because of this, the *Imagination* <note>original: "Phansy"</note> cannot help but imagine this *Angle* to be indivisible. However, this is a complete contradiction and goes against the definition of an *Angle*, which is not the meeting but the *inclination* of two lines. Furthermore, if a smaller *Circle* is inscribed within a larger one so that they touch at one point, and we draw a common *Diameter* through both and drop a *Perpendicular* at the point where they touch, it becomes evident that one *Angle of Contact* is larger than the other. Yet, our *Imagination* previously accepted them both as indivisible. Thus, one and the same *Angle* would be both divisible and indivisible, which is once again a plain contradiction.

Just as the *Imagination* is puzzled by things we are certain of through *Reason*, it is also confused by things we are certain of through *Sense*. For who can imagine how it happens that we see our image behind a *looking-glass*? It would be easier to imagine that we should perceive <note>original: "deprehend"</note> our faces either on the very surface of the glass or in the place where they actually are. If reflected rays were enough to explain it, then we would find the distance of our image to be no greater than the distance to the glass. But if we are also affected by direct rays, it seems to me that we should be led by them to the original place from which they came and find our faces in their real position.

7. To give examples that are more relevant to our purpose: we see in some kinds of Matter an almost invincible union of parts, such as in *Steel*, *Diamond* <note>original: "Adamant"; historically referring to the hardest known substances, like diamonds or lodestones.</note>, and the like. What is it that holds them so tightly together? If you say it is some inward *Substantial form* <note>A philosophical term for the essence or "organizing principle" that gives matter its specific properties.</note>, then we have found what we were looking for: a Substance distinct from Matter. If you say it is the quality of *Hardness* in the Matter that makes it thus hard, that is nothing more than saying "it is so because it is so." If you say it is because the parts are at a more perfect state of rest next to each other than in other Matter, even if that were true, it is still utterly unimaginable. For example: imagine Matter that is perfectly flat—flatter and more solid than a marble table. If a person laid a little *Cube* of similar flatness and solidity upon it, the idea that this *Cube*, merely by touching the table, should form as firm a union with it as the parts of the *Cube* have with each other is something that the human *Imagination* cannot accept. Suppose you first slid this *Cube* along the table, which it would do easily since both surfaces are so smooth, and then you stopped moving it. The idea that these two smooth bodies should suddenly stick together so tightly that a hammer and chisel could scarcely separate them is utterly unimaginable.

Therefore, since the *union* between the parts of Matter is so strong, and yet it is unimaginable how this happens, why should we not admit an equally strong or even stronger union between a *Spirit* and a *Body*? This remains true even if our *Imagination* suggests that a spirit would simply pass through a body, just as it suggests that smooth bodies will...

He concludes that if we cannot imagine how physical matter sticks together, we should not reject the idea of a spirit-body union just because it is difficult to visualize.</summary>

# C H A P. III. An Appendix to the foregoing Antidote.

will always remain loose unless there is some cement to hold them together? Once this *union* is admitted—and since *Motion, Activity,* and *Agitation* are such easy and natural ways to conceive of the properties of a *Spirit*—it follows just as easily and naturally that a spirit *moves* or *stirs* the *Matter* to which it is united.

8. But to answer more specifically, I say that this present objection is nothing more than a trick of the *imagination* <note>original: "Sophism of the Phansy"</note>. It mistakenly imagines a *Spirit* to be like a *Body* passing through a hole or passage that is too wide and open for it, and in which it therefore cannot stick or be firmly settled. Against this *imagination*, we argue that although *Spirits* do penetrate *Bodies*, they are not such thin and flimsy things that they must necessarily slip through them, or be unable to take hold of them or unite with them. Instead, they can fill up the entire capacity of a *Body* that is penetrable by *Spirits*. When this *penetrability* of a *Body* or *Matter* is saturated or filled, the *Spirit* that fills it is more strongly fixed or united with that *Body* than one part of *Matter* can be with another.

Therefore, we will recognize one special faculty of a *Spirit*, which it exerts either naturally or by its own will after *penetration*: the power to fill the *receptivity* or *capacity* of a *Body* or *Matter*, as far as that matter is capable of receiving a *Soul* or *Spirit*.

For the sake of brevity, we will call this quality of a *Spirit* by the Greek term <term>Hylopathia</term> <note>original: "ὑλοπάθεια"; from the Greek 'hyle' (matter) and 'pathos' (affection or feeling). It refers to the spirit's ability to 'feel' or 'interact with' matter.</note>. So that there is no suspicion of fraud or academic nonsense, we will define it as plainly as we can: *A power in a Spirit to produce something so similar to a physical substance from its center of life that it perfectly fills the capacity of the matter it has entered. This prevents any other spirit from occupying the same space, and thus creates a bond so firm that the spirit can both move the body and be affected by it.*

Now, let us ask the *imagination* itself if *Matter* does not fit as closely—even closer—to a *Spirit* than any one part of *Matter* can fit to another. In this case, the *union* spreads through the entire substance, whereas physical conjunction only happens where two surfaces touch, as is usually imagined and accepted. Furthermore, I would add that this <term>Hylopathia</term>, which we assume exists in a finite *Spirit* or *Soul*, may well be seen as a smaller version of that power to create *Matter* which is necessarily part of our *Idea* of *God*.

9. Finally, if the way a *Spirit* acts upon a *Body* (or is affected by one) seems so complex that it must be considered unexplainable, consider this: we accept the mobility of a perfect *Globe* upon a flat *Plane* as an obvious and undeniable property, according to our *Understanding*. Yet we cannot *imagine* how, by touching only at a single *point*, it can describe a continuous *line* through its motion. (The same could be argued from other examples of complexity and confusion.) Therefore, when we see clear operations in Nature that *Reason* demonstrates cannot come from *Matter* itself, we must acknowledge there is some other Substance—a *Spiritual* one—acting within it and upon it, even if we do not know exactly how *Motion* is communicated from a *Spirit* to *Matter*.

<page-num>154</page-num>
# An Appendix to the foregoing Antidote. CHAPTER III.

10. The strength of our third and last answer lies in this: there are indeed several operations that clearly go beyond the power of *Matter*. We will briefly repeat the main points here, having discussed them more fully in the previous treatise.

First, I will give a general example acknowledged by *Descartes* himself, who attributed the highest possible effects to the Laws of Matter that any man could rationally claim. It is this: the Matter from which all things are made is, in itself, *uniform and of one kind*. From this, I infer that, by itself, it must either all be at *rest* or all be in *motion*. If it all *rests*, there must be something besides *Matter* that *moves* it, which is necessarily a *Spirit*. If it *all moves*, it would be impossible for anything to come together; every imaginable particle would be loose from every other. Therefore, a Substance besides Matter is required to bind together what we find fixed and joined.

The second instance is found in the remarkable *Wisdom* visible in all the works of Nature, which I discussed extensively in my Second Book. These works clearly prove that all things are designed by a *wise* Principle. Only a fool would say that *Matter* itself is *wise*. Yet, from the decaying parts of the Earth, from drops of dew, or from rotten wood and similar materials <note>original: "geer"</note>, the bodies of Animals arise, so skillfully and exquisitely formed that human Reason cannot study them without great pleasure and admiration.

Thirdly, the many undeniable stories of *Apparitions* clearly prove that an Intellect resides in various *Airy* bodies. It would be utterly impossible for *Air* to be changed so arbitrarily into specific shapes and held together as a living vessel <note>original: "actuated vehicle of life"</note> if there were not something besides the *Air* itself that possessed and controlled it, and could expand, contract, and guide it as it pleased. Otherwise, it would have no better shape or stability than tobacco smoke or the steam from a chimney.

Fourthly and lastly, it is obvious that the part of us which *understands*, *remembers*, and *perceives* is the same part that *moves* our bodies. These cognitive faculties <note>original: "Cognoscitive Faculties"</note> cannot be a function of mere Matter. From this, it is evident that there is an *intellectual spirit* in our bodies that *moves* them as it wishes, as I have sufficiently proved in the final chapter of the first book of my *Antidote*, and will confirm further when we address the objections against it.

<header>CHAPTER 4. An Appendix to the previous Antidote.</header>

# CHAPTER 4.

1. *That Existence is a Perfection, verified from common examples.* 2. *Further proved from Metaphysical principles.* 3. *An appeal to ordinary reason.* 4. *That at least "Necessary Existence" is a Perfection, even if simple Existence is not.* 5. *An illustration of that last conclusion.*

1. To avoid the necessity and evidence of our demonstration of the existence of God—drawn from the inseparable connection of the concept with his *Idea* (since we argue *that necessary existence must be included in the Idea of a Being who is absolutely perfect*)—there are some who do not hesitate to claim that *Existence* is not a quality of intrinsic *perfection* in anything. For, they say, imagine two pieces of gold equal in weight, purity, and all other respects, except for duration or the necessity of existence; we cannot justly, without being capricious <note>original: "humoursome"</note> or imaginative, attribute superiority to one more than to the other. To this I answer: just as two pieces of gold are better than one, so one piece of gold that will last twice as long as another is twice as good as the other, or at least much better than the other. I think this is so evident that it requires no further proof.

But furthermore, so that we may not only apply ourselves to answering objections, but also absolutely confirm the present truth, *that Existence is a Perfection*: First, it is clearly obvious according to that sensible aphorism of *Solomon*: *Better is a living dog than a dead lion.* <note>Ecclesiastes 9:4. The author uses this to show that life/existence is inherently more valuable than non-existence or death.</note>

2. But then again, to argue more generally, the *Metaphysicians* <note>Philosophers who study the fundamental nature of reality, being, and existence.</note>—as is very well known—view *Existence* as the formal and actual part of a *Being*. "Form" or "Act" is acknowledged as the more noble and perfect principle in every essence; therefore, if they can be distinguished in God, it is so there as well. If they cannot be distinguished, then it is thereby admitted that we cannot think of the *Idea* of God without it immediately informing us that he does *Exist*. And I recommend to the inquiry of Hebrew scholars <note>original: "Criticks"</note> whether *havah* <note>original: הוה; a Hebrew root meaning "to be" or "to become"</note>, from which *Yahweh* <note>original: יהוה; the personal name of God in the Hebrew Bible</note> is derived, does not signify *Existence* rather than *Essence*.

3. Thirdly, let the *Metaphysicians* conclude what they please; it is evident to ordinary reason that if there is one concept better than another that implies no imperfection, it must be attributed to what is most perfect. But *Existence* is better than non-existence, and implies no imperfection; therefore, it must be attributed to the *Idea* of a *Being who is absolutely perfect*.

4. But fourthly and finally: though it were possible to argue against the simple notion of *Existence*—claiming it argued for neither *perfection* nor *imperfection*, nor belonged to either—yet there can be no appearance of an exception against the highest and most perfect manner of existing. That manner of existence is naturally and undeniably included in the *Idea* of a *Being who is absolutely perfect*. Therefore, we rightfully contend that *necessary existence* is inseparably contained in the *notion of God*.

5. For example, while it is confessed that *Matter* is finite and cannot be otherwise, for a *Body* to be *shaped* <note>original: "figured"</note> implies neither Perfection nor Imperfection, but is a natural and necessary property of it; yet to be *shaped in an orderly way* is an undoubted *Perfection* of a *Body*. So, in the same way, even if it were confessed that mere *Existence* is neither Perfection nor Imperfection, yet such a noble mode of it as necessarily to *Exist* must, without any evasion <note>original: "tergiversation"</note>, be acknowledged as a concept of *Perfection*. Therefore, it naturally belongs to the *Idea* of a *Being* who is absolutely perfect.

### CHAPTER 5.

1. *That there is a vast difference between arguing from forced fabrications <note>original: "Figments"</note> or fancies and from the natural Ideas of our own minds.* 2. *That the Idea of a Being absolutely Evil does not imply necessary Existence, whether it signifies a Being who is absolutely Imperfect,* 3. *Or absolutely Wicked,* 4. *Or absolutely Miserable,* 5. *Or absolutely Harmful <note>original: "Mischievous," which in this period meant destructive or injurious rather than playful</note>.* 6. *That if by a Being absolutely Harmful one meant only the infinite power of doing hurt, this is God, whose absolute Goodness prevents the execution of it.* 7. *That the right method of using our Reason is to proceed from what is plain and beyond suspicion to what is more obscure and suspicious.* 8. *That according to this method, being assured first of the Existence of a Being absolutely Perfect from his Idea, we are thereby enabled to answer that the impossibility of Existence belongs to a Being who is either absolutely Miserable or absolutely Harmful.* 9. *That the natural appearances <note>original: "Phaenomena"</note> of the world further prove the impossibility of the Existence of a Being who is absolutely Harmful.* 10. *And that the counsels and works of God are not to be measured by the vain opinions of men.*

1. As for those who admit that necessary *Existence* is included in the *Idea* of a *Being who is absolutely Perfect*, but want to show that our conclusion from that—namely, *that this perfect Being exists*—is false and deceptive <note>original: "sophistical"</note>, they argue that *necessary Existence* is contained in the *Idea* of a *Being who is absolutely Evil*. They claim that because such a being would not be admitted to *exist* (for, they say, that which is absolutely *Evil* is immutably and always unavoidably so, and cannot be otherwise, and therefore it cannot help but *exist*, and has always *existed*): to these people we answer that we shall easily discover the grand difference between such arbitrary and forced fabrications <note>original: "Figments"</note> and fancies, and the natural and consistent *Ideas* of our own mind. This is clear if we look more carefully and precisely <note>original: "curiously"</note> into the nature of what these objectors have ventured to utter, and sift out what they either mean themselves, or what must necessarily be understood by this *Idea* of a *Being absolutely Evil* which they have concocted.

2. By the *Idea* of a *Being absolutely Evil*, one must mean either the *Idea* of a *Being who is absolutely Imperfect*, or *absolutely Wicked*, or *absolutely Miserable*, or *absolutely Harmful*.

Now, the *Idea* of what is *absolutely Imperfect* removes from it what-

Therefore, a being that is *absolutely imperfect* cannot possibly *Exist*. However, *necessary Existence* is a quality <note>original: "Term"</note> of *Perfection*, as was clearly demonstrated before.

3. The *Idea of a Being who is absolutely Wicked* excludes from it all manner of goodness, fairness <note>original: "Equity"</note>, decency <note>original: "Decorum"</note>, and righteousness. It implies a firm and unchangeable turning away of the will from all these things, and a settled and unalterable purpose of acting wickedly. But this says nothing about either the *Necessity* or the *Contingency* <note>meaning: the possibility of something happening or not happening; dependent existence</note> of the *Existence* of the *Substance* of this *Being*; that fact has nothing to do with its moral depravity, as is clearly obvious at first sight.

4. The *Idea of a Being who is absolutely Miserable* is the *Idea of a Being* that endures the fullest and most complete torments imaginable. This must occur in a conscious <note>original: "knowing"</note>, sensitive <note>original: "passive"</note>, and self-aware <note>original: "reflexive"</note> subject. Now, I argue that this torture arises partly from the sensation of present pain <note>original: "smart"</note>, and partly from reflecting on what it has suffered, combined with a total conviction that it shall suffer in this way eternally. This *miserable Being*, even if it were only a *Creature* <note>meaning: a created being, rather than a self-existent one</note>, is as perfectly tormented as it could possibly be even if it necessarily existed by itself. For if it existed forever, even if its existence were dependent on another, the torture would be just as complete; therefore, *necessary Existence* is not a required part of its *Idea*.

Furthermore, the objector must prove that a being who is entirely immaterial can suffer any torture at all. Until he does so—since it seems more reasonable that such a being cannot—I shall flatly deny that it can. I assert, therefore, that a being capable of being tortured is a *Spirit joined with a body* <note>original: "Spirit incorporate"</note>. I also maintain, as a most rational point, that if a very great pain were inflicted upon this *Spirit*—so great that it would be better for him not to exist at all than to exist in that state—the anguish would be so increased by its continuation (pain infinitely overpowering the vital strength and outweighing the capacities of life and sensation) that the spirit would "die" to the body in which it is thus tormented. But if its condition is not so bad as to break its connection to the body, and the torture proves tolerable, then *necessary Existence* would not be its misery, but rather a form of happiness. Thus, there can be no such thing as a being *absolutely Miserable* in the world. For *Misery* pushed to the highest degree would cause the being to cease to exist. Just as one cannot speak of an *absolutely large Triangle*—because a *Circle* will always be larger—or rather, no *Shape* <note>original: "Figure"</note> can be *absolutely large* because its very nature is to be limited.

Thirdly, the *Idea of a Being who is absolutely Perfect* is composed of concepts <note>original: "Notions"</note> of the same kind, all of which represent absolute *Perfection* in themselves. But the *Idea of a Being who is absolutely Miserable* is not compiled of concepts that represent absolute *Misery* on their own. For what *Misery*—as opposed to goodness—is there in *necessary Existence*? Therefore, if we should argue that an inference from the *Idea* of a thing to its *necessary Existence* is only valid when the *Idea* consists of consistent concepts, the objector must explain away this distinction.

### An Appendix to the foregoing Antidote. CHAPTER V.

But *Self-existence* is the highest and most perfect mode of existence that can be imagined, and is therefore appropriate only to what is most absolutely *Perfect*. Therefore, to transfer *self-existence* to such a pitiful *Idea* as the *Idea* of a Being who is absolutely *Miserable* is as absurd <note>original: "absonous"</note> and unnatural <note>original: "prodigious"</note> as to attach the head of a lion to the body of a snail. Indeed, it seems even more contradictory; the latter is merely a misplacing of physical parts and shapes, while the former is the planting of an internal property into the wrong subject—indeed, joining infinitely contrary properties in the same subject.

5. Fourthly and lastly, regarding a Being who is *absolutely Malevolent* <note>original: "Mischievous"</note>, such a concept seems to include *necessary* and unavoidable *Existence* as well as *Omnipotence* and *Omniscience*; otherwise, this *Sovereign Malevolence* is not as full and absolute as we can imagine. These traits, added to a stubborn and unchangeable desire or will to do all possible evil simply for the sake of evil, fully complete the concept of this *absolutely Malevolent Being*.

But how fake <note>original: "spurious"</note> and unnatural this *Idea* is becomes evident because it again forcibly ties together concepts of a completely opposite nature—the greatest imperfection with the highest perfections. It joins the unique <note>original: "incommunicable"</note> attributes of God with something that is perhaps <note>original: "haply"</note> worse than what we can prove exists in any Devil; indeed, it combines things that seem to be a contradiction in any subject whatsoever.

Therefore, as I suggested before, if anyone claims our argument is a logical trick <note>original: "Sophism"</note> and tries to reveal a fallacy by imitating it in some other matter, he must strictly follow the rules of logic in his imitation. He must create an *Idea* made of concepts that fit the same *Title*, as they perfectly do in the *Idea* of a Being who is *absolutely Perfect*; for in that concept, every single idea represents the highest perfection.

But in this *Idea* of a Being who is *absolutely Malevolent*, there is nothing that by its own nature signifies evil except for that wicked and malicious desire to do harm merely for harm's sake. This is a degree of imperfection that sinks into the realm of inconsistency and contradiction. Yet, to be able to accurately destroy all good whatsoever would require an *Omnipotence* in power and an *Omniscience*. However, a being that is omnipotently and absolutely malevolent must also destroy itself; just as an infinitely large triangle implies no triangle at all. Thus, this *Idea* is not free from the entanglement of many various contradictions in how it is conceived.

6. But if by a Being *absolutely Malevolent* one meant a Being that has the power and skill to do all imaginable harm—and indeed, harm far beyond all human imagination and thought—and to do so so effectively and universally that nothing can possibly stop him: this is indeed the Eternal God. He necessarily exists of himself and comes before all things, and his actions can be limited by none but himself. But since he is that absolute and unchangeable *Good*, and full and pure Perfection, he cannot help but include in his *Idea* that precious attribute of *Kindness* <note>original: "Benignity"</note>. Therefore, acting according to his entire Nature, he is not only *Good* himself, but, by the power <note>original: "prerogative"</note> of his own Being, he prevents such *malevolent sovereignties*...

### CHAPTER V. An Appendix to the foregoing Antidote.

7. Therefore, to bring our answer to a conclusion, I say that we ought to use the same natural method in this speculation that people who know how to use their mental faculties observe in all others—namely, to agree first to what is most simple, easy, and plain, and of which there can be no doubt that the concept <note>original: "Notion"</note> is fitting and consistent. Such is the *Idea* of a *Being absolutely Perfect*. This is no arbitrary or accidental fiction, nor a forced compilation of concepts that clash with one another, or which may be justly suspected (if not proven) to be incoherent and mismatched—such as, for example, a *walking tree* or an *intelligent stone*. Rather, it is a concept where the various attributes naturally and necessarily come together to complete the definition of one single title, being of the same nature and essential to it.

8. What I am arguing for is this: that by attending to this natural *Idea* of God, or a *Being absolutely Perfect*, we unavoidably discover the necessity of *actual existence* as inseparable from Him, as it is necessarily included in this *Idea of absolute perfection*. This is even more undeniably established in the final thrust of my argument, where I urge that either *Impossibility*, *Contingency*, or *Necessity of actual existence* must belong to a *Being absolutely Perfect*. Since it is neither *Impossibility* nor *Contingency*, it must therefore be *Necessity of actual existence*.

And therefore, being so well secured in this truth, I require the objector to bring his argument to this same clear framework. Let him also argue that either *Impossibility*, *Contingency*, or *Necessity of actual existence* belongs to either a *Being absolutely Miserable* or *absolutely Malevolent* <note>original: "Mischievous"; in this context, it refers to a being of pure evil or harm</note>. To this, I shall confidently answer: *Impossibility of existence*. I would give him a further reason beyond what I hinted at before regarding the inconsistency of the concepts themselves—that such a being is also incompatible with the existence of God. By attending to the natural and undistorted suggestions of our own faculties, we have already demonstrated that God *exists* without any obstacle or doubt.

9. To make our answer even more certain concerning a *Being absolutely Malevolent*, it is most evident that He does not exist. Since such a being would have to exist by its own power if it existed at all, it is therefore impossible for it to exist. That he does not exist is plain, because if he did, things would be infinitely worse than they are, or would not exist at all. On the contrary, I dare say things are currently as well as it is fit or possible for them to be, if only we had the wisdom to conceive or comprehend the entire counsel and purpose of *Providence*, and knew clearly and particularly what is past and what is to come.

10. However, we sometimes adopt principles concerning the *Providence* of God that are inconsistent with his *Idea* out of our own blindness or rashness. An example of this is the *Ptolemaic System* <note>The ancient astronomical model where the Earth is the center of the universe, which was becoming increasingly complex and "cluttered" with mathematical corrections by the 17th century</note> of the heavens. Some say that *Alfonso* <note>Alfonso X of Castile, known as "The Wise," who famously quipped that if he had been present at Creation, he could have given God some good advice on the design of the universe, mocking the complexity of the Ptolemaic model</note> looked upon this system (though others tell the story regarding the placement of certain mountains on the Earth) as such a perplexed bungle that, transported with zeal against that foolish hypothesis, he mockingly and audaciously claimed that if he had stood by while God made the world, he could have directed its framework better. ### CHAPTER VI.

1. *That the meaning <note>original: "sense"</note> of his argument from the Idea of God in the first position <note>original: "posture"</note> is not simply that the Idea is true, and if God existed, his existence would be necessary; but that this Idea, being true, presents to our mind an absolute, necessary existence as belonging to Him. 2. That the Idea of the God of the Manichees <note>The Manichees were followers of a dualistic religion that believed in two equal, opposing powers: one good and one evil.</note> does not include necessary existence in itself. 3. That to say that the necessary existence included in the Idea of an absolutely perfect Being is only conditional is a contradiction. 4. The second position of his argument is confirmed, and by virtue of its form, the existence of the Manichean God cannot be concluded. 5. The invincible evidence of the third position of his argument in the judgment of his opponent <note>original: "Antagonist"</note> himself. 6. That the force of his argument in the fourth and last position is not that we conceive of the Idea of Matter without necessary existence; but that, look as closely as we can, we find no necessary existence included within it, as we do in the Idea of God. 7. That the faculties of our mind, to which he constantly appeals, are to be assumed, not proved, to be true.*

1. And now having thus clearly satisfied the objection taken from the *Idea* of an absolutely evil being, it will be easy to turn back the edge of any argument of a similar nature, no matter how skillfully and cunningly it is directed against us. Such as that which I received from a clever <note>original: "ingenious"</note> person, which because it seems very witty to me as well as invincible to the objector, I shall present in his own words; the meaning <note>original: "tenour"</note> of which runs like this:

> If a man may have a true *Idea* or notion of that which does not exist—yes, and of that which does not exist and yet would necessarily exist if it did—then your argument for the existence of God (based on necessary existence being included in his *Idea* or notion) is inconclusive. How you can deny this argument, I cannot possibly conceive, since the substance of your first argument from the *Idea* of God is contained within it in its first position.

> But a man may have a true notion of that which does not exist—yes, and of that which does not exist and yet would necessarily exist if it did; as for instance, the evil god of the Manichees.

<margin>Antidote, Book 1. ch. 8. sect. 1, 2.</margin>
But I answer briefly to this proposition like this: it does not apply to our case. We do not argue that God exists simply because the *Idea* of him is true and that *if* he existed, he would necessarily exist. "Conditional" necessary existence, being less perfect than "absolute" necessary existence, cannot belong to an absolutely perfect Being. Instead, we argue that because this true *Idea*, without any "*if*" or "*and*," suggests to our natural faculties that necessary existence is involved in his *Idea* alone—a thing that does not happen in any other *Idea*—he does, without any more fuss <note>original: "a-do"</note>, absolutely and really exist of himself.

<summary>Henry More refutes the objection that the "Idea" of an evil god could imply its necessary existence, arguing that only an absolutely perfect Being possesses inherent, non-conditional existence.</summary>
