# CHAP. VI. An Appendix to the foregoing Antidote.

To the minor premise <note>original: "Assumption"</note> I answer, that the God of the Manichees <note>The Manichees were followers of a dualistic religion that believed in two equal, opposing powers: one good and one evil.</note>, if he could exist at all, would do so *necessarily*; and my reason is that God would never create such a foul monster.

2. But if you still insist that the *Idea* of this *Evil God of the Manichees* includes *necessary existence* within it (being the concept of a God), and yet he does not exist—and that therefore the true God cannot be proved to exist simply because *necessary existence* is involved in his *Idea*—I further answer: that the concept of the Manichean God does not naturally include *necessary existence* because it is not the concept of a Being who is *absolutely Perfect*. The concept of an *Evil God* is a mere forced or accidental fiction. It makes no more sense than a *Wooden God* <note>A "Wooden God" is used here as an example of a "contradiction in terms," like a "square circle."</note>, whose *Idea* implies not *necessary existence*, but the *impossibility of existence*.

<margin>*Antidote, Book 1. chapter 8. section 3.*</margin>
3. But the objector proceeds, and we must follow his movements. However, before he reaches the second position <note>original: "posture"</note> of our argument, he takes notice of my charge against all those who acknowledge that *necessary existence* is contained in the *Idea* of God (or a Being *absolutely Perfect*), and that this signifies that *necessary existence* belongs to him, yet then take it back by adding, "If he exists at all." I answer that my charge is true. For to say that *necessary existence* belongs to a Being, while simultaneously claiming he might not exist, is to admit a contradiction. By doing this, the same thing is acknowledged by our minds to be both *necessary* and *contingent*—that is, that it both "must be" and "might not be." If that is not a contradiction in this case, I do not know what is; for nothing less than *absolutely necessary existence* must be comprised in the *Idea* of a Being who is *absolutely perfect*.

<margin>*Antidote, Book 1. chapter 8. section 4.*</margin>
4. But the argument will appear even more plain in the second position. For if there is any fraud or fallacy, it lies in this term, *Necessary*, which I have truly explained (and it is not denied) to signify nothing else but an inseparable connection between the *Subject* and the *Predicate*. Therefore, because *existence* has an inseparable connection with God, it must follow that this axiom, *God exists*, is eternally and immutably true. But to reply here, "*If he existed*," is to suggest that despite this, he might not exist, which is to say that what is immutably true is not immutably true—which is a palpable contradiction.

But the objector here flies for help to the God of the *Manichees*, asking me to substitute the *Manichean* God for the God whose *existence* I want to prove, so that I might see my own sophistry <note>original: "Sophisme"; a clever but false argument.</note>. Well, if it is not idolatry, let us place him there. But you may see how puny <note>original: "shrimpish"</note> and unfit he is to fill this place from what I said before: that the *Manichean God* no more implies *necessary existence* in its concept than a *Wooden God* does. In fact, it actually implies the *impossibility* of *existence*. For the concept of *God* is the same: a Being *absolutely Perfect*, which must involve the highest *absolute goodness* possible. Now, bring the *Manichean God* into view and let us look at his label: He is *an evil being who is absolutely good*. This, as I said before, is in my opinion far worse sense than a *Wooden God*. Therefore, *impossibility*, and not *necessity of existence*, is contained in his *Idea*.

<margin>*Antidote, Book 1. chapter 8. section 5.*</margin>
5. The third position of my argument is formidable even to the ob-

### CHAP. VI. An Appendix to the foregoing Antidote.

...the objector himself. For whereas I argue that either *Impossibility*, *Contingency*, or *Necessity of Actual Existence* belongs to a *Being who is absolutely Perfect*, he admits here that the "Manichean God" <note>The Manichees believed in two equal gods, one good and one evil. More previously argued that an evil god cannot truly possess "perfection" or "necessary existence."</note> will no longer help him. Instead, like a man left in distress, he complains that it is a "hard case" that he must be forced to prove that God's *Existence* is impossible, or else be forced to admit that He exists. But later, being better advised, he notices that if God does not exist, it is impossible for Him to be. Therefore, I say, it is only fair that we expect anyone who denies God exists to prove His *Being* impossible—especially since the force of our *Argument* necessarily drives him to that point. 

In my opinion, however, he would be better off saving his effort than venturing on such a useless <note>original: "frustraneous"</note> undertaking. He should remember that the *Idea* of this *Being who is absolutely Perfect* is designed so that, in the judgment of any person using their natural faculties, there is no inconsistency or impossibility within it, nor the slightest reason for suspicion or hesitation. Furthermore, since the "impossibility of existing" is the most imperfect <term>relation or state</term> <note>original Greek: "σχέσις" (schesis)</note> <margin>Chapter 5, section 2.</margin> that any Being can have toward existence, it must be an outrageous inconsistency to attribute that impossibility to a *Being who is absolutely Perfect*. Such an impossibility naturally and undeniably belongs to a *Being who is absolutely Imperfect*, as has been noted before.

Therefore, if either the doubting or stubborn Atheist says that the existence of God is impossible, that will not prove any weakness or vanity in my argument, but rather the rash boldness and blind impudence of the one who gives such an irrational answer.

<margin>Antidote, Book 1. chapter 8. sections 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11.</margin> 
6. Against this, he alleges that just as thousands of people have the *Idea* of a *Triangle* and yet have no knowledge of that property where its three angles equal two right angles <note>In Euclidean geometry, the sum of a triangle's angles is 180 degrees, the same as two "right" (90-degree) angles.</note>, so a person may have the *Idea* of *Matter* and yet know nothing of the necessity of its *existence*, even if it has that property within it.

But I answer: this does not address the strength of our argument. For look as curiously and skillfully as you will into the *Idea of Matter*, and you can discover no such property as *necessity of existence* within it. Furthermore, the weight of my reasoning lies mainly in this: that *necessity of self-existence* is plainly and unavoidably discoverable in the *Idea* of a *Being who is absolutely Perfect*, but it is not at all discernible in the *Idea* of *Matter*. We do manifest violence to our <term>faculties</term> <note>Faculties refers to our innate mental powers of reason, logic, and perception.</note> when we acknowledge *Self-existence* in *Matter* (when no faculty informs us it is so) while denying it in God (whose *Idea* so clearly informs us that *necessary self-existence* belongs to Him). So, all I contend for is this: that he who denies a God runs counter to the light of his natural faculties, to which I constantly appeal.

## CHAP. VII.

1. *That the necessity of existence which seems to be included in the Idea of Space is the same as that which offers itself to our mind in that more full and perfect Idea of God.* 2. *That there is the same logic regarding Eternal Duration, whose immediate subject is God, not Matter.* 3. *That Space is only the possibility of Matter, measurable only in the same way that many different possible species of things are countable.* 4. *That Distance is not a physical property <term>affection</term> of any thing, but is only conceptual.* 5. *That the distance between bodies is only the absence of physical contact <term>privation of tactual union</term>, measurable by parts, just as other absences of qualities are measured by degrees.* 6. *That if distant Space, after the removal of matter, is any real thing, it is that necessary Being represented by the Idea of God.* 7. *That Self-Existence and Contingency are terms inconsistent with one another.*

We do obvious violence to our own mental faculties when we claim that *self-existence* belongs to *matter*—even though no faculty tells us so—while denying it to God, despite the *idea of God* so clearly showing us that *necessary self-existence* belongs to Him. My entire contention is simply this: whoever denies God goes against the light of their own natural faculties, which I constantly call upon as witnesses.

In that case, we would simply be whatever we find ourselves to be, and we could seek no further. We could not assure ourselves that we were not made with a nature that is most mistaken exactly when we think we are most certain, and when we have used the greatest caution and care to avoid error.

### CHAPTER VII.

1. *That the necessity of existence which seems to be included in the idea of space is the same necessity that presents itself to our minds in the more complete and perfect idea of God.* 2. *That the same reasoning applies to eternal duration, whose immediate subject is God, not matter.* 3. *That space is merely the possibility of matter, measurable only in the same way that different possible species of things are countable.* 4. *That distance is not a physical property of anything, but exists only as a mental concept.* 5. *That the distance between bodies is only the absence of physical contact, measurable by units just as other absences of qualities are measured by degrees.* 6. *That if empty space remaining after the removal of matter is a real thing, it is actually that necessary Being represented by the idea of God.* 7. *That self-existence and contingency are mutually exclusive terms.*

2. The same reasoning applies to *Time* (by *Time* I mean *Duration*) as it does to *Space*. For we cannot imagine anything other than a continued *duration* that has no beginning and no interruption. Anyone would agree it is nonsensical to suggest such a necessary duration could exist without a real Essence that must, by its very nature, always and forever endure. What or who is it, then, to whom this eternal, uninterrupted, and never-fading duration must belong? 3. We cannot free our minds from this, but must necessarily acknowledge that there is indeed such a possibility for matter to be measured upward, downward, and in every direction infinitely <note>original: "in infinitum"</note>, whether this physical *matter* were actually there or not. Although this potential for *matter* or *space* can be measured by furlongs, miles, or the like, it no more implies a real essence or being than when a person counts different types of possibilities; the mere counting or numbering of them does not mean those possibilities actually exist.

This is because more or less of it may be attributed to an object even when nothing at all has happened to the object itself. For instance, suppose one of these mentioned balls was first an inch away from another; the distance between them could become many miles, and yet the ball might not be touched or moved at all, even though it is now much further away than before.

5. The greater the *distance*, the greater the lack; and the greater the lack, the more work must be done to regain the previous state of contact. This lack of physical contact is measured by *parts*, just as other lacks of qualities are measured by *degrees*. These *parts* and *degrees*, and other such concepts, are not *real* things themselves anywhere, but are simply our way of conceiving them, and therefore we can [bestow]...

To ensure we omit nothing that might seem worth answering: there are those who try to avoid the force of our argument... by saying that *contingency* <note>the quality of being possible but not certain; happening by chance</note> is not incompatible with God or anything else. They argue that all things in the world just happen to exist, even though they might have done otherwise. But no one would answer this way if they paid attention to their own logic, or to the light of their own reason, which would instruct them better. For example, if *matter* existed by its own power, it is evident that it exists *necessarily* and could not have done otherwise. This is because *self-existence* prevents all possible obstacles that might have caused a thing to fail to actually exist.

And as for God, it is equally evident that it is either impossible for him to be, or else he exists by his own nature. And if he exists by his own nature, his existence is unpreventable and necessary; as anyone must acknowledge if they understand the terms they are venturing to speak.

### An Appendix to the foregoing Antidote. Chapter VIII.

1. ...part of the world never had any such *idea*; and that those who have had it, have erased it from their souls; and those who have it most deeply imprinted upon them are not as certain of it as that two and two make four. I briefly answer: all men ever had and still have this *idea* in their souls. It is no more in their power to erase it than it is to blow out the sun with a pair of bellows. Personal interest, the mind being distracted by other matters, or a physical illness caused by indulgence or depression <note>original: "Sensuality or Melancholy"</note> may hinder the actual contemplation or discovery of this *idea* in the mind, but it cannot fundamentally <note>original: "radically"</note> erase it.

2. Regarding the last allegation—that it is not as clear as two and two make four—even if that were true, it does not invalidate our position. The truth we argue for is natural and undeniable. Many truths that are less easy or clear than basic math must still be acknowledged as naturally and undeniably true.

3. I answer that what is already naturally within a man, they cannot put there. I confess they may use it for political purposes. Indeed, it is as dreadful and detestable as it is true that mere politicians <note>original: "States-men"</note> have no conscience about corrupting the most sacred things for their own lowly, trivial goals. It would be like arguing that there is no natural self-love, love of wife and children, or desire for liberty, riches, or honor except what politicians and statesmen have placed in the hearts of men. Because politicians skillfully appeal to these affections, they can lead and manipulate people as they please. By inflaming their spirits with persuasive speeches <note>original: "plausible Orations"</note>, they often hurry people into the danger of losing the very things they hoped for, which the politicians had so beautifully and fully promised them.

# CHAPTER IX

> 1. *The natural structure of the conscience is such that it suggests fears and hopes which imply that there is a God.* 2. *The fact that various religions may seem ridiculous is no proof that being affected by religion is not an innate faculty of the human soul.*

1. The strength of my argument from *natural conscience* is this: that people naturally fear misfortunes and hope for success according to how they behave. But I must admit that this proof or line of reasoning is the most slippery <note>original: "lubricous"</note> and difficult to manage of any I have used, because it is clearly vulnerable to the objection or excuse that the fears and hopes of the conscience do not come from a natural knowledge of God, but from the power of *upbringing* <note>original: "Education"</note>, which becomes a second nature.

Since there is hardly any nation that has not awed its children with some basic principles of religion, we cannot provide a genuine example that perfectly demonstrates the validity of our argument. Therefore, we must rely on a *supposition*.

We will, therefore, imagine a man of average character. (I admit that some people are born with such distorted inner natures <note>original: "ingeny"</note> that one can no more judge human intellectual or *moral qualities* <note>original: "Moral property"</note> by them than one can judge the true human form by looking at a physical deformity or a monster.) Suppose this man has not been taught any religious principles or specific doctrines about God, but is of such a temperament (whether by nature or upbringing, it is all the same) that he considers some things *fitting* and *right* to do, and others *unfitting* and *unjust*. To some people, what is *just* and *unjust*, *good* and *evil*, *lovable* and *hateful* <note>original: "amiable and execrable"</note> is more obvious and clear than the *existence* of a deity. I say, suppose such a man should commit crimes he considers heinous and abominable—such as *murdering his father or mother*, *incest with his sister*, *betraying his truest friends*, or the like—and he is not punished by the law (having done these things so cunningly that they escaped notice), but immediately afterward he suffers a string of misfortunes. Suppose his barns and stacks of grain are burned by lightning from heaven, his cattle die in his fields, and he himself is later tormented with the most foul <note>original: "noisome"</note> and painful diseases—all of which can happen to anyone in the natural course of things. I ask anyone: is it not likely that this man will naturally and unavoidably feel such a sting of conscience that he suspects these misfortunes have fallen upon him as a *punishment* from some invisible power or divine hand that orders all things justly?

*Regarding religious veneration: namely, the many ridiculous religions in the world, from which it is inferred that the human mind has no innate principle of religion at all, but is instead moldable into any shape or form of worship that the supreme power in any country pleases to propose; I answer to this:*

First, if every religious person would look upon foreign <note>original: "extraneous"</note> religions with the same respectful sincerity and solemn seriousness <note>original: "venerable candor and awfull sobriety"</note> with which he views his own, he might find them more worthy of pity for their falsehood than laughter for their ridiculousness. However, it no more follows that all religions are false because so many are, than it follows that no philosophical opinions are true because so many are false.

But, secondly, regarding the multitude of various and—if you will—foolish <note>original: "fond"</note> religions in the world into which the nations of the earth are moldable: the more ridiculous they are, the better they serve our purpose. We argue that *religion is a natural property of man*. The necessity of religion's connection to our nature is more clearly proven by this variety; for humanity can no more exist without religion than *matter* can exist without *shape* <note>original: "Figure"</note>. Although few parts of matter have the good fortune to be framed into something *regular* or *orderly* <note>original: "Ordinate"</note>, or to have any beauty or proportion in their shape, nonetheless, however you break the *matter*, it will still take some shape or another.

But this communication seems impossible; for if perception is caused by an impression from an external object, no particle in the <term>Conarion</term> shall perceive any part of the object except that which it receives an impression from. But if you still wish to say that every part of the object impresses upon every part of the <term>Conarion</term> where the image is, it will be utterly impossible for the whole image not to be confused, and the distinctness of colors would be lost, especially in smaller objects.

...The object projects its *sensory images* <note>original: "Species"; in medieval and early modern philosophy, these were the forms or "images" of things that traveled from the object to the eye.</note> through the air to the eye. Since *perception* occurs by physical impression, and that impression was lost in the *pineal gland* <note>original: "Conarion"</note> although retained in the *brain*, how can the *pineal gland* ever know that it had any such impression before? For once the impression is wiped out, it is as if it never had *any*, and therefore it can never *remember* that it had. Besides, the *perception* of this image in the *brain* is as incompatible with the *pineal gland* as the *perception* of any external object, a point upon which we have already insisted.

4. And thirdly, concerning the power of free *imagination*, by which the *pineal gland* is supposed to invent the various forms or shapes of things which it never actually saw; I ask, whether it is the thin membrane, or the internal and somewhat soft and fuzzy pulp it contains, that raises and represents to itself these arbitrary fantasies and monsters <note>original: "Figments and Chimeras"</note>? And then, what part or particle of either of them can perform these fine feats? And (what is most important) since the representations are corporeal <note>physical or bodily</note>, is there not a necessity that the *pineal gland* be affected or impressed just as it is by external physical objects? I then demand how this passive, soft substance should be able to impress or mark itself, or how one part of this body should be able to act upon another for this purpose. Furthermore, since there is also a *memory* of these imagined impressions, how can they be stamped upon the brain, which is the seat of *memory*? For if we admit that the *pineal gland* imitates the manner in which outward objects leave an impression when she invents images of her own, and she then stamps these images upon the *brain*, it would be like using the impression of a seal on some hard material to then stamp some softer material. In that case, the two impressions will be notoriously different: those parts that project outward in the first will be pressed inward in the second.

5. Fourthly, regarding *reason*: in addition to the fact that it is obvious when we use reason that we simultaneously grasp the images or mental representations <note>original: "Phantasms"</note> of not only different but contrary things in the very same part or particle of the *pineal gland*—for if they are in different parts, what faculty shall judge both of them? For example, when we conclude that "hot is not cold," or "a crooked line is not a straight line," this cannot be conceived without a confusion of both impressions. There is also another consideration regarding *notions that are clearly immaterial*, which do not impress themselves upon the *pineal gland*, nor any part of the *brain*, nor on the outward organs from sensible objects, but are our own *innate concepts* discovered in the contemplation of things. Such are various *logical*, *metaphysical*, and *mathematical notions*, as I have proven elsewhere. Therefore, it seems altogether incredible that the *pineal gland*, being so dense and tangible a body as it is, should have any *notions* or *concepts* that are not physical and conveyed to it from material objects from the outside.

6. 7. Nor does it invalidate the force of our proof when some claim our arguments are fallacious <note>original: "Sophistical"</note> because they suggest there is an **incorporeal substance** in **animals** <note>original: "Beasts"</note> just as certainly as they do that there is one in **Humans**.

For I answer, first, that these arguments conclude absolutely regarding **Humans** because we are certain that humans perform operations that clearly prove such a nature. However, we are not as certain about what exists in **animals**. Indeed, very learned men with a more mechanical **mindset** <note>original: "Genius"</note> have at least doubted whether **animals** have any **thought** <note>original: "Cogitation"</note> at all; yet they have also stated that if animals *did* think, they would necessarily possess **immaterial souls** truly distinct from their **bodies**.

Secondly, even if our arguments proved that there were **Souls** in **animals** <note>original: "Brutes"</note> truly distinct from their **bodies**, is this anything more than what all philosophers and scholars who held the theory of **substantial forms** <note>A philosophical concept suggesting that every physical thing has an internal essence or "form" that gives it its qualities.</note> have already acknowledged to be true? But if these souls are **incorporeal**, they say, then they must also be **immortal**—which they find ridiculous. If by **immortal** they mean "indestructible," like **Matter**, why shouldn't they be as indestructible as **Matter** itself? This active substance of the **Soul** (even that of an **animal**) is a more noble essence and shares more in its Creator's perfection than dull, decaying **Matter** does. But if by **immortality** they mean a capacity for eternal life and happiness after the death of their bodies, that is a ridiculous conclusion of their own making, which I happily allow them to laugh at; it does not concern us or our current argument. For we believe that the **Soul** of an **animal** may be of such a nature that it can only perceive or be "vitally affected" while in a **physical body** <note>original: "Terrestrical Body"</note>; once outside the body, it may have neither sense nor perception of anything, so that it utterly perishes as far as its own consciousness is concerned.

## An Appendix to the foregoing Antidote. CHAP. X.

8. There is another objection that seems to carry more weight: since there are *properties* that we must admit exist in a *body* or *matter*, yet which involve strange contradictions in how we conceive of them—for instance, that confusing property of *divisibility* <note>The philosophical problem of whether matter can be divided forever or if it eventually reaches an unbreakable "point."</note> (which must either be into points or *to infinity*, both of which baffle our imagination)—why can we not also admit that a *body* may have *sense* and *understanding*, even if that seems entirely contradictory upon closer consideration? 

But I answer: this reasoning is very deceptive <note>original: "Sophistical"</note>. By the same logic, we would have to admit that the head of an *onion* understands and perceives as well as the *pineal gland* <note>original: "Conarion"</note> in a human being. For you can bring no greater argument against the onion than that it is contradictory and illogical for it to be so. 

But you will reply that we clearly see that some part of the human body must have *sense* and *understanding* in it, but we discern no such thing in an *onion*. To this I ask: by what faculty do we discern this? If you answer, "*our own senses tell us so*," I say that *our own senses*, if we did not correct them, would confidently suggest to us that our *finger feels* and our *eye sees*. However, it is clear they do not; for the very same thing that *feels* and *sees* also moves our body. But neither our *eye* nor our *finger moves* the body, and therefore they neither *feel* nor *see*.

And yet, without our *eye* we cannot *see* in this joined state of body and soul, just as without the proper structure and condition of our *brain* we cannot well *understand*. But it no more follows from this that the *brain understands* (rather than something distinct from it) than it follows that the *eye sees*. Therefore, it is apparent that there is no faculty in us that can clearly inform us that any part of our body is endowed with *sense* and *understanding*.

From this, we see the great difference between admitting *divisibility* in *matter* (however confusing the concept) and admitting *sense* and *understanding* in a *physical body* (which actually brings more confusion than the other, if examined closely). We are fully assured by *sense*—and I would say by *reason* as well—that *matter is divisible*; however, no faculty at all can pretend to assure us that a *body* is capable of either *sense* or *reason*.

9. But there seems to be an even worse objection still remaining: even though we have clearly proved the impossibility of *sense*, *understanding*, or *spontaneous motion* <note>Self-initiated movement, as opposed to being pushed by something else.</note> existing in *matter* or a *body*, we are no closer to an answer. For the same difficulties may be raised against there being any *sense* or *understanding* in a *spirit*. Since a *spirit* must be *extended* <note>Occupying or stretching across space.</note>, and if it is extended it must be *divisible*, and if it is divisible it must be *incapable of sense or understanding*, according to the same arguments we used against *matter*.

To this I answer: if by *extension* you mean a *juxtaposition* of parts (placing them side by side, one by another, as it is in *matter*), I utterly deny that a *spirit* is *extended* in that sense at all. But if you mean only a certain *amplitude of presence*—that it can be present in every part of a certain amount of *matter* at once—then I say it is *extended*. However, this kind of *extension* does not imply any *divisibility* in the substance thus *extended*. This is because the *juxtaposition of parts*, *impenetrability*, and *divisibility* go together, and therefore where

But when I speak of *Indivisibility*, so that *Imagination* does not create new troubles for itself, I do not mean such an *Indivisibility* as is imagined in a *Mathematical point*; but rather as we conceive in a *Sphere of light* created from one shining point or radiant *Center*. For that *Sphere* or *Orb of light*, though it is in some sense *extended*, yet it is truly *indivisible*, assuming the *Center* is such. For there is no imaginable way to tear away <note>original: "discerp"</note> or separate any one ray of this *Orb* and keep it apart by itself, disconnected from the *Center*.

10. Now, to slightly invert the property of this *luminous Orb* when we apply it to a *Soul* or *Spirit*: Just as there can be no change in the radiant *Center* without it necessarily affecting every part of the *Orb*—for instance, if it were redder, everything would be redder; if dimmer, everything would be dimmer, and so on—there is also that unity and indivisibility of the exterior parts (if I may call them that) of a *Spirit* or *Soul* with their inmost *Center*. If any of these exterior parts are affected, the *Center of life* is also necessarily affected. Because these exterior parts of the Soul are affected by the parts of an *Object* and the circumstances they are in, the inward *Center* receives all the details so that it necessarily possesses the entire and clear images of things outside, even though they are compressed into such a small compass and are in the very center of this *Spiritual Substance*.

I used this *Symbolic representation* before, and I cannot think of <note>original: "excogitate"</note> anything that will better explain the *nature of a Spirit*. This nature implies a power of receiving a multitude of specific shapes into one indivisible Principle of *Sense*, where all are exactly united into one *Subject* and yet distinctly represented. This cannot be performed by the <term>Conarion</term> <note>The pineal gland, which many 17th-century thinkers believed was the seat of the soul.</note> itself, as I have demonstrated; therefore, it remains that this function must belong to a *Soul*, whose primary seat may perhaps be there regarding the act of *perception*.

11. But if anyone should abuse our *Courtesy* in trying to help his *Imagination* (or at least to satisfy it) with this *Symbolic representation* we have made—by thinking of this *Center of the Soul* as merely some dull, divisible point in *Matter*, or by viewing its vital or voluntary *extension* so crudely that he argues it must be as divisible and separable as a *Body*—to prevent all such nitpicking <note>original: "cavils"</note>, we shall set aside those thorny details <note>original: "spinosities"</note> regarding the *extension* or *indivisibility* of a *Soul* or *Spirit* and conclude briefly thus:

The many contradictions and inconsistencies we find in the nature of *Matter*—which make it unable to either think or *spontaneously move itself*—assure us that these operations do not belong to it, but to some other *Substance*. Therefore, finding those operations within us, it is manifest that we have within us an *Immaterial Being* truly distinct from the *Body*, which we ordinarily call a *Soul*. Although the study of its bare *Essence* may well puzzle us, those *Properties* we find to be incompatible <note>original: "incompetible"</note> with a *Body* sufficiently inform us of its different nature. For it is plain she is a *Substance* endowed with the power of *cogitation* (that is, of perceiving and thinking about *Objects*) as well as the power of *penetrating* and *spontaneously moving* a *Body*. These *Properties* are as fundamental to her...

## CHAPTER XI.

1. *That Subtlety is not inconsistent with the strongest Truth. 2. That the secondary usefulness of things in the world exists in the things themselves, not merely in our imagination <note>original: "Phanſy"</note>. 3. That the difficulty of obtaining such useful commodities is an argument for Providence rather than against it. 4. That Beauty does not result necessarily from the mere motion of Matter. 5. That it is an intellectual object, not noticed by animals <note>original: "Brutes"</note>. 6. That the preying of animals upon one another is very consistent with the goodness of the First Cause. 7. That the immediate matter of the fetus is homogeneous <note>original: "homogeneal"; meaning: uniform in its physical makeup</note>. 9. That the notion of the Archei <note>vital principles or "seminal forms" believed to direct the growth of living things</note> or seminal forms is not such an intricate speculation.*

1. We have now gone through all the objections against the first book of our *Antidote*. If those of a coarser disposition—so they may still seem to have something further to object—shall mockingly cavil, claiming we have used too much *subtlety* in the management of our arguments, I can only remind them of this: that *subtlety* is as consistent with *truth* as the most basic theories. This is evident in many *mathematical speculations*, which are more certain and undeniable to human reason than anything else. But the idea that the connection of concepts that are subtle in themselves should be as easily plain and obvious as the physical objects of the senses is an illogical thought; it can be expected by none but those who are utterly unskilled in the nature of such contemplations.

But the defense of our second book will be not only shorter but less obscure. Our arguments there for the most part are such that even the unlearned can judge them, and few of them are not so evidently convincing that nothing significant can be argued against them. However, I shall briefly set down and answer such objections as there are.

They argue: how easy is it for the wit of man to bring things together that are of a distant nature in themselves, and to imagine many *series of means and ends* in matters that have no dependence on one another but what he himself makes? Therefore, since it is true that there is such a subordinate *usefulness* in the things themselves that are provided for us, it is only reasonable for us to attribute it to a *Cause* that was aware of the *usefulness* and *serviceability* of its own works.

3. Nor should we complain <note>original: "cavil"</note> because these *useful* things—such as *stones*, *metals*, *coals*, and the like—must be obtained with so much labor. Some might argue that men would be better off released from all such drudgery so that they might have more time to contemplate the *world*, seek after *God*, and exercise the better *faculties* of human *nature*. However, we see plainly that the fallen <note>original: "lapsed"</note> condition of *man* is such that *idleness* does not encourage *virtue* or *piety*, but rather fosters all kinds of *beastliness* and *sensuality*. Besides, few men's minds are of such a *contemplative* <note>original: "Speculative"</note> temperament that they can, with any great pleasure, attend to such meditations as would be worth abandoning a more *practical* and laborious life—a life which, certainly, does not exclude men from being pious and honest, as no *calling* does. Therefore, the fact that for the majority of men all *useful* things are hard to come by is actually an *argument* for *Providence*. It shows that the *Cause* that framed the *Earth* knew well beforehand what the disposition of terrestrial *man* would be.

4. The second objection is against our *argument* from the *beauty* of *plants*, which I contend has its primary origin in an *intellectual cause*, as *beauty* itself is an *intellectual object*. But two things are objected against this. First, that *beauty* is a necessary result of the mere motion of *matter*. Second, that it is not an *intellectual object* at all, since *women* and *children* seem to be more taken with it than *men*, and *animals* <note>original: "Brutes"</note> as much as either.

The objectors attempt to prove the first point as follows: they say that *color*, which is one part of *beauty*, is the result of mere *matter*. This is plain, they say, from the *rainbow*, which is assuredly such a purely natural result. As for *symmetry*—the other part of *beauty*, which in *plants* consists of their leaves and branches matching each other in parallel, as well as the various parts of the same leaf—they say there is a kind of *natural* necessity for such a uniform correspondence. They argue that the nourishment must follow the path of the *vessels* of the *seed*; because these vessels are regular in their initial formation, the branches and leaves that sprout out must also be regular. This regular formation of the *seed* came from the uniform motion of particles in the *parent plant* <note>original: "Mother-plant"</note>; and finally, the first *parent plant* of any kind came from the regular motion of *matter*.

But I answer: it is true that the *arrangement* <note>original: "Poſiture"</note> as well as the *colors* of the *rainbow* are necessary results of mere *matter*. But what I insist upon most, and contend proceeds from an <term>Intellectual principle</term>, is their <term>symmetry</term>. The objection against this seems very weak, the reasoning being this: you plainly see that the regular motion of matter created the <term>first plant</term> of every kind. We must ask: what regulated the motion of that matter so as to guide it to form itself into such a state that it eventually appears as a very pleasant intellectual spectacle? Such a result is exceedingly difficult (if not impossible) to hit upon without some other Director distinct from blind matter. 

A man will easily believe this if he does not think so much about the <term>trunks and branches of trees</term>—whose shooting out of the ground, and then having arms shooting out of the trunk and branching themselves into many subdivisions, is not so difficult to conceive—as upon their <term>blooms, fruits, and leaves</term>. Consider the leaf of the <term>oak</term> and of <term>holly</term>, and the abundance of leaves of <term>herbs</term> and their flowers, such as <term>monks-hood</term>, <term>snap-dragon</term>, and sundry sorts of <term>fly-flowers</term> (including the <term>fly-flower</term> properly so called, the <term>butterfly-satyricon</term> <note>an archaic name for a type of orchid</note>, and the <term>gnat-satyricon</term>). To these, add the <term>wasp-orchis</term>, the <term>bee-flower</term>, and the like. Matter could never have hit upon such difficult and yet regular shapes had it not been regulated by something besides itself. The elegance <note>original: "concinnity"</note> of these figures pleases those of us who are <term>rational</term>, and we ought in all reason to conclude that they came from an <term>intellectual principle</term>.

However, if children can also discover a lack of symmetry and correspondence—for instance, in a flower that has some leaves torn off—it is because the <term>spirit</term> within them is intellectual; it is not at all unreasonable that it should begin to exercise itself on such simple objects early on. Otherwise, there is no question that if they could be free from other employments, they would be as devout admirers of beauty as women themselves, and be as well pleased with women's beauty as women themselves are.

Lastly, even if we should admit at any time that <term>brutes</term> <note>animals, as distinguished from rational humans</note> may be more pleased with a *beautiful* object (taking *beauty* in its entire sense) than with one less beautiful, it is only a confused delight. They no more relish it as *intellectual* than *children* do—who are often well pleased to see mathematical instruments made of brass or ivory—when they look at the exact carvings of the characters and lines on them, which are actually rational and mathematical in nature. Therefore, we may very well conclude that the *beauty* of bodies is naturally intended no more for *animals* than such mathematical instruments are for *children*. 6. The third objection is against animals preying upon one another, and man preying upon them all. For this, they say, is inconsistent with that *Eternal Goodness* that we claim has created and ordered all things. To which I answer, that it is not at all inconsistent. For the nature of that *absolute, universal*, and *eternal goodness* is not to dote upon any one individual, as we do—whose temperaments may perhaps make us more than ordinarily compassionate (though most men have too little of that natural kindness) and whose short-sightedness plunges us too much into the feelings of the present moment. Instead, taking a full and free view of the capacities for *happiness* in these kinds of creatures, this Goodness contrived their condition to be what was best for the majority of them, even though the necessity and <term>incompossibility</term> <note>original: "incompossibility"; the state of being unable to exist together or be true at the same time</note> of things would surely burden some individual creatures with greater inconvenience than the rest.

# CHAP. XI. An Appendix to the foregoing Antidote.

Now it is evident that the *main powers* of *animal life* are *natural cleverness, strength,* and *physical activity*. Anything gained through these is far more pleasant to a living creature than what comes easily without them. Therefore, what could be more gratifying to a land animal than to hunt its prey and catch it? But not all kinds of creatures are capable of this special happiness. Some, therefore, are made to feed on the fruits of the earth, so that they may not only enjoy themselves but also occasionally provide game and food for other *creatures*. In this, the *wisdom* of God as well as His *goodness* is manifest: while these creatures are a sport and prey to others, they are still abundantly preserved in their various generations. But I have treated all such doubts against Providence so fully and systematically in my *Enquiry into the Causes and Occasions of Atheism* <note>Referring to Henry More's own work, *An Antidote against Atheism* (1652), which explored these philosophical arguments in depth</note> that we will satisfy ourselves with this brief response here.

We will only add that if the *souls of brutes* <term>brutes</term> <note>original: "brutes"; a common term for animals, implying they lack the rational soul of humans</note> *prove to be immortal* (an idea which the best philosophers have not been against), the tragedy of predation is even less horrifying. Yet, that should not encourage us to needlessly and stubbornly kill them, because we do not know how long it will be until they have the opportunity to form other *bodies* for themselves; the interval of time between is, to them, a perfect death, wherein they have neither the sense nor enjoyment of anything. And for my own part, I think that he who disregards the life or welfare of an animal is naturally so *unjust* that, if outward laws did not restrain him, he would be just as cruel to man.

7. The fourth objection is against our argument for *Divine Providence* <note>The protective care of God or nature as a spiritual power</note> drawn from the consideration of that happy mitigation of the *trouble* and *annoyance* of some animals by *others* that are natural *enemies* to them and feed upon them as their prey—as the *cat*, for example, does to the *mouse*. Now, some say it would be a more precise sign of *Providence* if there were no such *offensive* creatures in the world to trouble us at all, rather than bringing on the trouble by creating these animals and then removing it again by creating others to correct the mischief that would follow.

But no man would argue this way if he had not over-carelessly adopted this false principle: *that the world was made for man alone*. Assuredly, the blessed and kind Maker of all things intended that *other living creatures* should enjoy themselves as well as *men*, which they could not do if they did not exist. Therefore, *Providence* is more precise in that she can thus spread her *goodness* even further, reaching the enjoyments of the lower ranks of creatures without any considerable inconvenience to the more noble and superior ones.

Besides, all these creatures that are thus a *prey* to others serve as their sport and nourishment, and so they please others by their death, just as they enjoy themselves while they are still alive and free from their enemies. This is to say nothing of how they are all, in one way or another, *useful* to man himself, and therefore would sometimes be missed if they were gone.

### CHAP. XI. An Appendix to the foregoing Antidote.

8. The fifth and last objection is against our concluding that there is a *substance distinct from the body* based on the *homogeneity* <term>homogeneity</term> <note>original: "Homogeneity"; the quality of being uniform or consisting of parts that are all of the same kind.</note> of that *immediate crystalline matter* out of which the *fetus* is shaped—for instance, in an egg, which is also observable in other types of generation. To avoid the force of this *argument*, it is denied that there is any such *homogeneity* of parts. Instead, it is argued that there are various *heterogeneous* <note>original: "Heterogeneal"; diverse in character or content; made of different types of particles.</note> particles, though invisible to us, which are set into motion by the heat of the *hen* or some equivalent warmth. These similar particles are supposedly driven toward one another, and so the *chicken* is formed. They argue that to acknowledge any other *Archeus* <term>Archeus</term> <note>original: "Archeus"; in Paracelsian and Neoplatonic philosophy, this is the "master-workman" or vital force that governs the growth and functions of a living organism.</note> brings inescapable difficulties along with it.

For where, they ask, were all the *Archei* which shaped the *wasps* out of a *horse's carcass*? <note>This refers to the then-common belief in "spontaneous generation," where it was thought insects grew directly from decaying organic matter.</note> Are they parts of the *horse’s soul*, or are they new guests who intrude once the old soul has been ejected? If the former, then the *soul* of a *horse* is divisible and consequently material—or, if you prefer, truly *matter*. If the latter, where were those little intruders before? Or are they so many sprouts or branches of the common *soul of the world*? <term>soul of the world</term> <note>original: "Soul of the world"; translated from the Latin *Anima Mundi*, the idea that a single spirit animates all of nature.</note> But if so, why do they not all share one common sense of pain and pleasure? But to all these questions, I answer in order.

To the first part of this objection, I say that it must be a very strong presumption that *Nature* intends an utter *homogeneity* of *matter* before she begins her work of formation, since she constantly brings it to as perfect a *homogeneity* as we can possibly discern with our senses. Since there is no conceivable benefit at all in having *heterogeneous* parts at that stage, I think the conclusion is not rash if we assert that the *immediate matter* used to form the *fetus* is either accurately *homogeneous*, or if there is any diversity of parts in it, it is only by accident. Such diversity contributes no more to the first work of shaping or organizing the *matter* than the specks of dust that land on a painter's colors contribute to the better drawing of a picture. For to say that those various sorts of particles, set in motion by external warmth, gather together by virtue of their similarity to one another, is to claim something without any evidence at all, and against all grounds of *reason*.

For what can this *similarity of parts* consist of, if not either in a likeness of shape, or in an equality of movement or size? Now, if bodies of a similar shape are set in motion, they will not direct their courses toward one another any more just because they have the same shape. Indeed, in a state of confused agitation, bodies of similar shape, movement, and size may very likely come together. We see this happen in the thinner spirits of distilled liquors that all rise upward; in the *tartarous parts of wine* <note>original: "Tartarous parts of wine"; the sediment or cream of tartar that settles in wine casks.</note> that are driven outward to the sides of the vessel; in the *feculency* <term>feculency</term> <note>original: "feculency"; the dregs or impurities that settle at the bottom of a liquid.</note> of urine that sinks to the bottom of the glass; and in the sinking of this dreg-like part of the world, the *Earth* (if it can be said to sink to the bottom as much as it sits in the midst of the more refined and subtle elements). In a similar way, the *fermentation* of matter which precedes the formation of creatures may perhaps achieve some such crude effect as seen in those examples; but it can never amount to such an artistic arrangement of organs as is found in living creatures.

### CHAP. XI. An Appendix to the foregoing Antidote.

But if by *likeness of parts* they mean only the *fitness of parts for shape* and *motion*—where both are so framed and regulated that, upon external warmth, their agitation will necessarily cause them to lock into one another and be linked into this admirable and useful frame of an animal's body—that design would be so particularly precise and sophisticated that it is utterly inconceivable. It must imply either the attendance, or at least the original design, of a *Knowing Principle* <term>Knowing Principle</term> <note>original: "Knowing Principle"; a conscious, intelligent agency or mind (God or a Spirit) as opposed to blind, random matter.</note> that put the *Matter* into such a wonderful order as to be able, by such *precise laws of shape* and *motion*, to present such noble objects to our senses and understandings. And thus, our adversaries will gain nothing by this theory.

<margin>* See my treatise *The Immortality of the Soul*, Book 3, chapters 12 and 13.</margin>

But though this may seem barely possible, I believe it is very improbable that such an infinite number of particles, which must come together to make up a *fetus*, should have such a specific shaping and law of motion impressed upon each of them as to enable it to take its right station or posture in the structure of a living creature. For it seems to me that this is "going about the bush" <note>An idiom meaning to take an unnecessarily indirect or complicated route.</note>, whereas the more efficient way would be to make use of some *Immaterial Substance*, such as those conceived to be the *Seminal Forms* <term>Seminal Forms</term> <note>original: "Seminal Forms"; the non-physical blueprints or "seeds" that direct the growth of physical organisms.</note> of plants and animals, or the *Archei* <term>Archei</term> <note>original: "Archei"; plural of Archeus, the vital force or "master-workman" that governs the growth of a living thing.</note>, as others call them. For this *Form* or *Archeus* is something more simple and plain, and requires a simpler qualification of the subject it works upon: namely, that the material be only *homogeneous* <note>Uniform in composition.</note> and *ductile*, or yielding to the gentle influence of that substantial power of life that resides within it.

9. Nor is this opinion of the *Archei* or *Seminal Forms* entangled in any such difficulties that it cannot be easily answered.

As for those many pretended intricacies in the example of the formation of *wasps* out of the carcass of a horse <note>A reference to the outdated belief in spontaneous generation, where insects were thought to grow directly from decaying matter.</note>, I say that the *Archei* that framed them are not parts of the horse's soul that is dead. Instead, they are several distinct *Archei* that naturally join with the *Matter* of his body, once it is putrefied and prepared, just as crows come to eat his flesh.

But you ask where these *Archei* were before. To which I answer: Can there be a lack of room for such small pieces of *spirituality* in so vast a compass as the entire universe? I shall rather reply, Where were they *not*? The *world of life* is excluded from no place, and the various sorts of souls are as plentiful and as common there as those *magnetic particles* are in this physical world. You can hardly place your *lodestone* and *iron* anywhere without finding their presence by their noticeable effects. Or, if you prefer a coarser comparison, they are as cheap and common as dust flying in the air in a dry and windy summer.

<margin>* This is the usual phrase used by the ancient philosophers, but to see how far it is justifiable, see *The Immortality of the Soul*, Book 3, chapter 16, section 8.</margin>

To the last puzzle proposed—whether these *Archei* are so many branches of the *common Soul of the world* <term>Soul of the world</term> <note>original: "Soul of the world" or *Anima Mundi*; a common Neoplatonic concept of an animating spirit that permeates all nature.</note>, or particular substances existing by themselves—there is no great inconvenience in acknowledging that it may be either way. For it does not follow that if they are so many branches or distinct *rays of the great Soul of the world, they are therefore that very Soul itself. If they are not, they may have their pleasures and pains apart and distinct from one another. And what is pleasure and pain to them may perhaps be *neither* to their source, affecting her no more than the chirping of a cricket affects those who are listening to a full concert.

But suppose we say that they are as many distinct substances, as independent of the <term>Soul of the World</term> <note>original: "Soul of the world"; a concept in vitalist philosophy where a single spirit permeates all nature, giving it life and order.</note> as <term>Matter</term> itself is (though all depend on God); there is no difficulty or inconvenience at all in that position. For a <term>Substance</term>, whatever its nature may be, cannot perish without a miracle. And I think no man can think of <note>original: "excogitate"</note> any reason why God should annihilate something that, in the passage of time, may again have the opportunity to play its part and prove useful to the world.

And as for the **Children at Amsterdam** <note>This likely refers to a famous 1566 case where dozens of children in an orphanage reportedly suffered from demonic possession, exhibiting strange behavior like vomiting pins and needles.</note>, the spectacle was so miserable, and their reported torture so great, and the parties involved so numerous, and all attempts of medical Art or Religion so **futile** <note>original: "frustraneous"</note>, that it seems very incredible that there should be either fraud or foolery in the matter. 3. The third Objection is against the **Mirth** of some of the stories recorded, such as that of **John of Hembach** and **John Michael the Pipers**. There are such passions and affections in them as are found in wicked men and beasts; some of them especially bear the same relationship to an unfallen Angel that an ape or monkey does to a sober man. Thus, all their pleasure is in unlucky, ridiculous tricks. They bear a secret hatred for whatever is comely and proper, and in perpetual scorn of it, they distort all their actions into the opposite style, applauding themselves only in an unlimited liberty to do whatever their foolish or foul imaginations suggest to them; desiring nothing but the gratification of their own wills and a power to make themselves wondered at and feared.

Secondly, even if we admit that the *Angel* spoke to him in that way, the *Angel* in this case is not properly speaking as a *Person*, but as an *Instrument*—much like how a man's *Tongue* speaks, even though the man's *Soul* or the man himself is more truly the speaker than the tongue. Therefore, if *God* takes full possession of all the powers and faculties of an *Angel* so that the Angel loses the sense of his own personality for a time and becomes a mere passive *Instrument* of the *Deity*—becoming, as it were, the *Eye* or *Mouth of God*—what he speaks in this state should be understood as coming from *God*, and not from himself.

In this way, I hope I have resolved the difficulties concerning all the *historical passages* of this *Third Book* that still remain in it. I must confess that I have removed <note>original: "expunged"</note> some that did not seem accurately consistent with the rules I set for myself upon closer review. It is not that I know them to be false, but because they lack that consistency, I must admit they are not convincingly true.

### An Appendix to the preceding Antidote. CHAPTER XIII.

*12. That if Spirits or Demons are nothing but mere compositions of Airy or Fiery Atoms, every Devil is many millions of Devils. 13. The superiority of arguments drawn from the history of Spirits over those from the operations of the Soul in the Body for proving an immaterial substance.*

1. THE first Philosophical Objection is against the *Transformation* of a human body into the shape of, for instance, a *Wolf* or any such creature. For it is thought that this cannot be done without a great deal of pain to the person transformed. To which I answer: that although this *Transformation* is made in a very short time, it may still be performed without any pain at all. For that part in the Head which is the seat of *Common Sense* I conceive to be very small (suppose it to be the *Conarion* <note>original: "Conarion"; the pineal gland, which many 17th-century thinkers, including Descartes, believed was the "seat of the soul" where all sensory information was integrated.</note>, it is not very big). Therefore, if the Devil gets into the body of a man and possesses that part along with the rest, he can intercept or block all the transmissions of motion from other parts of the body. Thus, let him do what he will with them, the person shall feel no *pain* at all. He may *soften* all the parts of the body besides into whatever consistency he pleases and work it into any form, just as he can his own Vehicle of Air <note>original: "Vehicle of Aire"; the Neoplatonic idea that a spirit or soul inhabits a subtle, semi-material body made of air or ether to interact with the physical world.</note>, and the person will not be aware of it the entire time. There is the same reason for reducing the body back into its own shape again, which is just as painless to the person who undergoes it. Nor is there any fear that a body once loosened this way will remain in this loose, melting condition forever; for it is acknowledged even by those who oppose *Bodinus* <note>original: "Bodinus"; Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and author of "De la démonomanie des sorciers," a major work on witchcraft and demonology.</note>, whose cause I undertake, that a *Spirit* can just as easily stop and fix a body as move it. Therefore I say, when the Devil has fixed the body again in its original shape, it will—according to the undeniable laws of Nature—remain in that state he left it, until something more powerful unsettles and changes it; and every body is overpowered at last, and we must all yield to death.

2. The second Objection is against our acknowledging an *actual separation of Soul and Body without death*. Death is properly defined, as we state it, as a separation of the Soul from the Body because the Body is *unfit* any longer to host the Soul, which may be caused by extreme disease, by outward violence, or old age. Now, they say, "What is violence, if this is not: for the Devil to take the Soul out of the Body?" But the answer is easy: any separation by violence is not *death*, but rather such a violence in separation that makes the body unfit to host the Soul again. This happens when the blood is let out by wounding the body, or by hindering the course of the spirits <note>original: "spirits"; in early medicine, these were "vital spirits," subtle substances in the blood believed to power life and movement.</note> by strangling, drowning, or the like. For to revive such a body as this would be a miracle indeed; in such cases, death has seized upon the body in a true and proper sense, and then none but God himself can thus kill and make alive.

3. The third Objection is against the notable *coldness* of the bodies of Devils. For at the great trial of Witches at the *St. Edmundsbury Assizes* <note>original: "S. Edmonds-Bury Assises"; a famous series of witch trials held in Suffolk, England, in 1645 during the height of the English Civil War.</note> in *August* 1645, I heard some of them openly confess at the bar, says the Objector, that when the Devil lay with them, he was *warm*. To which I might answer, if I had a mind to dodge the question rather than precisely satisfy it...

# CHAPTER XIII. An Appendix to the preceding Antidote.

...the exceptions made against what we have written—suggesting that perhaps some warm young man had taken the place of the "cold Devil"; for who knows what tricks <note>original: "juggles"</note> there might be in these things?

<margin>* Antidote, Book 3, chapter 9, section 8. * Chapter 7, section 6.</margin>
But to answer more directly to the point, I admit that the *bodies* of *demons* <note>original: "Devils"</note> may be not only *warm*, but *searingly <note>original: "findingly"</note> hot*. This was the case with the spirit that took one of *Melanchthon’s* <note>Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560) was a famous German Protestant reformer.</note> relatives by the hand and scorched her so badly that she bore the mark of it until her dying day. However, examples of *cold* are more common, as in the famous story of *Cuntius* <note>original: "Cuntius"; refers to Johannes Cuntius, a reported "revenant" or ghost in Silesia whose body allegedly remained cold and touchable after death.</note>. When he touched the arm of a certain woman of *Pentsch* as she lay in her bed, he felt as cold as ice. The same was true of the spirit's claw felt by *Anne Styles* <note>A witness in a 17th-century witchcraft case.</note>, and there are many other stories of that nature. Yet, I will not deny that their bodies may also be *warm*; otherwise, it is impossible to understand how those two wretched *sorcerers* <note>original: "Magi"</note> could reap such inexpressible pleasure—one from his *Armellina* and the other from his *Florina*—as they claimed to have done in a certain dialogue by *Gianfrancesco Pico* <note>original: "Franciscus Picus"; referring to Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola (1469–1533), an Italian philosopher.</note>. He titled this work *The Witch* <note>original: "Strix"</note>, or *On the Deception of Demons* <note>original: "De Ludificatione Dæmonum"</note>. In his introductory letter, he assures us that it is a true history and that he records only what he has either seen with his own eyes or heard from the confessions of witches themselves.

Therefore, the weight of the objection is aimed at something we do not claim: that the bodies of demons are found *only* cold. Rather, what we mean to suggest is simply this: since their *bodies* are nothing but *thickened* <note>original: "coagulated"</note> or compressed *air*, when they position themselves to compress their "vehicles" <note>A "vehicle" was the semi-material body of air or ether that a spirit was thought to inhabit to interact with the physical world.</note> much more than they agitate the individual particles within them, they will then seem not only *cold* (as frozen water does) but more piercingly and stingingly cold because of the extreme thinness <note>original: "subtilty"</note> of their parts.

But when they not only strongly *compress* <note>original: "constringe"</note> their whole vehicle but also fiercely *agitate* its individual particles, their body will become searingly <note>original: "findingly"</note> *hot*. In this state, it resembles heated brass or iron, where the particles stay close together, yet every one is vigorously moving. This is obvious if we spit upon such heated metals; they will make the spittle hiss and bubble, as the particles of the metal transfer their motion to the spittle resting on them. It will turn all liquid into vapors, as we commonly see when burning vinegar or rose water in a room to perfume it. For what is this perfuming but setting the water-based <note>original: "Aqueous"</note> parts of the liquid into such strong motion that they rise into the air and disperse as smoke <note>original: "fume"</note>, caused by the fierce and strong agitation of the solid <note>original: "inseparable"</note> parts of the heated fire shovel?

Finally, if a spirit uses his *active* <note>original: "Agitative"</note> power moderately and his *compressing* <note>original: "constrictive"</note> power forcefully enough to feel solid or touchable <note>original: "palpable"</note> to the man or woman he is dealing with, he may feel not only warm, but more pleasantly and agreeably warm than any earthly or fleshy body. This is because the refinement <note>original: "subtilty"</note> of the *matter* will more precisely target and more powerfully reach the sense organs, moving the nerves more exquisitely and enchantingly than any physical body possibly can. Yet, all the while, the *spirit* himself is neither hot, nor warm, nor cold, nor anything else that belongs to a body; he is a substance distinctly different from everything physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note>...

...any corporeal <note>original: "poreal"; referring to physical or bodily matter</note> matter whatsoever, as I have * already suggested in the section we are now defending.

4. The fourth objection is against our assertion that it is an inconsistent and self-contradicting position to hold *that there never was any man who was not born of a woman, even if we were to admit that the *successions* of mankind were *infinite*. For, the objectors say, a contradiction only exists if you can identify a *First* man. But in an *infinite succession*, they argue, there can be no *First* in any sense at all; for if there were a *First*, there would be a *Second*, and so on to our own times. In that case, the *series* would be countable and consequently finite—which would be a contradiction, because then the *succession* would be both *finite* and *infinite*.

But I answer, first, that I can demonstrate that there is indeed a *First* in an *infinite succession* based on the very principles that the *atheist* either does grant or must necessarily grant. That principle is that *Matter* has existed *from eternity* <note>original: "ab Æterno"</note>, and that at least some part of it has moved *from eternity* <note>original: "ab Æterno"</note>. Now, it is plain that this *matter* that moved *from eternity* either moved of its own accord or was moved by another. If the latter, then we have a *First* in an *infinite succession* of motions: for that which moved this *matter*—which has moved *from eternity*—is first in the order of causality <term>causality: the relationship between cause and effect</term>, as is undeniably plain to anyone who understands logic.

But you will say that this *matter* that moved *from eternity* <note>original: "ab Æterno"</note> was moved by itself. Even if that were so, no part of it can move in this full *ocean of matter* (which is excluded from no space) without hitting some other part of *matter* as soon as it moves, and that part hitting another, and so on. Thus, there might be a *succession* of motions *from eternity* <note>original: "ab Æterno"</note> or *infinitely*, and yet still be a *first* in the order of causality. For that original <note>original: "primordial"</note> motion of the *matter* is clearly first and the cause of all the rest. Our understanding can never be at rest until it has reached some such "first" in the order of causes.

Secondly, regarding that subtle argument intended to prove that this *infinite succession* would be both *finite* and *infinite*, I answer that it is a mere sophism <term>sophism: a clever but false argument</term> arising from the ambiguity of the term *first*. The word "first" can signify either a priority of *succession* or a priority of *causality*. In the first sense (succession), if we admit a *first*, the *succession* will be *finite* according to our own faculties; for we cannot help but look beyond it, finding the succession bounded by that *first*. But in the second sense (causality), *first* sets no bounds to succession, but leaves it free and infinite.

Or we may answer this way: if we begin from this moment and go back toward the *first* original motion—calling this present moment the *first* and the next moment before it the *second*—the sum will amount to a number that is truly *infinite*, and our human understanding can never finish counting it. However, even though God’s understanding can encompass it, it does not follow that the number is therefore *finite*; for an *infinite mind* may well comprehend an *infinite number*. But for us, whose capacities are *finite*, if we ventured to name a *first* in an *infinite succession*, we should call it the *first infinitesimal* <note>original Greek: "πρῶτον ἀπειροσὸν"</note> and acknowledge ourselves unable to complete the count, our understandings being finite.

5. The fifth and last objection is against that story from *Gerard* <note>John Gerard (c. 1545–1612) was a famous English herbalist whose "Herball" (1597) included the myth that "Barnacle Geese" hatched from trees.</note> regarding the *tree-geese* in the island of the *Pile of Foulders* <note>Piel Island, located off the coast of the Furness Peninsula in Cumbria, England.</note>. For it is objected by someone who inquired of people living near that place that the story was not confirmed to him. Instead, they told him only that at a certain time of the year it was...

But to this it may be answered, either that those parties who were consulted were men who did not look for such curiosities as these; or that the rotten pieces of ships or trunks of trees that were washed up there by the sea have been washed away again a long time ago. Thus, because the examples of this rarity have not been freshly renewed, the memory of it may have been lost in many of those parts. For it is nearly sixty <term>threescore: sixty</term> years since Gerard <note>original: "Gerard"; referring to John Gerard (c. 1545–1612), a famous English herbalist and author of *The Herball or Generall Historie of Plantes*</note> wrote his account; but while he was living, he offered to prove his story with sufficient witnesses; and he professes that he declares only what his eyes had seen and his hands had touched.

And he also adds a story of another sort of *tree-geese* <note>original: "Tree-geese"; a reference to the then-common belief in "Barnacle Geese," which were thought to grow from barnacles on driftwood rather than hatching from eggs</note> which he gathered in their shells from an old rotten tree on the shore of our English coast between Dover and Romney <note>original: "Rumney"</note>. He brought many of them with him to London; and opening the shells, which were somewhat like mussels <note>original: "Muscles"</note>, he found these birds in several degrees of development <note>original: "maturation"</note>. In some, he found only shapeless lumps; in others, the form of birds but bare; in others, the same form and shape with down also upon them, their shells gaping open and the birds ready to fall out.

I might add a third kind described to me by a gentleman from Ireland, which he has often observed upon those coasts; but it is not necessary <note>original: "material"</note> to insist upon the description of it. All that I aim at is this: that this truth of *birds being bred from rotting matter* <note>original: "putrefaction"; referring to the theory of spontaneous generation, where life was thought to arise from decaying organic substances</note> is very certain. I am so well assured of this by this gentleman’s information as well as by Gerard’s account that I must confess, for my own part, I cannot doubt it at all. And it might support my willingness to believe—if I could be justly suspected of that fault here—that the objector himself, upon further inquiry, is at length fully satisfied concerning the same truth.

6. We have now answered all the objections, both *philosophical* and *historical*, made against those particular passages in my third book. There remains only one of a more universal nature, and indeed of such importance that if I do not satisfy it, it would utterly undermine the main design of our whole third book against *atheism*. In that book, we intended to lead men to a more ready belief in God through the history of *spirits*. For even admitting all those stories to be true, they say it does not follow at all that there are *spirits* in the sense that I define *spirits*, and in the notion that is understood in my explanation of the *idea of God*. Specifically, they deny *that there should be an immaterial or incorporeal substance that can penetrate and move physical matter*. For they claim that spirits themselves are but a *thinner* kind of *body*, such as *air* or *fire*, or some similar subtle element, and not *pure spirit* according to our definition.

If this were true, I must confess that our last book against *atheism* is of no effectiveness <note>original: "efficacy"</note> at all and can do nothing toward the end for which it was intended. For if there is a *God*, He must necessarily be a *spirit properly so called*; otherwise, He cannot be *infinite*. Nor can He be this *universal matter* in the world, even if we suppose it to be boundless, because He could not then be *perfect*. Instead, He must be an essence upon which this *matter* depends, and in which He exists, penetrating and possessing all things. Which anyone will

# An Appendix to the foregoing Antidote. CHAP. XIII.

7. ...one could easily believe this if they were certain that there are specific *Spirits* that inhabit and move particular parts of *Matter*. I contend that the stories I have related clearly prove this to be true.

8. For I appeal to anyone who knows the nature of *Fire* and *Air*: are they not truly just a collection of loose particles of *Matter*, much like a *heap of sand*? The only difference is that they are so small that they are invisible and cannot be felt as individual pieces. Yet, they are as *truly disjointed atoms* (if I may call them that, though they are still theoretically divisible) as the *grains of sand* we just mentioned.

Now, this being granted—and only ignorance would deny it—we shall clearly see that the things done by *Spirits* (as we usually call them) are entirely impossible for any structure <term>original: "compages"; a complex structure or framework</term> made of these small grains or *atoms of matter* that compose *Air* and *Fire*. 

First, either all of these *grains* or *atoms* possess *Sensation*, *Imagination*, and *Understanding*, or only a few do, or perhaps only one. If all or a few possess these, it is plain that they are many distinct intelligent *beings*; and a distinct intelligent *being* is a *person*. This would mean that this one person is actually many persons, which is clearly a contradiction, or at least foolishly ridiculous. 

But if the seat of *Sensation*, *Imagination*, and *Understanding* is placed in only one atom, how is it possible for that single atom to *move all the others of its own accord*? The same problem arises if we place *Sensation* and *Reason* in a few internal atoms. How could they pull along those behind them, carry those beside them, or drive those in front of them without the group splitting apart and leaving atoms behind? Furthermore, there is a strong assumption that the *seat of sensation* is confined to a small area within the *vehicle of a spirit* <note>In the philosophy of the time, a "vehicle" was the subtle, airy, or ethereal body that a spirit inhabited to interact with the physical world</note>, just as it is in the *body of a man*. If it were not—if every part of the *vehicle* had *sensation* in itself—then an external object would seem to be in many places at once. Images of things would be utterly confused, or the atoms, when they began to move, would lose their way; by following their own individual senses, they would necessarily break away from one another and destroy the whole spirit.

9. Again, it is obvious that whatever has the power of *sensation* in a *spirit* also has the power of *memory*. They could not remember the objects of their senses if the same thing within them did not possess both *sensation* and *memory*. And that which remembers also *imagines*; and that which imagines, through the power of imagination, transforms its *vehicle* into various shapes and figures, holding it in that shape for as long as it sees fit.

Now I ask: how can this possibly be done by either one or a few particles or atoms residing in any part of the *vehicle*? How can they hold the others together, or grip them, to restrain and bind them into this or that form—such as a *dog*, a *colt*, or a *man*? But to say that *imagination* exists in every part of the *vehicle*—and to claim that particles can *imagine* even though they lack *sensation* (as most seem to, based on what was just argued)—is altogether unreasonable.

10. Thirdly, consider the argument that *Lucretius* <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and philosopher who argued that the soul was made of atoms and perished when the body died</note> uses against the *immortality* of the soul. He assumes the soul is a collection <term>original: "congeries"</term> of little *atoms*, much like the *spirits* discussed here are...
