11. Fourthly and lastly, the transportation of cattle and of witches themselves to their *nighttime meetings* <note>original: "Nocturnal Conventicles"; secret gatherings, often associated in this period with witchcraft</note> through the *air*—if *spirits* or *devils* are nothing more than a *mere* collection <note>original: "congestion"</note> of subtle *atoms of air* or *fire* without an inward *immaterial principle* that has the power to hold the particles together—is a thing altogether impossible. For it is evident that the weight of a *man* or a *beast* will sink through the *air* and never rest until they reach the *earth*. They would do the same through the vehicle <note>original: "Vehicle"; here meaning the subtle or spiritual body that a spirit inhabits</note> of a *spirit* that is as subtle, fluid, and yielding as the *air* itself, were there not an internal essence and principle able to bind <note>original: "constringe"</note> and hold together this fluid body or vehicle of the *spirit*, thereby making it able to sustain the weight. All bodies, whether hard or fluid, are equally impenetrable; therefore, if any power were to hold the air together so as to keep it within a certain space, and yet not change its usual consistency, it would be like wind in a bladder. A man might lie upon it as safely as upon a soft bed and never fear sinking through.

But in this loose arrangement <note>original: "composure"</note> of *atoms*, which they say is all there is in a *spirit* (even if we admit that ridiculous supposition that *every atom can imagine* and apply itself to one joint design of holding everything close together), it is still hard to conceive that this actual division of the whole into so many subtle, tiny <note>original: "exile"</note>, invisible particles does not so enfeeble the spontaneous efforts toward sustaining and carrying away the burden that their endeavors would always prove fruitless <note>original: "frustraneous"</note>.

12. But I need not insist upon that point, which may perhaps seem a bit more slippery <note>original: "lubricous"; here meaning difficult to grasp or uncertain</note>, when we have something even more clearly absurd <note>original: "palpably incongruous"</note> presenting itself to our view. For if this gathering of *airy* or *fiery particles* is the only substance acknowledged in a *spirit*, and every *atom* has *imagination* and *reason* in it to apply itself to one joint design, they must be—as I have suggested before—as truly *distinct persons* as *grains of sand* are distinct individuals of matter. Therefore, every single devil is actually 5,000 million devils and more—a thing that a person would hardly dream of, or admit to be anything more than a dream, if they thought of it while awake. But if such things as these are not acknowledged as absurd, but shamelessly admitted and swallowed as truth, I must confess that there is no argument <note>original: "Demonstration"</note> against impudence and stubbornness <note>original: "pertinacity"</note>, and that I am not able to prove to such people that even animals <note>original: "Brutes"</note> have life, or that the specks <note>original: "moats"</note> that dance in the sunbeams are devoid of *sense* and *reason*.

13. The substance of these arguments, as the reader may remember, I have used elsewhere to prove an *incorporeal principle* <note>a non-physical or spiritual essence</note> residing and acting in the *human body*. However, the structure and handling of them here is quite different, and their force is far more obvious and apparent. The fixed consistency and mechanical structure <note>original: "fabrick"</note> of a human body is able to perform many things that the fluid and unorganized vehicle of *fire* and *air* cannot possibly do, unless we admit an immaterial essence to be in it, and so thoroughly to possess...

### CHAPTER IX.
1. *The existence of God argued from the "final cause"* <note>original: "Final cause"; the purpose or end for which something exists</note> *of the implantation of the idea of God in the soul.*
2. *An evasion of the argument by supposing all things to be exactly as they are by chance.*
3. *That this evasion is either impossible or only barely possible, and therefore carries no weight.*
4. *That we should not focus on what is simply possible, but on what our natural faculties determine to be true.*
5. *He therefore urges again the final cause of the indelible idea or image of God in the soul, illustrating its force through a comparison.*
6. *That, supposing God did exist, he would have dealt with us no differently to make himself known than we are actually* <note>original: "de facto"</note> *dealt with; which therefore argues again that He does exist. 26*

### CHAPTER X.
1. *Several other attributes or properties in the human soul that argue for the being of God.*
2. *Such as natural conscience.*
3. *A pious hope or confidence of success in affairs when dealing righteously with the world.*
4. *An answer to an objection: that some men are entirely devoid of these divine senses.*
5. *That the universality of religious worship argues that the knowledge of God's existence comes from the light of nature.*
6. *An answer to an objection: namely, that this general acknowledgment of a God among nations might only be a universal tradition.*
7. *Another objection answered: namely, that what is universally received by all nations may nevertheless be false.*
8. *An objection regarding the general falsehood and perversity of the world's various religions. The first answer to this by way of apology.*
9. *The second answer, even supposing the religions of the nations were as depraved as you please.*
10. *A further objection regarding the long continuation of those false religions and the hopelessness of ever escaping them, with a brief answer. 28*

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER XI.
1. *An important inquiry concerning the essence of the human soul.*
2. *That the soul is not a mere modification of the body, as the body is incapable of the operations usually attributed to the soul, such as spontaneous motion, perception* <note>original: "Animadversion"</note>, *memory, and reason.*
3. *That the "animal spirits"* <note>The "spirits" were historically thought to be a subtle fluid in the nerves that controlled movement and sensation</note> *are incapable of memory, and consequently of reason, perception, and moving the body.*
4. *That the brain cannot be the source of spontaneous motion, as it has neither muscles nor sense.*
5. *That <term>fancy</term>* <note>original: "Phansy"; the faculty of imagination or forming mental images</note>, *reason, and perception are seated neither in any pore nor any particular part of the brain; nor is the whole brain, nor every particle of it, shaped into this or that specific concept.*
6. *That the formation of one part of the brain is not reflected to the rest, demonstrated from the physical position of things.*
7. *That the brain has no sense, further demonstrated from anatomical experiments.*
8. *How ridiculously the operations of the soul are attributed to the <term>conarion</term>* <note>The pineal gland, which some early modern philosophers believed was the seat of the soul</note>.
9. *The conclusion: that the impulse of spontaneous motion comes from neither the animal spirits nor the brain.*
10. *That the soul is not any physical* <note>original: "Corporeal"</note> *substance distinct from the animal spirits and the body.*
11. *And therefore it is an incorporeal substance* <note>A spirit or non-physical being</note>.
12. *The discovery of the soul's essence is of great use for more easily conceiving the nature of God.*
13. *And how there may be an eternal mind that has both understanding and the power of moving the matter of the universe. 32*

3. *Much less if matter were naturally at rest.*

### CHAP. IV.
1. *What notions are more particularly comprised in the* **Idea** *of a* **Being absolutely Perfect**. 2. *That the difficulty of framing the conception of a thing ought to be no argument against its* **existence**; *the nature of* **corporeal matter** *being so perplexed and intricate, which yet all men acknowledge to exist.* 3. *That the* **idea** *of a* **Spirit** *is as easy a notion as that of any other substance whatsoever. What powers and properties are contained in the notion of a* **Spirit**. 4. *That* **Eternity** *and* **Infinity**, *if* **God** *were not, would be cast upon something else; so that* **Atheism** *cannot free the* **mind** *from such intricacies.* 5. **Goodness**, **Knowledge**, *and* **Power** *are notions of the highest* **perfection**, *and therefore necessarily included in the* **idea** *of a* **Being absolutely Perfect**. 6. *As is also* **Necessity**, *since it suggests a greater* **perfection** *than* **contingency**. 14

### CHAP. V.
1. *What has caused various men to imagine that the Soul is a* **blank slate** <note>original: "Abrasa Tabula"; a scraped tablet ready for writing</note>. 2. *That the* **Mind of Man** *is not a* **blank slate**, *but has actual knowledge of her own, and in what sense she has it.* 3. *A further illustration of this truth.* 17

### CHAP. VI.
1. *Various instances arguing for actual knowledge in the Soul: such as that she has a more accurate* **idea** *of a* **Circle** *and* **Triangle** *than* **Matter** *can exhibit to her.* 2. *And that upon one single consideration, she assures herself of the* **universal property** <note>original: "Universal Affection"; a characteristic or attribute</note> *of a* **Triangle**. 3. *The same argued from the nature of* **Mathematical** *and* **Logical notions**, *which do not come in through the* **senses**, *as they are not* **physical properties** *of* **Matter**. 4. *Because they are produced without any* **physical motion** *upon the* **Matter**. 5. *And that contrary kinds may be entirely in one and the same part of* **Matter** *at once.* 6. *That there are certain sure* **complex notions** *of the* **Mind** *for which she was not beholden to* **Sense**. 18

<column-break/>

### CHAP. VII.
1. *Since the Mind of Man is not unfurnished with* **Innate Truth**, *we are to attend with confidence to her natural and unprejudiced dictates and suggestions.* 2. *That some notions and truths are at least naturally and unavoidably assented to by the Soul, whether she has* **actual knowledge** *within her or not.* 3. *And that the* **definition** *of a* **Being absolutely Perfect** *is one such truth.* 4. *And that this* **absolutely Perfect Being** *is* **God**, *the* **Creator** *and* **Designer** <note>original: "Contriver"</note> *of all things.* 5. *The certainty and settledness of this* **idea**. 20

### CHAP. VIII.
1. *That the very* **idea of God** *implies his necessary* **existence**. 2. *That his* **existence** *is not hypothetically necessary, but absolutely so, noting the occasion of that slippery* **evasion**. 3. *That to acknowledge* **God** *as a Being necessarily* **existent** *according to the true* **notion** *of him, and yet to say he may not* **exist**, *is a plain contradiction.* 4. *That* **Necessity** *is a* **logical term** *and implies an indissoluble connection between* **subject** *and* **predicate**, *from which this* **axiom** *is necessarily and eternally true:* **God** *does exist.* 5. *A further* **demonstration** *of his* **existence** *from the incompatibility of* **contingency** *or* **impossibility** *with his* **nature** *or* **idea**. 6. *That necessary* **self-existence** *belongs either to* **God**, *or to* **Matter**, *or to both.* 7. *The great* **incongruities** *that follow the admission of the* **self-existence of matter**. 8. *An* **answer** *to an* **evasion**. 9. *That a number of* **self-essential** <note>original: "Self-effentiated"; existing by their own essence</note> **Deities** *plainly takes away the Being of the true* **God**. 10. *The only undeniable* **demonstration** *of the unity of the* **Godhead**. 11. *The absurdity of admitting actual* **self-existence** *in* **Matter** *while denying it in* **God**. 12. *That this* **absurdity** *cannot be excused by the* **perceptibility** <note>original: "sensibleness"</note> *of* **Matter**, *since the* **Atheist** *himself is forced to admit things that do not fall under the* **senses**. 13. *That it is as foolish a thing to reject the* **being of God** *because he does not immediately fall under the* **senses**, *as it would be to reject the* **being of matter** *because it is so incomprehensible to the* **imagination** <note>original: "Phansy"</note>. 14. *The factions*

That there is a Divine Providence that at least approves, if not directs, all the motions of matter, with a reason why she <note>original: "she" refers to Nature or Divine Providence personified.</note> permits the effects of the mere mechanical motion of matter to go as far as they can.* 37

### CHAP. II.
*1. The constant parallelism <note>The fact that the Earth's axis stays pointed in the same direction as it orbits the sun.</note> of the Earth's axis is a clear argument for Divine Providence. 2. The great inconveniences that would occur if the position of this parallel axis were perpendicular to the plane of the ecliptic <note>The path of the Earth's orbit around the sun.</note>. 3. Or if it were aligned with the same plane. 4. The excellent advantages of its current tilted position, and what a clear demonstration of Providence it is. 5. The same argument made using the Ptolemaic hypothesis <note>The older astronomical theory that the Earth is the center of the universe.</note>. 6. Further consideration of the Earth's axis and the Moon crossing the celestial equator <note>original: "Æquinoctial Line"</note>. 7. A demonstration from the phenomenon of gravity that there is a principle distinct from matter. 8. That neither the air, nor any more subtle matter within it, possesses knowledge or free agency. 9. A notable demonstration from the piston <note>original: "Sucker"</note> of an air pump drawing up a great weight, proving there is a substance distinct from matter in the world. 10. That this phenomenon cannot be explained <note>original: "salv'd"</note> by the elastic power of the air, as shown by the phenomenon itself. 11. An excuse <note>original: "Evasion"</note> produced and answered. 12. Another excuse anticipated. 13. That this absolute force of nature—acting against the primary laws of mechanical motion and gravity—is a clear sign that where things function perfectly, there is the same immaterial guide, even if the force on matter is not as easily felt. 14. The ridiculous false reasoning <note>original: "Sophistry"</note> of the atheist—who argues from minor effects of the mere motion of matter that there is no higher principle—is plainly exposed and rightly mocked. 15. Providence concluded from the laws of day and night, winter and summer, etc.* 40

### CHAP. III.
*1. That there is nothing in nature that does not meet the approval of an intelligent principle <note>Refers to a conscious Creator.</note>. 2. The great usefulness of hills and mountains. 3. The condition of man in relation to the rest of creation. 4. The intended usefulness of stone quarries, timber, metals, and minerals. 5. How the glory and magnificence of both peace and war depend on these. 6. As well as the defense of men against wild beasts.* 47

### CHAP. IV.
*1. The distinction between land and sea is not without a Providence. 2. Also, the density <note>original: "Consistence"</note> of seawater so that it can carry ships. 3. The great convenience and pleasure of navigation. 4. The admirable series of provisions in nature for satisfying human intelligence in such an important interest <note>original: "concerning a Curiosity"</note>.* 50

### CHAP. V.
*1. That the form, beauty, seed, and "signature" <note>The "Doctrine of Signatures" was the belief that plants were marked by God with physical signs indicating their medicinal use.</note> of plants are arguments for a Providence. 2. That although the mere motion of matter might produce certain atmospheric phenomena <note>original: "Meteors"</note> like hail, snow, and ice, it does not follow that motion is the sufficient cause of animals and plants. 3. That it would be no great flaw <note>original: "botch"</note> or gap in nature if some cruder phenomena were acknowledged as the results of the mere mechanical motion of matter. 4. That the form and beauty of flowers and plants come from a higher principle. 5. That beauty exists and is an object of our intellectual faculties. 6. From which it follows that the beautiful forms and figures of plants and animals come from an intelligent principle.* 52

Certain examples of signatures. 5. An answer to an objection regarding signatures in plants that do not seem to relate to medicine.* 55

CHAP. I. 1. The author's reason for adding this Appendix to his Antidote. 2. A listing of the chief objections made against the First Book of the work. 145

CHAP. II. 1. That the strength of his argument for the existence of God from *the idea of Him* does not depend on there being *innate ideas* <term>Innate Ideas: concepts or knowledge considered to be universal and present in the mind from birth</term> in the human mind. 2. That the logic of arguing from the *idea of a thing*—whether it is innate or not—is the same, as proved by several examples. 3. The reason why he argues for *innate ideas*. 4. The fact that a triangle appears accurate to our outward senses is no proof against the idea that the exact *idea* of a triangle comes from the soul itself. 5. That it does not follow that, if there are *innate ideas*, a blind man could discuss colors. 6. That animals <note>original: "Brutes"</note> do not have knowledge of any logical or mathematical concepts. 7. Why *Zeno's* donkey <note>original: "Asse"</note> goes in a straight line to the bundle <note>original: "bottle"</note> of hay. 8. That those actions and movements in things that follow reason and mathematics do not prove that logical or mathematical concepts exist within the things themselves. 146

CHAP. III. 1. Considering the soul's descent into the physical world <note>original: "lapse of Man's Soul into Matter"</note>, it is no wonder it is so puzzled when contemplating non-physical things. 2. That all extension <term>Extension: the property of taking up space or having physical dimensions</term> does not imply physical

<column-break/>

divisibility or the ability to separate parts. 3. That the flow <note>original: "Emanation"</note> of the *secondary substance* from the *center* of a spirit is not actually "creation" in the strict sense. 4. How it happens that the soul cannot withdraw itself from pain using its own *ability to contract itself*. 5. That the soul's extension does not imply as many wills and understandings as there are imaginable parts, because of the *unique unity and indivisibility* of its substance. 6. Several examples of how the imagination <note>original: "Phansy"</note> is puzzled by the firm conclusions of the senses and of reason. 7. The impossibility of conceiving how some parts of matter are so strongly joined to one another. 8. What is meant by *hylopathy* <term>Hylopathy: the theory that spirit can act upon matter or suffer from it</term>, and how a spirit, though not solid <note>original: "impenetrable"</note>, may be the *mover of matter*. 9. That the fact that a spirit moving matter cannot be explained is no greater argument against its truth than the fact that the line produced by a globe moving on a flat surface is hard to conceive is an argument against the globe's ability to move. 10. That the strength of this last answer lies in the certainty that there are phenomena in the world that completely exceed the powers of simple matter; several examples of this are suggested from the previous treatise. 149

### CHAP. V.
1. That there is a vast difference between arguing from forced fabrications <note>original: "Figments"</note> or fancies and arguing from the natural ideas of our own minds. 2. That the idea of an "absolutely evil being" does not imply necessary existence, whether it signifies a being that is absolutely imperfect, 3. Or absolutely wicked, 4. Or absolutely miserable, 5. Or absolutely harmful <note>original: "Mischievous"; in this era, it meant causing great harm or destruction</note>. 6. That if by an "absolutely harmful being" one only meant an infinite power to do hurt, this power belongs to God, whose absolute goodness prevents Him from ever using it. 7. That the correct method of using our reason is to proceed from what is plain and certain to what is more obscure and doubtful. 8. That according to this method, once we are first assured of the existence of an absolutely perfect Being from the idea of Him, we are then enabled to answer that "impossibility of existence" applies to any being that is either absolutely miserable or absolutely harmful. 9. That the phenomena <note>original: "Phaenomena"</note> of the world further prove the impossibility of an absolutely harmful being existing. 10. And that the plans and works of God are not to be measured by the empty opinions of men. 156

### CHAP. VI.
1. That the meaning of his argument from the "idea of God" in its first position is not simply that the idea is true, and that if God existed, His existence would be necessary; but rather, that this idea being true shows our minds that "absolute necessary existence" belongs to Him. 2. That the idea of the God of the Manichees <term>Manichees: followers of a dualistic religion that believed in two equal, opposing powers of Good and Evil</term> does not include necessary existence. 3. That to say that the necessary existence included in the idea of an absolutely perfect Being is only conditional is a contradiction. 4. The second position of his argument is confirmed, and that by its very form, the existence of the Manichean God cannot be concluded. 5. The

<column-break/>

invincible evidence of the third position of his argument, even in the judgment of his opponent himself. 6. That the force of his argument in its fourth and last position is not that we simply imagine the idea of "matter" without necessary existence; but that, no matter how closely we look, we find no necessary existence included in it, as we do in the idea of God. 7. That the faculties of our mind, to which he constantly appeals, are to be assumed as true rather than proved to be so. 160

### CHAP. VII.
1. That the necessity of existence that seems to be included in the idea of "space" is actually the same necessity that presents itself to our minds in the more full and perfect idea of God. 2. That the same reasoning applies to "eternal duration," whose immediate source is God, not matter. 3. That space is merely the possibility of matter, measurable only in the way that many different possible types of things are countable. 4. That distance is not a physical property <note>original: "affection"</note> of anything, but only a mental concept. 5. That the distance between bodies is only the absence of physical contact <note>original: "tactual union"</note>, which is measurable by parts just as other absences of quality are measured by degrees. 6. That if "distant space" is anything real after matter is removed, it is that necessary Being represented by the idea of God. 7. That self-existence and contingency <term>Contingency: the state of being dependent on chance or other factors rather than being necessary</term> are terms that are inconsistent with one another. 163

### CHAP. VIII.
1. That the idea of God is a natural and permanent <note>original: "indeleble"</note> concept in the human soul. 2. That even if there were some small obscurity in the concept, it does not stop it from being natural. 3. That the politician's misuse of the concept of God and religion no more proves them to be his own inventions than his misuse of natural affection, the love of honor, or liberty does. 4. A twofold answer to an objection regarding God's implanting His idea in us through specific purpose or design. 165

### CHAP. V.
1. *That there is a vast difference between arguing from forced fantasies <note>original: "Figments"</note> or inventions, and from the natural ideas of our own minds.* 2. *That the idea of a being who is absolutely evil does not imply necessary existence, whether it signifies a being who is absolutely imperfect,* 3. *Or absolutely wicked,* 4. *Or absolutely miserable,* 5. *Or absolutely mischievous.* 6. *That if by an "absolutely mischievous being" one meant only the infinite power of doing hurt, this is actually God—whose absolute goodness prevents him from ever acting upon it.* 7. *That the right method of using our reason is to proceed from what is plain and certain to what is more obscure and suspicious.* 8. *That according to this method, once we are first assured of the existence of an absolutely perfect being from the idea of him, we are then enabled to answer that it is impossible for a being to exist who is either absolutely miserable or absolutely mischievous.* 9. *That the natural phenomena <note>original: "Phænomena"; the observable events and structures of the physical world</note> of the world further prove that it is impossible for an absolutely mischievous being to exist.* 10. *And that the plans and works of God are not to be measured by the vain opinions of men.* 156
